name: ETF NAV dislocation gate
one_line: Build a fair-value proxy for QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ and size down or skip entries when the ETF trades far from implied NAV.
parameter_choices: Use constituent time series, cash component, divisor, and constituent weights to estimate fair value; compare market price vs implied NAV before sizing.
disagreement: No source disagreement; this needs extra NAV/fair-value inputs that we do not currently have.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general premise that ETFs can trade away from NAV and that fair-value estimation uses constituents/cash/divisor/weights. It does not state, test, or quantify a rule to size down the Q desk when that happens. The proposed gate is our extrapolation from that general arbitrage concept.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a pre-trade filter to the intraday sleeve only: estimate TQQQ/SQQQ indicative value from QQQ’s move since the prior close, and if the ETF’s last price is more than 0.5% away from that estimate, cut that entry to 50% of normal size; otherwise trade normal size. Do not apply this to QQQ.
review.mechanism: If the ETF is temporarily rich/cheap versus its underlying, we avoid paying up into distorted prints or selling into stale quotes. In theory this should reduce bad fills during fast markets and volatile opens, but on liquid QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ the mispricings are likely tiny and rare, so the practical benefit is probably small.
review.data_missing: We do not have constituent holdings, cash component, divisor, or official intraday NAV data. We can only build a rough QQQ-based indicative-value proxy for TQQQ/SQQQ from minute bars. That is not the same as true NAV dislocation, and for QQQ itself the gap is usually too small to matter.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected-list of prior tests. The closest analogue would be a generic price filter, but this exact NAV-dislocation gate has not been tested.
review.overfit_note: This is a rare-event filter with at least one arbitrary threshold and a choice between skip vs size-down. A noisy price-only proxy can easily fit 2018-2026 quirks and fail elsewhere. The event frequency may also be too low to estimate reliably.
review.expected_effect: At best a small improvement from avoiding occasional stale or distorted ETF prints. More likely the effect is near zero after 1 bp per side costs and 5-minute fills, because QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ are very liquid and NAV gaps should be tiny.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one rule and compare it against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 first: same entries/exits, but halve size whenever |last price / indicative value - 1| > 0.5% on TQQQ or SQQQ intraday entries. Measure daily net return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in net return and Sharpe with no worse drawdown, and at least ~30 triggered cases so the result is not just noise. Only if that passes, re-check on 1999-2017 using the same QQQ-based proxy on synthetic leveraged series; do not treat that as true NAV validation. If the filter barely triggers or does not improve the live-period backtest, stop.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly an execution-quality filter, not a new alpha source, and the needed inputs are not in our dataset. A price-only proxy for NAV is crude, the liquid ETFs we trade are already close to fair value most of the time, and the likely edge is too small to matter after costs. The idea is not impossible in principle, but it is too weak and underpowered for our data/sample size to justify a test now.

name: Sector ETF trend sleeve
one_line: Run the existing trend/noise-area logic on sector ETFs so the bot can own the strongest sector trend instead of only QQQ.
parameter_choices: Select Sector SPDRs such as SPY, XLU, XLE, XLRE, XLP, XLY, XLV, XLI, XLB, XLK, and XLF; keep it long-only and apply the same trend sleeve rules.
disagreement: None stated.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B3 explicitly says Sector SPDRs are a practical way to play sector trends; B8 says to start from names already rising. Neither source gives a sector-rotation rule or says to pick the strongest sector, so this is an adaptation, not a direct quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: New overnight trend sleeve, replacing the current QQQ trend sleeve: at 15:55 NY, rank the legacy Sector SPDRs XLB, XLE, XLF, XLI, XLK, XLP, XLU, XLV, XLY by trailing 20-trading-day return; if the top-ranked ETF is above its 200-day SMA, hold that single ETF long with the existing 50% trend-sleeve allocation via MOC, otherwise hold cash. Keep the current intraday QQQ sleeve unchanged. Do not include XLRE in the confirmation test because its shorter history would shrink the sample.
review.mechanism: This tries to keep the overnight book in the strongest sector rather than forcing everything through QQQ. If leadership rotates away from tech, the bot can still own a live trend instead of sitting in cash or staying in the wrong sleeve. Best case: a modest return lift and some diversification. It is not a strong crash-exit fix, because sector ETFs are still equity beta.
review.data_missing: The daily trend version is feasible from the OHLCV history we have. The intraday noise-area version is not fully testable on sector ETFs before 2018 because we do not have sector-ETF 1-minute bars for the full 1999-2017 confirmation sample.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same as the rejected noise-area tests on IWM/DIA; this is a sector-rotation trend sleeve, which has not been explicitly rejected before.
review.overfit_note: A sector-rotation rule on 9-10 highly correlated ETFs has enough flexibility to look good on 2018-2026 by chance, especially with rank lookbacks and universe choices. The only way to trust it is if the exact same rule also works unchanged on 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: Probably modest at best: it may improve the trend sleeve when sector leadership is broad and QQQ is not the leader, but I would not expect a dramatic Sharpe gain or major drawdown reduction. It could also just add churn and dilute the clean QQQ edge.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one rule only: legacy Sector SPDR universe, selector = highest 20-day return subject to being above its 200-day SMA. Backtest it as a replacement for the current overnight trend sleeve on 2018-2026, using the same 50% allocation, MOC execution, and cost model. Then confirm on 1999-2017 daily data for the same legacy sector ETFs. Compare against the current QQQ trend sleeve and against the current full Q desk with only the trend sleeve swapped. Require improvement in net CAGR and Sharpe in both periods, with no meaningful worsening of max drawdown or turnover. If it only works in 2018-2026, or if it needs sector-list/lookback tuning after the fact, reject. The intraday sector-noise-area version should be a separate 2018+ experiment, not bundled into this test.
review.verdict_reason: The daily trend-rotation version is cheap, fully backtestable, and different enough from the rejected ideas to merit one clean test. The intraday sector variant is only partly feasible historically, so do not bundle it in; test the overnight sleeve now and only revisit minute-based sector noise-area logic later.

name: Defensive inverse or low-beta sleeve
one_line: When Nasdaq regime weakens, rotate capital into inverse ETFs or low/negative-beta ETFs instead of leaving that cash idle.
parameter_choices: Use the source's 3x bull/bear pairs such as TNA/TZA, NUGT/DUST, LABU/LABD, and SOXL/SOXS; alternatively select assets with beta at or below zero.
disagreement: Sources differ between explicit inverse exposure and beta-based diversification; both are defensive, but one is directional and the other is hedging.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients, not the rule. One excerpt says inverse ETFs can express a bearish view in a cash account; the other says zero/negative-beta assets can diversify a portfolio. Neither source justifies a regime-rotation sleeve or a scan across many leveraged bull/bear pairs.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not run a broad ETF scan. If we test a single defensive variant, change the trend sleeve so that when QQQ is below its 200-day SMA at the 15:55 decision, the 50% sleeve holds QID instead of cash; when QQQ is above the 200-day SMA, keep the existing 50% TQQQ rule. No low-beta basket search.
review.mechanism: It could make the bot earn something during sustained Nasdaq bear regimes instead of sitting in cash, which may reduce crash give-back. But it also adds another directional bet with inverse-ETF decay, tracking error and more whipsaw risk. A low-beta version mostly just turns idle cash into lower-return market exposure, so it is unlikely to add alpha.
review.data_missing: We can backtest the regime logic from QQQ daily history, but the exact inverse/low-beta ETF products do not exist across the full 1999-2017 sample, and minute data for those products is only available from our liquid-ETF dataset era. A true product-level history would need synthetic backfills or later-starting tests.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing on the rejected list is this rule. We have tested related Nasdaq trend and intraday sleeves, but not a dedicated inverse/low-beta defensive allocation.
review.overfit_note: The idea invites a large search space: which ETF, inverse vs low-beta, beta lookback, regime threshold, and allocation size. With only a few true bear regimes, it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and miss the earlier cycles.
review.expected_effect: Best case: smaller drawdowns and some profit during prolonged bear markets. More likely: lower long-run return after ETF decay, fees and whipsaws, especially if the regime filter is noisy. It does not address the bot's flat intraday years.
review.test_protocol: Only if narrowed to the single QID-on-QQQ<200d rule: pre-register it, run the full 2018-2026 backtest against the current Q desk with the same fills and cost model, then confirm on 1999-2017 using synthetic QQQ-based inverse returns. Compare net daily return, max drawdown and Sharpe. Accept only if both periods improve on net return and do not worsen drawdown; otherwise drop it. Do not test a multi-ETF low-beta search.
review.verdict_reason: As framed, this is a generic beta-shift idea, not a robust edge. Cash is already the best defensive asset in a cash account, while inverse ETFs add decay and whipsaw risk. The low-beta variant is just lower-return market exposure, and the broad ETF scan is a data-snooping trap. The only salvageable version is a single pre-registered inverse overlay, but the broad idea should be rejected.

name: Rolling pair-screen for long-only relative-value candidates
one_line: Use 3-month pair screens to identify liquid, similar instruments whose laggard leg might be worth buying in a cash account.
parameter_choices: Same industry or similar macro exposure; month-end 3-month lookback; moving 3-month co-integration window; 3-month beta similarity; normalize by price ratio; examples include ADBE/MSFT, JNPR/LUV, JNPR/MSFT, JNPR/QCOM, JNPR/SKYW, and JNPR/SPY.
disagreement: Sources vary on the selection metric—distance, co-integration, beta match, or example-pair similarity—but all favor liquid, mature, closely related names.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support rolling 3-month pair screens, same-industry/mature/liquid candidates, beta/cointegration/distance selection, and ratio normalization. They do not support the key leap to a long-only one-leg cash-account trade; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: New standalone sleeve, not a tweak to Q desk: on the last trading day of each month, screen a fixed hand-curated list of liquid same-sector/same-macro pairs with at least 3 months of daily history. Compute each pair’s 3-month daily close-price ratio z-score. If the laggard leg’s z-score is <= -2, buy one whole-share lot of that laggard at the next open; exit when the z-score reverts to 0 or after 20 trading days, whichever comes first. Use one position at a time.
review.mechanism: At best, this could harvest short-term relative underperformance mean reversion inside similar names and add a small extra return stream. But because we cannot short the leader, the trade keeps full market/sector beta and can easily turn into a noisy long-only factor bet instead of true relative value.
review.data_missing: We do not have sector/industry labels in the stated data store, so a fully automated same-industry scan needs external metadata or a hand-curated pair list. The price-ratio and rolling-screen calculations themselves are feasible from the stored bars.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tested as a pairs sleeve. But it is adjacent to the rejected cross-sectional momentum idea because it ranks names within a universe, so the same data-mining and regime-dependence risks apply.
review.overfit_note: Universe definition, pair metric (distance/cointegration/beta), lookback length, entry threshold, exit rule, and position sizing are all tunable. A long-only version gives you even more ways to fit 2018-2026 and fail 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: At best, a small uncorrelated swing sleeve from relative-value mean reversion. More likely, it adds another noisy long-only equity bet with weak edge and extra crowding on a $1,000 cash account.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register a fixed symbol-pair list first, to avoid optimizing the universe. Backtest the sleeve standalone with the exact month-end 3-month ratio rule, z<=-2 entry, z=0 or 20-day exit, whole-share fills, and our 1 bp/side plus SEC cost model. Then simulate replacing 25% of the current Q desk capital with it, since the account is already fully deployed. Compare 2018-2026 build vs 1999-2017 confirm on net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and fraction of PnL from the top 3 pairs. Keep only if both periods improve versus the current Q desk and drawdown does not worsen by more than 5 percentage points.
review.verdict_reason: The books support pair selection, not a profitable long-only version. Without shorting, the idea becomes an unhedged long-only bet that needs sector metadata we do not have, competes for scarce capital in a $1,000 cash account, and has too many knobs to overfit. It is too far from a clean improvement to the existing Q desk to justify production tests.

name: QQQ lead-lag basket filter
one_line: Only take QQQ entries when a basket of leading ETFs has already moved, using QQQ as the lagging target.
parameter_choices: Use SPY, IWM, DIA, or sector ETFs as the leading basket; apply as an entry gate to the existing QQQ sleeve.
disagreement: None stated.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B5 gives a generic lead-lag/stat-arb principle ('traded instrument should lag, reference portfolio should lead'), which is directionally related but not evidence for a QQQ ETF basket entry gate or any specific lookback/threshold. B8 is only about using movers/toplists as a watchlist, not about lead-lag timing.
review.exact_rule_change: At each existing QQQ intraday check, allow the trade only if the equal-weight 30-minute return of SPY, IWM and DIA is in the same direction as the QQQ signal (positive for longs, negative for shorts); otherwise skip the entry. Default basket = SPY/IWM/DIA, lookback = 30 minutes.
review.mechanism: If QQQ is truly lagging the broader market, a broad-market leader basket should confirm that the move is already underway before we spend an entry. That could cut QQQ-only fakeouts and reduce whipsaws in the intraday sleeve. Main downside: these ETFs are highly synchronous, so the gate may mostly delay good entries rather than add predictive power.
review.data_missing: We can test the basket gate from 2007 onward with SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA minute bars, and on 2018-2026 with the fuller ETF universe. But we do not have minute OHLCV for the candidate leader basket before 2007, so we cannot validate the rule on 1999-2006 as written; sector ETF minute data is also not available for the full pre-2018 span.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule, but it is adjacent to the rejected IWM/DIA noise-area experiment and other cross-ETF timing filters. We have already seen that simply swapping the benchmark ETF often does not create a durable edge.
review.overfit_note: Many degrees of freedom: basket membership, lookback, long/short asymmetry, and whether to use simple sign agreement or relative-strength thresholds. Lead-lag relations among liquid ETFs are tiny and regime-dependent, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and fail elsewhere.
review.expected_effect: If it helps at all, expect a small increase in intraday hit rate and fewer false QQQ entries; more likely it just reduces trade count and delays entries, leaving net PnL flat or worse after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one simple version only: basket = equal-weight SPY/IWM/DIA, lookback = 30 minutes, no sector ETFs, no threshold tuning. Run the current Q desk and the gated version with identical execution/cost assumptions. Evaluate net daily return after costs as the primary metric, with Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count as secondary checks. Build on 2018-2026, then confirm unchanged on 2007-2017. Keep it only if the gated version beats the baseline on net daily return in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: Plausible in concept, but the support is only a generic lead-lag rule and the real edge, if any, is likely tiny and unstable. More importantly, the missing pre-2007 minute data means we cannot validate the full historical regime set for this exact gate, so it is not a priority test right now.

name: Liquidity and tradability floor for any added sleeve
one_line: Before adding any stock or ETF sleeve, require instruments that are easy to enter/exit: tight spreads, high dollar volume, and no penny/OTC names.
parameter_choices: Candidate thresholds from the source items: average daily volume >= 200k shares; relative volume > 1.5; price > $2 (stress test > $5); exclude OTC and sub-$1 names; prefer persistently tight intraday ranges and high dollar volume; require enough liquidity that our intended size is a small fraction of ADV.
disagreement: A stricter tradability screen will cut off some explosive small names and may reduce raw upside, but should improve fills, reduce slippage, and make the bot more robust in a $1,000 cash account.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The books do support the broad principle: trade liquid markets, avoid OTC and sub-$1 names, and use basic volume/price floors. But the exact thresholds here (200k shares/day, $5 floor) are rule-of-thumb heuristics, not validated cutoffs, and the 'tight spreads' part is conceptual rather than measured with our data.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not approve any new non-ETF equity sleeve unless its tradable universe is U.S.-listed only, share price >= $5.00, and 20-day average daily volume >= 200,000 shares; OTC and sub-$1 names are ineligible. Leave the current Q desk unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is a hygiene filter, not alpha. It should reduce the chance that a future sleeve looks good gross but fails net because spreads, impact, and bad exits eat the edge. In a $1,000 cash account, a single wide-spread or hard-to-exit name can dominate daily PnL. For the current ETF-only Q desk, it likely does almost nothing.
review.data_missing: We can compute price and average volume from daily data, but we do not have bid/ask quotes, depth, or reliable spread/impact data. OTC/exchange metadata may also be incomplete. Our 1-minute universe is already filtered toward liquid names, so the very illiquid cases this rule is meant to exclude are underrepresented in minute history.
review.already_tried_note: The live bot already trades ultra-liquid ETFs (QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ), so the spirit of the screen is already implicit. What has not been tested is this as a separate, pre-registered gate for a new stock sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Few knobs, but the cutoffs are arbitrary and easy to tune to a sample. Because we lack quote data, any apparent improvement from a volume/price screen could be partly a proxy for other factors rather than true tradability.
review.expected_effect: For future stock sleeves: fewer fill problems, lower hidden transaction costs, fewer forced exits, and less tail risk from thin names. For the current Q desk: little to no effect, because the traded ETFs are already very liquid. Raw opportunity set may shrink.
review.test_protocol: Only test this as a gate on a candidate new equity sleeve, not as a standalone alpha. Pre-register fixed cutoffs: price >= $5 and 20-day ADV >= 200,000 shares, with OTC/sub-$1 excluded if metadata allow. Run the candidate sleeve twice on 2018-2026: (A) full eligible universe, (B) screened universe, using identical entry/exit rules and the same cost model, then confirm on 1999-2017 (daily-based where minute data are unavailable). Require the screen to improve net-after-cost Sharpe and max drawdown in both periods, and not materially reduce net CAGR unless it clearly lowers drawdown/slippage. If it only removes trades without improving net results, reject the screen as a live rule.
review.verdict_reason: This is a reasonable hygiene filter, but not a source of edge for the current bot. We already trade highly liquid ETFs, so it changes nothing today, and our data are too thin to validate the claimed spread/depth benefit on the names it is supposed to exclude. Use it as a pre-launch checklist for future sleeves, not as a separate test now.

name: Intraday session-window filter
one_line: Skip the opening burst and any low-quality midday lull; only allow intraday entries in the calmer parts of the session.
parameter_choices: No new entries for 15, 30, 60, or 90 minutes after the open; test first-trade times around 9:45, 10:00, and 10:30 NY; optionally block 11:00-14:00 ET and compare morning-only windows like 9:30-11:30 or 10:00-12:00.
disagreement: Some books say the first hour has the best volume and action, while others say the open is too volatile and unpredictable; the broad consensus is that the open is special, but they disagree on how long to wait.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources broadly support the microstructure premise: the open is noisy and spreads are wider early (B1-c006-03, B8-c001-02), and intraday activity/volatility has a U-shape with a midday lull (B1-c017-05, B3-c015-02). But Midas already starts intraday checks at 10:00 ET, so the 'skip the opening burst' part is only partly new; the actionable new change is mainly the midday no-entry window.
review.exact_rule_change: For the intraday sleeve only, allow new entries only from 10:30-11:00 ET and 14:00-15:30 ET; hard-block new entries from 11:00-14:00 ET. Keep all exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should cut the weakest part of the session: early post-open noise and the midday volume lull, when band breaks are more likely to be false and fills are less attractive. On this bot, that could reduce churn, false momentum entries, and slippage, especially in the intraday sleeve’s flat/losing years. The risk is that it also removes some profitable midday follow-through, so the only reason to keep it is if net expectancy improves after costs.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: The current live bot already delays intraday trading until 10:00 ET, so the open-avoidance component is already partially in place. What has not been separately tested is the added 10:30 start and the 11:00-14:00 no-trade window on the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: Time-of-day filters are easy to data-mine, and this idea offers several plausible cut points (15/30/60/90 minutes; morning-only; midday block). If we start searching across them, we will almost certainly fit 2018-2026 and disappoint on 1999-2017. This should only be tested with one frozen window, not a sweep.
review.expected_effect: Most likely outcome is fewer intraday trades, slightly lower turnover, and possibly better net expectancy per trade if the midday lull is the main source of bad entries. Best case: a modest Sharpe lift and cleaner fills. Worst case: gross return drops because the edge is actually concentrated in the morning or late-day continuation.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one rule only: first eligible intraday entry at 10:30 ET, no new entries 11:00-14:00 ET, exits unchanged. Backtest against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 using the same execution model and real TQQQ/SQQQ minute data. Score daily net return, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and average slippage. Then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 with the same rule applied to the available QQQ minute history and the existing synthetic-3x framework for pre-2018 ETF returns. Accept only if both periods improve on net return/day and Sharpe without materially worsening drawdown; if the filter only lowers trade count or gross exposure with no net gain, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully backtestable from existing minute data, and it targets a known weak spot of the intraday sleeve. The main caution is overfitting, so we should test exactly one frozen window and not optimize it after the fact.

name: Bar-cadence / event-driven execution
one_line: Recompute intraday signals on shorter bars or event triggers instead of a fixed 30-minute polling cadence.
parameter_choices: 1-minute vs 5-minute bar aggregation; timer-driven vs event-driven loop; instrument-specific minimum decision/holding horizon of roughly 3, 15, or 30 minutes; exit on bar-close back inside the band or VWAP rather than waiting for the next scheduled poll.
disagreement: One-minute bars preserve more detail around the open and close, while five-minute bars smooth microstructure noise and friction; the right choice depends on whether the signal is fast and noisy or slower and more stable.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general idea of shorter intraday aggregation and timer/event-driven strategy loops, but it does not specifically argue that the Q desk’s noise-area/VWAP rule should be polled more often. This is an adaptation of generic execution architecture, not a cited trading rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Change only the intraday sleeve’s scheduler: instead of checking QQQ every 30 minutes, run the existing band/VWAP logic on every 5-minute bar close from 10:00 to 15:55, with the same next-5-minute-open fills, same max one round trip per day, and no other rule changes.
review.mechanism: The current 30-minute cadence can leave the bot acting on stale conditions for up to half an hour. A 5-minute cadence should catch reversals and band re-entries sooner, so exits happen closer to the inflection and the bot gives back less on intraday swings. The risk is more false triggers and slightly higher turnover; if the underlying edge is real, the gain should come from lower giveback, not a big jump in hit rate.
review.data_missing: None for the bar-cadence version. We can build 5-minute bars from the 1-minute QQQ series and backtest the existing next-5-minute-open fill model. True quote/event-driven triggers would need tick/quote data, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: This exact cadence change has not been on the rejected list. The live desk already uses a 30-minute poll, so this is a clean baseline-vs-variant test rather than a rehash of a rejected strategy.
review.overfit_note: There is only one obvious knob if we pre-register 5-minute bars, but cadence is exactly the kind of execution detail that can be tuned to one regime. If we start sweeping 1/5/15/30 minutes or event-driven variants, overfit risk becomes high.
review.expected_effect: Small positive at best. It could improve the intraday sleeve by reducing stale exits and missed reversals, but I would not expect a large uplift; if the underlying edge is slower than 30 minutes, the extra turnover could cancel the benefit.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: 5-minute bar-close evaluation of the existing intraday sleeve, compared with the current 30-minute poll. Keep band math, VWAP exit, max one round trip/day, order type, and cost assumptions unchanged. Test on 2018-2026 first, measuring net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and trade count for both the intraday sleeve alone and the full Q desk. Then run the fixed 5-minute rule unchanged on unseen 1999-2017. Adopt only if the 5-minute version improves net return and Sharpe in both periods without worsening max drawdown materially; if the gain is only in 2018-2026 or disappears out of sample, reject.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with current data, cheap to run, and it is a real timing change to an existing sleeve rather than a new strategy. The source support is only partial, so I would not assume it works, but it is worth one pre-registered test because the worst case is a small change in turnover and the best case is lower intraday giveback.

name: Faster trend-regime gate
one_line: Replace the 200-day SMA trend filter with a faster or thresholded trend-state filter to exit crashes sooner and reduce whipsaws in sideways markets.
parameter_choices: Test 20/100, 50/100, or 50/200 moving-average crossovers; 20-day then 50-day confirmation; 20 EMA vs 50 SMA; x% filter values around 5-8%; moving-average ratio thresholds; APO sign filters; MACD(10,40,20) or MACD(12,26,9) regime gates.
disagreement: Fast filters and EMA crossovers react earlier but whipsaw more; the 50/200 golden cross is late but robust; thresholded filters and APO/MACD can be used either as momentum or as mean-reversion signals depending on polarity.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: B5-c018-01 states a 50/100 dual-MA long signal directly, and the other MA-cross examples support the same family of regime filters. The only leap is using it as the QQQ/TQQQ desk’s trend gate instead of a standalone textbook signal, but that adaptation is small.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current QQQ 200-day SMA gate on the 50% trend sleeve with a daily 50-day/100-day SMA crossover gate: at 15:55 New York, hold TQQQ overnight only when QQQ’s 50-day SMA is above its 100-day SMA; otherwise keep that sleeve in cash. Keep the intraday sleeve and cost model unchanged.
review.mechanism: A 50/100 crossover should turn the trend sleeve off earlier than the 200-day rule in selloffs, so the bot should give back less in crashes. It may also avoid some long, flat 200-day-whipsaw periods because the regime filter will stay out until the shorter average clearly leads. The tradeoff is slower re-entry after reversals and more false exits in noisy markets.
review.data_missing: None for this test; daily QQQ OHLCV back to 1999 is enough, and no news/options/L2 data are needed.
review.already_tried_note: The current live desk already uses a 200-day QQQ trend gate, but this exact 50/100 crossover was not listed among the already rejected ideas. So this is related to what we do now, not a repeat of an already-failed test.
review.overfit_note: If we pre-register one pair (50/100) the knob count is only two, so this is not a huge search. The overfit risk comes from trying many MA pairs/thresholds and picking the best in 2018-2026; don’t do that.
review.expected_effect: Best-case: smaller crash give-back and slightly lower drawdown versus the 200-day gate, with only a modest hit to trend capture. Worst-case: earlier exits in every minor pullback, so net return drops after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one A/B test: baseline Q desk vs the same desk with only the trend gate changed to QQQ 50-day SMA > 100-day SMA. Do not optimize any lookbacks or thresholds on the test set. Run 2018-2026 as the build period and 1999-2017 as the unseen confirmation period (daily data is sufficient for the gate). Compare full-bot net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trend-sleeve crash give-back after the same costs/fill assumptions. Keep the change only if it beats the baseline on net return/day in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly supported by standard MA crossover examples, so it is worth one clean preregistered test. But do not turn it into a crossover grid search; that would be classic overfit bait.

name: Pullback-to-support entry
one_line: In an uptrend, buy pullbacks into objective support instead of chasing strength.
parameter_choices: Define support with 20-day or 50-day SMA reclaim, pivot zones, Fibonacci 61.8% retracement, Bollinger lower-band pullbacks (e.g. 10/1.5 or 20/2), or nearby support/resistance zones; only enter after a bounce or reclaim, not after a multi-day extension.
disagreement: Some sources prefer the faster EMA for earlier entries, while others want a two-step confirmation such as reclaiming the 20-day and then the 50-day; support itself may be defined by pivots, bands, Fib levels, or moving averages.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The sources clearly support the general principle of buying dips in an uptrend, and several examples use quantified support ideas (20-day SMA support, Bollinger-band pullback/reclaim, rejection near support). But none of them backtests this exact QQQ/TQQQ 200-day + 20-day reclaim rule, so the link is adaptation rather than direct evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: keep the existing 200-day SMA uptrend filter on QQQ, but replace the unconditional 50% overnight TQQQ hold with a pullback entry. Enter/maintain the 50% trend sleeve only when QQQ has touched or breached its 20-day SMA during the session and then closes back above that 20-day SMA; otherwise that 50% stays in cash. Use the next 5-minute bar open for fills. Support lookback = 20 trading days.
review.mechanism: This could improve the bot by avoiding late chase entries and only adding leverage after a temporary pullback has reset the trend. If QQQ is truly trending, a reclaim of the 20-day SMA may give a better entry price and reduce whipsaws around the 200-day filter. The tradeoff is obvious: you may miss some strong straight-up days, so the effect could be modest or even negative if the pullback filter is too restrictive.
review.data_missing: None for the fixed 20-day reclaim version; daily OHLCV and 1-minute QQQ/TQQQ execution data are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule, but it overlaps with the already-known QQQ dip-buying theme (RSI(2) on QQQ) and with the current trend sleeve. The exact 20-day support-reclaim entry has not been rejected in the listed tests.
review.overfit_note: The idea family has a lot of degrees of freedom: SMA vs EMA, 20 vs 50 days, reclaim vs bounce, pivots vs bands vs Fib levels, and confirmation rules. If we do not freeze one pre-registered rule, it will be easy to fit 2018-2026 and fail out-of-sample.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trend whipsaws and slightly better entry prices, but also lower market exposure and more missed upside in persistent bull runs. Net improvement is plausible but not obvious; expect the effect size to be modest.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one fixed rule only: 200-day trend filter plus 20-day pullback/reclaim entry for the trend sleeve. Backtest the full Q desk baseline vs the modified version on 2018-2026 first, using the same costs and next-5-minute-open fill model. Then confirm on unseen 1999-2017; because execution depends on intraday fills, also run a minute-level sensitivity check on 2007-2017. Primary metric: annualized net return/day at the bot level. Secondary: Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and % of days invested in the trend sleeve. Adopt only if the modified version beats baseline in both sample blocks on net return and Sharpe, with no material worsening in max drawdown (say >5 percentage points) and no big turnover increase.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly aimed at a known weakness in the trend sleeve. But freeze one rule first; do not branch into Fib/Bollinger/pivot variants unless this exact 20-day reclaim test shows real out-of-sample value.

name: Confirmed breakout continuation sleeve
one_line: Add a separate breakout sleeve that enters only after a close outside a defined compression or range pattern, ideally with confirmation.
parameter_choices: Use 20-day highs/lows, 50-day Turtle breakouts, 2-day confirmation in a resistance tolerance zone, triangle slope thresholds around 0.01 with R² near 0.9, flag or pennant trendline breaks versus flagpole breaks, ascending-triangle closes outside the pattern, cup-and-handle breakouts, and volume-spike confirmation.
disagreement: Some books favor the earliest trendline break, while others wait for the final flagpole break or a confirmed close outside the pattern; wedges can be either reversals or continuations depending on trend context, so pattern context matters.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The source items support the *generic* idea of breakouts/continuation and waiting for confirmation (20-day/50-day breakouts, ascending triangles, flags, pennants, and volume spikes). They do **not** support this whole pattern zoo as a single robust sleeve, and most of the support is opinion or worked examples rather than real multi-market statistics. The only fairly concrete rules are the 20-day/2-day confirmation example and the Turtle-style breakout/mean exit; everything else is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a **new daily swing sleeve**, not a tweak to the intraday noise-area logic: at 15:55 New York, if QQQ has closed above its prior 20-day high for **2 consecutive closes**, buy TQQQ at the next session’s open with the sleeve’s fixed allocation; exit at the next open after QQQ closes back below its 20-day simple moving average. Do **not** include triangles, flags, cup-and-handle, or volume filters in the base test.
review.mechanism: If it works, this would get us into strong QQQ trends earlier than the 200-day SMA sleeve and avoid waiting for a slow regime flip. The best-case use is catching continuation after a real compression/breakout, not forecasting tops or bottoms. The downside is obvious: it is still a momentum chase rule, so most of the edge has to come from avoiding false breakouts after confirmation. In our bot, it mostly duplicates the existing trend sleeve rather than creating a clearly new return source.
review.data_missing: None for the narrow daily breakout test: we have daily OHLCV for QQQ and TQQQ-suitable ETF history back to 1999. What we do **not** have is objective labels for discretionary patterns like cup-and-handle, pennants, and flags, so those parts should not be tested as a free-form pattern scan.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact daily QQQ breakout rule, but the family is close to things we already rejected: ORB variants, noise-area momentum, overnight holding, and other momentum/continuation ideas. The more you widen this into pattern taxonomy, the more it starts to look like another overfit breakout system we have already spent time on.
review.overfit_note: The proposal bundles many degrees of freedom: 20-day highs/lows, 50-day Turtle breakouts, 2-day confirmation, triangle slope/R² thresholds, flag vs flagpole entry, ascending triangles, cup-and-handle, and volume confirmation. That is a classic pattern-mine. Even the narrowed version has arbitrary-looking choices (20 and 2) that can easily be tuned to 2018–2026 and fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a small improvement in trend capture and maybe slightly faster crash exit than the 200-day MA sleeve. More likely: extra turnover, more false breakouts, and little net improvement after costs because the bot already has a momentum sleeve and this mostly re-states 'buy strength.'
review.test_protocol: If we test anything here, it must be only the single preregistered rule above: QQQ 20-day breakout with 2-day confirmation and 20-day SMA exit, evaluated as a replacement for the current overnight trend sleeve while keeping the intraday sleeve unchanged. Compare current Q desk vs. breakout-replacement Q desk on 2018–2026 first, then on unseen 1999–2017. Primary metric: net CAGR/day after the stated costs; secondary: Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover. Require improvement in both in-sample and out-of-sample, or at minimum no degradation in OOS drawdown with a clear net return gain. Do not sweep pattern types or confirmation thresholds.
review.verdict_reason: As proposed, this is too broad and too discretionary: it is a pattern zoo, not a single falsifiable rule. The sources only justify generic breakout/confirmation heuristics, not a robust claim that flags, triangles, cups, pennants, and volume confirmation all add alpha together on our bot. The narrow 20-day/2-day breakout variant is testable, but the full idea should be rejected until it is reduced to one preregistered rule.

name: Failed-breakout and reversal-pattern sleeve
one_line: Add a separate reversal sleeve that fades failed breakouts and classic reversal structures at support or resistance.
parameter_choices: Double tops/bottoms, head-and-shoulders and inverse H&S neckline breaks and retests, springs or failed breakouts, engulfing and pin-bar/rejection candles, doji confirmation, fractal pivot windows around 3 bars, wick-to-body ratios above 3, body size thresholds around 0.5-1%, RSI thresholds of 20/80 or 30/70, and RSI divergence as a confirmer.
disagreement: Some sources treat Bollinger extremes as breakouts while others treat them as reversals; some reversal patterns want a retest after the break, while others trigger on the first neckline break.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support pieces of the idea: failed breakouts/springs, neckline breaks/retests, engulfing/pin-bar candles, RSI extremes, and fractal pivots. But they do not support the full bundled sleeve, and most of the evidence is qualitative; the only semi-quant result shown is weak (one rejection-candle example with poor accuracy).
review.exact_rule_change: Do not add the whole pattern zoo. If we test a salvageable version, add one daily QQQ reversal sleeve: define swing highs/lows with a 3-bar fractal pivot window, then buy TQQQ next open after a downside failed breakout that closes back above the last swing low with RSI(14) < 30, and buy SQQQ next open after an upside failed breakout that closes back below the last swing high with RSI(14) > 70; exit after 5 trading days or on a close back through the failed level.
review.mechanism: If this works, it would catch exhaustion reversals after false breaks and add a sparse mean-reversion stream that is less correlated with the trend sleeve. In theory it could help in sideways or climactic markets and slightly improve crash re-entry timing. In practice, it may just duplicate the bot’s existing RSI(2) dip-buying and add turnover.
review.data_missing: No missing market data for the salvageable version: OHLCV is enough. What we do not have is a way to validate the more subjective pattern zoo (H&S, doji, divergence, candle rejects) without arbitrary coding choices, but that is a rule-specification problem, not a data gap.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same as the rejected ORB/gap sleeves, but failed-breakout fades are adjacent to those ideas, and many of the proposed patterns are just reversal wrappers around breakout logic already tested and rejected in other forms.
review.overfit_note: The proposal has too many degrees of freedom: pattern type, timeframe, lookback window, support/resistance definition, retest logic, candle geometry thresholds, RSI cutoff, divergence confirmation, and exit logic. That is classic fit-the-past bait, especially with our finite sample and existing RSI(2) mean-reversion edge.
review.expected_effect: As a broad sleeve, likely small or negative after costs because the edge is weak and heavily overlap-prone with existing mean-reversion signals. The best-case scenario is a modest win in a narrow failed-breakout subset; the full pattern bundle is more likely to overfit than to add durable alpha.
review.test_protocol: If anyone insists on testing, pre-register only the narrow daily QQQ rule above. Use 2018-2026 to judge standalone performance and incremental lift versus the current Q desk, then confirm on 1999-2017. Score after-cost CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and incremental return when layered on the existing bot. Require improvement in both periods, not just one, and reject if the gain comes mainly from higher turnover or a few outlier years.
review.verdict_reason: The idea is a discretionary pattern zoo with too many knobs and weak evidence. It is not a single robust edge, and most of the proposed signals are likely just noisier versions of mean reversion that we already capture partly with RSI(2). The broad sleeve is more likely to overfit 2018-2026 than to add durable profit on 1999-2017.

name: Late-day strength gate for overnight holds
one_line: Only keep overnight exposure when the day ends strong, especially in the last 30 minutes.
parameter_choices: Keep or add overnight only if the close is in the top quartile or top 20% of the day range, the last 30 minutes are positive, or the first half-hour is positive as a tone filter; optionally test a midday probe plus an add-on into the close.
disagreement: One source emphasizes last-30-minute strength, another says the first half-hour predicts the last half-hour, and another uses a close-near-high rule; they agree on strength, but not on which clock window matters most.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the *components* of the idea: strong last-30-minute trading can predict next-day continuation, and a close near the day’s high can be bullish. But they do not directly test a rule that specifically gates an overnight hold in the Q desk. The first-half-hour item is only an indirect timing filter, not direct support for this overnight rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Change only the trend sleeve: at 15:55 New York, keep the existing 50% TQQQ overnight position only if QQQ closes in the top 20% of that day’s high-low range AND QQQ’s return over the last 30 minutes is positive; otherwise flatten that sleeve to cash. Do not change the intraday sleeve.
review.mechanism: This tries to keep overnight exposure only on sessions that finish with real bullish strength, which should avoid some weak-close days that often mean-revert or gap down overnight. If it works, it could improve the trend sleeve’s overnight drift and reduce whipsaw/give-back without adding new instruments or violating cash-account constraints.
review.data_missing: None for a first test. We can compute close location in range and last-30-minute return from existing 1-minute QQQ bars, and apply the rule to the current trend sleeve.
review.already_tried_note: Bare overnight holding has already been tested and rejected, and last-half-hour ideas were also rejected in the prior list. This exact close-strength gate was not explicitly listed as tested, but it is close enough to the rejected overnight-hold family that the prior failure is a real warning.
review.overfit_note: Even though the rule is simple, it sits on a large family of near-variants: top quartile vs quintile, 15/30/60-minute windows, positive vs thresholded returns, and adding the first-half-hour tone filter. That makes it easy to tune to 2018-2026 noise and miss 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: Best case: modestly better overnight expectancy and a bit less drawdown in the trend sleeve. More likely: smaller sample of overnight holds with a slightly higher hit rate, but possibly lower total CAGR if the filter throws away too many profitable trend days.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one version only: top-20%-of-day-range close plus positive last-30-minute return. Backtest the full Q desk with only this trend-sleeve gate changed, using the same costs and fills as baseline. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 and then on unseen 1999-2017. Primary metrics: net daily return/CAGR, Sharpe, and max drawdown of the full bot; secondary: trend-sleeve overnight expectancy and % of nights held. Accept only if both periods improve on net return and Sharpe with no worse max drawdown; if it helps one period but not the other, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with existing data, cheap to run, and directly targets the overnight trend sleeve without changing the bot architecture. The expected edge is probably small and the overfit risk is real, but this is still a clean pre-registered test rather than a wasteful data-miss or impossible idea.

name: Oscillator-based size overlay
one_line: Scale position size up or down with oscillator strength instead of treating every valid signal the same.
parameter_choices: Test full/half/zero sizing by RSI thresholds such as 20/80 versus 30/70, MACD settings like 12/26/9 or 10/40/20, APO sign or histogram strength, and distance from the moving average; sizing can be continuous rather than binary.
disagreement: RSI 20/80 and 30/70 are both used in the books, and MACD/APO can be read as momentum or mean-reversion depending on the polarity and regime, so the sizing map needs empirical testing.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients, not the exact overlay. We have RSI 30/70 and 20/80 heuristics, trend-conditioned RSI bands (45-85 in uptrends, 15-55 in downtrends), MACD/APO as momentum measures, and one example of state-variable sizing. None of the quoted items directly says to scale bet size by oscillator strength, so that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Change only the trend sleeve: keep the existing QQQ > 200-day SMA gate, but size the TQQQ allocation using QQQ’s last completed daily RSI(14) at the 15:55 decision. If QQQ is above its 200-day SMA and RSI(14) > 55, keep the current 50% sleeve; if QQQ is above its 200-day SMA and RSI(14) <= 55, cut that sleeve to 25%; if QQQ is below its 200-day SMA, hold cash.
review.mechanism: This is a conservative leverage filter. It reduces exposure when the market is only barely trending and momentum is weak, which is where the 200-day sleeve tends to get chopped up. If it works, we keep most of the upside on stronger trend days while trimming whipsaw losses and some late-trend giveback.
review.data_missing: None for this rule; daily OHLCV on QQQ is enough. Use the last completed daily close to avoid lookahead at the 15:55 decision.
review.already_tried_note: We have not already tested an oscillator-based size overlay on the existing QQQ/SMA200 trend sleeve. The rejected RSI(2) dip-buying and turn-of-month ideas are different, and the rejected noise-area variants were on IWM/DIA, not this rule.
review.overfit_note: The broad idea invites a search over oscillator family (RSI/MACD/APO), lookbacks, thresholds, polarity, and continuous-vs-binary sizing. That is a classic way to fit 2018-2026 noise. Only the frozen RSI(14)/55 cut is worth a fair test; do not sweep the family.
review.expected_effect: If the trend sleeve’s drag is concentrated in marginal bull-regime days, this should modestly improve risk-adjusted returns and maybe max drawdown. If the current sleeve mainly makes money on weak RSI pullbacks, it will just de-lever the good trades and underperform.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register this one overlay and do not tune it. Backtest the full Q desk unchanged except for this trend-sleeve sizing rule, using the same fill and cost assumptions as baseline. Compare baseline vs overlay on 2018-2026 and then on unseen 1999-2017. Score whole-bot net profit/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Accept only if net profit/day and Sharpe improve in both periods, and max drawdown is not worse than baseline by more than 3 percentage points in either period. If it helps only in 2018-2026 or only in 1999-2017, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, data-feasible, and directly targets a known weakness. The danger is not the single RSI cut; it is searching across many oscillators and thresholds. Freeze this one version and run it, but do not broaden the sweep.

name: Extreme-volume swing sleeve
one_line: Trade 1-day or 1-week volume shocks as a medium-horizon continuation or contrarian signal.
parameter_choices: Formation period of one day or one week; use relative-volume z-scores or top/bottom deciles; enter at the end of the formation period; hold up to about 20 trading days; high-volume winners can be traded as continuation, while low-volume losers can be traded contrarily.
disagreement: The literature points both ways: high-volume periods can predict positive continuation, while low-volume periods can predict negative excess returns, so the sign may depend on whether the stock is a winner or loser and on the regime.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: B1 directly supports the core claim that extreme high/low volume periods can be followed by positive/negative excess returns for roughly 20 days, and B1-c023-06 adds a winner-high-volume continuation tilt. But neither source states a QQQ-only, long-only, cash-account sleeve; the exact ETF implementation and the combined high-volume-winner / low-volume-loser rule are our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a separate weekly swing sleeve, keeping the existing Q desk unchanged: every Friday at 15:55 New York, compute QQQ's 5-trading-day return and its 5-day volume percentile versus the trailing 252 trading days; if volume is in the top decile and the 5-day return is positive, buy QQQ at the next open, sized at 25% of equity, and hold for 20 trading days; if volume is in the bottom decile and the 5-day return is negative, buy QQQ the same way and hold for 20 trading days; otherwise stay in cash.
review.mechanism: Extreme-volume weeks may mark information arrival or regime shifts. If the effect is real, the sleeve adds a medium-horizon return stream that is different from the 200-day trend sleeve and the intraday noise-area trade, without needing margin, shorting, or new data.
review.data_missing: none for the proposed daily/next-open backtest; no news, fundamentals, options, or order book data are required.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is not the same as ORB, overnight holding, last-half-hour, or noise-area on IWM/DIA. The closest overlaps are generic momentum/mean-reversion and RSI(2), but not a volume-shock swing sleeve.
review.overfit_note: This idea has several easy-to-fit choices: 1-day vs 1-week formation, continuation vs contrarian branch, top/bottom cutoff, lookback window for the percentile, and holding period. The sign can be chosen after the fact, and on QQQ alone the trade count will be modest.
review.expected_effect: Small positive at best; likely regime-dependent and noisy. If it works, the high-volume winner leg is the cleaner half, but I would not expect a large edge after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly the single rule above and do not search over variants. Backtest it as a standalone sleeve and then layered on the current Q desk using the same cost model and next-open execution. Compare to baseline on net CAGR/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Fit nothing on 2018-2026 other than the fixed rule. The rule passes only if it improves net return in 2018-2026 and again in unseen 1999-2017, with no material drawdown deterioration versus baseline. If it only works after splitting the branches or changing the hold/window, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our existing OHLCV data, cheap to test, and the literature is strong enough to justify one frozen backtest. It is not a priority edge and may overlap with momentum, but it is not obviously infeasible or cost-prohibitive.

name: Auction-aware execution regime
one_line: Treat the open and close as distinct execution regimes, with hard cutoff timing and MOC/MOO handling separate from continuous-session logic.
parameter_choices: MOO orders before 9:28; MOC/LOC by 3:55; model open/close auctions separately from regular-session bars.
disagreement: Whether auction-specific handling and cutoff discipline reduce slippage enough to matter after costs.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources correctly establish that the open and close are special auction regimes and give the Nasdaq timing rules (MOO before 9:28, MOC by 3:55). That supports the operational handling, but not a demonstrated profit edge; the return improvement is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add an auction-execution wrapper with two hard cutoffs: (1) any close trade for the trend sleeve must be sent as a Nasdaq MOC order by 15:55 ET, and no further signal updates are allowed for that sleeve after 15:55; (2) if we ever add an open-auction trade, it must be sent as a Nasdaq MOO order before 9:28 ET, and 9:28-9:30 auction-window data are ignored for decisions. No other strategy logic changes.
review.mechanism: The only plausible gain is cleaner execution: keep auction prints out of the continuous-session logic, reduce last-minute bar noise, and maybe shave a few bps of slippage around the open and close. It does not address the bot's real weaknesses, which are trend whipsaws, crash give-back, and weak intraday years.
review.data_missing: True auction prints/fills, auction imbalance data, and order-book/quote data. We can approximate with minute-bar open/close prices, but we cannot validate actual auction slippage.
review.already_tried_note: The current Q desk already treats the close separately via a 15:55 MOC-style trend decision and keeps intraday logic away from the open by starting at 10:00. The only genuinely new piece is an explicit open-auction MOO wrapper, which is not used by the current bot.
review.overfit_note: There are almost no tunable parameters if we fix the exchange cutoffs. The main risk is not overfitting; it is that the effect is tiny and gets lost in fill noise.
review.expected_effect: At best a very small reduction in execution slippage and late-day noise. Likely too small to move daily PnL materially after costs.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the cutoffs at 9:28 and 15:55 before looking at results. Run an ablation against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 and confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for any minute-bar open/close logic). Compare net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and average execution slippage versus the current fill model. Pass only if both periods improve or at least do not degrade, and the average slippage improvement is large enough to matter (>1 bp per round trip). If the gain is not visible in both periods, discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly execution plumbing, not a new edge. The close-side handling is already in the live design, and the open-side part cannot be properly validated without auction/quote data. With 1 bp assumed costs and our liquid ETF universe, any benefit is likely too small to survive sample noise and rounding.

name: Relative-value pairs sleeve
one_line: Add a cash-account pairs/stat-arb sleeve on liquid ETFs or large caps using spread divergence, correlation weighting, and session-aware timing.
parameter_choices: 12-month formation or rolling z-score; entry at z = +/-1 or 2 standard deviations; 6-month max hold; favor first and last hour entries; allow correlation-weighted multi-leg signals.
disagreement: Whether pair relationships are stable enough after costs, and whether session-specific timing materially improves edge.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the *general* pairs-trading idea, a 12-month formation / 2-sigma trigger / 6-month exit template, and the claim that intraday pairs alpha may be stronger near the open and close. They do **not** support the full proposed implementation for Midas: cash-account execution, inverse-ETF proxies for shorts, correlation-weighted multi-leg selection, or the specific ETF/large-cap universe we’d need here. Those parts are our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a **new standalone sleeve**, not a tweak to the current Q desk: each month, form one liquid-ETF pair using a 12-month rolling spread; compute the spread z-score; enter a long/short pair when |z| >= 2; exit when z returns to 0 or after 6 months; only open new trades in the first or last hour of the session. Default parameters: 12-month formation window, 2-sigma entry. Note: this requires true shorting/borrow; it is not implementable faithfully as a cash-account long-only/inverse-ETF proxy pair.
review.mechanism: In theory, a relative-value sleeve could add a market-neutral return stream that is less tied to QQQ trend direction and might monetize temporary mispricings between highly related instruments. Session-aware entry could reduce slippage and exploit the idea that pair reversion is strongest near the open/close. In Midas specifically, that mechanism is weak because we cannot short in a cash account, and inverse ETFs are not a clean substitute.
review.data_missing: We can compute spreads, rolling correlations, and z-scores from our OHLCV data. What we do **not** have is the ability to model or execute true short legs in a cash account: no borrow availability, locate costs, or actual short-sale mechanics. If we replace shorts with inverse ETFs, the economics change materially because of daily reset decay and path dependence, so it is no longer the same strategy.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is new relative to ORB/noise-area/overnight/momentum. But it is also not a close variant of the current Q desk because it needs a true long/short implementation we do not have.
review.overfit_note: Many degrees of freedom hide in pair choice, formation window, spread definition, z-threshold, hold cap, and session filter. With a small capital base and only one or a few concurrent trades, this is very easy to fit to 2018–2026 and fail out of sample, especially if we let ourselves search across many ETF/large-cap pairs.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a small uncorrelated swing sleeve that diversifies the trend book and maybe improves returns in range-bound markets. Realistically for Midas: likely weak or untradeable because the required short leg is missing, and inverse ETF proxies are not equivalent.
review.test_protocol: Only test if we first allow a faithful long/short simulation with borrow/short availability; otherwise do not test. Pre-register: choose a fixed liquid-ETF universe, 12-month rolling spread, 2-sigma entry, 6-month max hold, and first/last-hour entries only. Compare against (1) no sleeve and (2) the current Q desk. Evaluate net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and hit rate after the stated costs on 2018–2026, then confirm on 1999–2017. Require improvement in both periods and no material increase in drawdown or trade count. If we can only use inverse ETFs, test that as a separate strategy, not as pairs trading.
review.verdict_reason: The core idea depends on shorting, which a $1,000 cash account cannot do. Inverse ETF proxies are not a faithful substitute and introduce decay/path-dependence that undermines the pair-reversion premise. On top of that, the idea has too many knobs and is highly overfit-prone. This is exactly the kind of strategy that can look good in-sample and fail once we force it into our actual account constraints.

name: Intraday calm-regime gate
one_line: Only take intraday entries when realized volatility and participation are unusually calm versus expectation.
parameter_choices: 30-minute decision window; realized vol below predicted vol; cumulative volume below cumulative predicted volume; reevaluate every intraday check.
disagreement: Whether skipping noisy, high-volume periods improves net expectancy more than it reduces opportunity.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpt proposes essentially the same three-part trading gate: price signal + realized volatility below forecast + cumulative volume below forecast over a 30-minute window. What it does not provide is evidence on QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ or on a noise-area momentum sleeve, so using it on Midas is an adaptation rather than direct evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Add an entry gate to the intraday QQQ noise-area sleeve only: on each existing 30-minute check from 10:00 to 15:30, allow a TQQQ/SQQQ entry only if QQQ's realized volatility over the last 30 minutes is below its 14-session same-time-of-day average and QQQ's 30-minute volume is below its 14-session same-time-of-day average; otherwise stay in cash until the next check. Keep the current exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help if the bad intraday trades are mostly noisy, newsy, high-participation breakouts that whip back through the band. A calm-regime gate should cut those false entries and reduce churn. The trade-off is that many of the best momentum days are also high-volatility/high-volume days, so the filter may simply remove the most profitable opportunities.
review.data_missing: None. We can compute 30-minute realized volatility and same-time-of-day volume baselines from the 1-minute QQQ OHLCV/volume data we already have; no order book, news, or options data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not tested as a standalone gate, but it sits in the same family as the rejected intraday noise-area work and other attempts to make intraday breakouts more selective. It is not a completely new sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Only two obvious knobs, but the filter is still a regime label built from the same sample it is trying to improve. It can easily be tuned to skip losing 2018–2026 days and then underperform in older volatility regimes, especially if it mostly just suppresses trade count.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer intraday trades, slightly higher hit rate, lower whipsaw drawdown. My prior is modest at best; it may also lower CAGR by filtering out the strongest breakout days, so I would not expect a big edge.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the gate exactly as above (30-minute checks, 14-session same-time-of-day baselines, no other thresholds). Backtest the current Q desk versus the gated version on 2018–2026, then confirm on unseen 1999–2017 using the minute QQQ history, with 1999–2006 and 2007–2017 reported separately. Score the full bot and the intraday sleeve separately after costs. Accept only if the gated version improves net daily return and Sharpe in each period and does not worsen max drawdown; if trade count collapses without a return lift, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from our data, and directly targets the intraday sleeve's whipsaw problem. The evidence is weak and the expected lift is probably small, but this is still a legitimate one-pass backtest rather than a data-infeasible idea.

name: Multi-timeframe confirmation
one_line: Require higher-time-frame context to agree before taking the lower-time-frame entry trigger.
parameter_choices: Use 1-hour or daily context with 5-minute or 1-minute entries; require one-bar confirmation or a persistent trigger before entry.
disagreement: Whether the extra confirmation reduces whipsaws enough to offset later fills and fewer trades.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the *general* practice of using a higher time frame for context and a lower time frame for entries, but neither source gives this exact rule or any evidence that it helps on QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ. This is adaptation, not direct support.
review.exact_rule_change: For the intraday noise-area sleeve only: when a long/short trigger fires on the 30-minute check, execute it only if the last completed 1-hour QQQ close is on the same side of its 20-hour EMA (longs above, shorts below). Otherwise skip that signal. Leave the existing exits unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should filter out lower-time-frame fades that are fighting the current intraday drift, so we take fewer countertrend entries and fewer whipsaws. Best case, the sleeve’s hit rate and average trade improve; worst case, it just delays fills and cuts trade count. It may also overlap with the existing trend sleeve, so the main benefit would be on the noisy intraday sleeve, not the whole bot.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter. However, the bot already uses a higher-time-frame trend filter in the separate trend sleeve, and the rejected list shows we have already tried and rejected several price-only intraday ideas. This is a related context filter, not a wholly new edge.
review.overfit_note: If we lock the higher timeframe and the 20-hour EMA before testing, there are not many knobs. But this kind of regime filter is easy to overfit by changing the timeframe, lookback, or confirmation logic until 2018-2026 looks good and 1999-2017 does not.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small, mixed effect: fewer trades, fewer countertrend losers, and possibly a modest lift in intraday expectancy on trending days. It may also remove some good mean-reversion trades, so I would expect only a modest improvement if any.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: intraday noise-area signals gated by a 1-hour/20-hour-EMA context filter on QQQ. Compare against the current Q desk with all other rules and costs unchanged. Build/tune on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 minute data (and optionally 1999-2006 using the same QQQ daily/minute context if coverage permits). Primary metrics: after-cost daily expectancy and Sharpe of the intraday sleeve and of the full bot; secondary metrics: max drawdown, trade count, and average trade. Require the filtered version to beat baseline in both periods on net expectancy, and not worsen drawdown materially. If the only gain is fewer trades with flat or lower net return, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully data-feasible, and the rule can be made concrete with one fixed threshold. The source support is weak, so I would not spend much time on variants, but this is still worth one clean backtest because it could plausibly reduce intraday whipsaws.

name: Bollinger regime overlay
one_line: Use daily Bollinger-band position as a regime classifier for momentum versus mean reversion.
parameter_choices: 20-day Bollinger bands with 2-sigma outer bands; upper-band breaks favor continuation, lower-band excursions favor mean-reversion sizing or entry bans.
disagreement: Whether band-based regime labeling is robust enough to improve the Q desk instead of overfitting simple volatility states.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source says an outer Bollinger-band traversal can be read either as breakout continuation or as overbought/oversold reversal. That supports the general notion of using Bollinger position as a regime label, but it does not validate this exact overlay, these thresholds, or any edge on QQQ.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily overlay to the existing long trend sleeve: when QQQ is above its 200-day SMA, compute 20-trading-day Bollinger bands on the daily close with a 2-sigma envelope; use 100% TQQQ for the next session if the prior close is above the upper band, 0% (cash) if it is below the lower band, and keep the current 50% TQQQ otherwise. Below the 200-day SMA, stay in cash as now.
review.mechanism: This is trying to treat very stretched daily price action as a different regime. If QQQ is breaking out above its recent volatility envelope, the existing leveraged trend sleeve may deserve more exposure; if it is stretched below the lower band, the long trend sleeve is most exposed to whipsaw and crash give-back, so standing aside could cut the worst losses. The likely benefit is modest because Bollinger bands are mostly a volatility/z-score proxy and may be redundant with the 200-day SMA.
review.data_missing: None.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected-idea list. This is a new daily regime overlay, not the prior ORB/gap/overnight/noise-area tests.
review.overfit_note: Only one standard band specification, but the upper/middle/lower state machine can still be tuned to 2018-2026 and may just repackage volatility/trend information already captured by the 200-day filter.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small effect at best. If it helps, the gain should come from trimming some of the worst leveraged-long days in weak or stretched regimes; most of the time it may just duplicate an existing trend/volatility filter.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule above with no further tuning. Backtest baseline Q desk vs. overlay on 2018-2026 using the exact same fill and cost model, with the signal formed from the prior daily close and applied to the next session. Primary metrics: net CAGR and MAR (CAGR/max drawdown); secondary: daily Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Then run the same fixed rule on unseen 1999-2017. Require the overlay to beat baseline on net CAGR and MAR in both periods, and not worsen max drawdown by more than 5 percentage points. If it only helps the in-sample period or only raises leverage without improving MAR, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our data, cheap to test, and not already tried. The source support is weak and the edge is probably small or redundant, but this is still a legitimate pre-registered side experiment rather than a wasteful non-starter.

name: Cross-sectional technical ranker
one_line: Apply the same technical trigger across a liquid ETF or stock basket and allocate to the strongest names instead of trading a single instrument.
parameter_choices: Liquid ETF and large-cap basket; rank by technical score or acceleration; trade top-N names with pre-registered lookbacks.
disagreement: Whether cross-sectional technical alpha survives turnover and costs better than a single-symbol timing sleeve.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The cited book entry supports the general claim that technical analysis can have cross-sectional profitability, but it does not specify this exact ranker, universe, holding period, or cost-aware execution. The proposed basket-ranking rule is our extrapolation, not something the source states.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a new standalone sleeve, not a Q-desk tweak: each close rank a fixed basket of 12 liquid ETFs (SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, XLK, XLF, XLY, XLE, XLV, XLI, XLP, XLU) by 20-day total return; hold the top 3 equally weighted from the next 5-minute open to the next close, rebalanced daily.
review.mechanism: If it works, this would harvest relative strength across liquid names instead of timing one symbol, so it could add a somewhat different return stream and reduce dependence on QQQ-specific whipsaws. In practice it is still a momentum sleeve, so it will likely keep the same market beta and crash sensitivity unless the cross-sectional rotation meaningfully improves entry selection.
review.data_missing: None for the daily ETF version. We already have daily OHLCV across 1999-2026; quote/order-book data would only be needed for a more precise intraday execution variant, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: The exact ETF/stock basket version was not listed, but this is basically the same family as the rejected 12-1 cross-sectional momentum sleeve. Only the ranking window and universe change; the core idea is still cross-sectional momentum.
review.overfit_note: There are many free knobs: universe choice, technical score, lookback, top-N, rebalance frequency, and any cash/threshold filter. That makes it easy to fit 2018-2026 and disappoint on 1999-2017, especially with a small account and whole-share constraints.
review.expected_effect: At best a small, unstable improvement from relative-strength rotation; more likely a wash after turnover and share-size friction. It does not directly fix the known QQQ whipsaw/crash-giveback problem.
review.test_protocol: Do not run the broad stock-basket version. If you insist on a narrow sanity check, pre-register the fixed 12-ETF universe and the 20-day/top-3 rule above before looking at results. Backtest 2018-2026 first, then confirm on 1999-2017. Compare standalone net CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and average trade edge after 1 bp/side plus SEC fees against cash and against the current Q desk at the same capital weight. Require positive net performance in both periods and no material worsening of drawdown versus the current desk; otherwise kill it.
review.verdict_reason: This is basically the already-rejected cross-sectional momentum family under a new name. The source only gives a generic citation, not a concrete edge, and the broad stock/ETF ranker has too many knobs and too much overlap with existing momentum logic to justify another test. On a $1k cash account, the long-only top-N version is likely too fragile after turnover and whole-share constraints.

name: Year-end seasonality overlay
one_line: Use a year-end seasonal tilt to size QQQ/TQQQ exposure only during the historically strong mid-December to early-January window.
parameter_choices: Mid-December entry window; early-January exit window; size multiplier versus baseline trend sleeve.
