disagreement: Whether this seasonal pattern is strong enough after costs and already captured by turn-of-month effects.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the broad calendar claim 'buy early/mid-December, sell early January,' but it is an opinion about the FTSE 100, not a quantified result, and not specifically a QQQ/TQQQ sizing overlay. This is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current Q-desk trend sleeve unchanged except: if QQQ closes above its 200-day SMA and the date is Dec 15 through Jan 5 inclusive, raise the trend sleeve weight from 50% to 75% of equity (1.5x the baseline size) using the same TQQQ instrument; outside that window, stay at 50%.
review.mechanism: If year-end drift is real, we are already positioned long in the trend sleeve during strong market regimes. The overlay would simply lean a bit harder into the historically favorable holiday window, potentially adding a small amount of return without changing entry/exit logic or cash-account mechanics.
review.data_missing: None. Daily QQQ history back to 1999 is enough; no news/options/order-book data needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not explicitly on the rejected list, but it sits in the same broad seasonality bucket as turn-of-month, which is already a known small edge. It may just be a noisier subset of that effect.
review.overfit_note: This is a short calendar window with only a handful of annual observations in the build period. Date/multiplier tuning would be easy to overfit, and the apparent edge could be pure holiday noise or just turn-of-month.
review.expected_effect: Likely tiny. Best case: a small boost concentrated in late December/early January. Base case: no material improvement after costs because the trend filter and turn-of-month already capture most of the effect. It should not improve crash exits.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one configuration only: Dec 15-Jan 5 inclusive, trend-sleeve weight 75% when QQQ > 200DMA, otherwise 50%. Backtest the full Q desk with identical costs and fills on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Compare against the current Q desk on net CAGR/daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and the average return specifically inside the year-end window. Accept only if both subperiods improve versus baseline and max drawdown is not worse; if the lift disappears when you remove the existing turn-of-month days from the window, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap, but the source is only anecdotal seasonality, the edge is likely small, and it overlaps heavily with the existing turn-of-month effect. I would not prioritize it ahead of better trend/regime or crash-exit work.

name: Range-bound mean reversion sleeve
one_line: Trade stable ranges by buying near support and selling near resistance when the tape is genuinely range-bound.
parameter_choices: Rolling 200-day support/resistance or stable multi-day range; require range-width filter; enter near range edges and exit at the opposite edge.
disagreement: Whether range behavior is distinct and persistent enough to beat trend-following after costs.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B5 gives a worked daily GOOG example of rolling 200-day support/resistance; B8 is only a generic opinion about trading predictable ranges. Neither is a statistical test, and neither is specific to liquid ETFs or our cash-account constraints.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a separate long-only QQQ swing sleeve, not a tweak to the current sleeves: define support/resistance as the prior 200-trading-day low/high. If QQQ closes within 1% of the 200-day low and the 200-day high-low band is below its own 200-day moving average, buy QQQ at the next open. Exit at the next open after a close within 1% of the 200-day high, or flatten on a close below the 200-day low. Allocate 25% of equity to this sleeve.
review.mechanism: If QQQ really does oscillate inside a stable multi-week/month range, this can monetize sideways chop that hurts the 200-day trend sleeve. It adds a separate mean-reversion return stream and may reduce whipsaw dependence on trend continuation. It will still be vulnerable when the range breaks down or turns into a trend.
review.data_missing: None needed; daily OHLCV is enough to compute the 200-day band and backtest the sleeve.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the explicit reject list, but it overlaps with the existing QQQ RSI(2) dip-buying edge and broader mean-reversion logic. If the 200-day range filter does not add real regime selection, this is just slower dip-buying with more lag.
review.overfit_note: Range systems are regime-sensitive and easy to fit with one buffer, one lookback, one filter, and one asset choice. A 2018-2026 sample can easily make a bad channel-fade look good in chop and fail in 1999-2017 or 2022.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a small uncorrelated return stream in sideways QQQ regimes and a partial offset to trend whipsaws. Base case: modest or flat after costs. Bad case: it bleeds in strong trends or range breaks and adds drawdown.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact QQQ daily rule above with no threshold tuning after 2018-2026. Backtest standalone on 2018-2026, then confirm unchanged on 1999-2017. Use the same cost model as the bot. Compare against current Q desk both standalone and as an added sleeve with fixed 25% capital carved out of cash, not extra leverage. Pass only if the sleeve is profitable after costs in both periods and improves combined net CAGR and Sharpe versus the current Q desk without worsening max drawdown by more than 5 percentage points; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap with data we already have, and it targets a real weakness in sideways markets. The evidence is weak, so it only earns a pre-registered test if it can beat the current Q desk in both build and confirm periods.

name: Volatility sizing throttle
one_line: Cut or switch off sleeve size when realized volatility spikes or stays elevated, instead of treating every regime the same.
parameter_choices: Use 20- or 60-day realized vol; top-decile or rising-vol regime; OHLC proxy vol = 0.5(H-L)^2 - 0.386(C-O)^2; halve size or go to cash in stress.
disagreement: No major disagreement on using volatility as a risk brake; the choice is downsize versus full kill-switch.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: The sources strongly support the underlying fact that volatility clusters, market risk is heteroscedastic, and volatility can be used as a regime/risk proxy; they also give an OHLC volatility estimator. But none of them explicitly prove this exact 60-day top-decile throttle on the Q desk. This is an adaptation, not a quoted rule.
review.exact_rule_change: At each daily close, compute QQQ 60-day realized volatility from close-to-close returns. If that volatility is in the top decile of its expanding historical distribution, multiply every Q desk target weight by 0.5 for the next session; otherwise leave sizing unchanged.
review.mechanism: Volatility clusters are where 3x ETFs, daily rebalancing, and the trend sleeve are most fragile. A throttle should reduce exposure during noisy, gap-prone stress periods, which may cut crash give-back and whipsaw losses. The downside is that it also trims exposure on some of the bot’s best high-volatility trend days, so this is more of a risk brake than a clear alpha source.
review.data_missing: None; daily QQQ OHLCV is enough to compute the regime signal, and the rule can be applied without order book, news, or options data.
review.already_tried_note: Not this rule. The rejected items were different strategies or different assets; I do not see a prior volatility-based sizing throttle on the current Q desk.
review.overfit_note: Only one lookback and one fixed percentile gate, so the rule is simple. The risk is that once we start searching 20 vs 60 days, deciles vs quartiles, or half-size vs cash, it becomes a regime-mining exercise and will overfit 2018-2026.
review.expected_effect: Likely lower volatility and smaller drawdowns, especially in stress clusters like 2008/2020/2022, but probably some CAGR drag because exposure is cut exactly when the bot can also make big trend money. Net benefit is plausible only if high-vol days are net-negative after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one rule: 60-day realized vol, top-decile expanding-history gate, 0.5 multiplier. Backtest baseline Q desk vs throttled Q desk on 2018-2026 first using only information available by the prior close; then confirm unchanged on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level execution if needed). Primary metrics: net CAGR/day after all costs, max drawdown, Sharpe and Calmar. Keep the change only if both periods improve net CAGR/day and do not worsen max drawdown; if the improvement appears only in one period or only via lower risk with lower return, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully data-feasible, cheap to test, and plausibly helpful as a crash/whipsaw brake. But it is not a strong alpha claim, so we should only give it one fixed, pre-registered pass and not start tuning thresholds.

name: Volatility-adaptive signal parameters
one_line: Let the lookback, band width, and MA type adapt to volatility so the bands are not fixed across calm and noisy regimes.
parameter_choices: Shorter histories when vol is high; dynamic EMA smoothing and APO thresholds with stdev_factor; test SMA in high vol versus EMA in low vol; widen bands when volatility is noisy.
disagreement: Sources disagree on direction: some want faster, shorter lookbacks in high vol, others prefer SMA or longer smoothing in volatile markets.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: The books do support the general concept: volatility can be used to change MA type, lookback, and band width, and they explicitly say SMA is often better in volatile markets while EMA is faster in calm ones. But none of the sources gives an exact Midas rule or any performance evidence on QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ. Also, the intraday noise-area sleeve already uses a realized-move-based band, so the 'make bands adaptive' part is less novel here than it sounds.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not make the whole bot volatility-adaptive. For this test, change only the trend sleeve: compute QQQ 20-day realized volatility from daily close-to-close returns each morning. If realized vol is above 15%, use a 200-day SMA as the trend filter; if it is 15% or lower, use a 200-day EMA. Keep the intraday noise-area sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: In calm markets, the EMA should get us into the trend a bit sooner. In noisy markets, the SMA should filter more wiggle and reduce flip-flopping around the trend line. If it helps, the gain should come from fewer whipsaws and lower cost drag. The obvious failure mode is that the SMA branch slows crash exits, so this is a real tradeoff, not a free lunch.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact QQQ volatility-switch. We have tried adjacent ideas like stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot and noise-area on IWM/DIA, but not a trend-sleeve MA switch driven by realized volatility. The band-adaptation part is also partly redundant because the current noise-area band already adapts to recent move size.
review.overfit_note: Only one real threshold, but this can still turn into a sample-mined regime hack if we start tuning the 15% cutoff, the MA span, or adding extra filters. Keep it pre-registered and do not grid-search it.
review.expected_effect: Small-to-moderate at best. Best case: fewer trend whipsaws and a bit less churn in choppy markets. Worst case: slower crash exits and no improvement out of sample. I would expect a modest effect if any, not a step-change.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule exactly as written with the 15% volatility threshold fixed. Backtest current Q desk vs the volatility-switch trend sleeve on the full daily history, using identical costs and fills. Because the intraday sleeve is unchanged, minute-bar confirmation is not needed for this test. Score net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. First run on 2018-2026 to sanity-check, then confirm on 1999-2017 without changing anything. Require improvement in both periods, and reject if drawdown gets materially worse or if the gain only appears in one period. No threshold tuning, no MA-span search.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly aimed at the bot's trend-whipsaw weakness. I would not broaden it into dynamic lookbacks or band-width grids yet; just test the single realized-volatility MA switch and let the out-of-sample result decide.

name: Adaptive trend estimator
one_line: Replace the fixed 200-day SMA with a local-trend estimate that updates in real time and reacts faster to slope changes.
parameter_choices: Kalman filter or local linear trend; stochastic slope; rolling slope windows like 4, 5, or 10 bars; trend-strength confidence band or slope sign.
disagreement: Sources disagree on whether the adaptive trend state should come from Kalman/local-linear-trend estimation or a simpler EMA or slope proxy.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the ingredients, not this exact trade rule: Kalman/local-linear-trend estimation can update in real time, EMA reacts faster than SMA, and slope/angle can proxy trend strength. But none of the quoted items shows that replacing QQQ’s 200-day SMA gate in this bot with an adaptive estimator improves net profit after costs.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the QQQ 200-day SMA trend gate with a QQQ 200-day EMA trend gate, and only keep the 50% overnight TQQQ sleeve on when QQQ closes above its EMA200 and the EMA200 is rising versus 20 sessions ago; otherwise hold cash. Signal is checked at 15:55 New York using the latest available bar.
review.mechanism: A faster estimator may get the bot out of the trend sleeve earlier when the uptrend decays, which could reduce the big crash give-backs we already saw in the 200-day SMA sleeve. Requiring a positive slope should also keep the sleeve out of flatter, chop-heavy regimes where the SMA tends to whipsaw.
review.data_missing: None for this variant. We can compute EMA and 20-day slope from the daily or 1-minute QQQ bars we already have, with the same execution assumptions as the current trend sleeve.
review.already_tried_note: We have already tested the underlying idea of a QQQ regime gate for the trend sleeve, but not this exact EMA+slope variant. It is still just a nearby replacement for the current 200-day SMA filter, so expect incremental change rather than a new alpha stream.
review.overfit_note: If fixed מראש, this has only two obvious knobs (EMA length and slope lag). But once we start tuning those, it becomes another moving-average sweep that can fit 2018-2026 and fail 1999-2017. The Kalman/local-trend version would be even easier to overcomplicate.
review.expected_effect: Best case: earlier crash exits and slightly lower drawdown. More likely: small change in CAGR with some reduction in whipsaw losses, offset by extra false exits in sideways bull periods. This is a plausible improvement, but not a likely step-change.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly two trend gates: the current SMA200 baseline and the candidate EMA200+slope20 rule. Run the full Q desk with identical costs and intraday sleeve, using the same 15:55 decision time and next-5-minute-open fill logic. Evaluate on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Accept only if the candidate beats the baseline on net return after costs in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; if it improves return but increases turnover materially, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully feasible with existing data, and directly targets the bot’s biggest weakness (trend-sleeve whipsaw and crash give-back). The support is only conceptual, so keep the rule fixed and do not broaden into a Kalman-parameter search before seeing the out-of-sample result.

name: Multi-bar major trend gate
one_line: Only allow longs when the major trend has stayed aligned for several bars across price, moving averages, RSI, and VWAP.
parameter_choices: 5-10 consecutive candles; fast MA above slow MA; RSI above 50; price above VWAP; 20-day momentum positive; same-timeframe entry/exit with higher-timeframe filters.
disagreement: EMA-based versions react faster, SMA-based versions are cleaner; several books vary on the exact bar count and timeframe.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: No source states this exact four-factor gate. The books separately support the ingredients: keep entry/exit on one timeframe, trade with the major trend, confirm MA signals over several candles, require EMA and RSI agreement, and use VWAP as a trend reference. The proposed gate is our synthesis of those pieces.
review.exact_rule_change: At each 15:55 New York decision, keep the 50% trend sleeve in TQQQ only if QQQ has passed a 5-session confirmation gate: for the last 5 completed daily bars, QQQ's 30-day EMA is above its 50-day EMA and RSI(20) is above 50, and at each of those same 5 decision times QQQ traded above its session VWAP. Otherwise that sleeve stays in cash. Leave the intraday noise-area sleeve unchanged for this test.
review.mechanism: This should keep leveraged overnight longs out of weak, unstable rallies and sideways chop, which are where the current trend sleeve whipsaws. Requiring trend, momentum, and participation to agree for several sessions should reduce false re-entries after bouncebacks and may exit sooner when the regime breaks. The tradeoff is slower re-entry after sharp V-shaped recoveries and potentially fewer trades.
review.data_missing: None for this test. QQQ daily OHLCV covers the daily EMA/RSI pieces, and QQQ minute data lets us reconstruct session VWAP and the 15:55 decision-time check.
review.already_tried_note: We already run a simpler trend sleeve (QQQ above its 200-day SMA) and a VWAP-based intraday sleeve, so this is in the same family. But the exact multi-bar confirmation stack has not been separately tested and rejected.
review.overfit_note: This is a conjunction of highly correlated filters plus a 5-session persistence window. It is easy to tune 30/50/RSI/VWAP/persistence until 2018-2026 looks better by simply suppressing trades. Do not grid-search the thresholds on the first pass.
review.expected_effect: Likely fewer trend-sleeve entries and less whipsaw, with a chance of smaller drawdowns in sideways years. Best case: a smoother equity curve and faster de-risking when trend quality deteriorates; worst case: missed V-bounces and lower CAGR from underexposure.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register this exact gate and run only one locked version against the current Q desk. Compare 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017; because VWAP is minute-derived, also sanity-check 2007-2017 with the same code path. Primary metrics: net daily return after costs, Sharpe, and max drawdown for the full bot; secondary metrics: turnover and average time in TQQQ. Accept only if the gated version improves net daily return in both splits and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise stop.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our data, cheap to run, and it targets a real weakness of the current bot. The risk is overfitting and lower exposure, so this should be a single pre-registered test, not a search over many MA/RSI/bar-count variants. If the fixed version does not beat the baseline in both the build and confirm splits, kill it.

name: Price-structure trend regime
one_line: Use higher highs and lows, break-of-structure, trendline slope, and wedge or neckline breaks as a structural trend filter or exit trigger.
parameter_choices: HH/HL for uptrends and LH/LL for downtrends; two break-of-structure closes; 3-touch trendlines; wedge compression and neckline breaks as exhaustion signals.
disagreement: Some sources emphasize break-of-structure, others trendline slope or wedge exhaustion; the exact structural trigger differs.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the building blocks — HH/HL and LH/LL regime definitions, two break-of-structure closes, and a 3- to 5-day fractal/pivot heuristic — but they do not validate this exact QQQ/TQQQ rule. The wedge, trendline-slope and neckline parts are discretionary chart-pattern lore, not evidence-backed here.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current 200-day SMA trend sleeve, but add a structural fail-safe on QQQ daily bars: define confirmed swing highs/lows with a 5-day fractal pivot (two bars on each side); if QQQ closes below the last confirmed swing low for two consecutive daily closes, flatten the TQQQ sleeve to cash at the next rebalance; only re-enter after two consecutive daily closes above the last confirmed swing high and while QQQ is still above its 200-day SMA. Do not test wedges, neckline breaks, or trendline-angle rules in this first pass.
review.mechanism: This is a faster crash-exit overlay. If QQQ stops making higher highs/higher lows, the sleeve can get out before the 200-day average rolls over, which may cut some of the big give-back in 2008/2022-type selloffs. It may also keep us out of some choppy regimes, but because it is still a trend rule on the same market, I would expect only a small edge, not a new return stream.
review.data_missing: None for this version; daily OHLCV on QQQ is enough. A true wedge or neckline detector would need a separately defined algorithm, but not more data.
review.already_tried_note: The bot has tested the 200-day SMA gate, but not this formal HH/HL + break-of-structure exit overlay. The rejected ORB/overnight/noise-area tests are unrelated.
review.overfit_note: There are still lots of hidden knobs if we let the idea sprawl (pivot window, number of BOS closes, what qualifies as a swing point, whether to use highs/lows or closes). Pattern rules are especially easy to fit to 2018-2026 and then disappoint in 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: Small, uncertain improvement at best: earlier trend exits and slightly less crash give-back, but likely more whipsaw and delayed re-entry. If it works, it should show up mainly in the trend sleeve's drawdown, not as a big lift in average daily return.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact daily rule above with window=5 and BOS confirmation=2. Backtest the full Q desk unchanged except for this overlay, using the same costs/fill model as live. Compare against the current 200-day-SMA version on 2018-2026 first, then freeze the rule and test once on unseen 1999-2017. Primary metrics: full-bot net CAGR/day and max drawdown; secondary: Sharpe, trade count, and trend-sleeve drawdown in 2008/2022/2025-26. Accept only if the modified bot improves net CAGR/day and does not worsen max drawdown in both periods, with no more than 15% increase in turnover. If it only helps in 2018-2026 but not 1999-2017, reject.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with the data we already have, cheap to run, and it targets a real weakness of the trend sleeve. The chart-pattern version is too fuzzy, but the narrowed 5-day-fractal/two-close exit overlay is concrete enough to deserve one pre-registered test.

name: Regime shift kill-switch
one_line: Turn the bot off or cut to cash when a change-point or HMM says the market has moved into a new state.
parameter_choices: CUSUM with k = δ/2 and user threshold h; adaptive CUSUM; two-state HMM; cooldown after break; disable after sustained underperformance.
disagreement: Mean-shift, variance-shift, and combined mean/variance regime models are all proposed; test them separately.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general premise that markets switch regimes and that CUSUM / Markov-switching methods can detect those shifts. But none of them actually show that a regime detector improves a QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ desk, and none specify a bot-level kill-switch. The trading rule is our extrapolation from generic regime-detection theory.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily adaptive CUSUM gate on QQQ close-to-close log returns. If either side of the chart breaches h = 3× the trailing 20-day stdev of daily returns, disable the intraday sleeve for the next 3 trading days; leave the 200-day trend sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help only by keeping the intraday momentum sleeve out of unstable transition periods, where false breakouts and reversals are most likely. It is meant to reduce whipsaw losses and crash give-back without shutting down the slower trend sleeve that already handles the big regime filter. Best case: fewer bad intraday trades and slightly lower drawdown. Likely downside: missed trades and lower CAGR if the detector fires too often.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule. The current 200DMA trend sleeve is already a coarse regime filter, and prior stop/target tuning on the old ORB bot is the closest analogue. But no formal CUSUM/HMM kill-switch has been tested on the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: Regime detectors are easy to overfit because the threshold, cooldown, and state definition can be tuned to past crisis years. There are only a handful of true market-transition episodes in 1999-2026, so a detector that looks great in 2018-2026 can easily be a noise-fit.
review.expected_effect: Modest best case: fewer losing intraday trades and some crash-drawdown reduction. Base case: little change. Bad case: lower return because the gate turns off the intraday sleeve too often and misses profitable trend continuations.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one variant and do not retune after seeing results. Compare baseline Q desk vs. baseline plus the CUSUM gate on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and the 2007-2017 minute-data slice for the intraday sleeve behavior). Evaluate net return/day after all costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and fraction of days the intraday sleeve is disabled. Adopt only if the variant beats baseline on net return/day and max drawdown in both periods; if it only improves drawdown while reducing return, reject.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap, but the broad HMM/CUSUM regime-kill family is a classic overfit trap, and this bot already has a built-in coarse regime gate via the 200DMA trend sleeve. The only version worth testing is a very simple CUSUM gate on the intraday sleeve, and even that is likely to have only a small edge. I would not spend priority test time on the full kill-switch idea until simpler volatility or size filters have been exhausted.

name: Volume-confirmed breakout continuation
one_line: Require relative volume or volume surprise before taking momentum entries, so the bot only follows moves with participation behind them.
parameter_choices: Relative volume above 1.5; 30-minute volume above its time-of-day forecast; cumulative volume above EWMA forecast; confirm with strong candle body and rising volume.
disagreement: Volume is treated as confirmation in some sources, but other excerpts warn that high-volume moves can also reverse, so this should be tested against the fade variant.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general heuristic that high or surprising volume can confirm a move, and they give a usable relative-volume threshold (1.5x) plus time-of-day volume forecasting. But none of them tests this exact QQQ noise-area breakout filter, and one source explicitly warns that high-volume moves can also reverse, so the support is indirect and mixed.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday sleeve only: take the first QQQ noise-area momentum entry of the day only if the current 30-minute QQQ volume is at least 1.5x its 30-session average for that same 30-minute clock bucket; otherwise skip the entry. Do not change exits or the trend sleeve.
review.mechanism: This should cut low-conviction breakouts and chop on dead-volume days, which are a likely source of the intraday sleeve's flat or losing years. If volume really is a participation proxy, the filter should improve win rate and reduce churn/spread drag. It will not fix the daily trend sleeve's crash lag.
review.data_missing: None for this variant. We can compute same-clock-bucket relative volume from our existing 1-minute QQQ bars; no L2, news, or options data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter. But it is adjacent to already-rejected breakout/ORB-style ideas, so I would not expect a brand-new structural edge; only a possible quality filter on the existing intraday sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob (1.5x) plus a standard 30-session lookback, so this is not a huge parameter minefield. But volume definitions are easy to tune after the fact, and the effect may be regime-dependent.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small improvement in intraday Sharpe and drawdown if it helps at all, with fewer trades. It may also miss some profitable early breakouts, so I would not expect a large uplift.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule before looking: 30-session same-time-bucket average volume, entry allowed only when relative volume >= 1.5. Backtest baseline Q desk vs the modified desk on 2018-2026 and separately on 1999-2017 using the same fill/cost model. Primary metrics: net daily return after costs and Sharpe; secondary: max drawdown, trade count, and per-year stability. Accept only if the modified version beats baseline in both periods on net return and Sharpe without materially worsening drawdown; if it helps only 2018-2026, reject as overfit.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully computable from our existing minute data, and directly targets a known weak spot in the intraday sleeve. The source support is only partial and anecdotal, but the rule is concrete enough to pre-register and the downside of one test is small.

name: Intraday hysteresis and minimum hold
one_line: Add separate entry and exit thresholds plus a minimum hold time to stop the intraday sleeve from churning around the band.
parameter_choices: Entry and exit thresholds sufficiently apart; minimum holding duration; wider bands in noisy conditions to reduce catch-up risk.
disagreement: No real disagreement; the trade-off is lower churn versus slower re-entry.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general anti-churn idea: separate entry/exit thresholds and a minimum hold. But they do not give this exact QQQ band rule or any transferable numeric setting. The Donadio/Ghosh example is only a generic last-trade-distance filter, so the specific thresholds here are our own first-pass choice.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday sleeve only: add symmetric 0.10σ hysteresis around the existing QQQ band and a 60-minute minimum hold. Long entry requires QQQ to be 0.10σ above the upper band; long exit is allowed only after 60 minutes and only once QQQ has fallen back 0.10σ inside that same band. Mirror the rule for shorts around the lower band. Keep the rest of the Q desk unchanged.
review.mechanism: This can help only if the current sleeve is getting kicked out by short-lived noise after a real breakout. The hysteresis should avoid marginal entries and the minimum hold should prevent an immediate flip-flat on the first retrace. That said, the sleeve already allows only one round trip per day, so there is not much true churn to eliminate; the main effect may just be delaying exits. That could help on trend days and hurt when the move fails fast.
review.data_missing: None required for a first-pass backtest; quote/order-book data would only improve slippage realism.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact QQQ rule. But the live intraday sleeve already has a band/VWAP logic and a hard one-round-trip-per-day cap, so this is a small refinement rather than a new setup. Similar anti-churn tweaks were already rejected on the old ORB bot, though that is not the same signal.
review.overfit_note: Only two knobs, but both are easy to tune to 2018-2026 and the effect can be regime-specific. Because the sleeve trades at most once a day, a small in-sample lift can easily be noise or a lucky balance between skipping bad exits and missing good ones.
review.expected_effect: Likely small at best. If the sleeve is overly sensitive to noisy retracements, this may improve average trade quality and slightly lower turnover. More likely, it just delays exits and can worsen fast failure/crash days. I would not expect it to fix the flat/losing intraday years by itself.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register h = 0.10σ and minimum hold = 60 minutes before looking at results. Backtest the modified intraday sleeve alone and the full Q desk with identical fill/cost assumptions. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 and on the unseen 1999-2017 period (use the available minute data where present, with synthetic 3x earlier years only if that is already the standard framework). Judge on net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in both periods; if returns do not improve after costs, or if drawdown worsens materially, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully feasible with existing data and cheap to test. The expected edge is modest because the current sleeve already limits churn with a one-round-trip cap, so this is more of a smoothing tweak than a new alpha source. Still, it is concrete, falsifiable, and worth one clean backtest rather than hand-waving.

name: High-volume exhaustion skip
one_line: Skip or fade momentum after unusually large high-volume bars, because those moves often reverse.
parameter_choices: Abnormal high-volume price changes; large bars relative to recent range or ATR; fade back toward VWAP or simply block fresh momentum entries; cap size after volume spikes.
disagreement: This is the opposite-signed hypothesis to the volume-confirmation rule, so it should be tested as a separate branch.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: B1-c023-04 directly supports the core hypothesis: high-volume price changes are more likely to reverse. B1-c039-01 is weaker but consistent support for not leaning into volume spikes blindly. B1-c046-09 is only a generic liquidity/toxicity citation. None of the sources states our exact QQQ intraday filter, so this needs adaptation rather than a direct transplant.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday sleeve only: if the most recent 5-minute QQQ bar has volume > 3.0x the median volume of the prior 20 regular-session 5-minute bars, suppress any new intraday momentum entry for the next 30 minutes. Existing positions still use the normal VWAP/close exits. Do not add a fade branch yet.
review.mechanism: Large, high-volume bars are often exhaustion or liquidity events, not clean continuation. Our intraday sleeve is most vulnerable to entering right after those bars, when the move is stretched and adverse selection is highest. Skipping the next 30 minutes should cut false breakouts and churn, especially on opening/news-like spikes, without changing the trend sleeve or cash-account mechanics.
review.data_missing: No additional data is needed for the skip filter; 1-minute OHLCV is enough to aggregate 5-minute volume and rolling medians. News/order-book data would only be needed if we wanted to distinguish exhaustion from informed breakouts and build a true fade strategy.
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected related momentum/breakout systems (ORB, noise-area on IWM/DIA), but not this specific post-volume-spike entry filter on QQQ. So this is adjacent to prior work, not redundant with an exact prior test.
review.overfit_note: Only two real knobs are being proposed (spike threshold and skip duration), so this is not a giant curve-fit. But the effect can be regime-dependent and the threshold may be fragile, especially if we start searching many volume cutoffs or adding range-based confirmations.
review.expected_effect: Likely a modest improvement in the intraday sleeve’s trade quality: fewer bad breakout entries, lower turnover, and less slippage from chasing exhaustion bars. The tradeoff is that it may also skip some genuine continuation days, so the net effect could be small rather than dramatic.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule before looking at results. Apply it only to the QQQ intraday sleeve; leave the trend sleeve untouched. Compare baseline Q desk vs. Q desk + volume-spike skip on full 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017, with the minute-level split also reported for 1999-2006 and 2007-2017. Primary metrics: net daily return after costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and intraday trade expectancy. Success requires improvement in each period versus baseline, with no meaningful increase in max drawdown and no obvious degradation in trade count/expectancy. If the filter helps only in 2018-2026 but not in the older holdout, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, directly computable from our existing minute bars, and plausibly helps the intraday sleeve without changing the whole bot. The evidence is only partial and the edge may be fragile, but this is a reasonable, low-cost filter test rather than a new strategy or an infeasible data request.

name: Support/resistance retest sleeve
one_line: Trade only when price retests a recent multi-touch support or resistance zone instead of reacting to exact levels.
parameter_choices: Recent 10/20/40-day windows; 2-3 touches inside a tolerance band; treat levels as zones; broken resistance becomes support; round numbers can add confluence.
disagreement: Mostly agreement on zones rather than exact prices; sources differ mainly on how strict the touch count should be.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support components of the idea—zones not exact lines, recent levels matter, repeated touches matter, and broken levels can flip roles—but none gives a tested retest strategy or any stats. The actual sleeve is our extrapolation from charting folklore.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the trend-sleeve entry with a retest filter: while QQQ is above its 200-day SMA, only put the existing 50% trend allocation into TQQQ after QQQ has formed a 20-day support/resistance zone with at least 2 touches inside a ±0.5% band and then retests that broken level from the other side; otherwise that 50% stays in cash. No change to the current 200-day exit.
review.mechanism: If it works, it should skip the first impulsive breakout and only enter after the market proves acceptance at the level, which could reduce false breakouts and whipsaws and improve average entry prices. The cost is missing fast V-shaped breakouts; any edge would come from fewer bad entries, not more trades.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not on the explicit reject list, but it is very close to the already-rejected breakout/ORB family and to generic price-pattern folklore. We have not specifically tested daily QQQ retest filters, but the resemblance is close enough that it should be treated as adjacent, not novel.
review.overfit_note: Touch-count, zone width, window length, breakout definition, and retest timing are all flexible. On one ETF, the event count will be modest, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and look good by chance.
review.expected_effect: At best a modest reduction in whipsaw entries and a slightly better win rate on the trend sleeve; likely fewer trades and some missed winners. It does not directly fix crash give-back, so the upside is limited.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one version: 20-day window, 2 touches, ±0.5% zone, applied only as an entry filter to the existing trend sleeve. Backtest the current Q desk versus Q desk + filter on 2018-2026 with identical costs, fills, and sizing; then lock the rule and confirm on 1999-2017. Compare net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and the trend sleeve's whipsaw rate (losses within 5 sessions). Keep it only if the combined bot improves net return/day and Sharpe in both periods, does not worsen max drawdown, and reduces whipsaw trades materially.
review.verdict_reason: This is generic breakout/retest chartism with weak evidence and too much discretion for our sample. The only supported pieces are 'zones, recent levels, repeated touches,' which are just folklore-level heuristics. It is too close to the already-rejected breakout/ORB family and does not address our main failure mode—crash give-back—well enough to justify a new test slot.

name: Calendar and session-quality filter
one_line: Avoid low-quality trading windows: macro releases, Fed days, the open and close, holidays, DST shifts, early closes, August thinness, and halt or limit days.
parameter_choices: No-new-entry windows around major macro releases; Fed announcement days; skip first and last hour; reduce size on August, early-close, or DST-transition sessions; flat on halted days.
disagreement: Some sources prefer a full skip around events, others prefer smaller size or delayed re-entry after the event.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the general notion that liquidity/execution quality varies by session and calendar: several mention early/late-hour spread or impact deterioration, Fed days as a distinct regime, and the need to record holidays/DST/disrupted days. But none of them directly validates this whole bundled 'calendar-quality filter,' and most of the support is opinion or author experience rather than stats. The macro/Fed/August/DST pieces are mostly extrapolation unless split into separate tests.
review.exact_rule_change: For the intraday Q desk sleeve only, allow new entries only between 10:30 and 15:00 New York time on regular sessions; if the session is an exchange early-close day, take no intraday trades that day. Leave the trend sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is a pure execution-quality filter. It tries to avoid the noisiest/highest-slippage parts of the day, where ETF spreads and short-horizon whipsaws are typically worse, so the intraday sleeve should get fewer false starts and slightly better net expectancy after costs. It does not solve the bot’s main trend-sleeve drawdown problem; at best it trims the bad intraday windows.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed narrow rule. If we later add Fed-day or macro-release skips, we would need a reliable external event calendar, which is not in the current dataset.
review.already_tried_note: This overlaps with already-rejected 'last-half-hour' style ideas, and the current intraday sleeve already avoids the first 30 minutes and the final 30 minutes. So this is only an incremental tightening, not a new family of edge. The full macro/event bundle has not been tested, but that is exactly why it should not be bundled into one test.
review.overfit_note: The narrow time-window gate is simple, but the broader idea tempts you into many calendar labels and special-case filters (Fed days, August, DST, holidays, early closes, halts), which is a classic way to fit 2018-2026 and fail earlier years. Keep it to one pre-registered session window first.
review.expected_effect: Small at best. It may shave a bit of slippage and reduce some bad intraday trades, but it will also throw away valid signals. I would expect a modest improvement in intraday expectancy if anything, not a step-change in the whole bot.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one change only: intraday entries allowed 10:30-15:00 ET; early-close sessions = no intraday sleeve. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 first, then on unseen 1999-2017 (using the synthetic 3x handling already used in the backtests). Evaluate: (1) whole-bot after-cost daily Sharpe and CAGR/day, (2) intraday sleeve expectancy per trade after costs, and (3) max drawdown. Accept only if the modified rule improves intraday expectancy and does not worsen whole-bot Sharpe or max drawdown in either period. If it only helps 2018-2026, reject as overfit.
review.verdict_reason: The full calendar/Fed/August bundle is too broad, but the stripped-down session-hours filter is cheap, data-feasible, and specific enough to test. It is unlikely to be a big edge, but it is not a wasteful test if kept narrow and pre-registered.

name: Seasonal allocation overlay
one_line: Tilt exposure by month because some calendar windows are consistently stronger or weaker than others.
parameter_choices: Reduce risk in February-March and May-July; test higher risk in April and December; downweight September; use a simple month-of-year allocation schedule.
disagreement: April is the main conflict: some excerpts call it strong, one calls it weak, so this needs empirical testing.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The excerpts do support the general idea of month-of-year sizing: they explicitly suggest holding cash in February-March, trimming May-July, favoring April, downweighting September, and overweighting December. However, these are mostly opinion pieces / anecdotal seasonal claims from one author, aimed at broad market or FTSE behavior rather than QQQ/Midas specifically, and April is internally conflicting across the excerpts (strong in some, weak in another). So this is an adaptation, not a direct source-backed rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a monthly gross-exposure overlay to the whole Q desk (both sleeves scaled together) at the first trading day of each month. Use two fixed parameters: weak_month_mult=0.75 and strong_month_mult=1.25. Apply weak_month_mult in February-March, May-July, and September; apply strong_month_mult in April and December; use 1.0 in all other months.
review.mechanism: If Nasdaq seasonality is real, this can shift risk toward months with better average drift and away from choppier or weaker months. That could slightly improve net return and/or drawdown by reducing exposure when the base bot is more likely to whipsaw and by increasing exposure in stronger seasonal windows. The downside is that month effects are usually small and unstable, so this may just add noise or reduce CAGR by cutting exposure in a bull market.
review.data_missing: None. Month-of-year is derivable from existing timestamps, and the overlay can be tested on the same QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ price history already in the backtester.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is related in spirit to turn-of-month, but this is a different calendar effect and not previously rejected here.
review.overfit_note: Calendar seasonality is a classic data-snooping trap. If we search month-by-month or tune the month groups, we will almost certainly overfit 2018-2026 and fail out of sample. Even with a fixed schedule, the signal is weak and may not survive costs or regime changes.
review.expected_effect: Likely small at best. Best case: modest improvement in return/drawdown from slightly higher exposure in April/December and lower exposure in Feb-Mar, May-Jul, and September. More likely: no robust improvement once tested on 1999-2017, or a lower CAGR from simply running less risk in already-profitable periods.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact month map and do not search alternative month combinations. Backtest the unchanged Q desk versus the overlay variant with identical costs and fills. First evaluate on 2018-2026 (build); then freeze the rule and confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Compare annualized net return, Sharpe, and max drawdown. Require improvement in both periods, not just one, and do not accept any version that improves Sharpe by sacrificing too much CAGR or worsens max drawdown. Because the overlay only changes size, monthly turnover cost should be negligible; if the effect is not clearly positive in both samples, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully feasible with our existing data, and the rule can be fixed before looking at results. The edge is probably weak, but not obviously impossible, so a tightly pre-registered test is justified; just do not let it mutate into month-by-month optimization.

name: Regime-sliced validation and drawdown clustering
one_line: Backtest every candidate by regime slice, then monitor whether live paths resemble the worse drawdown cluster before allowing full size.
parameter_choices: Pre-register 2018-2026 and 1999-2017 splits; slice by volatility, trend, calendar, and event days; run 1000 bootstrap paths; disable a sleeve after sustained underperformance.
disagreement: None; this is a testing and monitoring method, not a trading rule.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: B2 is the closest support: it explicitly says 1000 Monte Carlo simulations produced two max-drawdown clusters. B1 supports the broader premise that returns are near white noise while volatility clusters, and B5/B11 warn about regime drift and broken assumptions. None of the sources actually proposes the specific live rule of "compare live path to the worse drawdown cluster before allowing full size," so that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to entries/exits. Add a hard sizing gate: pre-register regime slices using only data we already have (QQQ above/below its 200-day SMA and QQQ 20-day realized vol above/below its median), run 1000 bootstrap equity paths on 2018–2026 and confirm on 1999–2017, and do not promote a sleeve beyond shadow size unless it beats the current Q desk in both periods. In live paper trading, if a sleeve’s 20-day rolling PnL sits in the bad bootstrap drawdown cluster for 20 straight sessions, cut it to cash.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a risk-control overlay. It could stop us from running full size through a regime change where the strategy’s historical edge is weak, which is exactly when the trend sleeve whipsaws or gives back crash gains. It may lower max drawdown and reduce false confidence in a single good backtest, but it probably will not create new alpha by itself.
review.data_missing: True event-day labels (earnings, CPI/FOMC/news) are not in our current data. Volatility, trend, and calendar slices are feasible from existing bar data; event-day slicing would require an external calendar/feed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We already run shadow variants live, but this specific regime-sliced bootstrap gate and drawdown-cluster kill switch have not been tested as a formal rule.
review.overfit_note: Many degrees of freedom hide inside the slice definitions, bootstrap clustering, and the live disable rule. It is easy to tune the monitor until the past looks robust, then discover it just suppresses good regimes or delays size-up too long.
review.expected_effect: Best case: lower max drawdown and fewer bad full-size periods, especially for the trend sleeve. Likely downside: slower size-up and some CAGR drag if the gate is too conservative. This is a governance improvement, not a return stream.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the slice definitions before looking: build on 2018–2026, confirm on 1999–2017. For each sleeve, simulate the current Q desk versus the gated version with identical fills/costs. Primary metrics: net CAGR, Sharpe, and max drawdown; secondary: time spent at reduced size and number of false disables. Keep the gate only if both periods show lower max drawdown and better Sharpe, with no more than a small CAGR hit versus baseline; otherwise reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible and cheap, but it is a governance overlay rather than a source of alpha. The live cluster trigger is under-specified and can be tuned to death, so it should not compete with actual signal research time until we already have a candidate sleeve worth protecting.

name: Stationary preprocessing and bar hygiene
one_line: Convert raw OHLCV into clean stationary features before building regime signals: returns, differences, log volume, and bad-bar handling.
parameter_choices: Use log returns for price, first differences for nonstationary levels, optional seasonal differencing for weekly effects, log(volume), adjusted previous close for gap logic, and a cleaning rule set for zero-volume, zero-range, and missing bars; compare forward-fill vs drop vs flag.
disagreement: Whether these transforms materially improve out-of-sample regime detection or just add preprocessing complexity without real alpha.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients of the preprocessing layer: stationarity, first differencing/log returns, log(volume), adjusted prices, and dropping zero-volume/flat bars; they also show forward-fill as a generic cleaning step. But none of them demonstrate that this improves out-of-sample trading alpha or regime detection for our bot. The performance claim is mostly our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change the trading logic; add a fixed QC/preprocessing layer before computing the existing Q desk signals: use adjusted daily close for daily trend research, transform any price input used in diagnostics to log returns/differences, transform any volume input to log(volume), drop minute bars with Volume=0 or High=Low from indicator construction, and forward-fill at most one isolated missing minute bar (max_gap_ffill=1); if a longer gap exists, flag that timestamp and skip signal generation there.
review.mechanism: This can remove artifacts from corporate actions, stale prints, zero-trade minutes, and scale drift so the regime filter and intraday bands react less to junk. If it helps at all, it should be by slightly reducing false flips and unstable thresholds, not by creating a new edge.
review.data_missing: Nothing essential; OHLCV is enough for these hygiene rules. The only limitation is that without quotes/ticks we cannot distinguish a genuine no-trade minute from a bad bar except with heuristics.
review.already_tried_note: We have not explicitly listed this QC pipeline as a rejected idea, but the live/backtest stack almost certainly already uses cleaned data for the main QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ work. On this bot, it is likely baseline hygiene rather than a new sleeve or edge.
review.overfit_note: Very few fixed knobs if kept mechanical, but any apparent uplift may just be correcting sample-specific data quirks. If we start tuning gap thresholds or which bars to drop, it becomes data-massage rather than robust signal design.
review.expected_effect: Small at best. It may make the backtest cleaner and reduce a few spurious entries around bad bars or corporate-action artifacts, but it is unlikely to move net PnL meaningfully after costs.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on a smoke test, run a single A/B backtest only: baseline Q desk versus the same rules with this fixed QC layer, with no parameter tuning. Build on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017; for minute-level behavior also check 2007-2017. Compare net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and the number of bars affected by the cleaning. Require improvement in both periods and no drawdown increase; if the effect disappears out of sample or comes from only a handful of bad bars, do not promote it.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly data hygiene, not alpha. For our liquid QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ universe, cleaning obvious bad bars and using adjusted prices is sensible, but it is unlikely to change the bot’s edge enough to justify a strategy test slot. Forward-filling minute gaps is especially likely to introduce stale-price artifacts rather than improve performance.

name: Microstructure-noise benchmark
one_line: Before trusting a fast intraday edge, compare it against a short-horizon mean-reversion control net of costs to see whether the signal is just friction noise.
parameter_choices: Benchmark on 1-, 3-, and 5-minute returns using the same fill assumptions and round-trip cost model; judge by net expectancy and hit rate after costs.
disagreement: If the control matches or beats the signal after costs, the intraday sleeve is likely microstructure noise rather than robust momentum.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general microstructure premise—very short-horizon returns can be friction-driven and negatively autocorrelated—and it suggests comparing intraday returns to a mean-reversion control. It does not, however, validate this as a trading edge or as a standalone gate for our QQQ sleeve.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading-rule change; use the following pre-registered benchmark only: on QQQ 1-, 3-, and 5-minute bars, run a contrarian control under the same next-5-minute-open fill assumption and the same 0.02% round-trip cost, then compare its cost-adjusted expectancy and hit rate to the existing intraday sleeve.
review.mechanism: This is a sanity check against mistaking spread/impact noise for alpha. If the sleeve's apparent momentum is no better than a simple contrarian microstructure control, we should not allocate capital to it or should size it down.
review.data_missing: None for this benchmark; QQQ minute bars and the existing cost model are sufficient.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is not the same as the prior IWM/DIA noise-area test; this is a validation benchmark, not a new tradable sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Only a few discrete horizons, but the benchmark can still be cherry-picked after the fact and does not add much information beyond direct OOS sleeve backtests.
review.expected_effect: No direct PnL uplift. Best case: we avoid overtrusting a false intraday edge and can cut a weak sleeve. Worst case: it adds a placebo benchmark that doesn't change decisions.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the benchmark before looking at results. For each of the 1-, 3-, and 5-minute contrarian controls, enter using the same timing/fill conventions as the live intraday sleeve and apply the same 0.02% round-trip cost. Evaluate cost-adjusted expectancy per trade and per day, plus hit rate, on 2018–2026 and then on 1999–2017 (minute-data years only). Decision rule: keep the intraday sleeve only if it beats the best benchmark in both periods; otherwise set the intraday sleeve weight to zero. Do not retune horizons or thresholds after seeing results.
review.verdict_reason: Useful as a reporting sanity check, but not a standalone bot improvement. It does not create a tradable edge, and the conclusion is mostly redundant with the existing cost-adjusted OOS backtests. If we want this information, fold it into standard research reports rather than spending a separate test on it.

name: Long-horizon mean-reversion sleeve
one_line: Add a separate slower QQQ mean-reversion sleeve that trades deviations from trend on a longer horizon, distinct from the intraday momentum desk.
parameter_choices: Define stretch by distance from a long MA, z-score of deviation, or overextension after a trend regime; test holding periods of days to weeks and only run when the trend sleeve is flat or underweight.
disagreement: Whether a second-horizon mean-reversion sleeve adds independent edge or just fights the existing trend logic.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B1 supports the broad claim that short-term trend and longer-horizon mean reversion can coexist; B8 adds a generic post-shock rebound anecdote. Neither source gives a concrete QQQ trading rule, so this is our adaptation, not a directly supported setup.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a third sleeve that uses the currently idle trend bucket: if QQQ closes 5% or more below its 200-day SMA, buy QQQ at the next open with that bucket; exit on the first close back above the 20-day SMA or after 10 trading days.
review.mechanism: If there is a real post-selloff rebound effect on QQQ, this can monetize it on a slower horizon than the intraday desk and turn some cash periods into return-generating periods. The logic only makes sense if it is treated as a capital carve-out, not extra leverage; otherwise it just fights the trend sleeve and crowds the intraday desk.
review.data_missing: None; daily QQQ OHLCV is enough.
review.already_tried_note: We already have a known QQQ mean-reversion edge via RSI(2) dip buying, which is a nearby family. This is a slower, deeper-drawdown variant, so it is not identical, but it is not a wholly new idea either.
review.overfit_note: This family has obvious knobs if we start tuning it: deviation threshold, lookback anchor, exit rule, and capital carve-out. It is easy to make 2018-2026 look good and then discover it is just buying falling knives in 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: At best a small extra return stream during sharp rebound periods; more likely it adds drawdown and capital crowding in the same weak regimes that already hurt the trend sleeve.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule exactly as written, with no threshold/exit search beyond the fixed 5% and 10-day settings. Test it as a capital carve-out, not as leverage on top of the current Q desk: when the swing sleeve is open, it must use only the idle trend bucket and not increase gross exposure. Backtest the combined Q desk on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on 1999-2017. Compare net daily CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and turnover versus the current Q desk. Also check the standalone sleeve so we can see whether any gain is just a transfer from the existing trend/intraday sleeves. If there are fewer than about 20 total entries across the full history, treat it as too sparse to trust.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully testable from existing daily QQQ data, costs are low, and the implementation is concrete. The edge is weakly supported and likely modest, but this is still cheap enough to backtest under a strict pre-registered capital-allocation rule rather than guess about it.

name: Latent factor regime model
one_line: Compress OHLCV and market proxies into a few latent factors with reduced-rank regression or PCA to create a compact regime state.
parameter_choices: Use a rolling window, choose rank r / number of PCs, and compare hand-built regime scores versus low-rank state vectors built from returns, range, volume, and market proxies such as VIX.
disagreement: Whether a learned low-rank regime state is more stable and useful than a hand-crafted filter built from a few obvious indicators.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports reduced-rank regression and PCA as dimensionality-reduction tools, but it does not show that a latent factor state improves trading regime timing. The trading use here is our extrapolation from the math, not something the book demonstrates.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the trend sleeve’s 200-day SMA gate with a rolling 252-trading-day rank-1 reduced-rank regression on standardized daily QQQ features [1-day return, 20-day realized volatility, 20-day high-low range, 20-day relative volume, VIX level]. If the model’s fitted next-day QQQ return is > 0, keep the existing 50% TQQQ trend sleeve on; otherwise move that sleeve to cash. Do not change the intraday sleeve.
review.mechanism: If it works, this would compress several noisy regime clues into one smoother risk-on/risk-off score, which could cut some whipsaws around the current 200-day gate and maybe exit faster when the market shifts into a noisy/high-vol state. The catch is that PCA/RRR does not create new information; it only repackages the same price/volatility data, so any benefit would have to come from better smoothing and state estimation, not a new edge.
review.data_missing: None for the daily version; we already have daily OHLCV and can add VIX for free. A minute-level latent-state version would be harder because we do not have full minute history for all names back to 1999, but this proposal does not need minute data.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact model. We have already used hand-built regime logic in the current Q desk and have rejected several other ETF timing ideas, but we have not directly tested a rolling latent-factor gate like this.
review.overfit_note: There are many hidden degrees of freedom even if we freeze the headline knobs: feature choice, normalization, window length, rank, and how the factor score maps to on/off exposure. PCA/RRR can fit sample-specific covariance structure very well and then fail when the regime changes across 1999-2017 vs 2018-2026.
review.expected_effect: At best, a modest reduction in false trend signals and a small crash-giveback improvement; more likely it ends up close to the current filter after costs, or looks good only in one subperiod. It is unlikely to add a new uncorrelated return stream.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one model before looking at results: daily 252-day rolling rank-1 reduced-rank regression gate on the fixed QQQ/VIX feature set above. Keep the rest of the Q desk unchanged. Compare against the current 200-day SMA trend gate on net CAGR/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover after costs. Evaluate 2018-2026 and 1999-2017 separately, then the full sample. Only consider it viable if it beats the current trend gate in both subperiods on net CAGR and does not worsen max drawdown materially; if it improves one era but not the other, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, but too generic and too easy to overfit to be worth immediate attention. The latent factor is just a rotated view of the same inputs, so it is unlikely to outperform a simpler hand-built regime score unless it shows a clean out-of-sample gain in both eras. I would not spend test budget on a broader PCA/RRR sweep until a simpler fixed regime filter benchmark has been run.

name: Volume-conditioned swing sleeves
one_line: Only take swing entries in favorable return/volume bins or after price+volume overreaction conditions, so participation helps filter the setup.
parameter_choices: Test weekly return bins around 2% and volume-growth bins around 15% / 50%, plus a separate abnormal-volume threshold for price-filtered entries; keep the universe to liquid ETFs or stocks that fit a cash account.
disagreement: Whether volume confirmation is true signal or just an overfit confirmation filter.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: B1-c023-05 gives the exact 2% weekly-return and 15%/50% volume-growth binning and says these states can be used as portfolio filters. That supports the machinery, not the claim that a QQQ/TQQQ swing sleeve will have edge. B1-c046-04 is only a bibliography citation on price+volume overreaction.
review.exact_rule_change: New standalone weekly ETF sleeve: every Friday 15:55, compute QQQ's trailing 5-trading-day non-market-adjusted return and trailing 5-trading-day volume growth (current 5-day volume divided by prior 5-day volume, minus 1). If return is in the +2% winner bin and volume growth is between +15% and +50%, buy TQQQ at the next open and hold until the next Friday close; otherwise stay in cash. No short leg.
review.mechanism: It is trying to keep only weeks where participation confirms the move, so it may skip thin, noisy rallies and improve hit rate on directional swing trades.
review.data_missing: None. Daily OHLCV is enough to compute weekly return and weekly volume growth; no news, order book, options, or fundamentals needed.
review.already_tried_note: Conceptually close to the already-rejected overnight/multi-day momentum family. The volume gate is new, but the underlying bet is still 'hold after recent strength' rather than a fresh edge.
review.overfit_note: Multiple discretionary choices are hidden inside the filter: bin width, volume band, universe, direction, and holding period. On ETFs the weekly sample is modest, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: At best a small hit-rate improvement on a narrow subset of weeks; more likely flat after costs, with fewer trades and a fragile edge.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on a test, pre-register one version only: QQQ signal, long TQQQ only, Friday-to-Friday hold, +2% return bin, +15% to +50% volume band, no other tuning. Compare to the same 5-day swing without the volume filter and to cash/current Q desk. Success requires higher net CAGR, Sharpe, and MAR in both 2018-2026 and 1999-2017, with no worse max drawdown and at least ~150 trades; otherwise kill it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic confirmation filter, not a proven edge. The source only justifies the binning scheme, while the predictive claim is our extrapolation. It also sits very close to the already-rejected multi-day/overnight momentum family and is likely too sparse and tunable to survive the 2018-2026 / 1999-2017 split.

name: Age cap on trend positions
one_line: Reduce or exit trend positions once the signal gets too old, before late-cycle reversal risk rises.
parameter_choices: Set a maximum signal age in trading days, with either a hard exit or staged de-risking; test short, medium, and long age caps separately on the trend sleeve.
disagreement: Whether a signal-age cap improves realized trend capture more than it sacrifices from late-stage winners.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general premise that momentum tends to last about a year and then reverse. It does not specifically recommend an age cap on this QQQ/TQQQ trend sleeve, so the exact rule is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard age cap to the existing trend sleeve only: start counting regime age on the first day QQQ closes back above its 200-day SMA after being below it. Hold the 50% overnight TQQQ trend allocation only while that regime age is <=252 trading days. On the first day age >252, liquidate the trend sleeve to cash at the next 5-minute open, and do not re-enter until QQQ has first closed below its 200-day SMA and later closes back above it again. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could cut off stale trend exposure before the late-cycle reversal zone, which may reduce give-back in long bull runs and some crash tails. The downside is obvious: many of the best multi-month or multi-year Nasdaq trends last longer than a year, so the cap may simply amputate the right tail of returns.
review.data_missing: None for this rule. We can compute regime age from QQQ daily closes and backtest it with the same existing synthetic/real 3x ETF framework already used for the trend sleeve.
review.already_tried_note: The underlying 200-day trend sleeve is already live/backtested, but this exact age-cap overlay is not on the rejected list and has not been tested as such.
review.overfit_note: One free knob, but the 252-day cutoff is arbitrary and very easy to tune to 2018-2026. If you start sweeping short/medium/long caps or staged de-risking variants, the family becomes a multiple-comparison trap.
review.expected_effect: Likely small and uncertain. It may modestly reduce drawdown or late-stage give-back, but it is at least as likely to lower net return by exiting strong trends too early.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one candidate: the 252-trading-day hard cap. Backtest the full Q desk with only this change, keeping execution, costs, and every other rule identical. Compare baseline vs modified bot separately on 2018-2026 and 1999-2017 using net CAGR as the primary metric, with max drawdown and Sharpe as secondary checks. Accept only if net CAGR improves in both periods; if the cap only reduces drawdown while hurting return in either period, reject. Do not sweep alternate caps unless you are counting that as a separate experiment.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and directly tied to a real empirical claim about momentum aging. The edge is probably small and may be negative, but it is worth one locked test rather than a parameter sweep.

name: Sentiment/fear regime overlay
one_line: Use a slow public sentiment proxy such as VIX or a FEARS-style search index to size down risk-on exposure in fearful or low-sentiment regimes.
parameter_choices: Test simple percentile buckets, positive/negative regime splits, and lagged smoothed versions such as a 12-month PCA-style index or a daily FEARS proxy.
disagreement: Whether public sentiment measures are too lagged or noisy to help tactical sizing.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the broad premise that sentiment regimes matter (Baker-Wurgler buckets, FEARS, and different technical performance in high vs low sentiment). They do not give a direct rule for TQQQ/SQQQ or for VIX-based sizing, so using VIX as the live proxy is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a slow regime throttle: compute the trailing 252-trading-day percentile rank of VIX using only information known as of yesterday's close. If yesterday's VIX percentile is above 75%, scale both Q desk sleeves to 50% of their normal target size for the next session; otherwise leave sizing unchanged. Do not change the existing entry/exit rules.
review.mechanism: High VIX is a cheap proxy for fear/instability. In those regimes the leveraged ETF sleeves are more likely to get chopped around or give back gains, so cutting size should reduce the worst left-tail days and some whipsaw. The downside is that it can also cut exposure during strong crash-trend days, so the likely benefit is lower drawdown, not higher raw return.
review.data_missing: No missing data if we use daily VIX, which can be added for free. The FEARS/Google Trends version is not available in the current dataset and would require a new feed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest existing filters are price-based (200-day SMA) and the shadow desks; no sentiment/fear overlay has been tested.
review.overfit_note: If we keep it to one VIX percentile cutoff and one downsize factor, the knob count is small. But the whole idea is still a proxy choice plus a threshold, so it is easy to fit stories after the fact if we start trying many sentiment variants.
review.expected_effect: Best case: modestly lower max drawdown and fewer whipsaw losses, with a possible Sharpe/Calmar lift. Base case: little change. Worst case: lower CAGR because the throttle cuts good high-volatility trend days.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one version only: 252-day VIX percentile, threshold 75%, size factor 0.50, applied from the next session using only prior-close VIX. Backtest current Q desk vs throttled Q desk on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for any minute-level implementation details). Success requires improvement in both periods on net return and a drawdown-adjusted metric such as Sharpe or Calmar, with no material increase in max drawdown. Also run a control that uses the same 75% threshold on 21-day realized QQQ volatility; if VIX does not beat that control, treat the effect as plain volatility targeting rather than sentiment.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with data we can add for free, cheap to test, and at least directionally tied to known regime effects. But the expected edge is small and may just be a volatility throttle in disguise; kill it if it only helps one period or if a simpler realized-vol control matches it.

name: Oscillator-confirmed band and reversal entries
one_line: Require Williams %R or RSI divergence to confirm band breaks or reversal setups instead of trading the raw trigger alone.
parameter_choices: Try Williams %R thresholds around 20/80, RSI divergence confirmation, or both; test confirmation only on the band side that matches the setup direction.
disagreement: Whether oscillator confirmation improves precision enough to justify the delayed entries and missed early moves.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The books support the ingredients, not the exact Q-desk rule. One source gives explicit Williams %R overbought/oversold thresholds; the other says RSI divergence can help confirm turning points and should not be used alone. Neither source tests oscillator-gated intraday band breaks on leveraged ETF momentum entries, so this is an adaptation, not a near-identical published rule. The RSI-divergence version is especially under-specified.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily Williams %R(10) gate to the intraday QQQ band sleeve only: at each 30-minute check, take an upper-band long in TQQQ only if QQQ’s Williams %R on the last 10 completed daily bars is <20; take a lower-band short in SQQQ only if Williams %R is >80. Otherwise skip the trade. Keep all other entry/exit rules unchanged. Do not include RSI divergence in the first test.
review.mechanism: This could reduce false band breaks in choppy tape by requiring the daily oscillator to agree with the intraday signal, so we only trade when the market already has directional pressure. That may lift hit rate and cut some whipsaws. The downside is obvious: it will also block some good early moves, so the main risk is lower total capture rather than a cleaner edge.
review.data_missing: None for the Williams %R version; daily OHLC is enough. The RSI-divergence version would need an explicit swing-high/swing-low definition and lookback rules, which are not supplied, so I would not test that first.
