review.already_tried_note: No direct test of oscillator-gated band entries on the current Q desk. The rejected ideas list covers ORB/gap/overnight/last-half-hour etc., not this kind of daily oscillator filter on the intraday sleeve.
review.overfit_note: If you keep it to a fixed Williams %R(10) gate with the source thresholds, there is only one real knob and the overfit risk is manageable. But the likely edge is small and regime-dependent, so it is easy to convince yourself on 2018-2026 and lose it out of sample. The RSI-divergence variant would push this toward high overfit risk, so don’t bundle it in.
review.expected_effect: Most likely: fewer trades, somewhat higher win rate, and flat-to-worse net return once missed moves are counted. Best case is a modest reduction in chop-year losses. I would not expect this to fix the trend-sleeve crash give-back or create a new return stream; it is just a precision filter.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: Williams %R(10) on completed daily QQQ bars, gated at <20 for upper-band longs and >80 for lower-band shorts. Compare the gated intraday sleeve against the current raw band sleeve on identical costs, fills, and one-round-trip-per-day constraints. First run on 2018-2026; then confirm on the unseen 2007-2017 minute backfill/synthetic-3x version. Success requires improvement in both periods in net profit per day and Sharpe, with max drawdown no worse in either period; also watch trade count, and reject if the filter cuts trades by >30% without a clear expectancy gain. Do not tune thresholds after seeing the test.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, data-feasible, and mechanically compatible with the current bot. The support is weak-to-partial, but the parameter count is low enough that the test is worth running. The RSI-divergence idea is too vague to bundle, but the fixed Williams %R gate is concrete enough to try once.

name: Single-active-trade concurrency cap
one_line: Allow only one open trade at a time when testing alternative exits or swing ideas, to keep cash management and attribution clean.
parameter_choices: Set len(open_trades)==0 for all non-core entries, or test a per-sleeve cap versus a global cap.
disagreement: Whether overlapping positions add enough return to justify the extra complexity and cash-lockup risk.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The cited book explicitly gates entries with `len(self.trades)==0`, which is the same single-open-trade concurrency rule. That is direct support for the rule itself, but only as a coding pattern, not as evidence that it improves returns.
review.exact_rule_change: For any non-core/experimental sleeve, set `max_open_experimental_trades = 1` and block a new experimental entry whenever `open_experimental_trades > 0`; do not apply this gate to the existing core trend/intraday sleeves.
review.mechanism: This would keep cash usage and T+1 settlement from being tangled across simultaneous trial trades, so you can attribute P&L to one idea at a time and avoid accidental overexposure from overlapping experiments. It does not create alpha; it likely lowers capital efficiency and can reduce total return if the signals are actually complementary.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not as a formal global cap. But the live intraday sleeve already has one-round-trip-per-day logic and the core bot already manages two sleeves against the same small cash account, so the operational problem is familiar.
review.overfit_note: Very few knobs. The main risk is not curve-fitting the cap itself; it's using the cap to mask whether the underlying candidate really has edge.
review.expected_effect: As a research control: cleaner attribution and fewer settlement/cash conflicts. As a live rule: probably slightly worse net return from reduced concurrency, with at best a small drawdown reduction.
review.test_protocol: Do not test this as a standalone alpha. Use it only as an A/B research control on any future swing sleeve: backtest the same candidate with cap=1 vs cap=∞ on 2018–2026, then confirm on 1999–2017. Keep the cap only if it improves OOS net CAGR and Sharpe in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown or cut trade count to noise. Otherwise leave it in the research harness only.
review.verdict_reason: This is a bookkeeping constraint, not a source of edge. It does not address the Q desk's whipsaws or flat intraday years, and applied live it would fight the intended two-sleeve capital allocation. Useful for research hygiene, not as a bot rule.

name: Sector relative-strength alignment
one_line: Only allow longs when the stock or ETF’s sector is strong on both weekly and monthly relative-strength views.
parameter_choices: Require the sector ETF to be in the top half on both 1-week and 1-month returns, or require the market and sector both to be above their chosen trend filters.
disagreement: Whether sector alignment matters beyond the underlying chart, especially for liquid ETF and stock swing setups.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The quoted book excerpts explicitly recommend aligning trades with market/sector direction and checking whether a sector is aligned on the 1-week and 1-month views. That is the same trading logic as this idea, just turned into a quant rule. The source is still practitioner opinion, not statistical evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change the current QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ desk. If we later add a separate long stock/ETF swing sleeve, only allow a long when its sector ETF is in the top half of the 11 GICS sector ETFs on both trailing 5-trading-day and trailing 21-trading-day returns; otherwise skip the long.
review.mechanism: In a diversified stock-swing universe, this is a leadership filter: it tries to avoid buying names whose sector is still weak on both weekly and monthly horizons, which can reduce false breakouts and improve follow-through. On the current QQQ-only bot, though, the information is mostly redundant with the existing market-trend filter and may mainly reduce trade count or delay entries.
review.data_missing: We can compute the 5d/21d return ranks for sector ETFs from daily OHLCV, but the brief does not give us a ticker-to-sector classification for the general stock universe. So this is testable for a sector-ETF proxy or a manually curated ETF sleeve, but not cleanly for all stocks without adding sector metadata. On the current QQQ-only desk, the concept is also ambiguous because QQQ spans many sectors rather than one sector.
review.already_tried_note: No direct sector-alignment filter has been rejected already, but this is close to the failed relative-strength/momentum family: 12-1 cross-sectional momentum already failed on 1999-2017. For the current desk, the existing 200-day QQQ trend filter already captures much of the same broad-market information.
review.overfit_note: The rule looks simple, but it is easy to tune the sector universe, the proxy mapping, and the lookbacks until 2018-2026 looks good. The edge is likely weak and regime-dependent, and on a QQQ-only bot the filter is probably just a lagged version of the existing trend rule.
review.expected_effect: Small at best. It may help a future stock-swing sleeve by avoiding weak sectors and improving hit rate, but on the current QQQ/TQQQ desk I expect little incremental benefit because sector strength is largely embedded in the instrument already.
review.test_protocol: Do not test this on the live QQQ-only desk. If we revisit it as a separate stock-swing sleeve, pre-register one rule only: use the 11 GICS sector ETFs, fixed before analysis, and require the candidate’s sector ETF to rank in the top half on both trailing 5-day and 21-day returns; otherwise no long. Compare that sleeve to the identical sleeve without the sector filter on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on 1999-2017. Accept only if net CAGR, Sharpe, and max drawdown all improve in both periods, with no large drop in trade count or average holding period.
review.verdict_reason: This is a reasonable textbook filter for a future stock-swing sleeve, but it is not a good test for the current QQQ-only bot. The filter is mostly redundant with the existing market trend gate, the source is only opinion, and the likely edge is too small and too easy to overfit to the 2018-2026 tech regime. Save testing for a separate stock universe with sector labels.

name: Binary event-risk avoidance for swing sleeves
one_line: Skip or flatten around scheduled earnings or other binary company events instead of treating them as ordinary calendar days.
parameter_choices: avoid holding through earnings; optionally block trades within X days of scheduled binary news; use a simple event calendar cutoff
disagreement: Some traders think the lost upside from skipping event days outweighs the gap-risk reduction.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The quoted passages explicitly recommend avoiding holdings through earnings reports and other major pending company announcements. That is essentially the proposed filter; the only adaptation is making it mechanical and calendar-based. The support is practitioner advice, not empirical evidence, and it applies to single-name swing trades rather than the current ETF-only Q desk.
review.exact_rule_change: Not a Q-desk tweak; this is only for a future single-name stock swing sleeve. Default rule: if a position’s next scheduled binary company event is within 1 trading day, do not open the trade, and if already in the position, flatten at the close of the last trading day before the event. Start with earnings only; do not add other event types until we have a reliable event calendar.
review.mechanism: The point is to avoid discontinuous overnight gaps from company-specific news. Those gaps can dominate the normal edge of a swing trade and create the rare large loss that matters most in a small cash account. It could lower tail risk and drawdown for a stock-swing sleeve, but it also removes some positive gap captures and reduces trade count. For the current QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ ETF desk, the benefit is minimal because we do not trade individual names.
review.data_missing: We do not have a historical earnings/news event calendar with announcement dates and, ideally, before/after-close timestamps for candidate names. Price bars alone are not enough to know ex ante which days are binary event days, so the filter cannot be backtested cleanly with the current data.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected news/catalyst gap swing ideas, which live in the same event universe. But a pure defensive 'avoid the event' filter has not been separately tested. Even so, it is outside the current ETF-only bot.
review.overfit_note: Binary events are sparse and heterogeneous, and the cutoff can be tuned many ways (0/1/2/3 days, earnings only vs. all events). It is easy to fit away a few disastrous names or windows in 2018-2026 and then fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: If we had a stock swing sleeve, this would likely reduce the worst overnight gap losses and max drawdown, but it would also cut exposure and probably some winning trades. Net expectancy is uncertain. On the current ETF-only Q desk, I expect little to no benefit.
review.test_protocol: Only test after sourcing a real event calendar. Fix the cutoff at 1 trading day before the event before looking at results. Backtest a liquid single-name swing sleeve with the filter versus the identical sleeve without it on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017. Compare net CAGR after costs, max drawdown, average overnight gap P&L, and trade count. Require improvement in both periods and no severe drop in trade frequency; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: We cannot backtest this properly with the data we currently have, because the needed earnings/news calendar is missing. It also does not help the existing ETF-only Q desk in any direct way, so testing it now would be a waste of time.

name: Breadth-based market regime filter
one_line: Use market breadth to decide when the Nasdaq tape is healthy enough for risk-on exposure.
parameter_choices: % advancing vs declining, % new highs vs new lows, % above 50-day and 200-day SMAs; thresholds can gate size or turn sleeves off
disagreement: Breadth may be useful as a slow macro filter, but it can also lag price and add complexity.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly recommends using breadth metrics to judge whether the market is trending or churning, so the general regime-filter idea is supported. But it is opinion-only, not a measured claim, and it does not establish that a breadth gate will improve our specific Q desk.
review.exact_rule_change: At 15:55 NY each day, compute the percentage of names in our existing prior-day $5M+ dollar-volume US universe that closed above their 50-day SMA; if that breadth measure is below 50%, keep the trend sleeve in cash for the next session, otherwise run the current trend sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: Breadth should help identify when the uptrend is narrow and fragile, which is exactly when the QQQ 200-day trend sleeve tends to whipsaw or give back gains in selloffs. A daily breadth gate could therefore reduce bad overnight trend exposure in weak regimes without changing the intraday sleeve or transaction costs.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed daily rule. We can compute breadth from the daily OHLCV database we already have; no news, fundamentals, options, or L2 data are needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest thing we have tested is generic regime logic, but breadth itself and this exact breadth gate have not been tried.
review.overfit_note: The idea invites a knob farm if we start mixing 50-day vs 200-day breadth, new highs/lows, and different universes. If we freeze one metric and one threshold pre-test, the risk is manageable; if not, it will almost certainly overfit 2018-2026 and disappoint 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: If it works, expect a modest reduction in trend-sleeve whipsaws and some crash avoidance. The likely downside is missing early recovery legs, because breadth lags price and is partly redundant with the existing 200-day trend filter. Net edge is plausible but probably small.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one breadth definition only: % of names above their 50-day SMA in the prior-day $5M+ dollar-volume universe, threshold 50%. Backtest the current Q desk versus the breadth-gated version on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Use the same cost model. Compare net CAGR/daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trend-sleeve turnover/whipsaw count. Accept only if both windows improve net return and do not worsen drawdown; if the gate merely reduces risk while giving up too much return, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with data we already have, cheap to backtest, and directly aimed at the known trend-sleeve weakness. The evidence is weak, so we should not search across many breadth variants, but the single pre-registered version is worth one test because it could reduce whipsaws without adding execution cost.

name: Liquid momentum scan for future stock sleeves
one_line: Only consider stocks or ETFs that are liquid, already rising, and showing fresh early-day attention before adding any non-core swing sleeve.
parameter_choices: minimum average daily volume, positive relative strength, active/rising price, premarket 7-8am news/toplists where available
disagreement: A tight liquidity-and-momentum screen may improve hit rate, but it can also miss early turns and reduce trade count too much.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the generic screen logic: prefer liquid names, already-rising names, and premarket news/toplists. They do not provide a tested combined rule, a quantified threshold beyond the 200k ADV preference, or evidence that this filter adds edge in our setup.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the current Q desk. If we later add a separate stock/ETF swing sleeve, only allow candidates that meet two pre-entry gates: 20-day average daily volume >= 200,000 shares, and a positive 20-day return vs SPY with premarket volume >= 2x its 20-day median as the proxy for the "7-8am attention" idea (we do not have news/toplist data).
review.mechanism: The only plausible benefit is inside a future stock sleeve: liquid names should cut spread/impact noise, and names that are already strong and drawing early attention may have better follow-through. It does not address the current QQQ sleeves' whipsaws or crash give-back, and it does nothing by itself without a full entry/exit strategy.
review.data_missing: We do not have news feeds or toplists, so the exact 7-8am attention condition cannot be tested directly. We can only proxy it with premarket OHLCV/volume summaries; that is not the same signal.
review.already_tried_note: This sits right on top of already-rejected families: stocks-in-play ORB, gap-and-go, and news/catalyst gap swings. The screen is only a candidate filter for those kinds of trades, not a new edge on its own.
review.overfit_note: Several discretionary thresholds on a huge cross-section make it easy to mine a filter that looks good in 2018-2026 and then dies out of sample. With a $1k cash account, the tighter screen also risks leaving too few trades to matter.
review.expected_effect: At best, modestly better fill quality and maybe a higher hit rate in a future stock sleeve. More likely, the screen just reduces trade count and adds no edge to the current bot.
review.test_protocol: Do not test this standalone on the current Q desk. If we later build a complete stock/ETF swing strategy, pre-register this screen and run an ablation: same entry/exit rules with and without the screen on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017. Judge on after-cost expectancy, Sharpe, drawdown, and trade count; require improvement in both periods and no collapse in sample size before accepting it.
review.verdict_reason: This is only a universe filter, not a tradeable strategy. The exact attention component needs data we do not have, and the strategy families it points to were already rejected. For Midas now, it is too indirect to justify tests.

name: Market quality and chop filter
one_line: Stand down or size down when the tape is choppy, low-quality, or clearly out of flow.
parameter_choices: trend-efficiency or ADX-like chop measure, repeated band failures, market-on/off indicator, downtrend confirmation, minimum swing significance
disagreement: The main debate is whether low activity is just low volatility or a distinct no-trade regime.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The books all argue for the general principle of avoiding choppy / low-quality / out-of-flow conditions and using market-on/off style filters, but none gives a tested chop metric or threshold. The ADX gate is our own translation of that advice, not a source-stated rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a session-level market-quality gate to the intraday sleeve only: compute QQQ ADX(14) from daily OHLC using yesterday's close; if ADX(14) < 20, skip all intraday QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ trades for the next session. Otherwise run the existing intraday rules unchanged. No change to the 200-day trend sleeve. One parameter: ADX threshold = 20.
review.mechanism: When QQQ is in a low-ADX regime, the intraday band-break system is more likely to get chopped up by false starts and pay spread/impact for nothing. A simple stand-down gate should reduce whipsaws, lower losing-day frequency, and maybe improve drawdowns, while leaving the trend sleeve untouched.
review.data_missing: None; daily OHLCV plus the existing QQQ minute data are enough to compute the gate and test it.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule, but it is adjacent to the already-tested noise-area / band logic and to the rejected IWM/DIA noise-area variant. So the concept is not novel, just the specific QQQ daily ADX gate.
review.overfit_note: There are many interchangeable chop definitions and thresholds (ADX, efficiency ratio, ATR compression, band-failure counts, lookback length). It would be easy to tune a gate that looks good on 2018-2026 and then disappears out of sample, especially since the base intraday sleeve already has its own band-based adaptation.
review.expected_effect: At best, a modest improvement in the intraday sleeve: fewer trades, fewer whipsaws, and possibly better drawdown behavior. The downside is that it will also skip some good low-ADX trend starts, so the net effect is uncertain and probably small.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one variant: QQQ ADX(14) < 20 on yesterday's daily bar disables today's intraday sleeve; otherwise no change. Compare modified Q desk vs current Q desk on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and sanity-check 2007-2017 for the minute-bar execution path). Primary metric: full-bot net CAGR/day after costs. Secondary metrics: Sharpe, max drawdown, intraday sleeve profit factor, and trade count. Accept only if the modified version improves net CAGR/day in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; if CAGR improves but drawdown worsens, require MAR to improve too. No threshold tuning after looking at results.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and directly aimed at the bot's whipsaw problem. The evidence is weak and overfit risk is high, but this is still simple enough to justify one preregistered test rather than dismissing it outright.

name: RSI extreme timing overlay
one_line: Treat RSI extremes as a timing filter for entries and exits, especially when paired with support or pullback context.
parameter_choices: RSI(2) or RSI(14); thresholds around 70/30 or 80/20; optionally require support, pullback, or overbought-avoidance context
disagreement: RSI can help time entries, but some traders see it as only a warning label rather than a usable trigger.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: Both sources say RSI extremes (roughly 20/80 or 30/70) are noteworthy and map to oversold/overbought conditions, so they support using RSI as a timing filter in a broad sense. Neither source gives evidence that an RSI overlay improves an existing trend or breakout system, and the support/pullback part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily RSI(2) gate to the trend sleeve: if QQQ is above its 200-day SMA and daily RSI(2) <= 20, hold the existing 50% TQQQ overnight sleeve; otherwise keep that sleeve in cash.
review.mechanism: Best case, this buys the uptrend only after a short-term pullback, which could reduce chasing and some whipsaws. But RSI is lagging, so it is unlikely to improve crash exits, and it will probably just suppress exposure to many of the strongest trend days.
review.data_missing: None for the RSI calculation itself; the vague 'support/pullback context' would need a formal price-rule proxy, which adds knobs rather than data.
review.already_tried_note: A very close cousin — RSI(2) dip buying on QQQ — is already one of our known small, robust edges. This exact overlay on the Q desk has not been tested, but it is not a fresh hypothesis.
review.overfit_note: RSI length, long/short thresholds, and any added support/pullback proxy are all easy curve-fit knobs. The signal is also a transformed version of the same price series we already trade, so it can easily look good in 2018-2026 and fade out-of-sample.
review.expected_effect: Likely small to negative after costs: it may slightly reduce chase entries, but it will probably miss a lot of good trend exposure and is unlikely to fix crash give-back or the weak intraday years.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register RSI(2)=20 as the only threshold. Compare the current Q desk versus the same desk with the RSI gate on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017. Success requires improvement in net daily return and Sharpe in both periods, with no material worsening of max drawdown or turnover. If the out-of-sample lift is tiny, unstable, or only appears in the in-sample period, discard.
review.verdict_reason: The source support is only generic RSI lore, not evidence for an overlay on this bot. The only clean backtestable version is basically a QQQ RSI(2) dip-buying rule, and we already know that edge exists. As an overlay, it is more likely to reduce useful trend exposure than to meaningfully improve whipsaws or crash exits.

name: Stable lead-lag ensemble
one_line: Use multiple lead instruments, but keep only the ones whose relationship to QQQ stays stable instead of flipping sign.
parameter_choices: rolling correlation window, minimum absolute correlation, zero-crossing count, and a small ensemble of lead instruments
disagreement: One stable lead may be cleaner, while multiple leads may be more robust across regime shifts.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general principle that sign-flipping correlations are unstable and that multiple lead instruments can help when one relationship breaks down. It does not specifically validate a QQQ ETF lead-lag ensemble or any numeric cutoff, so this is still an adaptation rather than a directly sourced rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the intraday noise-area sleeve to require broad-market confirmation: at each 30-minute check, compute 60-trading-day rolling correlations between QQQ’s forward 30-minute return and SPY/IWM/DIA 30-minute returns. Keep only ETFs with |ρ| >= 0.15 and no zero-crossing of ρ in the lookback window; average the surviving signals. Take the existing TQQQ/SQQQ trade only if at least 2 of the 3 surviving ETFs agree with the QQQ direction; otherwise stay in cash.
review.mechanism: This is a breadth-confirmation filter. If QQQ’s move is echoed by several stable, liquid ETF proxies, the move is less likely to be pure noise, so you should take fewer false entries and slightly better-timed trades. When the proxy relationships are unstable, you skip the trade instead of forcing one.
review.data_missing: Minute bars for candidate lead ETFs before 2007 (and for most non-SPY/QQQ/IWM/DIA ETFs before 2018) are missing, so a full 1999-2017 minute-level confirmation is not available. We can test the rule on SPY/IWM/DIA/QQQ from 2007-2026, but not the full requested minute-history span. No news/fundamentals/options data are needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not explicitly tested as a stable-lead ensemble, but it is close to the rejected IWM/DIA noise-area / broad-ETF intraday family. That prior failure is a warning that broad-market ETF tricks may not add much.
review.overfit_note: Several hidden degrees of freedom remain even after freezing the defaults: lead universe, lag horizon, correlation window, stability cutoff, and ensemble-vote threshold. Correlation/lead-lag edges at 30-minute horizons are notoriously regime-dependent, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and lose it out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly fewer intraday trades, a modest lift in hit rate/Sharpe, and lower day-to-day noise. Base case: flat after costs. Bad case: it suppresses valid QQQ-only moves and does nothing because broad ETFs mostly move contemporaneously with QQQ.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register SPY/IWM/DIA only, 60-day window, 0.15 absolute-correlation cutoff, zero sign flips, and a 2-of-3 majority vote. Backtest the current Q desk versus the same desk with this gate applied only to the intraday sleeve. Build on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 minute data. Primary metrics: net daily return after stated costs and Sharpe; secondary: max drawdown, trade count, and win rate. Require improvement in both periods; do not tune the universe or thresholds after looking.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap to rule in or out with data we already have, the rule can be kept small, and it could plausibly improve the intraday sleeve. But the expected edge is modest at best; if it does not beat the baseline in both 2018-2026 and 2007-2017, kill it immediately.

name: Stress-day inverse aggressiveness
one_line: When downside volatility is extreme, consider making the inverse sleeve more aggressive instead of only de-risking.
parameter_choices: realized-volatility percentile, downside breadth threshold, and a larger SQQQ/TQQQ inverse size on stress days
disagreement: Some will prefer always cutting risk in high-volatility regimes; others will want to press the inverse edge harder.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The quote only supports a broad observation: large-cap/index names can sell off faster during volatility. It does not state that inverse ETF sizing should be increased on stress days, so the trading rule is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a stress override to the existing intraday sleeve: if QQQ’s 14-day percentile rank of 30-minute realized volatility is at least 90% and the prior session’s breadth proxy is negative, then any intraday short signal uses 100% of sleeve capital in SQQQ instead of the usual 50%; otherwise sizing stays unchanged.
review.mechanism: This tries to press the inverse sleeve only when panic-like selloffs are already in progress. In those regimes, downside often persists long enough that a fixed-size short under-allocates the move; bigger SQQQ exposure could capture more crash continuation and offset the trend sleeve’s crash give-back. The risk is that high-volatility days also snap back hard, so the edge must be real and rare to survive costs.
review.data_missing: No essential missing data. QQQ minute bars are enough for the volatility percentile, and daily OHLCV for the universe is enough for the breadth proxy. If we wanted same-day breadth across the full universe before 2018, that would be the only limitation; the prior-session breadth proxy avoids that.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tried on the rejected list. The closest existing analogue is the volatility-adaptive noise-area band and the general use of regime filters, but not a stress-day inverse size-up rule.
review.overfit_note: Only two real knobs, but the effect is concentrated in a small number of crisis days, so a few episodes like 2020 or 2022 can dominate the fit. Small changes to the volatility percentile or breadth proxy could flip the result.
review.expected_effect: Best case: better capture of persistent selloff days and less crash give-back from the intraday sleeve. Base case: little change. Worst case: more whipsaw losses and decay from oversized SQQQ on violent V-shaped rebounds.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule at vol percentile >=90% and short-side size = 100% of sleeve capital. Backtest baseline Q desk vs. this overlay on 2018-2026 with the existing cost model, then confirm unchanged parameters on 2007-2017 and 1999-2017 using the same QQQ vol percentile and the daily breadth proxy. Score by net daily return, Sharpe, and max drawdown versus baseline, plus incremental PnL on activated stress days. Accept only if both the build period and the unseen confirm period improve net return and do not worsen max drawdown.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully implementable with our data, and directly targets crash-day give-back. The evidence is weak, but this is a reasonable sizing overlay to test before spending more time on it.

name: Indicator confluence and redundancy budget
one_line: Limit the model to a small non-redundant indicator stack and require confluence before acting.
parameter_choices: at most one momentum, one trend, and one volatility feature; require alignment between pattern, indicator, and regime filters
disagreement: More indicators can seem safer, but they also raise overfit risk and can create fake agreement.
books: Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: The sources give generic TA advice about avoiding redundant indicators and using confluence/context, but they are opinion, not measured evidence. They do not show that a confluence gate improves a QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ system specifically, so the link is only indirect.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one gate to the existing intraday noise-area sleeve: take TQQQ only when QQQ is above its 200-day SMA, and take SQQQ only when QQQ is below its 200-day SMA; otherwise skip the intraday trade. Keep the current 14-day σ band unchanged and add no other indicators.
review.mechanism: This may cut the noisiest countertrend breakouts, which are the most likely to whipsaw after costs. It turns the intraday sleeve into a trend-aligned continuation trade instead of a pure breakout trade, so hit rate and expectancy could improve modestly. It will also skip some good reversals and does not fix the trend sleeve’s crash give-back.
review.data_missing: None for the concrete 200SMA gate. If you want pattern-based confluence like head-and-shoulders, support/resistance, or cup-and-handle, our OHLCV data is too subjective to code cleanly without arbitrary rules.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already uses a 200-day trend filter in the trend sleeve and a volatility band in the intraday sleeve, so the ingredients are not new. What has not been tested is making the intraday sleeve conditional on the daily regime.
review.overfit_note: The specific gate has almost no free knobs, but the broader confluence idea is easy to abuse by searching across many indicators and thresholds. That makes the general concept prone to p-hacking even if this one version is clean.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer bad intraday trades and a small lift in net expectancy per trade. More likely: lower trade count with only a modest or zero improvement after costs. It is not expected to materially fix crash exits or the main trend whipsaw problem.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one variant: keep the current intraday noise-area logic, but only allow longs when QQQ > 200SMA and shorts when QQQ < 200SMA. Do not tune lookbacks or add RSI/extra filters in this pass. Backtest current Q desk vs gated Q desk on 2018-2026 with the existing cost model, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 minute data and 1999-2017 out-of-sample history. Compare net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in each period before adopting.
review.verdict_reason: The broad 'indicator budget' idea is just research hygiene, but this concrete regime gate is cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly targets the intraday sleeve’s false positives. The support is weak, so keep the search space narrow and test only this one gate, not a larger indicator-stack experiment.

name: Swing-structure early exit
one_line: Exit the trend sleeve when price breaks swing structure or fails a new high, rather than waiting for the 200-day SMA.
parameter_choices: Close below the latest swing low after a failed new-high attempt; break of a prior low; diagonal trendline/channel break; use as an earlier regime exit for the TQQQ sleeve.
disagreement: Sources disagree on the exact trigger: failed new-high + swing-low break, broader swing-structure break, or a trendline/channel break.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass

review.source_support_note: One source explicitly gives the near-identical change-of-character rule: close below a swing point after failing to make a higher high. Another source says a clear break of swing structure ends the trend. The trendline/channel source is only a looser, subjective cousin. So the concept is supported, but the exact automated implementation is still our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current QQQ>200-day-SMA entry rule for the trend sleeve, but add an exit override: while long TQQQ, if QQQ closes below the most recent confirmed 2-day pivot low (a low lower than the prior 2 and next 2 daily lows), flatten the trend sleeve at the next market close and stay in cash until QQQ is again above its 200-day SMA. Do not use hand-drawn trendlines/channels in live code.
review.mechanism: This could get the trend sleeve out earlier when the uptrend actually breaks, so it may cut the worst of the crash give-back that the 200-day SMA exit suffers in fast selloffs. The downside is more whipsaws and missed rebounds in sideways or choppy markets, which can easily erase the benefit if the stop is too tight.
review.data_missing: None for the fixed pivot-low version; daily QQQ OHLCV is enough, and no order book/news/options/fundamentals are needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list as a standalone Q desk test, but it targets the same known trend-sleeve weakness (late crash exit / whipsaw). We have not already tested this exact fixed swing-low exit on the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: The trap is obvious: if we start tuning pivot width, buffers, or high/low lookbacks on 2018-2026, this becomes curve-fit bait. Freeze the rule before testing and do not search over 3/5/7/10-day variants or trendline hacks.
review.expected_effect: Best case: smaller drawdowns and earlier crash exits in 2008/2020/2022. Base case: more whipsaws and slightly lower CAGR from being shaken out of normal pullbacks. Net effect is plausible but far from guaranteed.
review.test_protocol: Backtest baseline Q desk vs the variant with only this exit change, using identical costs/fill assumptions and no parameter search. Score full-desk net CAGR/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trend-sleeve giveback. Evaluate 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Accept only if net CAGR/day improves in both periods; if CAGR is flat within 5 bp/year, require max drawdown to improve by at least 5 percentage points in both periods and turnover not to jump enough to swamp the gain.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully feasible with the data we already have, and it directly attacks one of the bot’s main weaknesses. The fixed swing-low version is worth a clean pre-registered test; the subjective trendline/channel variants are not.

name: Opposite moving-average cross exit
one_line: Use the opposite moving-average cross as the trend-sleeve exit.
parameter_choices: 50/100-day dual MA cross; exit when the shorter MA crosses back through the longer MA in the opposite direction.
disagreement: No real disagreement in the source; only the MA pair is specified.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The cited book explicitly describes exiting/selling on the opposite dual-MA cross, with a 50-day short MA and 100-day long MA. Applying that same exit logic to Midas's QQQ trend sleeve is a direct match, not a stretch.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: keep the current 200-day SMA regime gate on QQQ, but replace the exit with a 50/100-day opposite-cross overlay on QQQ daily closes. At the 15:55 New York decision, hold the existing 50% TQQQ overnight only if QQQ is above its 200-day SMA and the 50-day SMA is above the 100-day SMA (default pair: 50/100 days from the source); if the 50-day crosses below the 100-day, go to cash at the next tradable open/MOC and stay there until the cross flips back up. This is a rule change, not a new sleeve.
review.mechanism: This could cut the worst part of the trend sleeve: giving back too much after momentum rolls over. A faster exit than the 200-day alone may reduce crash loss and late exits, but it will almost certainly create more whipsaws and may miss part of persistent bull runs.
review.data_missing: None. Daily QQQ closes are sufficient; no news, fundamentals, options, order book, or sentiment data needed.
review.already_tried_note: Nothing in the rejected list matches this exact 50/100 exit overlay on the Q desk. The prior stop/target work was on the old ORB bot, not this trend sleeve.
review.overfit_note: If we lock the pair at 50/100, there is only one obvious knob. But MA timing rules are regime-sensitive, and a faster exit can look good in 2018-2026 while quietly hurting 1999-2017 if we start shopping around for better lengths.
review.expected_effect: Plausibly lower drawdown and smaller crash give-back, but with a real chance of lower long-run return from extra whipsaws and reduced exposure. If it helps, the effect should show up most in bad tape, not in smooth bull markets.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the fixed 50/100 exit overlay before looking at results. Backtest the full Q desk with everything else unchanged, including the same cost model and fill assumptions, and compare A) current 200-day trend exit vs B) 200-day gate plus 50/100 exit gate. Score net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trend-sleeve turnover on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Require improvement in both periods; if B helps only the recent sample or worsens drawdown in the older sample, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully feasible with our data, and directly targets a known weakness of the trend sleeve. It is not obviously good enough to adopt, but it is worth one disciplined test with fixed 50/100 parameters.

name: APO sign-change exit
one_line: Exit when APO flips sign.
parameter_choices: Close positions when APO crosses zero or changes sign.
disagreement: Single-source rule; no alternative parameterization is given.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly says positions are closed when the APO signal changes sign, which is the exact exit concept being proposed. The only caveat is that it is a worked example in a book, not evidence that it works on our universe or costs.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: compute APO(12,26) on daily QQQ closes (APO = EMA(12) - EMA(26)). If APO crosses from positive to negative while a TQQQ position is open, flatten the position at the next 5-minute bar open. Keep the existing 200-day SMA entry rule unchanged; no change to the intraday sleeve.
review.mechanism: APO is a faster momentum gauge than a 200-day SMA, so it may get us out of TQQQ earlier when the market turns down. That could reduce crash giveback and some of the trend sleeve’s whipsaw pain from late exits. The tradeoff is more false exits in sideways markets.
review.data_missing: None; we already have daily QQQ OHLCV back to 1999 and can simulate the next-5-minute-open exit without extra data.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule, but it sits in the same family as our existing trend/regime work. The explicitly rejected list does not include APO sign-change, so this is not a duplicate, but it is also not a new market edge class.
review.overfit_note: If we lock APO(12,26) and do not search lengths, the knob count is low. The risk is mostly structural: zero-cross exits often look good in one sample and then whipsaw in choppy decades like 1999-2010.
review.expected_effect: Best-case: earlier exits from the 3x trend sleeve in downswings, smaller crash drawdowns, slightly better MAR. More likely: lower drawdown but some extra churn and missed upside in sideways periods.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register APO(12,26) and do not tune it. Backtest baseline Q desk vs. the same desk with the trend sleeve flattened on the first daily APO cross below zero, using the same fills/costs. Evaluate after-cost daily net return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017. Keep it only if the variant beats baseline on net return and max drawdown in both periods; if it helps only in-sample or worsens turnover materially, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully feasible with existing data, and directly targets a known weakness of the trend sleeve. The source support is real, the parameter count is tiny, and the worst outcome is quickly exposed by backtest whipsaw.

name: ATR-based stop
one_line: Use a volatility-scaled stop so exits expand and contract with ATR.
parameter_choices: ATR(14) with a 2.5x ATR stop; optional 1 ATR close-away shock exit; can be paired with a 1.5x target in the source example.
disagreement: Some sources use a static ATR multiple, while another treats a 1 ATR close-away move as the exit trigger.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The books support ATR stops in general, and one source gives a concrete 14-day ATR / 2.5x stop example with backtest stats. But neither source is for a QQQ/TQQQ sleeve in a 200-day trend system, so applying it to Midas is an adaptation, not a direct citation.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: after the 15:55 entry into TQQQ when QQQ is above its 200-day SMA, track the highest QQQ daily high since entry and set a stop at (highest high) minus 2.5 × ATR(14) of QQQ. If QQQ closes below that stop, liquidate the TQQQ sleeve at the next market open and keep that sleeve in cash until the 200-day SMA signal turns off and later back on. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This is meant to cut the trend sleeve sooner when a real breakdown starts, while letting the position breathe during normal volatility. If it works, it should reduce crash give-back and maybe some whipsaw loss in the leveraged trend sleeve without touching the intraday sleeve.
review.data_missing: Nothing required beyond the price data we already have. QQQ daily OHLCV is enough to compute ATR(14) and the stop; synthetic 3x history already exists for the pre-2010 TQQQ sleeve.
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected generic stop/target tuning on the old ORB bot, but that is a different strategy. This exact ATR stop on the current Q desk trend sleeve has not been tested yet.
review.overfit_note: Only two fixed choices are involved (ATR length 14 and 2.5x), but ATR stops are still path-sensitive and can be mined easily if we start varying the multiplier, lookback, or re-entry logic. Keep those fixed and do not optimize them on 2018-2026.
review.expected_effect: Best case: smaller trend-sleeve drawdowns in sharp reversals and crash periods. Base case: little change because 2.5 ATR may be too loose to matter before the 200-day flip. Downside: some extra churn and lower CAGR from cutting good trends early.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact stop rule above before looking at results. Run the full Q desk unchanged except for the trend-sleeve ATR stop. Compare baseline vs variant on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Use net %/day after all costs, Sharpe, and max drawdown for the full bot, plus trend-sleeve give-back from entry to exit. Accept only if both periods improve net daily return and do not worsen max drawdown; otherwise keep it as shadow-only and do not promote.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, feasible with our data, and directly targets a known weakness of the trend sleeve. The expected edge is modest and the stop may do nothing or hurt returns, but that is exactly why it is worth a quick pre-registered test rather than more discussion.

name: Trailing stop for winners
one_line: Let winners run with a trailing stop instead of a time-based exit.
parameter_choices: Fixed 2% trail; highest-high minus 2 or 3 ATR; preset drop from the high watermark; trailing exit after the first favorable move.
disagreement: A tight 2% trail was reported as weak; the other sources prefer ATR-based or high-watermark trails.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support trailing stops in general and the 'let winners run' principle, but mostly as opinion. One concrete 2% trailing-stop example is actually reported as worse than the author's prior approach. None of the sources validate this on a leveraged QQQ/TQQQ regime sleeve, so the support is generic rather than direct.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: keep the existing QQQ > 200-day SMA entry filter and 50% allocation, but replace the current hold-until-200-day-flip exit with a daily trailing stop on TQQQ set to the highest daily high since entry minus 3×ATR(14); if TQQQ trades below the stop, exit at the next session open. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could cut the trend sleeve's worst crash give-back and get us out faster after a clear reversal, which is exactly where the current sleeve is weakest. The main risk is that TQQQ is noisy enough that a trailing stop may fire during normal pullbacks and truncate the big bull-trend gains that pay for the sleeve.
review.data_missing: None for a daily trailing-stop test. We already have the needed daily OHLCV for QQQ/TQQQ; pre-2010 TQQQ can be handled the same way as the bot's existing synthetic 3× backtests.
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected stop/target tinkering on the old ORB bot, but not this trend sleeve. So this is the same family of exit-management changes, just applied to a different sleeve and regime filter.
review.overfit_note: There are several hidden degrees of freedom behind a 'trailing stop' idea: ATR multiple, high vs close watermark, daily vs intraday triggering, and possible activation thresholds. The 2018-2026 sample is also dominated by a huge bull run plus one major crash, which makes it easy to fit a flattering stop after the fact.
review.expected_effect: Best case: lower max drawdown and faster crash exits with only modest return loss. More likely: some drawdown reduction, but a real risk of giving up too much upside in the strong Nasdaq trends that already drive most of the sleeve's return.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one variant: the trend sleeve exit becomes a 3×ATR(14) daily trailing stop off the highest daily high since entry, with the existing 200-day SMA still used for entry. Compare this modified Q desk against the current baseline on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Primary metric: net profit per day after costs. Secondary metrics: Sharpe and max drawdown. Accept only if net profit/day improves in both periods and max drawdown is not worse in either period; if it only helps 2018-2026, treat it as overfit and reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with the data we have, cheap to backtest, and directly targets the trend sleeve's known crash give-back. The evidence is weak and the stop is likely to overfit, but this is still a sensible one-shot test because the implementation is simple and the downside is only a small amount of testing time.

name: Scale out and protect the remainder
one_line: Take partial profits in pieces and move the stop on the leftover shares to breakeven or just beyond the first target.
parameter_choices: Half off at 1R; thirds or quarters; two profit targets plus a trailing runner; stop to entry or near the target; final exit at a higher-time-frame swing.
disagreement: Sources disagree on split size (half vs thirds vs quarters) and on whether the remainder stop should be exactly breakeven or near the target.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The cited sources explicitly describe the same trade-management family: take part of a winner off at a predefined profit threshold, then move the stop on the remainder to breakeven or near the first target. One source even gives a small backtest with stats. The only disagreement is the split size and exact stop placement.
review.exact_rule_change: No direct change to the current Q desk. The only source-faithful version is a new fixed-stop sleeve: sell 50% of the position at +1R, move the stop on the remainder to breakeven, and let the runner exit on the existing rule. This does not map cleanly onto the current trend sleeve because it has no predefined R.
review.mechanism: In principle this could lock in some small favorable excursions and prevent winners from turning back into losers, which can reduce left-tail giveback. On Midas, though, the main edge is from letting trend and momentum trades run; scaling out usually truncates the right tail that pays for costs. So the only plausible benefit is on a very specific mean-reversion style sleeve, not the current trend hold.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot, which is the same family of exit-management rule. This exact split-exit rule has not been tested on the Q desk, but it is not novel.
review.overfit_note: There are multiple free knobs: split fraction, first target, and remainder stop/trail. Those interact with whole-share rounding and trade path, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: smaller drawdowns and fewer winner-to-loser reversals on a mean-reverting sleeve. Base case: lower average winner and lower total expectancy, especially on the trend sleeve, because the right tail gets clipped.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on testing, pre-register exactly one variant and do not sweep parameters: use the intraday sleeve only, sell 50% at +1R, move the remainder stop to entry, and otherwise keep the existing band/VWAP/close exit. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026, then confirm on 2007-2017, using the same fills/costs. Judge by net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, win rate, average winner, and turnover. Require improvement in both periods after costs; if the gain comes only from smaller winners or higher turnover, reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is generic trade-management folklore, not a bot-specific edge. It needs a predefined R that the current Q desk does not have, adds multiple knobs, and is likely to hurt the trend sleeve's convex payoff. Similar stop/target tinkering already failed on the old ORB bot, so the expected value is too low for a test slot.

name: Profit-lock exit
one_line: Close a winning position once open PnL crosses a profit floor, even if the signal has not reversed.
parameter_choices: Fixed profit floor such as $10; shares × 10; volatility-normalized threshold; or a 20% profit target.
disagreement: Some sources use a fixed dollar amount, others scale by position size; one source prefers a 20% target but says not to auto-sell mechanically.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The Donadio/Ghosh excerpts explicitly close profitable positions once unrealized PnL exceeds a threshold, regardless of the original signal, which is essentially this rule. Burns/Douglas only add generic profit-taking advice, not performance evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Apply a profit-lock exit to the intraday noise-area sleeve only: at each existing 30-minute check, if the open TQQQ/SQQQ position shows unrealized profit of at least $10, exit the full position at the next 5-minute bar open even if the band/VWAP exit has not triggered. Leave the trend sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could cut some giveback when a quick intraday burst reverses before the normal band/VWAP exit. The only plausible gain is a slightly smoother intraday PnL path and fewer scratch-to-loss reversals. The downside is obvious: it also truncates the right tail of momentum winners, which is where the edge usually lives.
review.data_missing: none for this rule; 1-minute OHLCV is enough to mark unrealized PnL and trigger the exit.
review.already_tried_note: Not tested verbatim, but it is a close cousin of the previously rejected stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot and of the current band/VWAP profit-giving-exit logic. No reason to think this is materially different.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but it is arbitrary and easy to tune to 2018-2026. Fixed profit caps often look good in-sample by reducing volatility while quietly destroying the big winners.
review.expected_effect: Likely lower average winner and lower trade expectancy; maybe slightly lower variance and fewer give-backs on some reversal days. Net PnL is more likely flat-to-negative than meaningfully better after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one variant: intraday sleeve only, profit-lock threshold = $10, no other changes. Compare baseline Q desk vs modified desk on 2018-2026 using actual TQQQ/SQQQ minute data, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 using synthetic 3x from QQQ minute bars with the same fill and cost model. Primary metric: net daily PnL after costs. Secondary metrics: Sharpe, max drawdown, win rate, average trade, and trade count. Accept only if both periods improve on net daily PnL and do not worsen max drawdown; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic profit cap, not a new source of edge. It is very likely to clip the profitable right tail of the intraday momentum sleeve more than it reduces giveback, and similar stop/target tweaks have already failed for this team. Cheap to simulate, but not promising enough to spend validation budget on.

name: Daily stop once green
one_line: Shut down intraday trading once the day is green.
parameter_choices: Stop after the first profitable round trip; stop after a fixed daily profit; or stop after a time window once green.
disagreement: Single-source behavioral rule; no numeric consensus is provided.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The source states the same trading guardrail explicitly: stop for the day once you are green. The catch is that it is one author’s behavioral rule, not quantified evidence, and our bot already has a hard one-round-trip/day cap, so the adaptation is narrower than the book’s advice.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a session-P&L gate to the intraday sleeve: at each 30-minute decision point from 10:00 to 15:30, if the bot’s total session P&L (realized + mark-to-market across both sleeves) is > 0, do not open any new intraday position for the rest of that day; keep the trend sleeve unchanged. Default threshold = 0.0% of equity.
review.mechanism: The only possible benefit is avoiding giving back a good day once the account is already ahead. On choppy days, the intraday sleeve may have negative expected value after an early win, so this could trim some giveback and lower variance. But because the current desk already allows only one intraday round trip per day, the rule has very little room to improve anything and will mostly just turn off the only intraday opportunity on green days.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: The exact green-stop has not been tested, but the current intraday sleeve already has a max-one-round-trip-per-day limit, which removes most of the behavior this rule is supposed to fix.
review.overfit_note: If we keep the threshold fixed at 0, there are not many knobs. But the implementation choice between realized vs mark-to-market session P&L, and whether to apply it at the bot level or just the intraday sleeve, gives enough flexibility to fit a small 2018-2026 bump that may not survive 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: Small reduction in trade count and maybe a little less giveback on days that are already green, but likely neutral to negative on net profit because it suppresses the only intraday edge on those days. Any drawdown benefit is likely tiny.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register threshold = 0 and do not tune it. Compare baseline Q desk vs the same desk with the session-green gate applied only to the intraday sleeve. Run the full 2018-2026 sample first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level behavior). Primary metrics: net CAGR/day after costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and average intraday trades/day. Accept only if both periods improve on net return and do not worsen drawdown; if the rule merely lowers volatility or trade count without a clear return gain, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly redundant with the existing one-round-trip/day cap, so the only meaningful version is a broad account-level 'skip intraday once green' filter. That may avoid a few giveback days, but it is more likely to cut the bot’s only daily intraday edge than to create new alpha, so it is not a good use of tests.

name: Gap-aware overnight exit
one_line: For overnight longs, treat a gap through the stop as an emergency exit, with a short stabilization window only if the open reclaims part of the gap.
parameter_choices: Immediate exit at the open if the stop is gapped through; or wait the first 5 minutes, then use the day's low as the new stop; sell by the close if it still cannot reclaim the original risk level.
disagreement: Immediate exit versus a 5-minute wait; the sources disagree on how much post-open patience to allow.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The book explicitly says to exit immediately when a gap blows through a stop, to wait the first 5 minutes only if the open starts reclaiming the gap, and to sell by the close if the reclaim fails. The adaptation is that Midas currently has no explicit overnight stop, so we must choose one (e.g., prior session low) before the rule is testable.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: hold TQQQ overnight with an emergency stop anchored to the prior session low. If the next regular-session open gaps below that stop, exit at the first 5-minute bar open. If the first 5 minutes reclaim the stop, keep the position but trail the stop to that day’s low; otherwise flatten at the close.
review.mechanism: This is a crash-risk filter for the overnight trend sleeve. It should cut the worst gap-down losses when the Nasdaq breaks hard overnight, which is exactly when the 200-day trend filter is slow. The trade-off is that it will also dump some V-shaped opens that later recover, so the likely win is lower tail risk and lower drawdown more than higher raw return.
review.data_missing: No additional market data. The only missing specification is the overnight stop anchor; with our bars we can test a concrete choice such as the prior session low.
review.already_tried_note: Broad overnight holding was already tested/rejected, so this is not a fresh return stream; it is a narrow exit tweak on the existing overnight trend sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Only a couple of knobs if pre-registered, but the effect may depend heavily on the chosen stop anchor and on 2018+ gap behavior, so it can still be fit to recent crash patterns.
review.expected_effect: Likely reduces overnight tail losses and max drawdown in crashy periods; likely small drag on CAGR from exiting some gap-down opens that would have recovered. Net effect on Sharpe/MAR is uncertain but plausible.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant and compare it with the current Q desk. Variant: overnight TQQQ trend sleeve uses a prior-session-low emergency stop; if the next open gaps below it, exit at the first 5-minute bar open; if the first 5 minutes reclaim the stop, keep the trade and trail to that day’s low; otherwise flatten at the close. Backtest on 2018-2026 with real TQQQ minute data, using the same spread/impact assumptions and the existing intraday sleeve unchanged. Confirm on 1999-2017 using synthetic 3x QQQ. Pass only if net CAGR and max drawdown improve versus baseline in both periods; if drawdown improves but CAGR falls materially, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully price-testable with our data, and it directly targets the trend sleeve's crash give-back. The source support is only partial and the edge may be small, but this is a valid risk-management tweak rather than a new strategy, so it is worth one pre-registered test.

name: Hard loss backstop
one_line: Put a hard percentage stop on leveraged ETF positions so no trade can turn into a large loser.
parameter_choices: 10% initial stop; 15% review/stop region; 20% hard stop as a backstop.
disagreement: Thresholds vary from 10% to 20%, and one source recommends reviewing at 10% rather than auto-exiting.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books do support the general loss-cutting idea: 10% initial stops, a 10% review threshold, and a 20% hard stop are all explicitly recommended or described. But that is generic practitioner opinion, not measured evidence, and none of it is specific to 3x Nasdaq ETFs or to this QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ bot.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard 20% stop-loss backstop to every open TQQQ or SQQQ position: if mark-to-market loss from the entry fill reaches -20%, exit at the next 5-minute bar open and do not re-enter that sleeve again that day. Leave all other entry/exit rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help only if the current trend or intraday exit lags a real regime break or a sharp overnight selloff. In that case it would cap rare large losses on the 3x ETF sleeve and reduce drawdowns. The downside is that TQQQ/SQQQ are noisy enough that a 20% stop will also fire on ordinary volatility, so the more likely outcome is fewer large losers but more whipsaws and lower expectancy.
review.data_missing: Nothing material. The rule is price-only and can be simulated with the existing minute bars plus the synthetic 3x history used before real TQQQ/SQQQ data exists.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot, so this family of idea is not novel. That said, a hard stop overlay has not been tested on the current Q desk specifically.
review.overfit_note: The stop threshold is arbitrary and easy to tune after the fact. Even with a fixed 20% rule, the result can depend heavily on whether the test window is dominated by crash regimes or grindy mean-reversion.
review.expected_effect: Most likely a small reduction in max drawdown at the cost of lower CAGR and more churn. Best case, it trims a few crash legs in the trend sleeve. Base case, it stops out on normal 3x ETF noise and underperforms the existing exit logic.
review.test_protocol: Backtest the current Q desk versus the identical Q desk with the 20% stop overlay on all TQQQ/SQQQ positions. Keep the same fills, costs, and signal logic; do not scan 10/15/20 after the fact. Use 2018-2026 as the primary build period, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 using the same synthetic-3x methodology where real ETF data do not exist. Primary metric: net CAGR / average daily return after costs. Secondary metrics: max drawdown and turnover. Adopt only if the stop version improves net CAGR in both periods, or at minimum preserves CAGR while cutting max drawdown materially in both periods.
review.verdict_reason: This is cheap, fully price-testable with our existing data, and only adds one fixed knob, so it is worth a pre-registered test. I do not expect a big edge, but it could plausibly reduce tail losses on the trend sleeve; the main risk is that it just adds whipsaw exits and lowers returns.

name: Minimum reward-to-risk filter
one_line: Skip entries unless the planned exit is at least 1.5R–2R away from the stop.
parameter_choices: 1.5R minimum; 2R minimum; 2:1 default reward-to-risk.
disagreement: One source sets the floor at 1.5R, another at 2R.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The books do support the generic idea of demanding 1.5R to 2R reward-to-risk before taking a trade. But they are discretionary swing-trade examples with explicit stop and target placement, not evidence that this works for our QQQ noise-area sleeve or the trend sleeve.
review.exact_rule_change: Reject for the current Q desk: a 2.0R minimum is not a valid rule change unless we first add an explicit stop-loss framework to the intraday sleeve, which would turn it into a different strategy rather than a filter.
review.mechanism: In theory it would skip marginal setups whose upside is too small relative to risk. In practice, our intraday edge is short-horizon mean reversion with condition-based exits, so a minimum R:R gate is likely to remove the highest-hit-rate trades and force an arbitrary stop definition.
review.data_missing: None for a backtest; minute bars are enough to compute entry, the existing planned exit, and any hypothetical stop you choose.
review.already_tried_note: This is the same family as the stop/target tweaks we already tested and rejected on the old ORB bot. The current intraday sleeve also already uses band/VWAP/close exits, so this is mostly a repackaged stop-target optimization idea.
review.overfit_note: The threshold itself is easy to tune, and the bigger problem is that the stop definition is arbitrary. On a mean-reversion system, small changes in stop/target geometry can flip the result, so 2018-2026 is very likely to mislead us.
review.expected_effect: Probably fewer trades and a slightly better average R on survivors, but likely flat to worse net profit after costs because the current edge is not based on large reward-to-risk asymmetry.
review.test_protocol: If someone insists on quantifying it, compare the current Q desk to the same system with an R:R floor on the intraday sleeve only; keep the trend sleeve unchanged. Pre-register 2.0R and do not tune it after looking. Use 2018-2026 as the build period, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 and 1999-2017 QQQ minute data. Success requires higher net profit per day after costs, higher or equal Sharpe, and no worse max drawdown in both periods; if trade count collapses with no clear gain, kill it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic trading aphorism, not a proven edge for this bot. The Q-desk intraday sleeve is a mean-reversion system with condition-based exits, so a minimum reward-to-risk filter either forces a new stop/target strategy or just deletes the best short moves. Not worth a test on the current bot.

name: Partial rebalancing toward target exposure
one_line: Move exposure toward the target gradually instead of flipping all the way in or out at once.
parameter_choices: Rebalance 25%–50% of the gap to target each check; only rebalance when drift exceeds a set threshold (e.g. 10%–20% of target exposure).
disagreement: Reduces turnover and slippage on choppy days, but can lag hard trend continuations.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpt is essentially the same trading principle: with transaction costs, you should not trade all the way to the target every time. That is direct support for partial rebalancing, though it is generic portfolio guidance rather than a Midas-specific result.
review.exact_rule_change: Apply partial rebalancing only to the intraday sleeve: at each 30-minute signal check, if the sleeve’s current exposure is at least 10% of book away from its target (cash/TQQQ/SQQQ), trade 50% of the gap toward the target at the next 5-minute bar open; otherwise hold. Leave the 15:55 trend sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This should cut churn on noisy intraday reversals, so we pay fewer spread/impact costs and avoid some flip-flopping around the band. It may also smooth the equity curve by making the sleeve less sensitive to brief signal flickers. The tradeoff is slower participation when QQQ runs hard after a signal.
review.data_missing: No extra data needed; existing minute bars and portfolio accounting are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is closer to an execution/position-sizing tweak than to the ORB stop/target changes that were already discarded.
review.overfit_note: Only two knobs, but it is easy to tune them on 2018-2026 until the backtest looks nicer. The unseen 1999-2017 check is important.
review.expected_effect: Probably a small reduction in turnover and slippage, with a small chance of slightly better drawdown on choppy days. Net profit improvement is plausible but likely modest; it could also underperform by lagging strong intraday moves.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register 50% gap and 10% drift threshold, then backtest the current Q desk versus the same desk with partial rebalancing in the intraday sleeve only. Use identical fills, costs, and whole-share rules. Score full-system net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and same-day flip count over 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (using synthetic 3x before 2018 as in the existing framework). Keep the change only if net return and Sharpe both improve in both periods, max drawdown is not worse, and intraday turnover falls by at least 15%.
review.verdict_reason: This is directly supported by the literature, needs no new data, and is cheap to test. The expected edge is small, but it is a sensible cost/turnover tweak rather than a speculative new alpha.

name: Structure-based stop placement
one_line: Place exits just beyond recent structure levels instead of using a purely fixed percent stop.
parameter_choices: Use the signal candle high/low, recent swing high/low, or nearby support/resistance with a small buffer (for example 0.25–1.0 ATR); cap risk by exact dollar or fraction-of-equity risk.
disagreement: Structure stops can cut noise better than fixed stops, but they may still be too tight in fast, volatile tape.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: B2 explicitly recommends candle/swing-based stops, B8 says support/resistance can guide stops, and B11 argues for exact structure-based risk. None of them gives a quantified rule or evidence on leveraged ETF momentum, so the fit is an adaptation, not direct proof.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: keep the existing 200-dma regime filter and 50% TQQQ sleeve, but add an emergency exit. If QQQ closes below the most recent confirmed daily swing low (use a 2-bar fractal low) minus 0.5 ATR(14), flatten the TQQQ sleeve at the next close. No profit target.
review.mechanism: This could shorten the bot's exposure during fast selloffs, so it may cut the worst crash give-back before the 200-dma flips. The trade-off is that TQQQ is 3x leverage, so a swing-low stop will likely increase whipsaws and may trim bull-market upside; it only helps if the drawdown reduction is real.
review.data_missing: None for a prototype. Daily OHLCV is enough to define the swing low and ATR. Exact intraday stop-fill slippage through gaps is not observable without quotes/order-book data, so the fill model will be approximate.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot, so this is the same family of exit tweak even though it is being applied to the Q desk trend sleeve rather than ORB.
review.overfit_note: There is only one real knob if we pre-register the swing definition and the ATR buffer, but stop rules are still fragile and regime-dependent. If we start tuning lookback length, buffer, and whether to apply it to intraday vs trend, the test turns into stop-shopping.
review.expected_effect: Best case: smaller crash-month losses and a lower max drawdown. More likely: modest drawdown improvement at the cost of more whipsaw and some return drag. I do not expect a large lift in average daily PnL.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one candidate only: 2-bar daily swing low, 0.5 ATR(14) buffer, trend sleeve only, all else unchanged. Backtest 2018-2026 first, then lock the rule and confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Compare against the current Q desk on after-cost net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and worst month/year. Adopt only if both periods show higher net return and Sharpe with no worse max drawdown; if the stop merely reduces drawdown but cuts the long-run return too much, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible and cheap, but the support is thin and the expected edge is small. This is a generic stop-placement tweak with prior negative history in our ORB work, so I would not spend an early test on it unless higher-priority regime/sizing changes have already been exhausted.

name: Bracket profit targets and measured-move exits
one_line: Test fixed profit targets, including 2R brackets and midpoint targets, as explicit exits.
parameter_choices: Compare full exits at 1.5R–2R versus scale-outs; for gap-style setups test a midpoint target versus the full measured move.
disagreement: Higher hit rate and less giveback, but the trade may cap upside too early.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)

review.source_support_note: B2 supports the generic idea of a fixed stop-loss with a 2R take-profit. B6 supports a midpoint target, but only in a fair-value-gap/futures example. Neither source supports applying these exits to the current QQQ 200-day trend + noise-area desk without adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not alter the current Q desk. The only source-consistent test would be a separate gap-style sleeve: on a defined gap entry, exit at the midpoint of the gap/measured move (0.5x target) instead of the full measured move; use a 1R stop and 2R take-profit only as the comparator variant.
review.mechanism: The only plausible benefit is banking profits earlier and reducing late giveback on fast reversals. On Midas, that likely helps only if the setup mean-reverts quickly; otherwise it cuts off the occasional large Nasdaq trend that pays for many losers. For the existing intraday sleeve, the current band/VWAP/close logic already exits winners and losers, so a hard target mostly caps upside rather than fixing a real problem.
review.data_missing: No critical market data is missing. Minute and daily OHLCV are enough to backtest bracket exits and opening-gap midpoint targets. The blocker is strategy fit, not data.
review.already_tried_note: Classic stop/target tinkering was already tried on the old ORB bot and did not help. Gap-style setups were also already rejected, so the midpoint-target version is not a fresh family.
review.overfit_note: There are multiple tuning knobs here (stop size, target multiple, scale-out, trailing vs fixed exit), and the edge would be easy to fit to 2018-2026. Gap trades are likely sparse, so a few good years could dominate the result and then fail on 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: If anything, expect a small rise in win rate and a larger drop in average winner size. Net expectancy is more likely to fall than rise, especially in the trend sleeve, because the big winners are what pay for the losers.
review.test_protocol: If forced to test, pre-register one simple comparison only: current Q desk vs the same entries with a hard 1R stop and 2R take-profit on the intraday sleeve, with no scale-out and no other exit changes. Fit on 2018-2022, validate on 2023-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level rules). Score by daily net return after costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Require improvement in every period and no material loss of net return or higher drawdown; if the edge comes from a tiny number of trades or one year, discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly exit tinkering. The source support is only generic, the midpoint version needs a separate gap strategy that we have already rejected, and the fixed-bracket version is likely to cap the best winners in the current Q desk. Cheap to test, but not a good use of bandwidth.

name: Thesis or edge invalidation abort
one_line: Exit as soon as the setup fails to confirm, instead of waiting for a deeper stop or end-of-day exit.
