parameter_choices: Abort if price re-enters the signal band, fails to confirm within 1–3 bars after entry, or crosses back through the regime trigger; optionally add a simple market-regime proxy.
disagreement: Can get out faster before crashes or failed breakouts, but increases false exits in noisy markets.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The books support the general principle of exiting when the trade thesis is no longer valid, but they do not specify an objective 5-minute time stop or a price-based confirmation rule. Converting that advice into a hard intraday abort rule is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Apply a 2-bar time stop to the intraday noise-area sleeve only: after entering TQQQ or SQQQ on a QQQ band break, if the trade has not closed outside the entry band by the close of the second 5-minute bar after entry, flatten at the next 5-minute bar open. Default confirmation window = 2 bars.
review.mechanism: This could cut failed breakouts and regime flips faster, so losers on noisy reversal days get smaller. The hoped-for gain is lower give-back on bad intraday entries. The likely cost is more whipsaws and more missed continuation days, especially because the current sleeve already has a thesis-invalidation exit via band/VWAP.
review.data_missing: none; this is computable from our existing 1-minute QQQ and ETF bar data and our simulated execution assumptions.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact 2-bar time stop, but the current intraday sleeve already exits on band/VWAP invalidation, and classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot were already rejected. So the proposed change is only a small extra layer on top of existing invalidation logic.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob, but it is a very fragile one: 1 vs 2 vs 3 bars can be fit easily to 2018-2026 and then fail out of sample. Because the current sleeve already has an invalidation exit, the incremental edge is likely tiny and unstable.
review.expected_effect: Small improvement in crashy intraday failures, but probably offset by more false exits and lower participation in trend days; net effect likely modest or negative.
review.test_protocol: If we insisted on testing, pre-register the 2-bar time stop and compare it against the current Q desk on 2018-2026, then confirm on 2007-2017 for the minute-level QQQ regime. Use the same costs, fills, and capital constraints. Compare daily net return, Sharpe, max drawdown, win rate, average trade, and trade count. Require improvement in both sample periods, not just the in-sample period, and no material increase in turnover or slippage drag. If the modified rule does not improve total net return and drawdown simultaneously, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly already baked into the current intraday exit logic, so the only new content is a tiny time stop. That is exactly the kind of stop tweak that is easy to fit and hard to generalize, and the historical evidence here is just trader opinion, not stats. With our existing band/VWAP invalidation and small sample of intraday trades, this is not worth burning tests on.

name: Pair mean-reversion exit on band re-entry
one_line: For pairs or spreads, close when the spread normalizes back inside the entry band.
parameter_choices: Exit when Z-score returns inside a band such as [-1,+1]; optionally compare against a tighter band like [-0.5,+0.5] or add a time stop.
disagreement: Usually shortens holds and cuts giveback, but may exit before full convergence.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source states essentially this exact exit rule for pair trades: close when the spread Z-score re-enters the band (e.g. [-1,+1]). That is direct support for the idea as a pair/spread exit. It is not evidence that the rule helps Midas specifically.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the current Q desk. This idea only applies if we add a new pair/spread sleeve: keep the entry rule as-is, and replace the exit with "close the spread when its Z-score returns inside [-1,+1]" (default exit band).
review.mechanism: For a true long/short spread, exiting once the spread is back in normal range can reduce giveback and shorten holds. For Midas, though, there is no pair sleeve and the current intraday noise-area exit already behaves like a band-re-entry exit, so there is no obvious new edge here.
review.data_missing: We can compute a spread Z-score from our price history, but the live bot cannot run the strategy as stated because the account is cash-only and cannot short. No extra market data is missing; the blocker is the trading constraint, not the data.
review.already_tried_note: The current intraday sleeve already exits on band/VWAP re-entry, which is the same logic family. What has not been tried is a true pair-trade implementation, but that is not live-tradable in this account.
review.overfit_note: Pair selection, hedge ratio, entry threshold, exit band, and time stop all create a lot of degrees of freedom. Mean-reversion edges in spreads are also prone to sample-specific decay, especially when you only have one main in-sample period to fit.
review.expected_effect: Likely modestly better for a genuine shortable pair strategy by cutting giveback; for Midas itself, probably no improvement because the bot cannot run pairs and already uses similar exit logic on its intraday sleeve.
review.test_protocol: Do not test this on the current Q desk. If a future shortable pair sleeve is added, pre-register a fixed pair universe and hedge rule, then compare two exits on the same entries: (1) fixed time stop, (2) exit when Z-score re-enters [-1,+1]. Evaluate net expectancy per trade after costs, average giveback from peak to exit, and max drawdown on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017. Require improvement in both periods before adoption.
review.verdict_reason: This is a pair/spread exit rule, but Midas is a cash account with no short selling, so the strategy is not implementable as stated. Also, the current intraday sleeve already uses the same band-re-entry concept in spirit, so there is no fresh bot edge to test.

name: Range-trading sleeve with boundary exits
one_line: Add a dedicated range-reversion setup that buys near one boundary and exits near the opposite boundary.
parameter_choices: Define the range with a recent N-day high/low, opening range, or tight volatility box; require a weak-trend filter; exit at the opposite boundary or on range failure.
disagreement: Should work better in sideways regimes, but it will underperform badly when trend strength picks up.
books: Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)

review.source_support_note: The excerpt supports the generic range-trading trope (enter near a range and exit at a predefined level), but it does not specify a concrete boundary rule, trend filter, holding period, or any evidence that the idea survives costs. The proposed sleeve is our adaptation, not something the source actually proves.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a new standalone sleeve, not a tweak to the existing Q desk: if QQQ’s 20-day ADX is below 20 and QQQ closes at or below its 20-day low, buy TQQQ at the next open using 25% of equity; exit on the first close at or above the 20-day high or on any close below the 20-day low. Otherwise stay in cash.
review.mechanism: If anything helps, it would be from monetizing sideways, low-trend QQQ stretches and diversifying the current trend sleeve. The boundary exit is meant to cap the trade when the range breaks. But this is basically another mean-reversion bet on QQQ, so the main question is whether it adds anything beyond the existing RSI(2) sleeve.
review.data_missing: None. Daily OHLCV on QQQ is enough for this exact rule; minute data is not required.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact setup, but it is very close to the already-known QQQ mean-reversion family (RSI(2)) and therefore likely to be redundant. It is not the same as the rejected ORB setups, but it is in the same broad bucket of range/mean-reversion betting.
review.overfit_note: Few knobs if we freeze N=20 and ADX<20, but the edge is likely regime-specific and easy to confuse with the existing mean-reversion sleeve. If we start tuning lookback, boundary definitions, or size, it will overfit quickly.
review.expected_effect: At best, a small choppy-market mean-reversion stream; more likely it is redundant with RSI(2) and not a crash fix. I would expect flat-to-slightly positive before costs in some subperiods and disappointment out of sample.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register only N=20 and ADX<20. Backtest the sleeve standalone and as a 25% overlay on the current Q desk on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017. Compare net CAGR, daily Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and incremental return versus the current Q desk and versus RSI(2) alone. Promote only if both periods are positive after costs and the combined bot improves Sharpe without worsening drawdown; otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic range-mean-reversion rewrite of a bet we already have in RSI(2), not a clearly new edge. The source is just a chapter heading, the mechanism is weakly evidenced, and the most likely outcome is more correlation and more churn rather than a meaningfully better bot.

name: Asymmetric short-side exit discipline
one_line: Manage inverse or short-side exposure more aggressively than longs, with faster exits on adverse moves and gaps.
parameter_choices: Use a tighter time stop for short-side exposure, and cover/exit if price makes a new adverse extreme after a gap or if the move fails to continue quickly.
disagreement: Reduces squeeze and gap risk, but can cut profitable short-side continuation too early.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: Both sources argue for being faster and more defensive on shorts, especially after an adverse gap and on a new high of day. That is directionally the same idea, but neither source states this exact QQQ/SQQQ rule for our bot, so this is an adaptation rather than direct support.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday inverse sleeve only: if QQQ prints a new high of day after an SQQQ entry, exit SQQQ at the next 5-minute bar open. Do not change the TQQQ sleeve or the 200-day trend sleeve.
review.mechanism: This is a tail-risk cut for the short side. Inverse ETF positions get hurt fastest when the underlying snaps back up or squeezes to a new high, so an immediate exit there should reduce the biggest losing short trades and may lower drawdown. The tradeoff is obvious: some valid downside continuations will be cut early, so this is only helpful if a small number of squeeze days are doing most of the damage.
review.data_missing: None. We can detect new highs from existing 1-minute QQQ bars and simulate the next 5-minute-open exit with our current fill model.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact asymmetric short-side exit on QQQ/SQQQ, but we have already tried generic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot, and the current Q desk already has exit logic that overlaps conceptually (band/VWAP/close exits).
review.overfit_note: Only one real rule, but the effect is likely concentrated in a small number of bad short-side days, so 2018-2026 could look better by luck. If we start tuning extra thresholds after that, it becomes a curve-fit quickly.
review.expected_effect: Likely lower left-tail loss on SQQQ trades and possibly lower max drawdown, but probably some reduction in average return because profitable short continuation gets cut earlier. This is a risk-control tweak, not an obvious alpha source.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: add the new-high-of-day emergency exit to the intraday SQQQ sleeve. Compare baseline Q desk vs modified Q desk with all other rules unchanged. Run 2018-2026 as the build period, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 using the same synthetic-3x/pre-2018 framework already used by the bot. Primary metrics: full-bot net CAGR/day after costs, max drawdown, Sharpe. Secondary metrics: SQQQ trade expectancy, worst-trade loss, 95th/99th percentile trade loss, turnover, and fee drag. Decision rule: accept only if the modified version improves full-bot net CAGR and max drawdown in both periods; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our existing data, cheap to backtest, and targets a real failure mode on the inverse sleeve. The evidence is weak and the likely effect is small, so this should be a single pre-registered run only. If it does not improve full-bot CAGR and drawdown in both periods, stop there.

name: Volatility-target the book
one_line: Scale sleeve size inversely to a QQQ volatility forecast instead of keeping fixed capital fractions.
parameter_choices: Use 1/σ sizing with a 20-day stdev, GARCH(1,1), IGARCH(1,1), Yang-Zhang OHLC volatility, Garman-Klass (a = 0.17), realized-range/scaled-range, ATR, or a 23-period OHLC forecast.
disagreement: All sources want inverse-vol sizing, but they disagree on the estimator and lookback; OHLC/range estimators are usually more efficient than close-to-close, while GARCH/IGARCH emphasize persistence.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the underlying principle (inverse-vol sizing, ARCH/GARCH/IGARCH forecasting, and OHLC-based volatility estimators), but they do not specifically validate this as a rule for our two-sleeve QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ cash-account bot. The leap from generic sizing advice to this exact implementation is ours.
review.exact_rule_change: At each rebalance, compute QQQ’s annualized 20-trading-day Yang-Zhang volatility from the last 20 completed daily OHLC bars. Set a book multiplier m_t = min(1, median(σ_YZ,20 over the trailing 252 trading days) / σ_YZ,20,t). Multiply the existing sleeve capital fractions by m_t: the trend sleeve remains 50% × m_t when QQQ is above the 200-day SMA, else 0; the intraday sleeve remains 50% × m_t when trend is on, or 100% × m_t when trend is off. No other rule changes.
review.mechanism: This cuts exposure when QQQ volatility is high, which is when TQQQ/SQQQ losses, trend whipsaws, and crash give-back are usually worst. It should smooth equity and reduce left-tail damage. Because this is a cash account, we can only scale down in volatile regimes, not lever up in calm ones, so expect a risk-control improvement more than a new alpha source.
review.data_missing: No additional data needed. Daily QQQ OHLC is enough for the volatility forecast; the existing minute data still handles the live intraday logic.
review.already_tried_note: We have not previously rejected book-level volatility targeting. The rejected items were ORB, gap/news, overnight holding, 12-1 momentum, noise-area on IWM/DIA, and stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot.
review.overfit_note: The estimator menu is large (std, YZ, GK, ATR, GARCH, IGARCH, range-based variants). Pre-register one formula and do not sweep alternatives after the fact.
review.expected_effect: Likely lower max drawdown and smoother daily P&L; Sharpe/MAR may improve modestly. Raw CAGR is uncertain and could fall a bit because we cannot scale above full cash exposure in this account.
review.test_protocol: Backtest the current Q desk versus this exact candidate with identical costs and fills. Pre-register the formula above; do not compare GARCH/GK/ATR variants unless you run a separate study. Evaluate 2018-2026 and unseen 1999-2017. Primary metric: net MAR (CAGR / max drawdown). Secondary: net CAGR, Sharpe, worst year, and turnover/costs. Keep it only if both periods improve MAR and do not reduce net CAGR versus baseline; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible, cheap, and directly targets the bot’s main pain point on 3x ETFs: oversized losses in volatile regimes. The downside is that this cash account cannot true inverse-lever up, so the upside is probably modest and mostly risk reduction. Still worth one pre-registered test, but not a menu-sweep of volatility estimators.

name: Cap loss per trade as a fraction of equity
one_line: Convert each trade to a fixed dollar-risk budget so a single loser cannot exceed a preset share of equity.
parameter_choices: Common cap is about 2% of equity per trade; examples also show fixed dollar risk like $20 on a $1,000 account, with size derived from stop distance.
disagreement: Most sources cluster around a 2% ceiling, but some examples imply smaller budgets or full-equity exposure only when leverage is not increased.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Several sources explicitly recommend risking no more than about 2% of capital per trade and sizing from predefined stop distance / dollar risk. That is the same money-management principle. The support is generic trader advice, though, not evidence that this specific leveraged-ETF Q desk will improve.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current fixed sleeve allocation with risk-budget sizing: on each new TQQQ/SQQQ entry, size the position so a 7% adverse move from the fill would lose no more than 2% of current equity, round down to whole shares, and place a hard 7% stop on the ETF. Keep the existing trend/intraday signals and their exit rules.
review.mechanism: This would cap the damage from a bad entry, gap, or whipsaw and make losses more uniform across trades. It could help the trend sleeve in crashy regimes and keep the intraday sleeve from having a few oversized losers, but it does not fix the slow 200-day exit or improve the signal itself; it mainly shrinks leverage.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule, but the bot already uses equity fractions for sleeve allocation, and classic stop/target tweaks were previously rejected on the old ORB bot. So the concept is not new and the likely benefit is mostly smaller sizing.
review.overfit_note: If the 2% and 7% numbers are fixed up front, there are only two knobs. The bigger risk is not classic overfit but that the rule just downscales the book enough to miss the return target. If anyone starts tuning the stop after seeing 2018-2026, overfit risk rises fast.
review.expected_effect: Lower max drawdown and smaller single-trade losses, especially on bad trend reversals or intraday whipsaws; likely lower CAGR/day because the bot is already signal- rather than size-constrained.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the 2% risk cap and 7% ETF stop, then backtest the risk-budget variant against the current Q desk with identical signals, fills, and costs. Compare after-cost CAGR/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and MAR on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level intraday behavior). Adopt only if both periods improve in MAR and CAGR/day is not materially worse (for example, no more than 5% lower) while max drawdown is meaningfully smaller (for example, at least 10% better).
review.verdict_reason: This is generic money-management advice, not an alpha source. The Q desk already has size knobs, and the real weaknesses are signal lag and whipsaw, not a lack of risk budgeting. A 2% cap would mostly reduce exposure and probably cut return more than it helps drawdown. I would not spend test budget here unless we also redesign the exit logic around a real stop.

name: Add hard or trailing stops to leveraged ETF positions
one_line: Force TQQQ/SQQQ exits on a predefined stop or trail rather than waiting only for band or 200-day exits.
parameter_choices: Examples: 3% below prior close, 7% / 10% / 20% max-loss stops, 2x or 3x ATR trailing stops, or candle-low / pattern-low / support-based stops.
disagreement: Tight stops cut losses faster but can whipsaw in volatile markets; wider ATR or pattern-based stops reduce premature exits but allow larger losses.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Several sources explicitly recommend stop-losses and trailing stops, including 10%/20% hard-stop examples and 2x/3x ATR trailing stops. That is close to the proposed change, but all of it is generic trader advice; none of the sources show that adding a stop to a leveraged Nasdaq trend sleeve with existing regime exits improves net profit.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: after a 15:55 entry into TQQQ, place a hard stop 20% below the entry price; if touched, exit at the next 5-minute bar open and stay in cash until the next scheduled 15:55 trend check. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could cap the left tail when a leveraged bull-trend breaks fast, so the 200-day filter does not have to absorb the whole crash. The upside is smaller crash losses and faster de-risking; the downside is that normal bull-market pullbacks will now become forced exits and likely whipsaws.
review.data_missing: No extra data is needed. We can backtest it from OHLCV, using next-bar-open fills as an approximation for stop execution across gaps.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact Q-desk rule, but stop/target tinkering has already been rejected on the old ORB bot, and the current Q desk already has band/VWAP/200d exits that function like implicit stops.
review.overfit_note: If we start shopping 3%, 7%, 10%, 20%, or ATR multiples, we will fit 2018-2026 noise. Fixing one 20% threshold before looking helps, but the rule is still fragile because it interacts with regime changes and volatility clustering.
review.expected_effect: Most likely a modest reduction in crash drawdown, but also lower CAGR from premature exits. I would not expect a clean improvement in net profit.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: 20% hard stop on TQQQ trend-sleeve entries, with next 5-minute-open fills, and no changes to the intraday sleeve. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 build and unseen 1999-2017 confirm, using the same synthetic-3x methodology already used for pre-2018 years. Primary metric: net CAGR/day after costs. Secondary metrics: max drawdown, Sharpe, and left-tail loss in crash windows such as 2020-2022. Promote only if it improves CAGR/day in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic risk-management overlay on a strategy that already has regime and intraday exits. It adds no new information and is more likely to truncate trend profits than to improve the return/drawdown trade-off. The only clear benefit is some tail-risk reduction, which is not enough to justify another live rule unless a pre-registered test shows an unusually strong win.

name: Add hard loss circuit breakers
one_line: Stop trading after a losing streak or drawdown breach so losses cannot snowball intraday or across days.
parameter_choices: 3 consecutive losers; daily max-loss boundary; weekly/monthly loss caps; warning→flatten-only→hard-stop ladder; immediate or gradual de-risking after sudden risk-profile changes.
disagreement: Thresholds vary: some books favor a simple streak stop, others time-based loss limits or a severity ladder.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: Several quoted sources explicitly advocate this family of control: stop after three consecutive losers, enforce a daily max-loss boundary, and use weekly/monthly limits or a risk-violation ladder. The exact cutoff for Midas is our adaptation, not something the sources validate numerically.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one desk-level daily kill switch: if combined realized+unrealized Q-desk P&L is down 2.5% or more from session start at any 5-minute check, flatten all positions at the next 5-minute bar open and disable new entries until the next NYSE session. Do not add weekly/monthly caps in this test; the 3-loser variant is source-backed too, but it is probably too slow to matter for a desk that usually gets only 1-2 entry/exit cycles per day.
review.mechanism: This is tail-risk insurance. It can stop a bad Nasdaq regime from compounding across both sleeves, which is where the current bot’s worst days come from. If it helps, it should show up as fewer deep red days and lower max drawdown, not as a new alpha source.
review.data_missing: None beyond normal trade/P&L bookkeeping; no news, options, order book, or fundamentals are needed.
review.already_tried_note: The team has already rejected classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot, but this exact desk-level kill switch has not been tested on the Q desk. So the concept is related, not redundant.
review.overfit_note: Only one threshold, so this is not a knob-fest. But the cutoff can still be tuned to a handful of crisis days in 2018-2026; if you start searching 1-4% or multiple ladder variants, overfit risk jumps fast.
review.expected_effect: Likely smaller left-tail losses and lower max drawdown, especially on days when both sleeves are wrong together. I would not expect higher raw expectancy; if the cutoff is too tight, CAGR will probably fall. The only acceptable win is better Calmar / survivability with a modest return hit.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the 2.5% daily stop before looking at outcomes. Backtest the current Q desk vs the breaker version on 2018-2026 with identical fills, whole-share sizing, and the existing synthetic-3x pre-2018 framework; then rerun unchanged on 1999-2017 (minute-level for QQQ, daily P&L for the stop logic). Compare net CAGR, Sharpe, Calmar, max drawdown, worst day, and count of >2.5% down days. Accept only if both periods improve max drawdown and Calmar, and CAGR is not down more than 5% versus baseline. If the stop fires on fewer than ~20 days in-sample, treat the estimate as too noisy and do not promote it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully feasible with our data, directly targets a real weakness, and the source support is decent. It is probably insurance rather than alpha, so the bar is whether it improves drawdown and compound return enough to justify the lost days. That is exactly the kind of thing worth a fast test, not a long debate.

name: Add a cooldown and no-repeat entry rule
one_line: Block back-to-back same-direction entries and small flip-flops until the signal or price has moved enough.
parameter_choices: One trade per direction until reset; minimum move from last trade such as 0.01; entry thresholds like 0.01/-0.01; optional grid-searched no-trade width α.
disagreement: No substantive disagreement on mechanism; only the reset threshold and band width need tuning.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the generic ingredients: no-trade zones chosen by grid search, minimum move / no-repeat entry logic, and execution caps. But they do not show that this exact cooldown improves the Q desk. Also, the intraday sleeve already has a one-round-trip/day cap, so the only clearly non-redundant place to apply this is the 200-day trend sleeve.
review.exact_rule_change: Trend sleeve only: replace the hard QQQ > SMA200 / QQQ <= SMA200 switch with a 1% deadband. At the 15:55 decision, keep the current state while QQQ is within [0.99 × SMA200, 1.01 × SMA200]; switch to TQQQ only if QQQ closes above 1.01 × SMA200, and switch to cash only if it closes below 0.99 × SMA200. Do not add extra trades to the intraday sleeve.
review.mechanism: This can reduce flip-flopping when QQQ chops around its 200-day average, which should cut needless turnover and spread/impact drag. The downside is that a deadband can delay exits in fast reversals, so it may improve sideways periods while slightly worsening crash give-back if the band is too wide.
review.already_tried_note: Not explicitly on the trend sleeve, but the bot already uses an anti-churn control in the intraday sleeve (max one round trip per day). So this is an incremental refinement, not a brand-new idea.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob, alpha, but it directly controls trade frequency and can be tuned to the exact chop regime of 2018-2026. A wider band can look good by suppressing whipsaws and then fail on crash years by delaying exits.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small reduction in churn and whipsaws, especially in sideways markets. If alpha is too wide, the delayed exit can hurt crash protection and max drawdown.
review.test_protocol: Backtest the current Q desk vs. the same desk with only the trend-sleeve deadband (alpha = 1%) on 2018-2026 first, with the intraday sleeve unchanged. Freeze alpha before looking at 1999-2017. Compare after-cost net profit/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Accept only if both periods improve net profit/day and Sharpe, max drawdown is not worse, and turnover falls meaningfully; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully price-data-feasible, cheap to simulate, and it targets a real weak spot in the current bot. The expected gain is probably modest, but the downside is limited to delayed exits, which a holdout test should expose.

name: Shift capital to the sleeve with the better recent edge
one_line: Replace the fixed 50/50 sleeve split with a rolling allocator that favors the sleeve with stronger recent risk-adjusted PnL.
parameter_choices: Equal-risk baseline; monthly PnL tilts; PnL/Sharpe weights; fractional Kelly from rolling win rate/payoff; slow ramp-in of new experts every d days; optional regime features like VIX.
disagreement: Some sources weight by raw PnL, others by PnL volatility or Kelly; equal-risk is the conservative baseline when edge estimates are noisy.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general idea of dynamic sizing and reallocation: monthly PnL-based rebalancing, PnL/Sharpe-based allocation, Kelly-style updates from recent wins/losses, and adapting aggressiveness to market conditions. None of them directly validate a rolling two-sleeve allocator on this Q desk, so this is an extrapolation rather than a directly cited rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the fixed 50/50 split with a monthly allocator. On the first trading day of each month, compute each sleeve’s trailing 20-trading-day net PnL per deployed dollar, divided by its trailing 20-day standard deviation of daily PnL. If the trend sleeve’s score is higher, set next month’s split to 75% trend / 25% intraday; if the intraday sleeve’s score is higher, flip it to 25% trend / 75% intraday; if the scores are equal, keep 50/50. Keep the existing rule that the trend sleeve is forced to cash when QQQ is below its 200-day SMA.
review.mechanism: If one sleeve has actually been working better recently, this shifts capital toward the live edge instead of funding the stale one. That can help if relative sleeve performance persists for a few weeks or months. The danger is that recent sleeve PnL is noisy, so the allocator may just chase luck; the 75/25 cap is meant to limit that damage.
review.data_missing: None. We can simulate both sleeve PnLs from the existing minute/daily bar history and use the bot’s own realized PnL stream.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule. We have a fixed split already, and there is a live 70% trend shadow, but not a pre-registered rolling PnL/Sharpe allocator between the two sleeves.
review.overfit_note: There are several free choices here: lookback length, score definition, rebalance frequency, and tilt cap. With only two sleeves, the recent-performance signal is noisy, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 and disappoint on 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: At best, a modest uplift in CAGR and possibly a smoother equity curve if relative sleeve edge really persists. At worst, it will simply rotate capital toward the last lucky sleeve and add rebalancing noise.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one variant: monthly rebalance, 20-trading-day Sharpe-like sleeve score, 75/25 cap. Backtest it with the same fills, costs, and whole-share rounding as the current Q desk. Compare against the current fixed 50/50 desk on 2018-2026, then freeze the rule and confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level implementation checks). Primary metric: net CAGR/daily return. Secondary: max drawdown and MAR. Keep it only if it beats baseline in both periods on net CAGR and MAR, with max drawdown not worse by more than 5 percentage points.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap, but the allocator is a noisy meta-signal on only two sleeves. It is more likely to re-slice luck than discover durable edge, and the live shadow 70% trend variant already covers part of the same territory. I would prioritize stronger regime filters or crash-exit work first.

name: Optimize sleeve weights with covariance and shrinkage
one_line: Use a long-only covariance optimizer for sleeve weights, then shrink the solution back toward equal weight if it looks brittle.
parameter_choices: Minimum-variance, tangency, or utility with λ; beta-neutral or cash-aware targets; long-only QP; force Σ positive definite; ridge/L2 or lasso/L1 shrinkage; combine model weights with 50/50 via δ.
disagreement: The books disagree on the objective: min-variance for defense, tangency for Sharpe, and some recommend shrinkage toward naive equal weight because unconstrained optimizers can be unstable.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books support the machinery: Markowitz min-variance/tangency, long-only quadratic programming, positive-definite covariance matrices, and shrinkage toward equal weight. They do not provide direct evidence that this improves a two-sleeve Nasdaq timing bot like ours; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current Q desk, but when both sleeves are eligible, replace the fixed 50/50 split with a long-only minimum-variance allocation computed from the last 63 trading days of each sleeve’s realized daily net returns. Project the covariance matrix to positive definite if needed, solve for w1+w2=1 and wi≥0, then shrink the optimizer 50% back toward equal weight: w_final = 0.5·w_opt + 0.5·(0.5,0.5). If only one sleeve is active, leave the other sleeve in cash as today.
review.mechanism: If one sleeve has recently been much noisier than the other, the optimizer will put less capital there and more in the smoother sleeve, which should reduce portfolio volatility and maybe drawdown. The shrinkage step is there because the covariance estimate is noisy and would otherwise overreact. This does not create a new edge; it only tries to stabilize the existing sleeves.
review.data_missing: None. We can estimate sleeve-return covariance from our existing backtest/live simulation outputs and use the same price data already available.
review.already_tried_note: We already run fixed-weight variants and shadow desks, but not a covariance optimizer with shrink-to-equal-weight. So this exact rule has not been tried, though it is close to existing allocation tinkering.
review.overfit_note: Only two sleeves, both driven by the same Nasdaq beta, means the covariance estimate will be unstable and regime-dependent. The lookback and shrinkage can be tuned to 2018-2026 very easily, and tangency/utility versions would add an even noisier expected-return forecast.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small reduction in volatility and turnover, with a chance of slightly better Sharpe. Raw return may not improve, and if the optimizer just chases recent low-volatility it could easily underperform the fixed split.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register L=63 trading days and shrinkage δ=0.5. Backtest baseline fixed 50/50 versus optimized+shrunk weights on 2018-2026 using identical execution and cost assumptions. Then lock parameters and run the same rule on unseen 1999-2017. Compare net CAGR/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Accept only if the optimized version beats baseline in both periods on net Sharpe and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible and cheap, but it is mostly a smoothing overlay on two highly correlated sleeves, not a new source of alpha. The likely gain is modest and the overfit risk is high, so it is not a priority test until we have exhausted more direct regime filters or simpler sizing rules like inverse-volatility.

name: Cap size by liquidity and validate orders strictly
one_line: Limit share counts and notional by liquidity, and reject malformed or oversized orders before they hit the broker.
parameter_choices: 30-day mean/median ADV; 66-day ADV; post-noon remaining-volume profile; per-asset notional caps; position caps; reject negative prices/quantities and unsupported order types.
disagreement: The main disagreement is the liquidity horizon: 30-day ADV is the common baseline, while 66-day or intraday remaining-volume estimates may fit specific order timing better.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books do support the general ideas of ADV-normalized sizing and pre-trade OMS risk checks, but they do not show that this exact change improves a tiny ETF-only bot. The liquidity cap is especially unlikely to bind on QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ at our account size.
review.exact_rule_change: For every QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ order, size shares off 30-day median daily volume and cap any single order at 5% of that ADV; if the capped size rounds to zero, skip the trade. In the OMS, hard-reject any order with price <= 0, quantity <= 0, or an unsupported order type.
review.mechanism: This mainly prevents accidental oversizing and reduces execution impact if the book ever scales up. On the current $1k book, though, these liquid ETFs are so deep that the cap will almost never bind, so it should not materially change returns or drawdowns. The validation piece improves operational safety, not alpha.
review.data_missing: None for the cap itself; we only lack quote/L2 data if we want a realistic impact model beyond simple volume-share caps.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, but we already have fixed-size, whole-share ETF trading with explicit fill-cost assumptions and live broker guardrails; the new piece is the ADV-based cap.
review.overfit_note: Very few knobs if fixed ex ante. The main danger is pointless optimization of cap fraction or horizon after seeing results.
review.expected_effect: Near-zero performance change on the current book; mostly a safety/ops improvement. If anything, a too-tight cap would slightly reduce return by shrinking an already tiny, highly liquid ETF book.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one cap: 5% of 30-day median ADV. Backtest the current Q desk with and without the cap on 2018–2026, then 1999–2017. Measure net CAGR, daily return, max drawdown, turnover, and how often orders are clipped or skipped. Require the cap to improve at least one risk-adjusted metric without hurting CAGR in either period; if it changes <1% of trades or the performance delta is within noise, do not pursue. Implement malformed-order checks separately as unit/integration tests, not as a market test.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly OMS hygiene, not an alpha source. On a $1k ETF-only book the ADV cap will not bind, so it cannot materially improve returns or drawdowns; the only useful part is safety validation, which should be implemented regardless of backtest results.

name: Require a minimum reward-to-risk before entry
one_line: Only take a new setup when the planned upside is large enough relative to the initial stop.
parameter_choices: 2:1 is the common floor; some sources prefer 3:1; one example uses a 4R target. Stops can sit at the pattern low/high, engulfing candle, or FVG candle.
disagreement: Sources disagree on the minimum acceptable R multiple, ranging from 2:1 to 3:1 to 4R.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the generic heuristic: several of them say a trade should have at least 2:1 reward-to-risk, and one says 3:1. But they are opinion-based swing-trading rules, not evidence that this filter improves our specific Q desk. They also assume an explicit stop/target framework, which our current sleeves do not have.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change the current Q desk as-is. If we add a separate swing sleeve, require an explicit stop and target at entry and only take the trade when projected reward / initial risk is at least 2.0x; default stop anchor = pattern low/high, default threshold = 2R.
review.mechanism: In theory this skips trades where the upside is too small relative to the loss, which can improve average trade quality and reduce cost drag. In practice, on Midas it only works if the setup already has a meaningful stop and target. The current trend sleeve has no stop/target, and the intraday noise-area sleeve already exits by rule, so the reward-to-risk ratio is not naturally defined. Without a new entry/exit framework, this mostly becomes a trade-count reducer, not an edge.
review.data_missing: We can backtest bar-based stop and target rules, but the live Q desk does not define an initial stop, so reward-to-risk is undefined for the existing sleeves. No order book, news, or options data is needed; the missing piece is a concrete strategy definition, not market data.
review.already_tried_note: We already tested and rejected classic stop/target tuning on the old ORB bot. This proposal is the same family of idea: a pre-entry gate based on stop/target geometry. It is not a new source of edge unless paired with a distinct setup.
review.overfit_note: There is a free threshold knob (2R vs 3R vs 4R), and the stop/target anchor can be adjusted endlessly. That makes it easy to fit 2018-2026 and disappoint out of sample.
review.expected_effect: At best, slightly fewer trades and slightly better average trade quality on a new swing setup. On the current Q desk, I expect little to no improvement because the rule is not naturally definable there.
review.test_protocol: Do not test this on the current Q desk as-is. If a new swing setup is proposed, pre-register one stop rule and one target rule, then compare no gate vs min_R = 2.0 on 2018-2026 and confirm on 1999-2017. Success means higher net expectancy per trade, net daily return, and Sharpe after costs in both periods, with trade count still sufficient. If performance only improves in-sample or collapses after costs, reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic trading aphorism, not a demonstrated edge, and it cannot be applied cleanly to the current bot because neither sleeve has an explicit initial stop and target. To test it properly, we would first need to invent a new strategy, and we already know that stop/target tuning on the old ORB bot did not help.

name: Sweep the risk-aversion lambda
one_line: Run the utility-based sizing formula at λ = 2, 3, and 4, then pick the smallest λ that still keeps drawdowns within the bot’s tolerance.
parameter_choices: λ ∈ {2,3,4}; choose by walk-forward performance and drawdown budget.
disagreement: Lower λ may maximize growth but higher λ may be safer and less brittle out of sample.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly says to evaluate λ = 2, 3, and 4, but it is only an exercise prompt, not empirical support. The drawdown-based selection rule is our own adaptation, not something the book states.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current fixed book sizing with the existing utility-based position sizer for the Q desk and set the live risk-aversion parameter to λ=3; keep the entry/exit logic unchanged. Use λ=2 and λ=4 only as pre-registered sensitivity checks, not as separate live rules.
review.mechanism: This only changes how hard we bet on the same signals. Lower λ raises exposure and can lift CAGR if the edge is real, but it also magnifies whipsaws and crash give-back in the leveraged ETF sleeves. Higher λ should de-lever the bot and reduce drawdowns/volatility, but it will not fix bad entries or exits.
review.data_missing: No external data is required. If the utility sizer is not already implemented, we still need to pin down its return-estimation window/lookback, but that is a model-spec choice, not a data gap.
review.already_tried_note: We have already varied exposure crudely (e.g., the 70% trend shadow desk and the fixed 50%/50% split), but not this formal λ sweep on a utility-based sizer.
review.overfit_note: This is a pure hyperparameter on leverage. With only three candidate values, it is easy to backfit the 2018-2026 sample, especially if the underlying μ/σ estimator is also a hidden knob. Integer-share rounding in a $1k account can make the apparent winner noisy.
review.expected_effect: Mostly risk control, not new alpha. Expect smaller λ to increase volatility and possibly return, larger λ to lower drawdown and smoothness. Any improvement is likely to be modest and second-order relative to the signal itself.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the utility sizer and do not tune any other sizing parameters on the full sample. Backtest current Q desk versus λ=2, 3, 4 on 2018-2026 using net returns after our stated costs, and compare daily CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Select one λ only once on 2018-2026, with the rule that it must beat the current Q desk on CAGR/Sharpe while not worsening max drawdown. Freeze that λ and run it unchanged on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for any minute-level segment). If the chosen λ does not improve both periods, or if the best λ changes by regime, reject the change.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap to run, uses only existing price data, and directly tests a real sizing lever rather than inventing a new signal. The evidence is weak, but the parameter set is tiny and the out-of-sample confirmation is clear enough to justify a pre-registered test.

name: Hard-cap gross leverage and sleeve notional
one_line: Limit total effective exposure from the 3× ETF sleeves to a fixed leverage cap instead of letting the book size float upward when signals are strong.
parameter_choices: Cap effective gross market exposure at 1.5x, 2.25x, or 3.0x equity (roughly 50%, 75%, or 100% of equity in 3× ETFs); test per-sleeve caps too.
disagreement: Strict caps may prevent wipeouts and crash damage, but they can also leave return on the table in strong trends.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general idea of not using extreme leverage, but it does not justify this exact hard cap or any sleeve-allocation rule for our Q desk. It is an anecdotal rule-of-thumb from one author ('I generally try not to exceed 10x, typically 5x'), not a backtest or multi-market result.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one sizing parameter: MAX_EFF_GROSS = 2.25x equity (75% of equity in 3x ETFs). Keep the existing entry/exit rules unchanged; if the trend sleeve and intraday sleeve together would exceed that cap, scale the intraday sleeve down so total 3x ETF notional never rises above 75% of equity.
review.mechanism: This can only help by shrinking the size of bad days: fewer losses from whipsaws, gap risk, and crash give-back when the bot is fully loaded. It does not improve signals or exits, and because the current desk already tops out at 3x effective gross exposure, this is mostly a blunt de-leveraging rule that is likely to cut upside as much as downside.
review.data_missing: None; this is pure price/position-sizing logic and can be backtested from existing minute and daily bars.
review.already_tried_note: The current desk already has an implicit exposure cap via fixed sleeve weights (50% trend, 50% intraday, 100% when trend is off). What has not been tested is a lower hard cap such as 2.25x or 1.5x gross exposure.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob, but it is easy to fit a lower cap to 2018-2026 and then discover it just reduced beta in the later period. Since the rule is monotone, the main risk is selecting a cap that flatters drawdown at the expense of compound return.
review.expected_effect: Likely lower max drawdown and lower day-to-day volatility, but also lower CAGR and probably lower absolute net profit. Any Sharpe improvement would only happen if current leverage is above the optimal point, which is not yet shown.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register MAX_EFF_GROSS = 2.25x and compare it against the current Q desk with all other rules frozen. Evaluate on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (using the synthetic 3x backfill where needed). Success requires higher out-of-sample net CAGR after costs and no worse max drawdown; if CAGR falls, or the gain is only in one period, reject the cap. Report daily net CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, and fraction of days at the cap.
review.verdict_reason: This is a blunt risk haircut, not an edge. It does not address the real weakness of the bot (whipsaw/crash timing), and the desk already has a practical exposure ceiling. A lower static cap is more likely to lower total profit than to create a durable improvement, so it is not worth a prime test slot unless you are specifically optimizing for lower drawdown rather than maximum net profit.

name: Size pair sleeves by equal notional and hedge residual beta
one_line: If a pair-trading sleeve is added, size both legs to equal dollar notional first, then hedge any meaningful leftover market exposure caused by whole-share rounding.
parameter_choices: Round to whole shares after equal-notional sizing; apply a portfolio hedge when residual beta exceeds 0.5%, 1%, or 2% of equity.
disagreement: Residual hedging can reduce drift and accidental directionality, but it adds cost and may be unnecessary for small leftovers.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the first half: pair legs should be sized by equal dollar notional rather than equal shares. It also gives a worked example that small rounding residuals can add up across many pairs and may warrant a portfolio hedge. But the specific residual-beta thresholds (0.5%, 1%, 2%) and the SPY-overlay trigger are our extrapolation, not stated in the source.
review.exact_rule_change: If we ever add a pair-trading sleeve, size both legs to equal dollar notional first, round to whole shares, and only hedge the aggregate residual market exposure with SPY if the open pair book’s net beta exceeds 1% of equity. This is bookkeeping, not a new alpha signal.
review.mechanism: It reduces accidental directional exposure from whole-share rounding, so a pair book behaves more like a market-neutral book and is less likely to drift with QQQ/SPY. In a larger multi-pair book that could trim drawdowns; in our $1k account the effect is likely tiny and the extra hedge trades may cost more than they save.
review.already_tried_note: No pair sleeve like this exists in the current Q desk, and it is not one of the explicitly rejected setups.
review.overfit_note: Few knobs and the rule is mechanical, so classic overfitting risk is low; the bigger risk is that any apparent benefit is just noise because the effect size is tiny.
review.expected_effect: At best a small reduction in accidental beta; likely no measurable alpha improvement on our account, and possibly slightly worse net returns after hedge costs.
review.test_protocol: Only as an ablation inside a future pair sleeve: freeze the pair-selection and entry/exit rules, then compare (a) equal shares, (b) equal notional with no residual hedge, and (c) equal notional with SPY hedge whenever residual beta >1% equity. Measure net CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, average net beta, and total trading cost on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 daily data. Keep it only if (c) beats (b) by at least 0.1 Sharpe or 5% max-drawdown improvement in both periods after costs; otherwise use equal-notional sizing only and drop the hedge.
review.verdict_reason: Equal-notional sizing is correct bookkeeping and should be built in if a pair sleeve is ever added, but the residual hedge is too small to matter in a $1k account and would likely be eaten by extra turnover. This does not improve the current Q desk’s known weaknesses and is not a standalone alpha idea.

name: Validate edge on 1R-normalized trades
one_line: Normalize every historical trade to 1R before comparing sleeves and regimes, so win rate, average win, average loss, and expectancy are measured on a like-for-like basis.
parameter_choices: Define 1R from the initial stop distance; aggregate results over 63-, 126-, and 252-day rolling windows and by sleeve/regime.
disagreement: Raw dollar PnL can mislead when size varies, but 1R normalization can hide how capital constraints affect compounding.
books: Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)

review.source_support_note: The source argues for uniform risk and judging trading by win rate, average win, and average loss, which is adjacent to R-based analysis. But it does not actually propose 1R-normalization, does not define an initial stop, and does not show that this re-expression would improve Midas specifically.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading-rule change; this is only a reporting layer. If we force a concrete definition, add an offline trade ledger that defines 1R as a pre-registered synthetic stop of 1.0x ATR(14) from entry, then report 63/126/252-day rolling expectancy in R by sleeve and regime. Do not use the metric to change live sizing unless it predicts out-of-sample PnL.
review.mechanism: In theory, R-normalization can separate 'good edge with small risk' from 'good dollars because the position was bigger,' which is useful when different sleeves use different risk budgets. For Midas, though, the live book is already sized mostly as fixed fractions of equity and the bot has no hard stops, so this is mostly a diagnostic. It may help future sizing decisions a little, but it does not directly fix whipsaws, crash give-back, or flat years.
review.data_missing: We have enough OHLCV data to simulate prices and trade paths, but true 1R is undefined unless we first pre-register an initial stop rule. No external data is missing; the missing piece is a stop convention, not market data.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We have compared raw PnL and sleeve performance, but not an explicit R-normalized ledger with a defined initial stop.
review.overfit_note: The result will depend heavily on the synthetic stop definition, the window length, and the regime buckets. That gives plenty of room to cherry-pick a version that looks better on 2018-2026 and fails on 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: Small indirect benefit at best. By itself it is unlikely to raise live PnL. At most it may improve how we rank sleeves/regimes for future sizing, but only if we add a real stop-based risk framework. Without that, it mostly relabels the same trades.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one stop proxy before looking at results: ATR(14) stop at 1.0x entry risk for every trade. Compute each completed trade in R, then compare current Q desk vs the same trades summarized by 63-, 126-, and 252-day rolling expectancy in R for each sleeve/regime. Build the sizing rule on 2018-2026, then freeze it and confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level rules). Keep the method only if the R-based ranking is stable across both periods and any size-allocation rule driven by it improves net CAGR/Sharpe without worsening max drawdown after costs versus the current Q desk.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly a reporting convention, not a trading edge. The current Q desk has no natural initial stop, so 1R has to be invented with a synthetic stop, which makes the result arbitrary and easy to overfit. Raw % equity and net PnL already capture the thing we actually care about for this bot; R-normalization is unlikely to change live decisions unless we add a separate stop-based sizing framework.

name: Stage down in crash regimes and hedge with inverse ETFs
one_line: When QQQ weakens enough, cut risk in steps and shift part of the exposure to cash or SQQQ until the market stabilizes, instead of waiting for a full trend flip.
parameter_choices: Use drawdown thresholds such as 5%, 10%, and 15% below a recent anchor; hedge fractions such as 0%, 25%, 50%, and 100%; restore only after a stabilization trigger.
disagreement: Faster crash protection may reduce drawdowns, but it can also cause the bot to miss violent rebound days.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book explicitly endorses scaling out during declines and using inverse ETFs as a hedge, so the direction matches. But it gives no objective trigger, anchor, or re-entry rule; the 10% below-200DMA threshold and the 50/50 cash-SQQQ split are our adaptation, not something the source proves.
review.exact_rule_change: Change only the overnight trend sleeve; leave the intraday noise-area sleeve untouched. If QQQ closes 10% or more below its 200-day SMA, replace the current cash-only below-200DMA state with a 50/50 split of cash and SQQQ inside that sleeve; otherwise keep the existing cash-only rule below the 200DMA. Restore the sleeve to normal TQQQ only after QQQ closes back above the 200DMA.
review.mechanism: This adds short exposure in deep bear regimes instead of sitting fully in cash, so the bot can offset some of the trend sleeve's crash give-back and recover faster after large drawdowns. The tradeoff is that it can lose money on sharp V-shaped rebounds and it adds inverse-ETF decay/spread costs.
review.data_missing: None beyond what we already have; the trigger uses QQQ daily closes/SMA, and the hedge can be backtested with real TQQQ/SQQQ data from 2018+ plus synthetic leveraged/inverse returns earlier.
review.already_tried_note: The current desk already has a binary trend/off regime at the 200DMA and already uses SQQQ intraday, but it has not tested a drawdown-triggered overnight hedge overlay on the trend sleeve.
review.overfit_note: There are many plausible variants (5/10/15 thresholds, different anchors, different hedge sizes, different re-entry rules) and only a few true crash regimes in the sample. This is classic curve-fit territory unless we freeze the rule before looking.
review.expected_effect: Likely lower max drawdown and faster recovery in deep selloffs, with some CAGR drag in sharp rebound periods. If it works at all, the benefit will show up in Calmar more than raw return.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: on the overnight trend sleeve, when QQQ closes 10% or more below its 200DMA, hold 50% cash / 50% SQQQ instead of cash-only; revert to normal TQQQ only after QQQ closes back above the 200DMA. Compare against the current Q desk with identical costs and fill assumptions on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Primary metrics: net CAGR, max drawdown, and Calmar. Accept only if both periods improve Calmar and reduce max drawdown versus baseline while losing no more than 10% of CAGR; otherwise reject. Do not tune the threshold after seeing results.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our data, cheap to test, and directly targets the trend sleeve's worst failure mode. The evidence is only conceptual and the overfit risk is real, but this is a bounded one-parameter overlay rather than a new strategy, so it is worth a pre-registered test.

name: Pyramid the trend sleeve on new highs
one_line: Add to the trend sleeve in fixed tranches as the position makes fresh highs, rather than keeping one static entry size.
parameter_choices: Add 25%, 50%, or 75% of the initial tranche after each new-high threshold or after a fixed percent advance above entry.
disagreement: Pyramiding can improve trend capture if persistence is real, but it can also magnify whipsaws and drawdowns when the trend fails.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The quoted passage supports the general principle of adding to winners as a trend extends, but it does not specify any trigger, tranche size, cap, or instrument. Turning that into a QQQ/TQQQ pyramiding rule is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Modify only the trend sleeve: while QQQ is above its 200-day SMA, keep the existing 50% overnight TQQQ starter tranche. Each time QQQ closes at a new 20-trading-day closing high since the last add, buy another 25% of equity in TQQQ at the next 15:55 NY close. Because the account is cash-only, that naturally takes the overnight trend sleeve from 50% to 75% to 100% if the trend keeps making new highs.
review.mechanism: This tries to compound into persistent upside instead of treating every trend day the same. If the rally keeps extending, the bot puts more cash to work only after the market has proven itself, which could lift CAGR in long bull runs. The downside is obvious: it increases exposure late in trends, so it can worsen crash give-back and whipsaws when the 200-day filter finally flips.
review.data_missing: None; this can be computed from QQQ daily closes, and the existing synthetic 3x pre-TQQQ backtest setup is enough for the trend sleeve.
review.already_tried_note: Not the same as the rejected ORB/stop-target tweaks, but it is still just a position-sizing overlay to an existing sleeve rather than a genuinely new edge.
review.overfit_note: Two tunables on one asset, with results likely dominated by a few regime shifts. It is easy to optimize the high-watermark window or tranche size on 2018-2026 bull runs and then disappoint in 1999-2017 or 2008-style drawdowns.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a modest lift in return during persistent uptrends. More likely: higher volatility and deeper drawdowns, with the out-of-sample edge depending on whether the added leverage in late-stage trends beats the extra crash give-back.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one rule: 20-trading-day new-high trigger, 25% add size, same fill/cost model as the current desk. Backtest three versions: current Q desk, pyramided Q desk, and a level-matched static trend control with the same maximum overnight gross exposure. Evaluate 2018-2026 first, then confirm on 1999-2017. Require pyramiding to beat the current desk on both periods in annualized net return and Calmar, and to beat the level-matched static control on at least the out-of-sample period; if it only wins because it uses more leverage, discard it.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible and cheap, but the prior is weak: this is mostly a leverage/money-management tweak on an already levered trend sleeve, not a fix for the bot's known whipsaw/crash problems. I would not spend priority on it before stronger trend exits, regime filters, or volatility sizing.

name: Conservative execution-cost model
one_line: Replace the flat 1 bp per side assumption with a decomposed model for spread, impact, partial fills, rejections, and cleanup trades.
parameter_choices: Spread proxy from observed prices or daily H/L/C; impact as square-root or log of size/volatility; explicit fill-rate, rejection, and residual-cleanup penalties; auction-aware fills for MOC/On-Close orders.
disagreement: Sources differ on the best spread estimator, the right realized-spread horizon, whether auction fills should be modeled explicitly, and whether large-order impact is better fit by square-root or logarithmic scaling.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients of the proposal: slippage/spread should be modeled, costs should be decomposed into spread plus impact, execution delay and partial fills can erase edge, and close/auction execution matters. But none of the excerpts validates this exact decomposed model or its coefficients for our ETFs and bar data; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No signal change. Replace the current flat 1 bp/side friction with a conservative all-in-shortfall model in the backtester: per side cost = max(1 bp, 20-day Roll half-spread estimated from 1-minute bars) + sigma20 × sqrt(order_notional / ADV20); if an order is not fully filled, cancel the residual and charge one extra half-spread for the cleanup trade. Model QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ MOC exits as fills at the close auction, not the last regular bar.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha; it makes us stop believing tiny intraday profits that vanish once spread, impact, and failed fills are priced in. If it helps, it will be by cutting marginal intraday trades and overconfident sizing, especially around the open/close where costs are worst.
review.data_missing: We can proxy spread, volatility, and ADV from 1-minute OHLCV, but we do not have bid/ask quotes, tick data, auction prints/imbalances, or broker fill/rejection logs. True partial-fill, rejection, and cleanup-cost calibration is therefore missing.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already uses a flat 1 bp/side plus SEC fees and next-5-minute fills, so cost modeling is not new. What is new here is only the decomposition and the attempt to model partial fills/auction execution.
review.overfit_note: With only OHLCV, spread, impact, and cleanup are weakly identified. A richer model can be tuned to make 2018-2026 look better or worse without telling us much about future live fills.
review.expected_effect: Lower and more realistic backtest PnL, lower trade counts, and likely fewer marginal intraday entries; useful for screening false positives, but unlikely to add alpha by itself.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact cost formula and do not tune coefficients on the outcome. Run the current Q desk twice on 2018-2026 and 1999-2017: (a) current flat 1 bp/side model, (b) conservative decomposed model. Compare net CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and the gap between simulated and realized paper-trade slippage where live fills exist. Accept the change only if it reduces the live fill-vs-simulated cost error by at least 25% and the strategy still beats the current desk in both periods; otherwise keep it as a stress-test only.
review.verdict_reason: Worth doing as a fixed pessimistic stress test, but not worth spending a scarce alpha-test slot on until we have quote or fill logs. With only OHLCV, the spread/impact/partial-fill decomposition is underidentified and can be made arbitrarily conservative without teaching us much about future live performance.

name: Delay intraday start past the open
one_line: Push the first intraday check later to avoid the wide-spread, noisy post-open period.
parameter_choices: Current 10:00 check vs 10:30 or 11:00 start; keep a hard no-trade window for the first 15-30 minutes after the open.
disagreement: No substantive disagreement; the sources are aligned that the open is the worst liquidity window.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources clearly support avoiding the first 15–30 minutes after the open because spreads are wider and price discovery is messy. But Midas already starts the intraday sleeve at 10:00 ET, i.e. 30 minutes after the 9:30 open, so extending the delay to 10:30 or 11:00 is an extrapolation beyond what the sources explicitly say.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the intraday noise-area sleeve so the first eligible signal check is 10:30 ET instead of 10:00 ET; keep the existing 30-minute check cadence and all other rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: The first hour of trading is often the noisiest part of the session, with wider spreads, opening-auction imbalances, and fast reversals that can fake out short-horizon band signals. Waiting until 10:30 ET should reduce bad fills and false breakouts in TQQQ/SQQQ, which may improve the quality of intraday trades even if it means missing some early moves.
review.data_missing: None for a pure price-bar test.
review.already_tried_note: This is not on the rejected-ideas list, but it is a close tweak to the live intraday sleeve, which already starts at 10:00 ET. We have not separately tested and rejected 10:30/11:00 starts.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob, but time-of-day effects are easy to data-mine. If we sweep 10:00 vs 10:30 vs 11:00 and pick the winner, that is likely overfit. Pre-register one start time.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small effect either way. Best case: fewer trades, slightly better average trade quality, lower slippage, and marginally higher net PnL. Worst case: we simply miss some of the sleeve's best early-day signals and underperform.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register a single variant: first intraday check at 10:30 ET, with the same 30-minute cadence afterward and the same band/VWAP exit rules. Backtest the modified desk against the current desk on 2018-2026 with real minute data, then confirm on the unseen pre-2018 period using the same synthetic-3x framework already used for Midas. Score primary success on total net daily return and Sharpe after all costs, and secondary on intraday-sleeve expectancy, trade count, and max drawdown. Adopt only if the modified rule improves out-of-sample net return and Sharpe in each period without worsening drawdown; otherwise keep the 10:00 baseline.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully price-data testable, and directly touches the intraday sleeve. The skeptical point is that Midas already avoids the first 30 minutes, so the incremental edge from pushing the start to 10:30 ET is probably small. Still, this is worth one pre-registered backtest because it costs nothing and could reduce bad early-session fills.

name: Daily spread gate for intraday trades
one_line: Skip or downsize intraday entries when QQQ's estimated spread is unusually wide.
parameter_choices: Use a daily spread proxy and trigger at a threshold such as the top decile or top quartile of recent spread estimates; optionally downsize instead of skipping.
disagreement: The estimator family varies, but the rule direction is consistent: wider-spread days are worse.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: B1 explicitly recommends estimating spread from daily OHLC/close and using that proxy to skip or downsize intraday trades on high-spread days. That is essentially this idea. The support is for the filter concept, not for a proven edge on liquid QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ or under our fixed-cost model.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday sleeve only: at the start of each session, compute QQQ’s Abdi-Ranaldo daily spread estimate from the last 20 completed daily bars. If that spread proxy is in the top quartile of its trailing 20-day history, set the intraday sleeve to 0% for that day; otherwise run the existing intraday logic unchanged. Do not change the trend sleeve.
review.mechanism: This is a cost/liquidity gate. On days when the tape is unusually expensive or stressed, the intraday noise-area trades are more likely to get eaten by slippage and false breakouts. Skipping those days should reduce bleed and maybe avoid some bad regime days. It does not fix the trend sleeve’s whipsaws or crash give-back; it only tries to improve intraday net expectancy.
review.data_missing: None.
review.already_tried_note: We have already stress-tested execution-cost assumptions and spread sensitivity on earlier bots, but not this exact rule that turns the intraday sleeve off based on a lagged daily spread proxy.
review.overfit_note: Only a couple of simple knobs, but the signal is weak and likely correlated with volatility rather than true spread. Easy to fit a threshold on 2018-2026 and discover it was just a volatility filter. QQQ is also very liquid, so the true effect may be tiny.
review.expected_effect: Probably small. Best case: a modest lift from avoiding the worst-liquidity days and slightly fewer bad intraday fills. More likely: near-zero impact, because QQQ spreads are already tight and the proxy may mostly identify volatile days that can also be good trading days.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule before looking. Use the same cost model as the current Q desk. Backtest the full bot with and without the spread gate on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and on minute-level years where applicable). Primary metrics: whole-bot net daily Sharpe and CAGR; secondary: max drawdown, intraday sleeve Sharpe, average trades/day. Require improvement in both periods on the primary metric, with no worse max drawdown. If the gate only helps one period or only reduces trades without improving net Sharpe, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is fully backtestable with data we already have, cheap to run, and it is a genuine execution filter rather than a rehash of an already-rejected setup. The expected edge is probably small, but the test is fast enough that we should settle it instead of guessing.

name: Volatility- and size-aware intraday sizing
one_line: Scale the intraday sleeve down when QQQ volatility, relative order size, or trading rate imply higher market impact.
parameter_choices: Penalty driven by realized minute volatility or ATR, order size as a fraction of ADV, and execution duration; baseline square-root impact (gamma around 0.5), but test a logarithmic alternative for larger clips.
disagreement: Most items point to higher volatility and size increasing impact, but one cited study says a logarithmic curve fits large orders better than square-root.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients of an impact model — volatility, relative size, duration and turnover matter, and square-root/log forms are common — but they do not directly justify a tiny-account QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ sizing rule. The leap from 'impact scales with size/volatility' to 'cut this bot's intraday sleeve' is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the fixed intraday sleeve size with a volatility-scaled size: at each 30-minute checkpoint, set intraday notional = base intraday allocation × clip(0.25, 1.00, sqrt(σ_med/σ_t)), where σ_t is the existing 14-day average absolute move-from-open volatility for QQQ at that time and σ_med is its 252-day rolling median; ignore the order-size term because it is effectively zero in our account.
review.mechanism: If the intraday sleeve is really paying for spread/adverse selection on noisy tape, cutting size on volatile days could reduce those losses and avoid the worst slippage days. But on a $1,000 account trading QQQ-family ETFs, true size-driven market impact is likely tiny, so any improvement would mostly come from a volatility regime filter, not from the size/impact model itself.
review.data_missing: We can backtest the volatility proxy from minute bars and the order-size-to-ADV proxy from daily volume, but we do not have quote/L2/tick data to validate actual spread/impact changes. That makes the size-aware part mostly unobservable.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly. We already assume flat 1 bp per side costs and run live shadow variants, but we have not tested volatility-scaled intraday sizing on the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: There are not many knobs if we pre-register the floor and exponent, but the expected edge is small, so a modest in-sample improvement can easily be noise. The size term is especially weakly identified without quote data.
review.expected_effect: At best a small reduction in losses and slippage on high-volatility days. More likely the effect is close to zero because the orders are tiny versus ADV, so shrinking size will mainly reduce gross exposure rather than true execution cost.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule: gamma = 0.5 via the square root, floor = 0.25, and no separate size penalty. Backtest current Q desk versus this variant with identical entries/exits and the same cost model on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (QQQ minute data where available). Compare daily net return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and average net PnL per intraday trade. Accept only if both periods improve versus baseline and max drawdown is not worse by more than 2 percentage points. If the gain disappears when you remove the volatility scaling, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: The market-impact rationale is valid for large orders, but this bot trades tiny clips in extremely liquid ETFs. Without quote/L2 data, the size component cannot be validated, and with a $1,000 account it is unlikely to matter enough to justify a dedicated test. If we want a cheap experiment, test the volatility filter alone; do not spend time on a full size-aware impact model.

name: Reduce intraday signal frequency
one_line: Test a 60-minute intraday check cycle instead of the current 30-minute cycle to cut churn.
parameter_choices: 30-minute checks vs 60-minute checks; optionally keep the same band logic and only change scan frequency.
disagreement: No substantive disagreement; the trade-off is simply fewer opportunities versus lower turnover.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The books support the general principle that frequent trading and high-turnover momentum are vulnerable to costs, so reducing scan frequency is a reasonable extrapolation. They do not specifically advocate an hourly scan or this exact QQQ noise-area rule.
review.exact_rule_change: Change the intraday noise-area sleeve from 30-minute checks to 60-minute checks: evaluate the same QQQ band once per hour at 10:00, 11:00, 12:00, 13:00, 14:00, and 15:00 New York time, while keeping the existing band logic, VWAP exit, next-5-minute-bar fills, and max-one-round-trip-per-day cap unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help only if a meaningful chunk of the 30-minute triggers are just noise. Fewer checks mean fewer entries and exits, so less spread/impact drag and less churn. The downside is obvious: you will also miss some short-lived moves and may delay exits, so gross alpha could fall faster than costs are saved.
review.data_missing: None; our 1-minute QQQ and ETF history is enough to backtest hourly versus 30-minute scans, including the synthetic-3x pre-2018 framework we already use.
