review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest rejected item is noise-area on IWM/DIA, but that is a different underlying and not a scan-frequency change.
review.overfit_note: Only one obvious knob is changing. The main risk is regime sensitivity, not parameter explosion; if we pre-register 60 minutes versus 30 minutes, there is little room to data-mine.
review.expected_effect: At best a small net gain from lower turnover; at worst a modest loss from slower exits and fewer captured breakouts. This is more of a cost/churn tweak than a new alpha source, so I would expect a small effect either way.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register a binary comparison: current 30-minute intraday scans versus 60-minute scans, with all else unchanged. Run on 2018-2026 as the build period and then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (using the existing minute/daily framework; 2007-2017 is the minute-data overlap check). Compare both the intraday sleeve alone and the full Q desk. Primary metrics: net return/day after the stated costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Adopt 60 minutes only if it improves net return/day and Sharpe in both periods, with no worse max drawdown than the current rule; otherwise keep 30 minutes.
review.verdict_reason: It is a cheap, fully data-feasible one-line rule change, and the only plausible benefit is lower churn in the noisiest sleeve. The support is weak-to-partial rather than direct, and I would not expect a big lift because costs are already low, but it is still worth one pre-registered test before discarding it.

name: Volume-profile-aware execution slicing
one_line: For larger ETF orders, slice fills across the session using the expected intraday volume curve instead of one-shot market orders.
parameter_choices: TWAP equal slices, VWAP slices proportional to historical minute volume, or POV fixed percentage of current volume; choose the number of slices n and smooth the volume curve first.
disagreement: Equal-split TWAP is optimal under linear impact, while VWAP/POV are preferred when the volume forecast is reliable; naive market orders are only acceptable on very liquid, tight-spread names.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly describe VWAP/TWAP/POV execution, splitting parent orders into child orders, and using historical intraday volume profiles with smoothing. That is essentially the same as volume-profile-aware slicing. The sources support the execution mechanism, though not a Midas-specific performance claim.
review.exact_rule_change: No new alpha sleeve. For any ETF order in the Q desk, replace the one-shot fill with a VWAP-style execution schedule: split the parent order into 6 child orders, weighted by the smoothed historical minute-volume curve for QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ (preserve the open/close spikes; use the curve shape rather than equal time slices). If we ever need a fallback, use TWAP equal slices with the same 6-child schedule.
review.mechanism: If the parent order is genuinely large relative to liquidity, filling more when the market naturally trades more should reduce impact and spread paid per share. Smoothing the curve avoids chasing noisy volume spikes. But for Midas’ current $1,000 account and liquid ETFs, the order size is so small that the benefit is likely tiny, while spreading fills across time adds drift/opportunity risk.
review.data_missing: We can backtest a bar-based proxy from our minute OHLCV/volume data, but we do not have order book, quotes, or true child-order fill data. Also, TQQQ/SQQQ minute data only exist in our main panel from 2018+, so any 1999–2017 confirmation would have to use QQQ as a proxy rather than the actual traded ETFs.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We have rejected other execution/ORB-style ideas, but not volume-profile-aware slicing itself.
review.overfit_note: There are only a few knobs, but the apparent benefit will be dominated by how we simulate fills, not by a stable edge. With no quote/order-book data, it is easy to backfit a schedule that looks good in 2018–2026 and then evaporates in a different regime.
review.expected_effect: Likely near-zero to slightly negative for the current bot. On 5–10 share ETF orders, the impact saved is probably smaller than the extra drift from delaying fills. It may matter only if the account becomes much larger or we trade less liquid names.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one simple comparison only: current one-shot fill rule vs a fixed 6-slice VWAP schedule using the historical minute-volume curve. Evaluate on the actual ETF trades in 2018–2026 first, then on an unseen earlier proxy set (QQQ-based execution proxy where TQQQ/SQQQ minute data are unavailable). Primary metric: implementation shortfall per executed dollar and net strategy return after costs. Decision rule: only adopt if the sliced version improves both periods, with no worse max drawdown, and saves enough to matter (at least ~0.5 bp per executed dollar). If the improvement is smaller than that, treat it as noise and stop.
review.verdict_reason: This is an execution micro-optimization for very liquid ETFs with tiny order sizes. With a $1,000 cash account and our current 1 bp/side cost model, the expected benefit is too small to measure reliably and likely too small to matter. We also lack quote/order-book data, so any apparent gain would be mostly a fill-simulation artifact. It is a better idea only after the book is much larger.

name: Passive-first, aggressive-finish execution
one_line: Try a passive limit near the band or VWAP first, then force completion on the next bar if the order is still unfilled.
parameter_choices: Passive-attempt duration: one bar or a short catch-up window; limit placement at the near side, band, or an ATR-based offset; completion with a marketable order if still short; be more aggressive on exits than entries.
disagreement: Some sources favor immediate marketable orders because they guarantee fills, while others favor limits for price improvement; the right choice depends on urgency and fill probability.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the generic execution tradeoff: limit orders can improve price but may miss fills, and a passive attempt followed by an aggressive catch-up leg is standard advice. None of the quoted items gives direct evidence that this exact passive-first / next-bar-completion rule improves this ETF sleeve.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday sleeve only: on each QQQ noise-area signal, enter the ETF with a passive limit at the near side (proxied by the current ETF last price) for 1 five-minute bar; if any shares are still unfilled at the next bar open, cancel/replace the remainder with a marketable order. Keep exits marketable immediately on the first bar.
review.mechanism: If the signal has a little more room to run, a passive entry can save spread/impact on the shares that would have filled anyway. The one-bar catch-up avoids missing the trade entirely. Making exits aggressive is sensible because unwind costs usually get worse once the move fades or reverses.
review.data_missing: We do not have bid/ask quotes, queue position, or true order-book fills, so passive-fill probability and partial fills can only be approximated from OHLC bars.
review.already_tried_note: The current bot/backtests already assume marketable next-5-minute-bar fills with a fixed slippage model. It has not tested passive-first entries with catch-up completion.
review.overfit_note: If the rule is fixed ex ante, there are only a couple of knobs. But the result will be sensitive to the unobservable fill model; tuning the limit offset or timeout would get fragile fast.
review.expected_effect: Small positive at best. It can reduce implementation shortfall on liquid ETF entries, but the gain is likely only a few bps per round trip and can be wiped out by missed fills or delayed entries. Aggressive exits should limit that damage.
review.test_protocol: Freeze signal logic and cost assumptions. Compare current execution (marketable at next 5-minute open for both entry and exit) vs passive-first entries with a 1-bar timeout and immediate marketable exits on the intraday sleeve only. Use 2018-2026 as the build set and 1999-2017 as the unseen confirmation set, with the same synthetic 3x proxy the desk already uses where needed. Score net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, fill rate, and implementation shortfall. Keep the change only if both periods improve net return and Sharpe without worse drawdown or a materially lower fill rate.
review.verdict_reason: This is cheap and mechanically testable with our bar data, and it is not a rehash of the rejected ORB/gap ideas. The expected edge is small, but execution savings are one of the few things that can still help this bot, so it is worth one pre-registered test rather than a bigger project.

name: Passive-order time-in-force test
one_line: For passive ETF entries, compare Day versus GTC persistence to see whether extra fill rate is worth the stale-fill risk.
parameter_choices: Day vs GTC; optional max-age before cancel/reprice of 1-3 bars.
disagreement: GTC should reduce missed entries, but Day may avoid stale fills and unwanted late executions.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general concept that Day and GTC are standard time-in-force settings that control order persistence. It does not provide evidence that GTC improves P&L, nor does it compare Day vs GTC on this bot’s kind of signals. The performance claim is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: For any passive ETF entry on the Q desk, submit the order as GTC instead of Day, with a hard cancel/reprice after 3 five-minute bars if still unfilled.
review.mechanism: GTC can reduce missed entries when a valid setup persists past the first bar or even the first session. The tradeoff is stale fills: the order may execute later after the edge has decayed or the market has moved away, which is especially dangerous for momentum-style entries.
review.data_missing: We can approximate touch-and-fill behavior from OHLCV bars, but we do not have quotes, queue position, or partial-fill data. That means the true fill rate and adverse-selection cost of resting passive orders are only roughly modeled.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and not the same as prior stop/target or breakout tests. This is an execution persistence tweak, not a previously tested alpha sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Only a couple of knobs, but the result can hinge on the chosen max-age and the exact passive limit price. With bar data, it is easy to make the fill model look better than it really is.
review.expected_effect: Small increase in fill rate, but likely tiny net impact. The most likely outcome is flat to slightly worse after stale-fill and adverse-selection costs.
review.test_protocol: Only test this on a passive-entry variant of the existing Q desk, keeping the signal logic, size, and limit price identical. Compare Day vs GTC on the same historical signals. Primary metric: net return per day and Sharpe after costs; secondary metrics: fill rate, missed-signal rate, and average adverse selection at fill. Run the comparison on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level validation). Keep the change only if GTC improves net return/day and Sharpe in both periods without worsening max drawdown.
review.verdict_reason: This is an execution-detail tweak, not a real edge for the current Q desk. The live bot mostly uses marketable/MOC logic, so TIF only matters if we redesign it to use passive limit entries. With our data we cannot model true resting-order fills or queue priority, and the likely benefit from slightly higher fill rate is too small versus stale-fill risk and already-low trading costs.

name: No-trade region around target sleeve weights
one_line: Only rebalance a sleeve when the current weight drifts far enough from target to justify the trading cost.
parameter_choices: Deadband in percentage points of sleeve weight; test roughly 1-5 pp or 10-20% of the target weight.
disagreement: A wider deadband cuts turnover and costs, but too wide increases tracking error and can miss timely reallocations.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly endorses a no-trade region for rebalancing momentum-style portfolios, so the core mechanism matches. But it does not test this specific two-sleeve QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ cash-account bot, and it does not justify a precise deadband width; 5 pp is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a 5 percentage-point deadband to every scheduled sleeve rebalance. At each allocation check, only trade if a sleeve’s current weight is outside target ±5 pp; otherwise leave the position unchanged. Use the same band for both sleeves; a true regime flip (e.g., 50%→0% or 0%→50/100%) still trades because it is far outside the band.
review.mechanism: Stops the bot from paying spread/impact and SEC fees to chase tiny drifts in sleeve weights. On a $1,000 cash account with whole shares, small price moves can force pointless one-share adjustments; a deadband should reduce turnover and slightly smooth P&L without changing the signal logic. It will not fix whipsaws or bad regime calls, only micro-friction.
review.data_missing: None; existing minute bars plus position/accounting data are enough.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list, and it is not the same as the old ORB stop/target tweaks. We have not already ruled out no-trade bands for the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but it is easy to tune the deadband on 2018-2026 until it fits small-sample noise. Because the account is tiny and shares are discrete, results may depend on price regime and rounding quirks.
review.expected_effect: Small positive at best. Expect a modest drop in turnover and trading costs, with little change in gross edge. If the current backtest already effectively rounds to whole shares, the gain could be near zero; if it rebalances often, Sharpe may tick up slightly from lower friction.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the current Q desk as baseline. Re-run it with a fixed 5 pp deadband on 2018-2026 using identical prices, fill assumptions, and fee model. Compare net CAGR, daily Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and total trading cost. Require the deadband version to beat baseline on net return or Sharpe and to cut turnover meaningfully (e.g. at least 10%) in 2018-2026; then confirm the same parameter on unseen 1999-2017 synthetic 3x history and require non-worse results there too. If it only helps one period or only reduces turnover with no net performance gain, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible, cheap, and directly aligned with transaction-cost control. The expected edge is small, and the bot may already approximate this via whole-share rounding, but it is a legitimate low-cost test rather than a new strategy.

name: Sparse long-only allocation for future multi-asset sleeves
one_line: For any added multi-asset sleeve, compare a sparse long-only optimizer against equal-weight or volatility-weighted baselines.
parameter_choices: Sparsity penalty or max-name cap; allow only positive weights and tune the number of active holdings.
disagreement: Sparsity should reduce turnover and trading costs, but it may concentrate risk too much versus simpler allocations.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source only says that long-only constraints tend to create many zero weights and higher turnover. That is a generic portfolio-theory warning, not evidence that a sparse long-only optimizer beats equal-weight or inverse-vol weighting in trading. The proposed comparison is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the current Q desk. If we later add a true basket sleeve, use a long-only allocation with a hard cap of 3 active names and compare it against equal-weight and inverse-vol baselines on the same sleeve.
review.mechanism: If a future sleeve has several liquid names, a sparse long-only cap could concentrate capital in the few names with the strongest forecast and avoid paying for weak marginal holdings. The downside is that, without a real cross-sectional edge, it mostly just increases concentration and estimation error. It does not address the current bot's main problems: QQQ trend whipsaws and crash give-back.
review.data_missing: No extra market data is needed, but this only makes sense after defining a real multi-asset sleeve and a forecast/ranking rule. The current Q desk has no basket sleeve to which this allocation method can be applied.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The current bot does use a 50/50 split between two sleeves, but that is not a sparse multi-asset allocation test.
review.overfit_note: This is mostly an allocation heuristic with several hidden degrees of freedom: universe, signal, covariance estimate, penalty/cap, and rebalance timing. On a $1k account, whole-share rounding and small cost differences make it easy to fit noise and call it skill.
review.expected_effect: At best, modest turnover reduction if a future basket sleeve has a few truly better names. More likely, no net improvement after costs and potentially worse drawdowns from overconcentration.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend test budget on this for the current bot. If a basket sleeve is added later, pre-register the universe, ranking signal, and rebalance rule; then compare equal-weight, inverse-vol, and sparse long-only cap-3 on 2018-2026, freeze the choice, and confirm on 1999-2017. Require the sparse rule to beat the better baseline on net CAGR and Sharpe in both periods, with turnover not higher and max drawdown not worse by more than 5 percentage points.
review.verdict_reason: This is not a current edge for Midas; it is a portfolio-construction choice for a future basket sleeve that does not exist yet. The evidence is only a generic warning about long-only sparsity, and the knob count is high enough to overfit our sample. It is not worth testing now on the live Q desk.

name: Liquidity-aware universe filter
one_line: Prefer larger, more liquid names when execution quality matters, and downsize or ഒഴിവe smaller-cap names with more asymmetric trading costs.
parameter_choices: Market-cap proxy and dollar-volume cutoff; compare liquid-large-cap universe versus broader universe.
disagreement: Tighter liquidity filters should lower spread and impact costs, but they shrink the opportunity set.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general proposition that smaller stocks have more asymmetric trading costs, so liquidity matters. But it does not directly prescribe this exact filter, and it does not show any benefit for a QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ-only desk.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the current Q desk. If we add a separate stock/ETF sleeve, hard-skip any name whose 20-day average dollar volume is below $50M; otherwise allow it. No market-cap input required.
review.mechanism: This only helps by avoiding slippage and fill asymmetry in thin names. That can matter for a broad stock sleeve, but it does not fix the current bot's real problems (trend whipsaws, crash give-back, or flat intraday years) because those trade only ultra-liquid Nasdaq-100 ETFs.
review.data_missing: We can compute 20-day average dollar volume from OHLCV, but we do not have shares-outstanding/market-cap data, bid-ask quotes, or L2 spread data. So the market-cap part of the idea is not directly testable.
review.already_tried_note: Not tested as a standalone filter on the Q desk. The only place it would matter is the thin-name stock sleeve world, which overlaps with already rejected small-cap/stock-in-play ideas.
review.overfit_note: Only one threshold, but it is easy to tune the cutoff to 2018-2026 and get a false win. Also the effect will likely be tiny on the current ETF-only desk.
review.expected_effect: Near-zero on the current Q desk. On a future broad stock sleeve it may cut slippage a bit, but likely at the cost of fewer trades and a smaller opportunity set.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend a current-bot test on this idea. If a separate stock sleeve is created, pre-register one filter: 20-day average dollar volume >= $50M. Compare identical strategy rules with vs. without the filter on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-bar rules). Judge by net PnL after costs, slippage-adjusted Sharpe, and trade count; require improvement in both periods.
review.verdict_reason: The current bot already trades only QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ, which are among the most liquid US instruments, so a liquidity universe filter will not materially improve execution or fix the desk's actual failure modes. This is only relevant if we build a new, broader stock sleeve.

name: Quote/LOB imbalance filter for intraday entries
one_line: If quote or order-book data is added later, use imbalance as a skip or size-up filter for the intraday sleeve.
parameter_choices: Imbalance threshold and lookback window; test a simple long/short cutoff versus no filter.
disagreement: Order-book imbalance may improve short-horizon follow-through, but it may add noise or be too unstable to help.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general microstructure claim that order-book imbalance can matter for short-horizon price moves. It does not actually state this Q-desk rule, a cutoff, a lookback, or show that using imbalance as an entry skip/size filter survives costs in this specific bot. The proposed filter is an extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: At each scheduled intraday entry check, compute QQQ top-of-book quote imbalance over the prior 5 minutes, I = (bid_size - ask_size) / (bid_size + ask_size). Take the existing TQQQ long only if I >= +0.20 and the existing SQQQ short only if I <= -0.20; otherwise skip the entry. Leave all exits unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help the intraday sleeve by avoiding entries when displayed liquidity is leaning against the trade, which should reduce false breakouts and chop-driven whipsaws and improve the chance the move continues to the band/VWAP exit. It may also cut turnover and slippage by skipping marginal signals. It will not directly fix the trend sleeve’s 200-day whipsaws or crash give-back, and quote imbalance can be noisy or spoofed.
review.data_missing: Historical quote or order-book data for QQQ (at least top-of-book bid/ask sizes, ideally depth snapshots) aligned to the 30-minute entry timestamps. Current dataset has OHLCV bars only, so we cannot compute imbalance.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tested. It is also not the same as the rejected ORB/noise-area ideas; this is a microstructure filter on the existing intraday sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Microstructure filters are unstable, regime-dependent, and easy to overfit. Even with only one cutoff and one lookback, the real design space explodes once we start choosing quote vs depth, averaging scheme, asymmetry, and venue handling. Without a large historical quote sample, any edge is likely noise.
review.expected_effect: If real, it should raise intraday trade quality more than trade count: fewer entries, slightly better hit rate, and lower slippage/false-trigger losses. The likely effect size is small and could disappear after costs or in different regimes.
review.test_protocol: Do not test with current data. If we later source historical quote/L2 data, pre-register one version only: 5-minute average QQQ top-of-book imbalance with a +/-0.20 cutoff. Compare the current intraday sleeve versus the imbalance-gated sleeve, with identical exits, timestamps, and cost model. Primary metrics: net daily return, Sharpe, and max drawdown; secondary: trade expectancy and turnover. Require improvement in both the build period and the holdout period, with no drawdown worsening. Do not tune the cutoff on the same data.
review.verdict_reason: Plausible as an intraday filter, but impossible to evaluate with our current dataset because we do not have historical quote/order-book data. It is not worth pretending we can validate it from bars alone. If we later buy L1/L2 history, it becomes a cheap, clean filter test; until then, defer it.

name: Staggered cross-asset switches
one_line: When flipping between TQQQ and SQQQ, test whether staggering the switch across bars beats trading both legs at once.
parameter_choices: Delay the second leg by 1-2 bars, or route the switch on the higher-volume bar only.
disagreement: Staggering may reduce cross-impact, but it can increase gap risk if the market moves during the delay.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The cited book supports the general notion that cross-impact exists across assets and matters in impact estimation. It does not actually recommend staggering a TQQQ/SQQQ flip; the proposed delay is our own execution extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: On any direct flip between TQQQ and SQQQ, execute the exit at the next 5-minute bar open, then wait exactly 1 additional 5-minute bar before entering the opposite ETF at that bar open. Keep all other Q-desk rules unchanged.
review.mechanism: The only plausible benefit is shaving a bit of transient spread/impact if two back-to-back ETF orders step on each other. But with TQQQ/SQQQ on a $1,000 account, any execution savings are likely tiny; the 1-bar delay adds 5 minutes of unhedged market exposure and can miss the reversal move.
review.data_missing: We can simulate the stagger on our minute bars and current fill model, but we do not have quote/order-book data to measure real cross-impact or spread improvement. Bar data only gives a coarse proxy for the execution effect.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and no direct prior test of staggered TQQQ/SQQQ flips is mentioned.
review.overfit_note: There is only one real knob if fixed at a 1-bar delay, but the effect size is likely tiny. If we start searching 1 vs 2 bars or adding volume-based routing, the in-sample winner will almost certainly be noise.
review.expected_effect: Probably flat to slightly negative. Any cross-impact savings are likely below the noise floor for liquid ETFs and a $1k book, while the delay adds gap risk.
review.test_protocol: If we ever test it, pre-register only one variant: 1-bar delay, no volume filter, no search over other delays. Compare against the current immediate flip on every TQQQ/SQQQ reversal event using the same signal timestamps and the same 5-minute-open fill model. Evaluate switch-level average net P&L, total CAGR, Sharpe, and max drawdown on 2018-2026 first; only if it improves net P&L per flip and does not worsen drawdown should we even look at 1999-2017 / proxy data. Do not tune parameters on the full sample.
review.verdict_reason: This is a micro-execution tweak, not a real edge, and our current assumptions already model fills at the next 5-minute bar with ~1 bp per side costs. On a $1,000 account trading ultra-liquid ETFs, any cross-impact savings are too small to matter, while the 1-bar delay introduces real market-risk. We also lack quote/order-book data to verify the supposed mechanism, so this is not worth a dedicated test now.

name: Order-flow speed bumps
one_line: Add hard throttles so the bot cannot churn too fast: cap daily entries/exits and block same-direction re-entry after an exit or stop.
parameter_choices: Max one entry and one exit per symbol per day; cooldown of 1-3 bars after exit; no same-direction re-entry after a stop.
disagreement: Speed bumps should cut churn and slippage, but they may also prevent useful re-entries in persistent moves.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B1 supports the generic execution idea of adding "speed bumps" so the strategy does not trade too fast, too aggressively, or send too many orders. B8 supports the generic concern that over-trading and wider spreads raise costs. Neither source proves that this exact throttle adds alpha for Midas, and neither source addresses the fact that the main throttle is already in the live bot.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday sleeve only: after any exit, block any new entry in that same symbol for 2 bars.
review.mechanism: In principle, this could cut flip-flopping and a few extra spread/impact hits if the sleeve were re-entering often. On the current Q desk, though, it is likely to do almost nothing because the intraday sleeve already has a max-one-round-trip-per-day cap. It does not solve the real issues: trend whipsaws, crash give-back, or flat intraday years.
review.data_missing: None for a pure rule simulation; minute bars plus the existing cost model are enough. We cannot measure true order-book slippage, but the incremental effect here is so small that that is not the bottleneck.
review.already_tried_note: The core part of the idea is already live: the intraday sleeve already has max one round trip per day. The only new piece is the post-exit cooldown, which is unlikely to bind under that existing cap.
review.overfit_note: Almost no degrees of freedom. The bigger problem is redundancy, not curve fitting. Any apparent improvement would likely be noise because the rule barely changes the trade path.
review.expected_effect: Probably near zero on net PnL; at best a tiny turnover/slippage reduction, and at worst lost re-entry alpha. It is not a meaningful fix for the bot's known weaknesses.
review.test_protocol: If we test it at all, pre-register a single variant: add the 2-bar post-exit cooldown to the intraday sleeve and leave everything else unchanged, including the existing one-round-trip/day cap and the 1 bp/side cost model. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 in-sample, then confirm on 2007-2017 unseen minute data. Success requires improvement in net daily return and Sharpe in both periods without worse max drawdown; a pure turnover reduction is only acceptable if it comes with no return loss. Because the current rule already blocks most churn, I would expect a near-no-op.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly already implemented: the live intraday sleeve already caps at one round trip per day. The proposed cooldown is therefore close to redundant, and it does not address the actual weaknesses of Midas (trend whipsaws, crash give-back, and weak intraday years). Do not spend scarce test cycles on it.

name: PIT data master and QA gate
one_line: Use a point-in-time, corporate-action-adjusted data master and reject any file or feed with timestamp or symbol-history problems before a backtest or live decision.
parameter_choices: As-of-date security master; delisted symbols included; split/dividend adjustments; null/gap/monotonicity checks; real-time feed for live trading; historical archive for research.
disagreement: No real disagreement on the need for this; the only practical tension is that live feeds can be delayed, so they should not be used as the sole research source.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The books strongly support the underlying hygiene pieces: point-in-time universes, delisted symbols, as-of-date symbology, corporate-action adjustments, timestamp/null/monotonicity checks, and avoiding delayed live feeds. But none of the sources shows that a hard fail-closed QA gate itself produces trading alpha; this is infrastructure, not a signal.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a fail-closed data gate: all research, backtests, and live signals must be built from an as-of-date security master with delisted symbols and split/dividend-adjusted prices. Reject the run if any required series has a null timestamp, duplicate/non-monotone timestamp, or missing session. New parameter: max_live_feed_lag_minutes = 0 (do not trade if the live feed is not real-time).
review.mechanism: This prevents bogus signals, bad joins, survivorship bias, and corporate-action artifacts from contaminating both backtests and live trading. For Midas, that mainly protects you from false discoveries and live/backtest mismatch; it is unlikely to fix trend whipsaws or flat intraday years by itself.
review.data_missing: We can implement PIT lookup, delisted-name coverage, split/dividend adjustment, and timestamp/gap/monotonicity checks from our archive. What we do not have is exchange-timestamped live reference data or a second live vendor, so we cannot truly audit live-feed latency or cross-vendor mismatches with the current stack.
review.already_tried_note: Some of this is already implicit in the existing minute archives and the use of real TQQQ/SQQQ data plus delisted coverage, but the explicit as-of-date security master and hard fail-closed QA gate have not been described as already in place or tested.
review.overfit_note: There are basically no PnL knobs to overfit. The risk is not overfitting returns; it is mistaking data-cleanup for alpha and wasting strategy-test budget on plumbing.
review.expected_effect: Mostly a hygiene win, not an edge. It may stop bad bars or symbol-history errors from creating fake performance, but if the current data are already clean it should have little or no effect on returns.
review.test_protocol: Run a one-time pipeline audit, not an alpha search. Apply the gate to all historical files and record: (1) null/duplicate/non-monotone timestamps, (2) missing-session gaps, (3) symbol-history mismatches, and (4) any trade/signal changes versus the current pipeline. Then rerun the current Q desk on 2018-2026 and the unseen 1999-2017 / 2007-2017 periods using the cleaned master. Decision rule: if the gate catches no material anomalies and changes fewer than 0.1% of trades, stop here and do not spend further strategy-test slots on it; if it changes results materially, fix the pipeline and rebaseline the existing bot.
review.verdict_reason: This is mandatory data plumbing, not a trading hypothesis. It has no standalone alpha to test, and the live-feed-delay part cannot be fully validated from our current data. Implement it once as baseline hygiene, but do not burn strategy-test budget on it.

name: Reproducible, test-driven research stack
one_line: Make every strategy change reproducible from a versioned notebook and protected by deterministic unit/regression tests for data, orders, and PnL.
parameter_choices: Versioned notebook; deterministic seeds; simulated clock from timestamps; unit tests for new/reject/fill/cancel states; order-manager validation; exact reruns of stored calibration data.
disagreement: No substantive disagreement; the sources all push toward more reproducible and testable code.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly recommend the core of this change: reproducible notebook-based research, stubbed simulation inputs/outputs, layered componentized research/TCA, automated regression tests, deterministic seeds, a dedicated order manager, exhaustive unit tests, and end-to-end PnL checks. The only extrapolation is turning those engineering practices into a hard promotion gate for Midas.
review.exact_rule_change: No trading-rule change. Require every Q-desk modification to be implemented in a versioned notebook/repo with a deterministic seed for synthetic fixtures and a timestamp-driven simulated clock; route all orders through one validated order manager with unit tests for new/rejected/partial/filled/cancelled states; before any live or shadow promotion, rerun the full historical backtest suite and require exact match to the stored baseline outputs (trades, positions, fees, and PnL).
review.mechanism: This will not create alpha directly. It should reduce implementation bugs, stop silent backtest/live mismatches, make comparisons between strategy variants reproducible, and let us tell whether a candidate edge is real or just a code or accounting error. For a small account, avoiding one bad deployment can matter more than squeezing out a tiny extra edge.
review.data_missing: No new market data is required. If we want realistic partial-fill, acknowledgment, and latency behavior, we still lack tick/quote/order-book data and an exchange test market, so those edge cases must be simulated.
review.already_tried_note: We already backtest and run shadow desks, but I do not see evidence of a formal versioned-notebook plus deterministic unit/regression-test gate with exact rerun hashes. So this is more disciplined infrastructure than a duplicate of the already-rejected alpha ideas.
review.overfit_note: This does not add market degrees of freedom. The main risk is false confidence from tests that only validate the code path, not the market edge, but that is an engineering risk, not a market overfit risk.
review.expected_effect: Better reproducibility, fewer silent bugs, cleaner attribution, faster parameter sweeps, and lower risk of live/backtest drift. No meaningful direct return boost by itself.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the current Q desk as the baseline. Implement the reproducible-stack gate on a fixed set of past strategy variants and a set of injected faults. On 2018-2026 and 1999-2017, require exact rerun match for baseline trades, positions, fees, and PnL hashes. Measure: (1) exact reproducibility rate, (2) bug-detection rate on seeded failures, and (3) time to rerun the full suite. Decision rule: adopt immediately if the stack reproduces the baseline exactly and catches essentially all injected faults; otherwise revise the tooling. This is an engineering validation, not a PnL contest.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with the data and code we already have, cheap to implement, and directly supported by the sources. It is not alpha, but it is the right gate before spending more tests on new strategy ideas.

name: Chronological walk-forward validation
one_line: Validate only with time-ordered splits and frozen validation windows, never with shuffled samples or moving parameters after the holdout is seen.
parameter_choices: 70/30 or 80/20 chronological split; rolling 5-year fit plus next-year test; four equal subperiods; moving-window evaluation; 30-day live-like replay before promotion.
disagreement: The sources disagree on split size, not on chronology: some favor 80/20 or 70/30, others favor rolling or subperiod checks.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The books repeatedly recommend exactly this class of guardrail: keep model-building separate from validation, use chronological train/test on time series, use rolling/moving-window checks, and avoid look-ahead. The support is for the validation discipline itself, not for any claim that walk-forward validation creates alpha.
review.exact_rule_change: Adopt a frozen nested walk-forward gate for every new Q desk change: develop only on earlier data, using a fixed 5-year rolling fit and 1-year next-window validation inside the development period, then lock the chosen parameters and evaluate once on a final 20% chronological holdout; no retuning after the holdout is inspected.
review.mechanism: This does not add a market edge by itself. It reduces false discoveries by forcing candidate rules to survive time-ordered out-of-sample checks across different regimes, so we are less likely to promote a lucky fit that dies live. For Midas, that matters because the bot’s weak spots are exactly the kind of things that look great in one regime and fail in another.
review.data_missing: None; the existing OHLCV history is enough.
review.already_tried_note: We already do chronological development vs unseen-period confirmation in the bot brief, so the core idea is not new. What is not clearly in place is a formal frozen walk-forward protocol with fixed window lengths and a strict no-peek rule after the holdout is opened.
review.overfit_note: Low if the protocol is fixed once. The only real overfit risk is if we keep changing the split scheme, lookback length, or acceptance rule after seeing results, which would just recreate the same snooping problem in a different form.
review.expected_effect: Better research hygiene, fewer bogus strategy additions, and a more honest estimate of live Sharpe and drawdown. It should not be expected to improve returns directly; it should improve the quality of the rules we allow into the bot.
review.test_protocol: Make this the default evaluation protocol for the next batch of candidate changes. Compare two selection methods on the same candidate set: current ad hoc split-versus the proposed frozen walk-forward. Score them on 2018-2026 and on the unseen 1999-2017 period using net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and the in-sample to out-of-sample Sharpe gap. Success means the walk-forward protocol rejects more fragile ideas without causing the current Q desk to fail its own unseen-period check; if it materially lowers the chosen strategy’s out-of-sample Sharpe or raises drawdown, keep the current process instead.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly reduces data-snooping. It will not create alpha by itself, but it is a sensible default gate for any future Midas tweak, and we already have the data to run it.

name: Minimum sample-size gate
one_line: Do not trust any signal until it has enough trades or labeled examples to beat noise, then keep the full sample complete.
parameter_choices: At least 20 trades for a first screen; 30-50 theoretical trades for a pre-live check; 100+ or 300+ trades for stronger confidence; 1000 labeled signals when classification is used.
disagreement: Some sources treat 20 trades as a minimum screening sample, while others want hundreds or even 1000 signals before drawing conclusions.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Multiple sources explicitly recommend minimum sample sizes before trusting a trading idea: ~20 trades, 30-50 theoretical trades, and hundreds/1000 labeled signals for larger-sample validation. The exact implementation as a promotion gate for Midas is our adaptation, but the underlying rule is directly supported.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a hard promotion gate for every new Q desk sleeve/filter: keep it in shadow until it has at least 30 completed qualifying trades; if the candidate is a classifier/skip filter, require 1000 labeled examples before promotion. Do not change its rules mid-sample, and keep the full sample intact (no cherry-picking wins/losses).
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself; it prevents us from mistaking noise for an edge. On a small account with few independent events, a handful of lucky trades can look great and then vanish. A minimum-sample gate should reduce false positives, make expectancy estimates less garbage, and stop us from promoting tweaks that only work in a tiny in-sample patch.
review.data_missing: No new market data is missing. We can count trades and labels from our bar data, but a 1000-label gate may be impractical for single-sleeve QQQ-only ideas unless we pool across many liquid ETFs/stocks or wait a long time.
review.already_tried_note: Our research process already uses long backtests, unseen confirmation, and shadow desks, which is similar in spirit. But we have not formalized an explicit minimum-trade gate like this, so the exact rule is new as a process control.
review.overfit_note: Very few knobs. The main risk is not curve-fitting PnL; it is choosing a threshold that is too loose to matter or so strict that it blocks useful slow-firing edges.
review.expected_effect: Lower false-positive rate in idea selection, fewer rule changes based on tiny samples, and slower but cleaner promotion of new sleeves. It should not improve returns directly; it should improve the quality of what we let into the bot.
review.test_protocol: This is a research-governance test, not a trading-edge test. Pre-register the gate at 30 completed trades (and 1000 labeled examples for classifier-style rules). Build a library of past and candidate Q desk tweaks. On 2018-2026, mark which ideas would have been promoted under the gate versus our current ad hoc process, then measure their unseen 1999-2017 expectancy/Sharpe after costs. Success means the gated process produces a lower false-promotion rate and higher median holdout expectancy/Sharpe than the ungated process, while not filtering out the current robust sleeves (QQQ RSI(2), turn-of-month, etc.).
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly useful as a guardrail. It is not an alpha idea, but it can stop us wasting time and capital on tiny-sample mirages.

name: White/SPA reality-check gate
one_line: Apply data-snooping controls to the whole rule family so the best-looking rule still has to survive a multiple-comparison test.
parameter_choices: White-style bootstrap with benchmark signal values 1/-1/0; SPA step-down across l rules; reject, remove, and recompute critical values iteratively.
disagreement: No direct disagreement; the methods are complementary ways to control false discoveries.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The source items directly support the core of this idea: White-style bootstrap reality checks for data-snooping bias and SPA step-down tests for a family of trading rules. Using them as a gate for the Q desk is an adaptation, but it is very close to the cited method.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a fixed research gate for every new candidate sleeve or rule tweak: treat cash as the benchmark signal (0), run a White-style reality check on the pre-registered rule family, then apply a stepwise SPA test across all l candidates at alpha=0.05. Only promote rules that survive the gate; otherwise they stay paper-only.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself. It should reduce the chance that we add a backtest winner that was only lucky across many tried variants. For Midas, that matters because the current bot already has several knobs and weak spots, so the main benefit is fewer false positives and fewer bad live additions.
review.data_missing: No extra market data is needed. The gate uses the same backtest return streams we already have from our price history; no news, order book, options, or fundamentals are required.
review.already_tried_note: We already do some out-of-sample confirmation and shadow testing, but not this formal multiple-comparison correction. It is related to current practice, not a duplicate of any rejected trading idea.
review.overfit_note: The method itself has almost no trading degrees of freedom. The real risk is defining the candidate family after looking at results, so the rule list must be frozen before testing.
review.expected_effect: No direct lift in the current desk’s live PnL. If used properly, it should lower the number of weak sleeves that survive research and slightly improve the chance that any future added sleeve actually survives live trading after costs.
review.test_protocol: Freeze a rule universe up front: all pre-registered trend filters, intraday band variants, sizing rules, and exits we would realistically consider. On 2018-2026, compute each candidate’s after-cost returns, run White’s reality check with benchmark signal 0, then SPA step-down at alpha=0.05. Compare the selected survivor set to naive best-in-sample selection. Confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level rules). Success means the gated selection has higher out-of-sample Sharpe or return, fewer negative-OOS selections, and no material loss versus the current Q desk.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and statistically sensible. It will not improve PnL by itself, but it is a good promotion gate for future rule mining and can be implemented immediately with our existing data.

name: Monte Carlo and bootstrap robustness
one_line: Stress-test each sleeve by perturbing prices, fills, sizes, and market scenarios so only edges that survive noise make it through.
parameter_choices: Blur OHLC by 0.5%-1%; 1000 repetitions; at least 10 assets; randomize entry/size/exit parameters; scenario slices for crash, bull, and low-vol regimes.
disagreement: Perturbing prices can erase real-looking signals; that is the point, but it means brittle pattern rules may fail even if their base backtest looks good.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The books explicitly recommend Monte Carlo blurring of price data, randomizing execution inputs, bootstrapping, and scenario slices. That supports the robustness-testing method, but not the exact 1% blur/10-asset gate as a trading edge; those defaults are our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Leave the Q desk signal logic unchanged; add a pre-launch robustness gate: rerun every candidate variant 1,000 times with OHLC blurred by 1% and reject it unless it also holds up in separate crash, bull, and low-vol slices. Only variants whose median perturbed CAGR and max drawdown still beat the current Q desk proceed to paper/live.
review.mechanism: This is an edge filter, not an edge. It should reduce false discoveries caused by exact bar shapes, lucky fills, and one-regime overfitting, which matters because Midas’ round-trip cost is small but nonzero and the sample is finite. The downside is that a coarse blur can also kill real but fragile minute-bar edges.
review.data_missing: None for a coarse version; quote/order-book data would only improve fill realism, but the Monte Carlo and bootstrap test itself is computable from our OHLCV history.
review.already_tried_note: We already do long-history backtests, explicit cost modeling, and live shadowing, which are crude forms of validation. We have not yet done explicit Monte Carlo blur / bootstrap resampling of prices, fills, or regime slices.
review.overfit_note: The method has only a couple of knobs, but it is easy to p-hack the blur size or pass/fail threshold after looking. At 1% blur, it may become a false-negative machine for minute-bar rules and reject genuine but small edges.
review.expected_effect: Small positive as a selection filter, not as a direct return source. It should lower live-vs-backtest disappointment by killing brittle variants earlier, but it may also discard some profitable noisy edges.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the candidate set before looking: current Q desk plus any proposed variants. On 2018-2026, rerun each candidate 1,000 times with the existing cost model and 1% OHLC blur; record median daily return, 10th percentile CAGR, max drawdown, and trade count. Also split results by crash, bull, and low-vol regimes. Select by robustness score, not raw backtest. Then lock the same rule and confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level sleeves). Success only if the robustness-selected variant beats both the raw-selected variant and the current Q desk in both periods without worse max drawdown; otherwise keep this only as a diagnostic and do not let it change trading decisions.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and useful as a pre-deployment filter. It will not create alpha by itself, but it can save us from deploying brittle variants. The main caution is that 1% blur is likely harsher than our real execution noise, so treat this as a stress test rather than a realistic fill model.

name: Expectancy-first performance scorecard
one_line: Judge strategies by expectancy, drawdown, and tail-aware ratios, not by hit rate or raw backtest equity alone.
parameter_choices: Expectancy in R; Sharpe/Sortino/Calmar; max drawdown; winning/losing trades; invested-days versus calendar-days; exposure-adjusted benchmark comparisons.
disagreement: Sharpe can be misleading because returns are often non-normal, so it should be paired with downside and drawdown measures rather than used alone.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Multiple sources explicitly recommend evaluating backtests with expectancy/profit, win-loss counts, drawdown, Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, exposure, and benchmark comparisons. Several also warn that Sharpe alone can mislead because returns are not normal. The exact phrase 'expectancy-first scorecard' is our synthesis, but the underlying evaluation rule is well supported.
review.exact_rule_change: No trading-rule change: every candidate Q-desk variant must be promoted only if its after-cost expectancy is > 0R/trade and its max drawdown is no worse than the current Q desk; report Sharpe, Sortino, Calmar, win/loss counts, and exposure-adjusted benchmark stats as secondary diagnostics (good bands: Sharpe 1-2, Sortino 2-3, Calmar 1-2).
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself; it stops us promoting rules that only look good on hit rate or raw equity. For Midas, that should reduce false positives, surface high-payoff/low-hit-rate variants, and make crash risk and idle-capital costs visible when comparing trend, intraday, and new sleeves.
review.data_missing: No new market data is required. We only need a consistent per-trade R definition in the backtester for sleeves that currently have no stop, plus the existing trade logs and equity curves.
review.already_tried_note: We already evaluate variants with return, Sharpe, and drawdown. The new part here is formalizing expectancy in R and exposure-adjusted comparisons as the standard promotion gate, which is mostly a reporting change rather than a new market hypothesis.
review.overfit_note: The metrics themselves are fine, but if we start tuning pass/fail cutoffs on 2018-2026 we can easily overfit the scorecard. Treat the thresholds as pre-registered hygiene, not optimized parameters.
review.expected_effect: Better research triage and capital allocation, fewer fragile variants admitted live, and clearer separation of true edge from market beta. Not a direct PnL edge.
review.test_protocol: Meta-test only: take the current Q desk, the shadow variants, and any archived candidates. Rank them two ways on 2018-2026: (a) raw CAGR/Sharpe-first, and (b) the proposed scorecard (positive expectancy, max DD, Sharpe/Sortino/Calmar, exposure-adjusted benchmark). Then check 1999-2017: whichever method would have selected the variant with the best unseen expectancy/Calmar and no worse max DD wins. If the scorecard does not improve unseen selection versus the current process, keep it as reporting only and do not spend more alpha tests on it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a useful bookkeeping rule, not a tradable edge. It should be adopted as the default research report, but it does not justify a dedicated strategy test because it cannot by itself improve returns beyond helping us choose among already-tested candidates.

name: Nonstationarity and differencing screen
one_line: Test every candidate feature for nonstationarity first, and only difference it when the data support that choice out of sample.
parameter_choices: d = 0, 1, or 2; sample ACF compared with ±2/sqrt(T) bounds; unit-root tau and tau_mu tests; keep the simplest transformation that works.
disagreement: Over-differencing is a real risk: it can wipe out useful structure, so the simplest stationary representation should win.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources clearly support the econometric pieces of the idea: nonstationary series can be differenced, ACF can be used as a diagnostic, unit-root tests (tau/tau_mu) are the right screen, and over-differencing is a real risk. What they do not show is that this screening step improves trading PnL or that it should be applied to every candidate feature in a live bot.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the current live Q desk rules. For any future price/volume-derived auxiliary feature X, fit on the 2018-2026 training window only and choose the smallest d in {0,1,2} such that the transformed series passes an ADF tau_mu test at the 5% level and its early-lag ACF stays within about ±2/√T. If no d passes, drop X. Do not difference the existing SMA trend or noise-band entry/exit rules themselves.
review.mechanism: This is mainly a hygiene gate for future regime or sizing models: it can stop us from feeding trending, nonstationary levels into a predictor and mistaking drift for signal. That can reduce fake predictability and unstable parameters. It is not a direct alpha source for the current hand-built Q desk, and if forced onto the existing level-based rules it could destroy useful structure.
review.data_missing: None; the existing OHLCV history is enough for the screen.
review.already_tried_note: We have not explicitly run a stationarity-gated preprocessing study on the Q desk. Related transformed-price ideas have already been used/tested indirectly (returns-based ideas like RSI(2), turn-of-month, 12-1 momentum, and the existing open/prev-close band logic), but not this exact ADF/ACF differencing gate.
review.overfit_note: The rule itself has few knobs, but feature-by-feature transformation choice can become a multiple-testing filter. It is easy to rationalize a transform on 2018-2026 that does not survive 1999-2017, and unit-root tests are noisy on shorter rolling windows.
review.expected_effect: At best, a modest robustness improvement for any future auxiliary model built on price levels. On the current Q desk, likely no measurable gain and possibly worse performance if applied to the core trend/noise rules.
review.test_protocol: If we add one concrete auxiliary model or regime filter, test three versions of every candidate input: d=0, d=1, d=2, with all other rules, costs, and sizing held fixed. Build on 2018-2026 only, using walk-forward validation, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level inputs). Compare against the raw version and against the current Q desk using net after-cost PnL, Sharpe, and max drawdown. Accept only if the same transform wins in both periods and does not worsen drawdown; otherwise discard the feature or keep d=0.
review.verdict_reason: This is feasible and statistically orthodox, but it is not a standalone edge for the current Q desk. The bot already uses transformed/relative price relationships, so forcing a generic stationarity screen onto the live rules is more likely to strip signal than add it. Keep this as a development gate for future auxiliary models, not as an immediate trading change.

name: Residual tail and volatility diagnostics
one_line: After fitting a model, check whether residuals are normal-ish, independent, and free of volatility clustering before trusting the signal.
parameter_choices: QQ plot; Jarque-Bera; ARCH test with q = 5; Ljung-Box on squared residuals at h = 12, 24, 36, 48; residual and squared-residual ACF.
disagreement: Returns are often fat-tailed, so the point is not to force normality but to detect when Gaussian assumptions are unsafe.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The sources explicitly recommend residual ACF/squared-residual checks, Ljung-Box/ARCH tests, and QQ/JB diagnostics after fitting a model. But they describe this as model validation, not as a trading rule or alpha source, so the support is direct for the diagnostics and indirect for any bot change.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading signal change; add a pre-launch gate for any candidate sleeve or volatility-sizing model: fit on the training sample, then require residual Ljung-Box on squared residuals at h=12, 24, 36, 48 and ARCH(q=5) to have p>0.05. Use QQ plot and Jarque-Bera only as informational checks, not as a pass/fail gate.
review.mechanism: This can catch misspecified models that have hidden autocorrelation or volatility clustering before we trust them for sizing or regime switching. That may prevent deploying a fragile rule that looks good in-sample but breaks in clustered-volatility periods. It does not create edge by itself.
review.data_missing: None for the diagnostics themselves; we already have enough price data to fit simple models and compute residuals.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact residual-diagnostic gate, but the team already uses backtests, subperiod checks, and stress-period validation. This is research hygiene rather than a new predictive sleeve.
review.overfit_note: Easy to tune the model, lag lengths, and pass/fail threshold until the chosen candidate looks good in 2018-2026 and then disappoints out of sample. Also easy to misuse normality rejections to discard useful fat-tailed models.
review.expected_effect: Mostly model hygiene, not PnL. Best case: fewer bad live deployments of misspecified rules. Worst case: over-filtering and rejecting useful but fat-tailed strategies. No obvious direct improvement to the current Q desk.
review.test_protocol: Do not allocate a standalone strategy backtest to this. If you operationalize it, pre-register alpha=0.05 and ARCH q=5 with Ljung-Box h=12,24,36,48 as a go/no-go screen for a specific candidate sizing model. Compare the candidate with and without the gate on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017: out-of-sample Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count must improve in both periods. QQ/JB should not block deployment. If the gate rejects the current Q desk or any profitable shadow desk without a clear OOS improvement, discard it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a diagnostic method, not a return-generating rule. It can help research hygiene, but it does not itself improve the bot, and a hard normality gate will reject many perfectly usable financial-return models because fat tails and volatility clustering are normal in this data. Not worth a standalone test as a trading idea.

name: Lagged-volatility regime filter
one_line: Use lagged realized volatility and volatility-clustering tests as a gating or sizing input, but test the effect separately by sleeve.
parameter_choices: Lagged sigma_t-1; 60-day EWMA volatility; 5-lag LM test; use volatility only for sizing first, then for threshold scaling if justified.
disagreement: Volatility scaling can help some mean-reversion or selection rules, but it hurt trend-following in one cited example, so the effect is sleeve-specific.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the ingredients, not this exact trading rule: they show volatility clustering/ARCH effects exist, recommend using lagged ex-ante volatility to avoid look-ahead, and give one example where a volatility-adjusted strategy improved. But one source also warns that dynamic volatility scaling can hurt trend-following, so the Midas application is still an extrapolation and likely sleeve-specific.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a sleeve-specific size gate using only lagged data: compute QQQ’s 60-day EWMA realized volatility from daily close-to-close returns, using yesterday’s value only. If that lagged volatility is above its expanding median, halve the active sleeve’s notional; otherwise leave it unchanged. Test this separately on the trend sleeve and the intraday sleeve first, and do not change the entry/exit thresholds in the first pass.
review.mechanism: Volatility tends to cluster before the worst whipsaws, gap risk, and crash reversals. A lagged vol gate would shrink exposure after the market has already turned noisy, which could reduce the amount the 3x ETFs give back in late-trend chop and could keep the intraday sleeve from trading aggressively on eventful days. This is mostly a risk-control idea; the upside is lower tail loss, not a new alpha source.
review.data_missing: none; daily OHLCV and the available minute bars are enough to compute lagged realized volatility and ARCH/LM diagnostics. No news, options, fundamentals, or order book data are required.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact filter on Midas, but it is close to the already-warned-against idea of volatility-scaled trend thresholds. Also, the current intraday band already uses a volatility-like term, so this is not a totally new state variable.
review.overfit_note: There are only a couple of real knobs if we keep it to sizing-only, but regime filters are easy to fit to 2018-2026 and disappoint in 1999-2017. The risk jumps if we start optimizing the lookback, cutoff, or separate sleeve thresholds.
review.expected_effect: Best case: lower drawdown and fewer bad days, especially in the trend sleeve during high-volatility chop and crash periods. Most likely case: some drawdown relief but a lower CAGR because the filter will also cut size when the bot is making money. I would not expect a large standalone edge.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register three runs: current Q desk; trend sleeve with the lagged-vol size gate; intraday sleeve with the same gate. Compute the gate from QQQ 60-day EWMA realized vol using only prior data, and size down by 50% whenever lagged vol is above its expanding median. Keep all other rules unchanged. First evaluate on 2018-2026; then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 for the daily trend sleeve and 2007-2017 for the minute-based intraday sleeve. Compare net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover to the current desk. Require the same variant to improve in both periods; if drawdown improves but net return falls materially, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully feasible with our data, and it might reduce drawdown, but the evidence is only partial and the likely benefit is modest. Test it as a sizing-only, sleeve-specific gate; do not move on to volatility-scaled thresholds unless this first-pass variant clearly survives out of sample.

name: Special-day calendar regimes
one_line: Treat half-days, month-end/quarter-end, rebalance days, and other calendar anomalies as separate regimes instead of averaging them into the normal-day model.
parameter_choices: Half-days before Christmas and after Thanksgiving; month-end and quarter-end; triple witching; index rebalance dates; weekday seasonality if auxiliary data are used; cluster-level out-of-sample tests.
disagreement: Some sources say model normal days first and special days separately; others go further and add separate special-day profiles. Both agree the days should not be pooled blindly.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The quoted sources do support the general principle: special liquidity days should be handled separately because they have different intraday volume/return patterns than normal sessions. But they do not specifically validate a QQQ/TQQQ intraday noise-area bot, nor do they show that a skip rule improves PnL. The exact action here is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the trend sleeve unchanged. For the intraday noise-area sleeve, estimate the 14-day sigma band using normal sessions only. Mark a session as special if it is a US half-day, month-end, quarter-end, or triple-witching Friday. On special sessions, do not open any new intraday noise-area trades from 10:00 to the close; only manage exits already in force.
review.mechanism: These sessions have atypical liquidity and close pressure, so the normal-day band is likely miscalibrated and the next-bar fills are worse. Skipping new intraday entries on those days should reduce false breakouts and bad fills, which could improve the intraday sleeve without touching the trend sleeve.
review.data_missing: None for half-days, month-end/quarter-end, and triple-witching; if you want true index-rebalance days too, you would need a public rebalance calendar, but I would leave that out of the first test.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. The closest rejected items are other day/session anomalies like last-half-hour and overnight holding, but there is no prior rejection of a special-day calendar regime for this bot.
review.overfit_note: A fixed calendar flag has few knobs, but the sample of special days is small and the effect can be very regime-specific. If we start fitting a separate profile per day type, overfit risk jumps quickly.
review.expected_effect: Likely a modest positive at best: fewer bad intraday trades and less execution slippage on odd sessions, with little or no effect on the trend sleeve or crash exits. This is more of a variance-reduction filter than a new alpha source.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one variant only: same current Q desk, but the intraday sleeve excludes special-session new entries and the sigma band is fit on normal sessions only. Build on 2018-2026 with the same cost model, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 QQQ minute data; the daily trend sleeve can still be sanity-checked on 1999-2017, but the special-day rule itself is a minute-level test. Compare net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and intraday sleeve PnL split into special vs normal days against the current Q desk. Use cluster-level bootstrapping by day type because special days are sparse. Accept only if both 2018-2026 and 2007-2017 improve on net return and Sharpe without a drawdown penalty; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully calendar-driven, and directly aimed at a real weakness of the intraday sleeve. It is not a big expected edge, but it is feasible, low-cost, and specific enough to deserve one pre-registered test.

name: Intraday bar-size optimization
one_line: Pick the intraday sampling interval by backtesting a small grid of bar sizes and choosing the one that best balances friction and information.
parameter_choices: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, and 15-minute bars; 5-minute volatility estimates; avoid sub-minute complexity unless it clearly wins after costs.
disagreement: Five-minute sampling is favored for volatility estimation, but the best signal bar size still needs to be chosen empirically by net PnL.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The sources support intraday aggregation in the 1–15 minute range and specifically favor 5-minute sampling for volatility estimation, but none says the Q desk’s noise-area signal itself should be optimized this way. The step from generic intraday guidance to this exact sleeve is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the intraday sleeve’s 30-minute check interval with 5-minute checks on QQQ bars (decision cadence = 5 minutes; volatility estimate remains 5-minute).
review.mechanism: If the current 30-minute checks are too slow, a 5-minute cadence should catch QQQ breakouts/reversals earlier and exit losers sooner. If the tape is noisy, the bar-size search can avoid overreacting to microstructure bounce. The only plausible gain is in the intraday sleeve; the trend sleeve is unchanged.
review.data_missing: Historical 1-minute QQQ data is enough to backtest the grid, but the current live stack only has Yahoo 5-minute bars. Any live winner below 5 minutes would need a new real-time feed.
review.already_tried_note: We already use 5-minute fills and 5-minute volatility inputs, and the intraday sleeve has been stress-tested in other variants, but there has not been a dedicated bar-size sweep for the Q desk signal.
review.overfit_note: Only one knob, but six candidate bar sizes on a single asset/single regime family is still a classic snooping problem. The best 2018–2026 cadence can easily be the luckiest one unless it also survives 2007–2017.
review.expected_effect: Modest at best. A better cadence could raise intraday PnL by reducing lag and/or noise, but I would expect small gains and plenty of chance for the improvement to disappear after costs. If anything helps, 5 minutes is the most credible candidate.
review.test_protocol: Backtest the current Q desk unchanged except for the intraday decision cadence: 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, and 15-minute bars on QQQ, with the same 5-minute fill assumption, same 1 bp/side costs, same max-one-round-trip rule, and the same 5-minute volatility estimate. Pick the cadence on 2018–2026 only using net daily return/CAGR as primary and Sharpe as secondary; require it to beat the current 30-minute cadence on both 2018–2026 and 2007–2017 after costs, with no material increase in drawdown or turnover. If the winner is only an in-sample winner, reject.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap and directly relevant, but only worth doing as a pre-registered one-knob sweep. The main caveat is live execution: anything faster than 5 minutes may not be implementable with the current Yahoo 5-minute feed, so do not confuse the grid-search result with a deployable rule unless the winner is 5 minutes.

name: Confirmed breakout and pivot validation
one_line: Test breakout-style entries only with strict confirmation rules and explicit no-look-ahead implementation.
parameter_choices: Close beyond prior high/low; fractal confirmation delay equal to the right-side window; R-squared above 0.9 for channel fits; backcandles of 20, 40, or 60; gap_candles of 5 or 10; zone_threshold of 0.001 to 0.002; price_diff_threshold of 0.01 to 0.02; MACD and RSI confirmation.
disagreement: Strict confirmation reduces false positives but can also miss valid trades, so looser and stricter versions should be compared head-to-head.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the narrow mechanics: wait for a close beyond the prior extreme, delay fractal/pivot signals until future bars exist, and use an R-squared cutoff (e.g. >0.9) to reject sloppy channels. But they are mostly cautionary notes and worked examples, not performance evidence, and they do not validate the full combo of breakout + pivot + MACD/RSI + threshold grid for Midas.
review.exact_rule_change: If we test this at all, tighten the current QQQ intraday breakout rule to: only treat the breakout as valid if the 5-minute bar closes beyond the band, then wait a fixed 2-bar fractal confirmation delay before entering on the next 5-minute open; if a regression-channel filter is used, require R² >= 0.90. Do not add MACD/RSI or any backcandles/grid search in the first pass.
review.mechanism: In theory this filters out some one-bar fakeouts and prevents look-ahead leakage, so you get fewer trap entries and a cleaner live/backtest match. In practice, on QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ a 2-bar confirmation often means the move is already partially gone, so the main effect is usually lower turnover and lower missed-trade risk, not a durable alpha boost.
review.data_missing: None for QQQ/ETF bar-based testing; 1-minute OHLCV is enough to compute closes, pivots, fractals, MACD, RSI, and channel fits. No news, fundamentals, options, or L2 data are required.
review.already_tried_note: This sits in the same family as the rejected ORB/breakout variants, and the current intraday sleeve is already a breakout/band system. The exact confirmation stack is not identical, but it is not a fresh alpha family either.
review.overfit_note: There are many knobs here (lookback horizons, confirmation delay, R², gap/zone/price thresholds, MACD, RSI). That makes it easy to make 2018-2026 look good and then have the edge disappear in 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly fewer fakeouts and a cleaner implementation. More likely: fewer trades, later entries, and flatter or worse net expectancy after costs. If anything survives, it is more likely a robustness fix than a new return stream.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the rule before looking: current QQQ intraday breakout signal plus a fixed 2-bar confirmation delay, with R² >= 0.90 only if a channel filter is used; no MACD/RSI tuning and no threshold grid search. Backtest against the current Q desk on 2018-2026, then confirm on the unseen minute-level holdout (2007-2017 for this kind of rule). Compare net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and profit per trade after the same fills/costs. Accept only if the strict version beats the baseline in both periods on net return and Sharpe, with no worse drawdown and no meaningful turnover increase; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly a no-lookahead coding discipline wrapped around an already-tested breakout family. The sourced pieces justify the implementation hygiene, but not a new profitable sleeve. With our costs, 5-minute execution, and small sample, the added confirmation lag and extra knobs are more likely to reduce edge than create it. If you want to test something, test the timestamp/leakage audit, not this as an alpha idea.

name: Formation/trading split for pair sleeves
one_line: If a pair or relative-value sleeve is added later, require a separate formation window, residual stationarity, and a related-instrument universe before trading it live.
parameter_choices: Engle-Granger residual test; separate formation and trading periods; avoid arbitrary +/-1 Z-score thresholds; restrict to structurally related ETFs or names.
disagreement: The books warn that arbitrary thresholds are not universal and that scanning the whole market creates false positives; both point toward tighter, study-specific pair selection.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly support the component ideas: Engle-Granger residual stationarity, a separate formation period before trading, and not using universal +/-1 z-score thresholds; they also warn that scanning arbitrary pairs produces false positives. But they do not present this exact Midas-specific policy as a standalone alpha source, only as pair-screening/validation hygiene.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to the current Q desk today.
