If we add a future pair/relative-value sleeve, only allow pairs from a pre-fixed list of structurally related ETFs/names; build each pair on a 252-trading-day formation window, require an Engle-Granger residual stationarity test with p < 0.05, and then trade that same pair for the next 252 trading days before re-forming. Do not use a universal +/-1 z-score or a whole-market scan.
review.mechanism: This would reduce false-positive pair selection and data-mined spreads. If we ever add a pair sleeve, it should cut down on broken relationships that only looked good in-sample, which means fewer blowups and better out-of-sample stability. It does not create alpha by itself; it is a gate for a new sleeve.
review.data_missing: None for a daily pair-screening study. If we wanted intraday pair execution back before 2018 on broad non-QQQ/SPY names, minute data would be missing.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tested as a pair-sleeve gate. The closest rejected cousin is the noise-area test on IWM/DIA, which is a related ETF relative-value idea and underwhelmed, but this specific formation/cointegration workflow has not been tried.
review.overfit_note: The gate itself has only a couple of knobs, but pair selection can still be mined through the related-universe definition and the chosen rolling windows. It reduces overfit risk versus naive scanning, but it does not eliminate it.
review.expected_effect: Lower false discoveries and fewer spread blowups in any future pair sleeve, at the cost of fewer trades and likely lower gross return. The main gain would be better stability, not a proven edge.
review.test_protocol: If we ever define a concrete pair sleeve, test the same spread strategy two ways on daily data: (1) ungated baseline that uses the full allowed universe and no formation/trading split, and (2) the proposed gate with a fixed related-universe list, 252-day formation, and Engle-Granger p < 0.05. Keep the downstream entry/exit logic identical in both arms. Pre-register the universe and parameters before looking. Evaluate net return/day after costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and number of live pair candidates on 2018-2026 as the development set, then confirm unchanged on 1999-2017. Adopt only if the gated version improves Sharpe and net return in both periods without worse drawdown; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is sensible validation for a future pair sleeve, but it is not a standalone trading edge and does nothing to the current Q desk unless we first define an actual pair strategy and candidate universe.

name: Parsimonious model and feature selection
one_line: Keep any predictive model small and regularized, and choose the simplest version that survives walk-forward validation.
parameter_choices: Standardize inputs; PLS components chosen by cross-validation/PMSE; AIC/BIC for lag order; ridge penalty lambda > 0; bagging with M bootstrap samples; boosting stopped on validation loss; kernel bandwidth chosen by cross-validation.
disagreement: Boosting can overfit, PCA is unsupervised while PLS is supervised, and some pattern methods are more stable than others; the common rule is to keep the simplest surviving model.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The sources do support the *general* principle: prefer fewer parameters, standardize inputs, use ridge/early stopping/bagging/PLS/CV/BIC to avoid overfitting, and keep model complexity small. But they do not show that 'parsimonious model and feature selection' is itself a profitable trading edge for Midas. The trading connection is mostly our extrapolation from generic model-selection advice.
review.exact_rule_change: No standalone trading rule. If we add a learned overlay to Midas, make it: z-score all inputs, fit a ridge-regularized PLS meta-model, default to r=1 component, choose λ by rolling cross-validation, and deploy only the smallest model within 1-SE of the best validation PMSE. No feature set larger than the pre-specified small candidate list.
review.mechanism: If we ever add a predictive overlay, this should reduce coefficient noise and regime-fitting, which is the main way small samples fool us. A tiny regularized model is less likely to chase 2018-2026 quirks, less likely to blow up when the regime changes, and more likely to keep the current bot's simple rules from being buried under unstable signals. By itself, though, it does not create alpha; it only makes a future model less fragile.
review.data_missing: Nothing missing for a price/volume-only overlay. We can build standardized features, lagged returns, volatility, and volume signals from the data we already have. If the proposal were to use news, fundamentals, options, or order book features, we do not have those.
review.already_tried_note: We have not specifically tested PLS/ridge/bagging/early-stopping on Midas. But the existing bot is already a small, hand-built rule set, and the team has already rejected several 'add more indicators / more analysis' style ideas. So the spirit is already in use; only a concrete learned overlay would be new.
review.overfit_note: A feature-selection pipeline can hide a lot of degrees of freedom: candidate universe, lag choice, scaling, number of components, penalty strength, bootstrap count, stopping rule, and thresholding. With only one main in-sample span (2018-2026) and a fairly small account/strategy sample, it is easy to fit noise and fail on 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: As a modeling discipline, it should lower the chance of a bad overlay surviving. As a standalone bot change, expected effect is near zero because it is not itself a signal, exit, or sizing rule. If turned into a specific meta-filter, it might modestly improve out-of-sample stability and reduce whipsaw in the overlay.
review.test_protocol: Do not test 'parsimony' in the abstract. First define one explicit prediction task, such as next-day QQQ direction or intraday trade/no-trade for the 10:00-15:30 sleeve, using only a pre-specified small OHLCV feature set. Then compare: (1) current Q desk baseline, (2) unregularized model, (3) ridge-regularized PLS with r=1 and λ chosen by rolling CV, using nested walk-forward so the feature-selection step never sees the test slice. Build/tune on 2018-2026, then confirm unchanged settings on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level rules). Require improvement in net Sharpe and drawdown after costs in both periods; otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is a good modeling rule, but it is not a bot edge and not a concrete standalone strategy. Testing 'use simpler models' without specifying a target, feature set, and decision rule would waste time and likely just reward overfitting in the selection process itself. If the team wants to test it, it must be attached to one explicit overlay; until then, reject it as too abstract to be actionable.

name: Equal-weight and shrinkage allocation benchmark
one_line: Benchmark any allocator against equal-weight and shrinkage baselines before trusting an optimized weight vector.
parameter_choices: 1/N benchmark; CAPM-style shrinkage target; bootstrap resampling of returns; upper weight caps as a secondary control; sample size m about one third to one half of T.
disagreement: Equal-weight can beat plug-in Markowitz, hard caps alone often do not help, and even weak strategies can deserve some weight if they diversify the rest of the book.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly support the ingredients: equal-weight as a hard benchmark, the instability of plug-in Markowitz, and shrinkage/bootstrapping as stabilization tools. They do not directly state the meta-rule 'benchmark any allocator before trusting it'; that is our extrapolation from those points.
review.exact_rule_change: No live Q-desk rule change: keep the current 50/50 sleeve split as the default 1/N baseline. For any future allocator proposal, require a Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage covariance estimator toward a CAPM target (alpha chosen by Ledoit-Wolf) and reject the allocator unless it beats the fixed 50/50 baseline after costs on both 2018–2026 and 1999–2017.
review.mechanism: This is mostly a guardrail against estimator noise, not a return source. It prevents us from trading an unstable optimized weight vector that is just fitting sample error. On this bot, the practical effect is limited because the live allocator is already a simple 50/50 split; the main benefit is protecting future multi-sleeve experiments from overfitting and allocator churn.
review.data_missing: None for the benchmark itself; daily or intraday sleeve returns are enough, and we already have the underlying price data.
review.already_tried_note: The live Q desk already uses a fixed 50/50 sleeve split, so the equal-weight baseline is already embedded. Shadow desks also exist. What has not been tried is a formal Ledoit-Wolf/CAPM shrinkage allocator, but with only two sleeves the allocation problem is close to trivial.
review.overfit_note: As a benchmark, this has almost no tuning freedom. It only becomes overfit-prone if we start adding many allocator variants, caps, or bootstrap/window choices and then selecting the winner on the same history.
review.expected_effect: Mostly negative or neutral as a standalone proposal: it will not add alpha by itself. Best case, it keeps us from promoting unstable optimizers and slightly reduces allocator noise. On the current bot, any direct PnL lift is likely negligible because the baseline is already fixed 50/50.
review.test_protocol: Do not test this as a standalone alpha rule. Use it as a gating benchmark for any future allocator: compare candidate weights to the current fixed 50/50 split on daily sleeve returns, with walk-forward re-estimation on a trailing 252 trading days and monthly or quarterly rebalance. Report after-cost CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and allocation stability for 2018–2026, then freeze the exact same rule and confirm on unseen 1999–2017. A candidate only survives if it improves net CAGR and Sharpe in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown. If testing more than two sleeves/factors, keep the test dimension small relative to sample length; do not tune hard caps or bootstrap settings unless they beat the baseline in both periods.
review.verdict_reason: This is a validation method, not a tradable edge. The one meaningful baseline it promotes—equal weight—is already the live Q-desk split, and with only two sleeves there is little room for a covariance optimizer to add value after costs. Useful as governance for future experiments, but not worth a standalone backtest or live change now.

name: Event-driven, latency-aware fill simulator
one_line: Replace replay-only fills with an event-driven simulator that models latency, fill probability, rejections, and look-ahead-safe timestamps.
parameter_choices: Next-bar or next-5-minute-open fills; explicit latency variances; pessimistic fill modes; partial fills and rejection rates; simulated clock; market-impact and slippage assumptions.
disagreement: Simple replay is too optimistic, and paper trading can diverge from live fills; the simulator should therefore be pessimistic enough to survive real conditions.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The quoted sources repeatedly recommend essentially this: event-driven backtesting, a simulated clock driven by timestamps, explicit latency/slippage/fees, fill probabilities/rejection rates, and pessimistic fill modeling. They do not give a calibrated Midas-specific parameter set, but the simulator change itself is directly supported.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current replay-only fill layer with an event-driven simulator for the Q desk: every signal/order is timestamped, the simulated clock advances on market timestamps, execution is deferred to the next 5-minute bar open (1-bar latency), and a pessimistic stress mode applies a 10% fill ratio to intraday orders, rejecting the rest.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself; it makes the backtest stop lying about fast entries/exits. That is most valuable for the intraday sleeve and any future short-horizon variants, where replay-only fills are most likely to overstate edge. The practical benefit is fewer false positives and better selection of rules that can actually survive live trading costs and timing frictions.
review.data_missing: We can build a bar-based event simulator from our 1-minute OHLCV and existing next-5-minute-open assumption. But we do not have tick/quote/order-book data, OMS acknowledgements, or actual queue position, so true latency calibration, partial fills, and venue-level fill probability cannot be identified from our data. This can only be a coarse stress model, not a faithful microstructure simulator.
review.already_tried_note: Partly already in place: the brief already uses next-5-minute-bar-open fills and explicit cost assumptions, plus live shadow desks for comparison. What is new here is the timestamp-driven event queue, simulated clock, and rejection/partial-fill layer.
review.overfit_note: The core idea is sensible, but every extra latency/fill knob is another way to tune the backtest to a preferred story. Keep the assumptions fixed before looking at results; otherwise the simulator becomes a narrative generator instead of a validator.
review.expected_effect: Backtest returns should fall, especially for the intraday sleeve and any fast variants, but the surviving edge should be more believable and closer to live/paper reality.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register two execution modes: the current replay fill model vs the new event-driven model with 1-bar latency and a 10% intraday stress fill ratio. Run the existing Q desk and the closest candidate variants on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-sensitive pieces). Success means the event-driven model does not flip the sign of the current Q desk in-sample, does not radically reshuffle the top variants, and exposes only modest degradation relative to the replay model; if a strategy only works under optimistic replay fills or loses most of its edge under the event-driven model, reject that variant.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly relevant to Midas' main weakness: short-horizon execution realism. It will not produce alpha, but it is a worthwhile validation upgrade and should be done before trusting any more intraday backtests.

name: TCA and execution benchmark control
one_line: Measure execution with spread-normalized, impact-aware benchmarks and a stateful schedule rather than a naive VWAP replay.
parameter_choices: VWAP, TWAP, and PWP comparisons; spread-normalized slippage; arrival-to-close penalties for unexecuted inventory; one- to five-minute schedule bins; state variables for target, current, next, opportunistic, and lower-band quantities; dynamic cost calibration by regime.
disagreement: VWAP can distort behavior, TWAP can beat VWAP when the volume curve is noisy, and effective-spread metrics can miss impact; the benchmark must therefore be chosen carefully and compared to a stateful schedule.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book excerpts explicitly recommend the same building blocks: spread-normalized execution benchmarks, arrival-to-close penalties for residual inventory, 1–5 minute schedule bins, and a state machine with target/current/next/opportunistic/lower-band quantities. It also warns that VWAP/TWAP-style benchmarking can distort behavior and that static schedules are brittle. The only adaptation is applying that TCA framework to Midas' ETF sleeves.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change the trading signal. For every intraday Q-desk order, replace the current VWAP-style replay/cost check with a stateful 5-minute execution schedule: set a linear target path over 5-minute bins; at each bin compute target/current/next/opportunistic inventory; if we are more than 1 bin behind target, catch up on the next bar open, otherwise only trade the next-bin quantity. Benchmark the fill with arrival-to-close slippage and spread-normalized cost. (Defaults: 5-minute bins; catch-up trigger = 1 bin behind.)
review.mechanism: This should stop us from thinking execution was good just because it matched VWAP while actually bleeding alpha to drift or impact. It also gives a simple rule for when to be more aggressive in fast adverse-momentum periods and when to wait, which could reduce missed exits and late catch-up trading in the intraday sleeve. The main win is cleaner cost control and better live-vs-backtest matching, not a new alpha source.
review.data_missing: We can implement the schedule and bar-based proxies from our minute bars, but true spread-normalized and impact-aware TCA needs quote/tick/order-book data and actual arrival/completion prices, which we do not have.
review.already_tried_note: We already use a simple next-5-minute-open fill assumption and fixed cost model, but we have not tested a stateful 5-minute schedule, lower-band catch-up logic, or residual-to-close penalties as a separate execution layer.
review.overfit_note: Only one or two knobs, but the effect is mostly in cost accounting. It would be easy to tune the benchmark to 2018–2026 and declare victory without improving real trade quality, so it needs strict out-of-sample confirmation.
review.expected_effect: Small to moderate improvement in estimated net PnL attribution and a modest chance of better intraday execution; probably little direct alpha. Best case is fewer over-trades in hostile regimes and more honest sizing/skip decisions; worst case is no change.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the trading signal and compare two execution layers: (A) current 1bp/side cost model with next-5-minute-open fills, and (B) the new stateful 5-minute schedule with arrival-to-close residual penalty and spread-normalized slippage proxy. Run on 2018–2026 using actual TQQQ/SQQQ minute bars, then confirm on 2007–2017 with synthetic 3x QQQ. Success metrics: intraday-sleeve net PnL/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and absolute cost-model error versus realized fills. Require improvement in both periods and no drawdown worsening; otherwise keep the current simple execution model.
review.verdict_reason: It is feasible with our bar data, costs almost nothing to test, and the sources directly support stateful execution control and better benchmarks. It is not a new alpha, so treat it as a TCA/validation upgrade, not a standalone return stream.

name: Trade journal and signal database
one_line: Log every trade and signal in a structured journal so winners, losers, regime effects, and parameter decay can be reviewed later.
parameter_choices: Record setup, entry and exit, indicators, regime, expected versus actual R, actual versus intended prices, and a unique record for each signal/parameter tuple; review weekly or monthly.
disagreement: No substantive disagreement; the sources reinforce journaling as a way to turn live experience into testable data.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Day Trade (sample)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Roadmap to Profitability (YouTube transcript)
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Multiple sources explicitly recommend keeping a trade journal/diary with pre-trade and post-trade fields, and one source explicitly recommends a signal database keyed by <signal, instruments, parameters> to compare performance across regimes and detect decay. The weekly/monthly review cadence is also directly supported. The only extrapolation is expecting the journal itself to create trading edge; the sources support it as a review/diagnostic tool, not alpha.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a mandatory journal row for every Q desk signal and every fill, keyed by a unique <sleeve, signal state, parameter tuple>. Log: timestamp, sleeve, regime label, intended entry/exit, actual fill, realized R, exit reason, and a rule-violation flag. Default review cadence: weekly (every Monday). Default logging granularity: one row per signal, even if no trade is taken. No change to entry/exit rules.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself. It makes failures visible: separates signal edge from execution error, shows which sleeve/parameter tuples decay, and lets us throttle or kill a sleeve before a small edge disappears. For Midas, that is useful for diagnosing whether the trend sleeve is whipsawing or the intraday sleeve is degrading in specific regimes.
review.data_missing: No external data is missing for the logging layer. Historical rows can be reconstructed from our existing backtests using price/signal state; subjective notes and live operator comments are forward-looking only.
review.already_tried_note: Not in the rejected list. We have shadow desks and backtests, but not a formal structured trade/signal database with the required fields and review cadence.
review.overfit_note: The logging change itself has no fitted knobs. The risk is downstream cherry-picking from the database; any follow-on filter should be pre-registered and out-of-sample validated before it changes the bot.
review.expected_effect: Indirect only: better attribution, faster detection of drift/regime shifts, fewer bad parameter changes, and cleaner post-mortems. No standalone return edge expected.
review.test_protocol: Implement the journal now and backfill it on historical trades to verify completeness. Pre-register a small diagnostic pack: expectancy by sleeve, by regime, by parameter tuple; slippage vs intended vs actual; and rule-violation counts. Compare the current Q desk against itself with and without the logging layer for operational completeness only; do not expect a P&L change from journaling alone. Success = 100% of trades/signals logged with required fields, and any follow-on rule change discovered via the journal must beat the current Q desk after costs on 2018–2026 and also hold on unseen 1999–2017. If the journal never produces an OOS-valid rule change, keep it as ops only and stop mining it for alpha.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and useful as an instrumentation layer. It is not a standalone trading edge, so do not burn strategy-test budget on the journal itself; just implement it and use it to police future rule changes and execution errors.

name: Mechanism-and-failure pre-registration
one_line: Before backtesting any new sleeve or filter, write down the mechanism, the failure mode, and what would falsify it.
parameter_choices: Require a one-paragraph thesis plus a named failure mode and a pre-set validation metric before first backtest; no free-form tuning after seeing results.
disagreement: Theory-led hypothesis testing versus open-ended data mining.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: B1 supports the general principle of iterating between theory and empirical testing instead of data-mining; B8 warns about confirmation bias. Neither source gives a trading edge or a specific preregistration rule, so this is only a process extrapolation, not direct evidence that the rule improves returns.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a mandatory research gate: before any first backtest of a new sleeve/filter, the proposer must submit a one-paragraph mechanism thesis, one named failure mode, and one preset validation metric. Default metric: out-of-sample net Sharpe on the unseen period. No parameter retuning is allowed after the first 2018–2026 pass unless the idea is re-preregistered.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself; it reduces the chance that we waste time on stories that only fit the backtest window. For Midas, the benefit is indirect but real: fewer p-hacked variants, less parameter churn, better use of scarce unseen data, and a cleaner funnel toward ideas that actually fix whipsaw, crash give-back, or flat intraday years.
review.data_missing: None for the process rule itself; it can be applied to any candidate idea using the data we already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list and not the same as the existing shadow desks. This is a research workflow change, not an already-tested trading rule.
review.overfit_note: The rule itself has almost no degrees of freedom and should reduce overfit risk. The only mild risk is metric-shopping if we keep changing the preregistered success metric after the fact.
review.expected_effect: Low direct P&L impact. It should improve research hygiene and reduce wasted backtests, but it is unlikely to move live returns by itself.
review.test_protocol: This is not a trading backtest. If you insist on evaluating the process, apply it to the next 10 proposed ideas and compare them with the last 10 ad hoc ideas on (1) number of ideas that survive unseen-period testing, (2) number of retunes requested after the first pass, and (3) eventual shadow/live performance. Success means fewer false positives and no worse out-of-sample performance than the old process.
review.verdict_reason: Good research discipline, but not a bot edge. It does not change trades, costs, or sample size, and there is no meaningful P&L backtest to run on the rule itself. Adopt it as an internal SOP if you want, but do not spend strategy-testing budget on it.

name: Aggregation-aware feature sanity check
one_line: If a feature is built from pivots, mid-ranges, or other aggregated bars, test whether its edge survives when the mechanical autocorrelation is stripped out.
parameter_choices: Compare raw-return features against aggregated-bar versions; include a null model for the expected lag-1 autocorrelation from the aggregation window.
disagreement: Real predictability versus autocorrelation created by the feature construction itself.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the warning: aggregated OHLC/pivot/mid-range features can manufacture lag-1 autocorrelation by construction. It does not explicitly prescribe this exact null-adjustment workflow; that part is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading rule change. Add a pre-deployment gate for any future signal built from m-bar pivots, mid-ranges, or other aggregated bars: de-serialise the feature against the aggregation-induced AR(1) null before considering it for Q desk deployment. Default m=3, with expected rho1≈0.21 from the source; only keep the feature if the corrected signal remains positive OOS in both 2018-2026 and 1999-2017.
review.mechanism: This would not create edge by itself; it would keep us from mistaking smoothing and autocorrelation created by bar aggregation for real predictability. The benefit is fewer false positives and less overfit, so future filters are more likely to survive out of sample.
review.data_missing: Nothing material. Minute OHLCV is enough to compute aggregated-bar features and the corresponding null adjustment; no order book, news, options, or fundamentals needed.
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected many price-based rules, but not this explicit aggregation-null screening protocol.
review.overfit_note: The method itself has almost no knobs if we fix the aggregation window and the null formula up front. The main risk is not overfitting the rule, but using it to justify weak signals afterward.
review.expected_effect: No direct PnL lift on the current bot. It should mainly reduce wasted tests and false discoveries from aggregated-bar features; any trading benefit would come only if a candidate signal survives the correction.
review.test_protocol: Do not run this as a live trading sleeve. Use it as a research screen: for each candidate aggregated-bar feature, backtest the raw version and the AR(1)-adjusted version on 2018-2026 with current execution costs, then confirm on 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level rules). Compare against the current Q desk and require positive OOS Sharpe in both periods plus no deterioration in max drawdown before promotion. If the adjusted version does not beat the raw version after costs, reject the feature.
review.verdict_reason: Good statistical hygiene, but not a trading edge and not a Q desk improvement by itself. It is a research filter, not a deployable strategy. Use it offline when vetting future features; do not spend bot test slots on it as if it were a sleeve.

name: Volatility model benchmark against a simple baseline
one_line: Treat GARCH as a candidate only if it beats EWMA or realized-volatility sizing out of sample after costs.
parameter_choices: Compare GARCH, EWMA, and realized-volatility forecasts on the same rolling windows; evaluate on unseen data and net PnL impact.
disagreement: Complex parametric volatility models versus simpler robust baselines.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the benchmarking logic: it warns that in-sample GARCH fit can look convincing while forecasts are poor, and it explicitly says to compare GARCH-based sizing against EWMA or realized-volatility baselines on unseen data after costs. What it does not prove is that volatility-targeted sizing itself will improve Midas; that part is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily inverse-vol sizing overlay to the Q desk: at 15:55, keep the existing entry/exit logic unchanged, but multiply both sleeves’ notional by an inverse QQQ volatility forecast. Start with a 20-day EWMA forecast (lambda = 0.94), normalized so its average multiplier over the 2018-2026 training set is 1.0; test GARCH(1,1) and 20-day realized-vol forecasts under the exact same sizing map, and only replace EWMA if a challenger wins after costs.
review.mechanism: If QQQ volatility clusters, the bot is currently leaning the same amount into calm and chaotic regimes. Inverse-vol sizing should cut exposure when the leveraged ETFs are most dangerous, which can reduce crash give-back and smooth the equity curve. GARCH only helps if it catches volatility spikes sooner than EWMA; otherwise it is just extra complexity.
review.data_missing: None for this test. We have enough QQQ minute and daily history to compute EWMA, GARCH(1,1), and realized-vol forecasts and to backtest the sizing overlay with the existing fills/cost model.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. We have rejected ORB, gap, overnight, last-half-hour, and noise-area on other indexes, but not volatility-targeted sizing or GARCH-vs-baseline model selection.
review.overfit_note: A single GARCH(1,1) versus fixed EWMA/realized-vol baseline is manageable, but the GARCH family is easy to overfit if you start searching over orders, distributions, or lookback windows. Lock the spec before looking.
review.expected_effect: Modest at best. If it works, expect a small improvement in Sharpe and drawdown, mostly by shrinking position size in volatile periods rather than by creating new alpha. If it fails, EWMA or realized vol will likely be as good or better.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one sizing rule and two challengers. Keep the current Q desk signals unchanged; only vary the daily risk scalar. Compare (1) current fixed size, (2) EWMA(lambda=0.94) inverse-vol sizing, (3) 20-day realized-vol sizing, and (4) GARCH(1,1) inverse-vol sizing. Primary metric is full-bot net CAGR/day after all trading costs and whole-share rounding; secondary metrics are Sharpe and max drawdown. Fit/calibrate on 2018-2026 only, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (minute-based realized vol where available). Keep GARCH only if it beats both simple baselines and the current fixed-size bot in both periods, with no worse max drawdown.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with our existing QQQ data and cheap to run, and it targets a real lever in the bot: position sizing. The skeptical caveat is that GARCH is unlikely to beat a fixed EWMA or realized-vol baseline by much, so the test should be narrow and pre-registered; but it is worth testing before we rule it out.

name: Low-rank factor regime model
one_line: Use a small rolling factor set, ideally from ETF returns or PCA, for regime detection and attribution instead of a single market proxy or full covariance matrix.
parameter_choices: Choose factor count by out-of-sample stability plus eigenvalue/chi-square screens; re-estimate on a rolling monthly or weekly schedule.
disagreement: Single-beta attribution versus multifactor/latent-factor explanations; full covariance versus low-rank structure.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source material supports the building block, not the trading edge: it argues against full covariance models, says a single market proxy can be inadequate, and recommends PCA/latent factors with factor-count checks. It does not show that a PCA regime gate improves PnL on a bot, so the trading use is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current QQQ 200-day SMA trend gate with a monthly re-estimated 2-factor PCA regime gate built on the prior 252 trading days of daily returns for QQQ, SPY, IWM, DIA, and TLT. Orient PC1 so the QQQ loading is positive; keep the existing 50% TQQQ overnight trend sleeve only when the month-end PC1 score is > 0, otherwise put that sleeve in cash. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: A low-rank cross-asset factor should capture broader risk-on/risk-off and breadth shifts than QQQ alone, so it might shut off the trend sleeve earlier in fragile regimes and reduce whipsaws and crash give-back. If the factor mostly just restates QQQ beta, it adds lag and noise instead of edge.
review.data_missing: None for the proposed daily PCA gate. If you wanted minute-by-minute factor updates, we do not need them and pre-2018 minute data for every ETF in the basket is not complete.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is adjacent to market-proxy trend filtering, but we have not tested a rolling PCA regime gate on the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: Latent factors can rotate or flip sign across subperiods, and there are many silent knobs if we start changing the ETF basket, lookback, or factor count. It is easy to make 2018-2026 look good and have it break earlier.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly fewer trend whipsaws and smaller crash give-back from the trend sleeve. Realistic case: modest or zero improvement once factor instability and extra lag are included.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the basket (QQQ, SPY, IWM, DIA, TLT), lookback (252 trading days), factor count (2), monthly re-estimation, and the PC1 > 0 gate before looking at results. Backtest the current Q desk versus the factor-gated variant on 2018-2026, then freeze the rule and confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Use the same fill and cost model as the live bot. Primary metric: net daily return/CAGR. Secondary metrics: Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover. Accept only if the factor version beats baseline on net return in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown in either period; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is cheap, fully data-feasible, and can be stated cleanly without new data or execution assumptions. It is not strong evidence of alpha, but it is a plausible risk gate worth one strict pre-registered test. Do not spend additional tuning cycles on ETF baskets or thresholds if the first pass does not beat the baseline.

name: Persistent regime filter with confirmation and sizing
one_line: Only change regime state after the signal persists for multiple bars, and compare binary switching with using the same signal as a position-sizing input.
parameter_choices: Confirmation window of 2-5 bars; optional confirmation by both price and volume; compare hard switch, partial sizing, and no switch.
disagreement: One-bar regime flips versus persistent shifts; binary switching versus alpha-style sizing.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The cited books do support the *general* idea: a one-off shock can be mistaken for a real regime shift, and switching should only be used when the trigger has predictive value; they also favor following established trends. But none of the sources specifies a 3-bar confirmation rule or a sizing ramp, so that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Modify only the QQQ trend sleeve: replace the binary 0/50% flip on a single close vs the 200-day SMA with a 3-day persistence ramp. Size the trend sleeve at 0%, 17%, 33%, and 50% of book after 0, 1, 2, and 3+ consecutive daily closes on the new side of the SMA, and let it decay back to cash symmetrically on the downside. Leave the intraday sleeve logic unchanged except that it can use the remaining capital.
review.mechanism: This should filter one-day head-fakes around the 200-day line, so we do fewer whipsaw flips and fewer round trips. The gradual sizing also makes false reversals less expensive because we do not jump to full size on the first confirming bar. The tradeoff is that genuine regime changes, especially selloffs, will be recognized later, so crash exits could get worse rather than better.
review.data_missing: none.
review.already_tried_note: The rejected list covers ORB, gap-and-go, overnight, last-half-hour, and noise-area variants on IWM/DIA, but not this QQQ 200-day persistence/ramp rule. The current trend sleeve is binary, so this exact confirmation-plus-sizing variant has not been tested.
review.overfit_note: Only one real parameter, but the payoff depends on a small number of crossover events, so results can swing a lot by regime. Do not tune 2-5 bars or different ramp shapes; fix 3 before looking and keep the rest of the bot frozen.
review.expected_effect: Likely a modest reduction in false flips and turnover in choppy periods; likely slower crash exits and possibly worse upside capture in fast reversals. Net effect is plausible but probably small rather than transformative.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one daily-bar ablation on QQQ only. Compare (1) the current Q desk baseline, (2) a hard 3-day-confirmation on/off flip, and (3) the proposed 3-day sizing ramp. Freeze all intraday rules and costs. Fit nothing beyond the fixed 3-day window. Evaluate 2018-2026 first on net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Then run the identical rules on unseen 1999-2017. Keep a variant only if it improves return and does not worsen drawdown in both periods versus baseline. If the sizing ramp helps only in 2018-2026, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly targets a known weakness of the current trend sleeve. The evidence is weak and the edge may be small, but this is a sensible pre-registered ablation before we spend time on more knobs.

name: Duration and intraday timing diagnostics
one_line: Check whether signal arrivals, fills, and opportunities are clustered in time instead of being independent, and whether the edge is concentrated early or late in the session.
parameter_choices: Run survivor-function and lag plots on event durations; bucket intraday returns by check time and compare first few half-hour bins to later bins.
disagreement: Independent opportunity arrivals versus clustered timing; uniform intraday edge versus time-of-day concentration.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The book explicitly supports the diagnostic part: survivor-function and lag-plot checks for event durations, plus the warning that short-interval dependence can matter and costs can kill frequent trading. The specific move from diagnostics to an early-window trading cut is our adaptation, not stated verbatim in the source.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current intraday entry schedule with an early-window-only variant: allow new intraday entries only at the 10:00 and 10:30 New York checks, and disable new entries after 11:00; keep the existing exit rules and one-round-trip-per-day cap unchanged.
review.mechanism: If the intraday edge is front-loaded, this stops us spending the day’s one trade on later checks that are mostly noise and cost. It also forces us to respect the possibility that signal arrivals are clustered rather than independent, which can make the current evenly-spaced assumption too optimistic.
review.data_missing: none; the needed 1-minute QQQ bars and the existing backtest fill model are enough.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already has time-of-day checks, so timing matters implicitly, but this exact bucketed timing diagnostic and the early-window-only variant have not been separately tested or rejected.
review.overfit_note: Only one real knob (the cutoff time), but time-of-day effects are notoriously regime-sensitive and easy to cherry-pick. If we search multiple cutoffs and keep the best, the risk jumps to high.
review.expected_effect: Small and conditional: if the alpha is concentrated early, the cutoff should lift net Sharpe and reduce wasted late-session trades; if the edge is spread through the day, this will likely hurt by throwing away valid entries.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register cutoff = 11:00 NY. On 2018-2026, run the current intraday sleeve and the early-window-only variant with identical costs and next-5-minute-open fills. For each 30-minute bin, record gross/net return, hit rate, trade count, and duration/fill survivor and lag plots to check dependence. Then lock the cutoff and rerun unchanged on unseen 1999-2017 (and 2007-2017 for minute-level overlap). Adopt only if the variant beats the current Q desk on net daily return and Sharpe in both periods without a worse max drawdown; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is cheap, fully backtestable with existing data, and directly answers whether the intraday sleeve’s edge is time-concentrated. It is not a new standalone alpha, but it is a sensible pre-registered filter that could trim dead late-session trades; the downside is only a few minutes of compute.

name: Cost-aware entry gate and turnover throttle
one_line: Skip trades unless the expected edge clearly exceeds round-trip cost, and stress-test the sleeve under heavier slippage and fee assumptions.
parameter_choices: Require expected edge to exceed estimated round-trip cost by a margin; rerun with doubled costs and whole-share/poor-fill assumptions.
disagreement: Trading every marginal edge versus only taking entries with a clear after-cost cushion.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general principle that transaction costs and over-trading can erase apparent technical-rule edges, and that high-turnover systems need hard trade controls. None of the sources directly justify a pre-trade 'expected edge > cost' gate for this exact QQQ noise-area setup, so the proposal is an extrapolation rather than a cited rule.
review.exact_rule_change: No live change recommended. If you insist on a testable variant, make the intraday sleeve require QQQ to clear the noise-area band by at least 0.04% (2× the current 0.02% all-in round-trip cost) before entering; otherwise skip the trade. Keep the existing one-round-trip-per-day cap.
review.mechanism: This could only help if the intraday sleeve's edge is concentrated in the strongest breakouts and the small breakouts are mostly cost noise. Then it might cut churn and remove weak fills. But your current desk already prices costs in, uses next-5-minute-open fills, and already limits to one round trip/day, so the extra gate mostly risks filtering out valid trades rather than fixing a real execution problem.
review.data_missing: We do not have order book/quote data, so we cannot measure true spread/impact or rejection risk; any fill-quality adjustment has to be modeled conservatively from bars.
review.already_tried_note: The current Q desk already includes 1 bp/side spread-impact, SEC fee, whole shares, next-5-minute-bar-open fills, and a max one round trip/day. So the 'turnover throttle' part is largely already live; only the extra entry margin is new.
review.overfit_note: If you turn this into a learned expectancy filter, it will be easy to fit 2018-2026 noise and disappoint out of sample. A fixed 2x-cost threshold is simple, but it is also arbitrary and may just discard good trades.
review.expected_effect: Likely a small reduction in trade count and maybe a small improvement in net expectancy if the weakest breakouts are mostly losers. More likely it lowers gross return faster than it improves Sharpe, because the signal already has cost-aware backtesting and a very low explicit cost burden.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one fixed threshold before looking: 0.04% minimum band excursion. Backtest current Q desk vs the gated version on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 minute data. Also rerun both with 2x the assumed round-trip cost (0.04%) and with conservative whole-share/next-5-minute-open fills. Success requires the gated version to beat the current desk in both periods on net daily return and net Sharpe, with no worse max drawdown and no collapse in trade count-adjusted expectancy. If it only helps in 2018-2026 or only under normal costs, reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly a robustness check, not a new edge. The bot already models costs, whole shares, and next-bar fills, and already caps turnover at one round trip/day. Without order-book data, an 'expected edge' gate is just a noisy proxy that is likely to undertrade and overfit. The only valuable output here is a cost-stress sanity check, not a live rule worth spending tests or complexity on.

name: Discrete-signal meta-label validation
one_line: Turn a candidate entry into a simple discrete label and validate it with ANOVA and chi-square before promoting it live.
parameter_choices: Use next-N average-price labels or 3-bin forward-return bins; tune the label threshold so class balance stays reasonable and test with ANOVA/chi-square.
disagreement: Continuous forward-return inspection versus coarse meta-label validation for discrete setups.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the building blocks: three-way forward labeling from the next N candles and ANOVA/chi-square as generic validation tools. It does not show that this kind of meta-label screen improves a trading bot, nor that significance on coarse labels survives out-of-sample under repeated testing; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: No live-trading rule change; for any new candidate entry on QQQ, label the next 10 five-minute closes by the average future price versus the entry close with a ±1.0% threshold into 3 classes (up / range / down), and only advance the rule if both a one-way ANOVA on forward returns and a chi-square test on the 3-bin outcomes are significant in the development window and still pass on the holdout.
review.mechanism: At best this is a research filter: it may reduce time and capital wasted on candidate setups whose forward returns are indistinguishable across categories. It does not create alpha by itself, does not fix the Q desk’s whipsaws or crash give-back, and can easily reject sparse but real edges because the bot already can backtest the actual rule directly.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejection list, but it is a validation wrapper, not one of the already-tested trading setups.
review.overfit_note: There are multiple hidden knobs (horizon, threshold, binning, p-value cutoff), and repeated testing across many candidate rules makes p-hacking easy. Minute-bar returns are autocorrelated, so nominal ANOVA/chi-square significance will overstate evidence unless we correct for dependence and multiple tests.
review.expected_effect: No credible standalone lift in live P&L. Best case, it reduces research noise and false positives among future candidate signals; worst case, it adds a brittle significance filter that discards real but sparse edges.
review.test_protocol: Treat this as a research gate, not a trading sleeve. Pre-register a fixed library of candidate rules you already want to consider. On 2018-2022, build the 10-bar / 1% three-class labels, run ANOVA and chi-square only as a gate, and record which rules survive. Then trade the surviving rules unchanged on 2023-2026 and 1999-2017, net of the bot’s costs, using contiguous folds or block bootstrap to respect autocorrelation. Compare against two baselines: (1) no label gate, select by raw in-sample expectancy; (2) the current Q desk. Success requires higher out-of-sample net expectancy and Sharpe in both unseen periods, plus fewer false positives than the baseline selection method. If the gate does not improve out-of-sample performance, do not adopt it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a research-quality screen, not a trading edge. We already can backtest the actual rule directly from the available data, and ANOVA/chi-square on coarse labels does not address costs, autocorrelation, or multiple testing. It is easy to overfit and very unlikely to change the bot’s live expectancy.

name: Band-trigger grace rule
one_line: For band-based intraday entries, test a small grace zone instead of requiring a perfectly strict band break.
parameter_choices: Strict trigger, partial penetration, or one-bar grace entry; compare all three on the same dates after costs.
disagreement: Strict band confirmation versus allowing a small tolerance to capture missed trades.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The source is directionally aligned: it warns that strict binary band filters can miss valid trades. That supports relaxing the trigger in spirit. But it does not propose a grace rule, does not give a tested threshold, and does not show that loosening the trigger improves expectancy after costs.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current Q desk noise-area bands, 30-minute checks, exits, costs, and one-trade-per-day limit unchanged. Pre-register one entry relaxation: allow a 1-bar grace entry on the next 5-minute bar if the signal direction is still intact after an initial miss (grace_window = 1 bar). Also run a touch variant as the lower bound, where penetration_threshold = 0 bp (band touch counts). Do not tune any other parameter.
review.mechanism: If the strict band rule is too picky, we may be missing late-confirming momentum bursts that still have continuation. A small grace/touch rule could recover some of those missed trades. The downside is obvious: borderline entries may just be noise, so the change could also add whipsaws and worse fills. This is a small entry-timing tweak, not a new source of alpha.
review.data_missing: none; 1-minute OHLCV is enough to rebuild the 5-minute entry bars and 30-minute checkpoints, and we do not need L2/news/options data.
review.already_tried_note: Not specifically this grace rule, but it is a micro-variant of the existing noise-area intraday sleeve, and the broader noise-area concept has already been tested live/backtested on similar instruments. Expect small deltas, not a new edge.
review.overfit_note: Only two tiny knobs if you include both touch and 1-bar grace, but these are easy to optimize on 2018-2026 and overstate the benefit. Freeze the thresholds before looking at 1999-2017 and do not scan more grace lengths or penetration levels.
review.expected_effect: Probably small. Best case: slightly more captured momentum on strong intraday days and a modest lift in net return. More likely: near-zero change after costs, with a real chance of extra false positives and no improvement in drawdown.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the current noise-area band formula, exits, costs, and one-round-trip limit. Compare three pre-registered entry definitions on the same dates: (1) strict current rule, (2) touch/partial-penetration with penetration_threshold = 0 bp, (3) one-bar grace with grace_window = 1 5-minute bar. Evaluate primary metrics on the intraday sleeve and full bot: net daily return after costs, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover. Run on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (use the available QQQ minute history). Accept only if the same variant beats strict in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown materially; if winners differ by period or the gain vanishes after costs, reject.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible with existing data, cheap to run, and directly tied to the live intraday sleeve. The expected edge is probably tiny, but the source does justify a narrow ablation instead of ignoring it outright.

name: Range-bound trend filter
one_line: Disable or downsize the trend sleeve when QQQ is chopping in a narrow range, even if volatility is not especially high.
parameter_choices: Use range width, moving-average compression, or support/resistance distance as the gate; compare on/off versus scaled exposure.
disagreement: Trend following through ranges versus blocking trend exposure in choppy markets.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: Both books make the general point that moving-average trend systems perform poorly in range-bound/choppy markets, which supports adding a regime filter. But neither source specifies this exact QQQ range-width gate, the 20-day lookback, or the choice to disable the existing 200-day trend sleeve.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a daily pre-close gate to the existing trend sleeve: at 15:55 New York, if QQQ’s trailing 20-trading-day high-low channel width is < 6% of QQQ’s close, set the trend sleeve weight to 0% (cash) for the next session; otherwise keep the current 50% TQQQ overnight allocation when QQQ is above its 200-day SMA.
review.mechanism: This could keep the leveraged overnight sleeve out of dead, mean-reverting zones where price is technically above the 200-day SMA but is really just chopping in a narrow band. That should cut whipsaws and leverage bleed in sideways regimes. The tradeoff is that some low-volatility consolidations are healthy trend pauses, so the filter may also throw away good exposure and reduce long-run CAGR.
review.data_missing: None; daily QQQ OHLCV is enough to compute the gate, so no L2/quotes/news/options are required.
review.already_tried_note: No direct prior test on this bot. The closest thing is the existing 200-day trend sleeve itself, but not a separate QQQ range-compression filter.
review.overfit_note: There are many easy ways to define ‘range-bound’ (lookback length, width threshold, binary vs scaled exposure). A single threshold can be tuned to 2018–2026 and then disappoint on 1999–2017, especially because the effect is regime-specific and probably small.
review.expected_effect: If it works, expect fewer trend-sleeve whipsaws and smaller drawdowns in sideways years, especially 1999–2010-type regimes. I would also expect a real chance of lower return in strong-but-compressed uptrends, so the net edge is likely modest rather than transformative.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the rule exactly as written (20-day high-low width < 6% => trend sleeve off). Backtest the full Q desk with costs on 2018–2026 versus the current baseline, then freeze the rule and confirm on 1999–2017. Primary metric: net daily CAGR; secondary: Sharpe and max drawdown. Accept only if the variant improves net CAGR and Sharpe in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise reject. Do not tune the threshold after seeing results.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully backtestable with our existing daily data, and directly targets one of the trend sleeve’s known failure modes. The idea is weakly evidenced and overfit-prone, but not so broken that it should be rejected without a quick pre-registered test.

name: Cluster-specific lookback tuning
one_line: Tune the history length used for intraday profiles separately by cluster instead of forcing one global lookback.
parameter_choices: Grid-search lookbacks such as 20, 60, 120, and 252 days per cluster; re-fit on rolling windows.
disagreement: One universal history length versus regime- or cluster-specific memory.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly says the history length for intraday profiles can be tuned as a hyperparameter on a per-cluster basis. That is the same modeling move, but it is only an opinion and not evidence for our QQQ noise-area bands specifically.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the single 14-day lookback in the intraday noise-area sigma(t) with two fixed lookbacks by the existing trend regime cluster: if QQQ is above its 200-day SMA, compute sigma(t) from the last 60 trading days; if QQQ is below its 200-day SMA, compute sigma(t) from the last 120 trading days. No other Q desk rules change.
review.mechanism: Different regimes may need different memory lengths. In trend-on markets, a shorter window could update the band faster and catch breakouts sooner. In trend-off or choppy markets, a longer window could keep the band from reacting to a couple of noisy sessions and cut false signals. The only plausible win here is a small improvement in the intraday sleeve from less stale calibration.
review.data_missing: none; this can be computed from the existing QQQ minute and daily price history and the current 200-day SMA regime filter.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact cluster split. But it is still just a lookback hyperparameter change inside the already-tested intraday sleeve, so it is adjacent to what we have already been tuning rather than a new edge.
review.overfit_note: This adds regime-specific parameter choice on top of a strategy that already has several moving parts. The source is only an opinion, and the gain is likely small enough that it could easily disappear out of sample, especially across very different market eras.
review.expected_effect: At best, a modest uplift in the intraday sleeve by making the noise band less stale in regime shifts. I would not expect a large portfolio-level change, and I would expect most candidate gains to be fragile.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the regime split as the current 200-day SMA trend state; do not search for other clusters. On 2018-2026, compare three versions: (1) current Q desk, (2) the same desk with one global lookback sweep over {20,60,120,252}, and (3) the cluster-specific pair where L_on and L_off are each chosen from that same set. Freeze the chosen pair after the 2018-2026 design pass and do not use 1999-2017 in selection. Then run the frozen rules on the unseen 1999-2017 history using the same synthetic 3x framework where needed. Success requires the cluster-specific version to beat both baselines in both periods on net daily return and Sharpe, with max drawdown no worse by more than 5 percentage points and no large increase in turnover. If it only wins in 2018-2026 or only against the 14-day baseline, reject it as overfit.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, but this is a small hyperparameter tweak with only opinion-level support and too much room to overfit. The likely effect is modest and unstable, so I would first prove that a single global lookback improvement is robust before spending complexity on per-cluster tuning.

name: Censoring-aware execution model
one_line: When modeling fills or cancels, include contemporaneous price move-away variables so censoring does not break the fit.
parameter_choices: Compare naive survival/fill models against censor-aware versions with price-departure covariates and cancel/replace states.
disagreement: Censoring is ignorable versus censoring depends on price moving away from the limit.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The cited book explicitly warns that a survival/fill model is invalid when censoring happens because price moved away from the limit and censor-time prices are omitted from X. That is directly adjacent to this idea, but it is a modeling caveat, not evidence that the fix improves trading PnL.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to Q-desk alpha signals. For any hypothetical limit-order or cancel/replace execution model, add one covariate `move_away_bps` = signed distance from the order limit to the current mid/last 5-minute price at order time (default lookback: current 5-minute bar), and if `move_away_bps > 1 bp` keep the order live only until the next 5-minute bar, then cancel/replace.
review.mechanism: If we ever use limit orders, the fill model will stop treating 'not filled yet' as harmless censoring when the market actually ran away from the order. That should make fill probabilities and cancel/replace decisions more realistic, reduce optimistic backtests, and slightly improve execution. On the current bot, which mostly uses market/MOC-style fills, this is mostly backtest hygiene rather than a new return edge.
review.data_missing: We do not have quote/L1-L2 data, order submission/cancel logs, or queue position. Minute bars can approximate limit touches and price move-away, but they cannot reconstruct true fill/cancel censoring or partial fills.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected-ideas list. However, the current Q desk does not depend on limit-order survival/cancel modeling, so there is no existing live edge to refine here.
review.overfit_note: A fill model can be made to look good on 2018-2026 with ad hoc covariates and thresholds, especially using bar data and sparse execution labels. Without quote/LOB data, it is easy to fit noise about touches and cancel timing.
review.expected_effect: Mostly better execution-model calibration, not a new alpha stream. If adopted with limit orders, it may shave a little slippage; as-is, expected impact on bot PnL is minimal.
review.test_protocol: Do not test as a trading edge unless we first start logging live order states. If we do, pre-register two execution models for hypothetical limit entries on QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ: (1) naive survival/fill model using only order age and side; (2) censor-aware model adding `move_away_bps`. Train on 2018-2023, validate on 2024-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 where possible using QQQ history. Compare out-of-sample fill log loss/Brier score, calibration by move-away decile, and realized slippage in a paper shadow book. Adopt only if calibration improves and average execution cost drops by at least 0.5 bp/side without reducing fill rate by more than 5%.
review.verdict_reason: This is a research hygiene fix, not a tradable improvement for the current Q desk. With our current bar data and mostly market/MOC execution, we cannot estimate true limit-order censoring or cancel/replace behavior well enough, and the expected PnL lift is negligible.

name: VWAP only when the volume curve is stable
one_line: Use VWAP scheduling only when the intraday volume profile is predictable; otherwise fall back to TWAP or a simpler schedule.
parameter_choices: Measure recent volume-curve stability over a rolling window; if instability is high, switch to TWAP.
disagreement: VWAP is always best versus VWAP fails when the volume forecast is noisy.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general warning: when the intraday volume profile is noisy or unpredictable, VWAP can be worse than TWAP. It does not propose a stability filter, a threshold, or a switch rule, so those parts are our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: For intraday TQQQ/SQQQ orders only, compute a 20-session rolling stability score on QQQ’s normalized cumulative 1-minute volume curve (mean absolute deviation from the 20-session median curve). If the score is above 0.10, execute the order with a 30-minute TWAP; otherwise execute it with a 30-minute VWAP schedule. Leave the 15:55 trend-sleeve MOC order unchanged.
review.mechanism: In theory this could reduce slippage on days when the market’s volume comes in on an unusual schedule, so the intraday sleeve would not chase a bad VWAP forecast. For this bot, though, the only plausible gain is a tiny execution improvement; it does not create new alpha or address the trend whipsaw/crash problem.
review.data_missing: We can compute the volume-curve stability score from our minute OHLCV data. What we cannot measure well is true implementation shortfall versus VWAP/TWAP because we do not have quotes, level-2, or an order-book impact model; with 1-minute bars the execution edge will be modeled, not observed.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list. It is adjacent to the existing VWAP exit reference, but this exact execution-schedule switch has not been tested.
review.overfit_note: At least two knobs (lookback and threshold) plus a schedule choice, with a very small expected effect. It would be easy to fit noise in 2018-2026 and get nothing in 1999-2017.
review.expected_effect: At best a tiny reduction in execution cost on unusual-volume days; likely too small to matter for a $1,000 cash account trading liquid ETFs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the 20-session lookback and 0.10 instability threshold. Backtest the current Q desk versus the modified desk on the same signals and the same cost model. Use 2018-2026 as the build period, then confirm on 1999-2017 (with synthetic 3x where needed, and 2007-2017 for minute-level validation). Track net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade-level slippage versus the current one-shot/next-5-min-open execution assumption. Adopt only if the modified version improves net return in both periods and shows a material reduction in modeled execution cost; otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is an execution-microstructure tweak, not a real edge for Midas. On a $1,000 account trading liquid ETFs, the order size is too small for VWAP-vs-TWAP choice to move the PnL materially, and our bar data cannot validate real slippage without quotes or L2. Any benefit is likely below the 1 bp/side cost model and below fill noise, so it is not worth spending tests on now.

name: Volatility-scaled stops
one_line: Size stop distance off realized volatility instead of using fixed tight stops that get chopped up in fast ETFs.
parameter_choices: Test fixed stop distance versus stops at fractions of realized volatility or ATR; compare small, medium, and wide settings.
disagreement: Fixed tight stops versus volatility-adjusted exits.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the broad warning that stops that are too tight get whipsawed, and that some form of stop-loss is prudent. They do not specifically advocate ATR/realized-volatility scaling, so the volatility-adjusted part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: On the 50% overnight trend sleeve only, replace any fixed stop with a hard stop at 2.0× the 14-day ATR of QQQ (ATR computed from daily bars and translated to the ETF position); if breached, exit at the next 5-minute bar open. Leave the intraday noise-area sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: In theory, a volatility-scaled stop gives TQQQ more room in fast markets, so normal noise should trigger fewer needless exits than a fixed-percent stop, while still limiting damage if the trend breaks hard. In this bot, though, the main edge is surviving multi-day trends, so the stop is more likely to cut winners early and add turnover than to materially improve crash protection.
review.data_missing: No new market data is required. We can compute ATR/realized volatility from our daily and minute bars. The only missing piece is exact stop-order slippage through gaps/fast moves, which we can only approximate with OHLC bars and next-5-minute-open fills.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected classic stop/target tinkering on the old ORB bot. This is the same family of idea, just repackaged for leveraged ETFs and volatility scaling.
review.overfit_note: There is at least one obvious knob (stop multiple) and one lookback choice, and the best setting can be cherry-picked to the volatile 2018-2026 sample. Stop backtests are also very sensitive to fill assumptions and regime mix.
review.expected_effect: Most likely little or no improvement in net profit, and a good chance of lower CAGR from premature exits and extra churn. Best case: slightly smaller drawdowns in sharp reversals; likely case: you give up trend profits faster than you save crash losses.
review.test_protocol: If we force a test, pre-register exactly one variant: trend sleeve only, 14-day ATR, 2.0× stop multiple, exit at next 5-minute open after breach. Compare against the current Q desk on 2018-2026 and then 1999-2017. Require improvement in both periods on net daily return and Sharpe, with max drawdown not worse by more than 2 percentage points and turnover not up more than 15%. No parameter sweep; anything else is a reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is generic stop-loss folklore, not a strong edge for this bot. The current desk already has volatility-aware intraday exits, and the overnight trend sleeve’s problem is crash give-back from a 3x ETF, which a stop is unlikely to fix without also chopping the profitable trend runs. We already learned that stop/target tinkering is usually not durable, and bar-based stop execution is too approximate to justify more testing unless a very specific risk-control goal is being pursued.

name: Paper-trade burn-in and reconciliation
one_line: Run every new sleeve in shadow/paper mode first, then compare intended signals, fills, exits, and PnL to the live-order logs before enabling real capital.
parameter_choices: Shadow for 2-4 weeks or until the sleeve has at least 30 trades, using the same fill delay, whole-share rounding, and cost model as live.
disagreement: Paper trading does not predict live PnL perfectly, but it is still useful as an implementation and execution audit rather than an alpha estimate.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The books directly recommend paper trading / simulator forward testing before risking money, and one source explicitly says to compare logs of intended vs executed orders. The exact 2-4 week / 30-trade burn-in is our extrapolation, but the underlying process is clearly supported.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a mandatory forward-testing gate for every new sleeve: run the live code in shadow mode with the same fill delay, whole-share rounding, and cost model as production for 14 calendar days or 30 trades, whichever comes later, and do not allocate real capital until the intended signal, order, fill, exit, and PnL logs reconcile to the simulated plan.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha; it reduces avoidable losses from broken code, timing mismatches, rounding errors, and optimistic fill assumptions before money is at risk. It can improve realized live PnL only by preventing deployment of sleeves that look good in backtest but fail in execution.
review.data_missing: Requires internal intended-order, broker-fill, and reconciliation logs. No extra market data is needed; this is an operational logging/replay task rather than a market-data problem.
review.already_tried_note: The bot already runs shadow desks on live prices, so this is mostly a formalization and hardening of existing practice rather than a new edge.
review.overfit_note: There are essentially no alpha knobs to fit. The only parameters are operational gates (burn-in time and trade count), so curve-fitting risk is minimal; the bigger risk is mistaking process quality for trading edge.
review.expected_effect: Low direct effect on strategy expectancy; potentially meaningful reduction in live implementation errors and model-vs-real slippage. Useful as a deployment safety check, not as a return source.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend historical backtest slots on this. For each new sleeve, run a forward shadow book on live prices with production timing, rounding, and costs. Reconcile every trade against the intended signal and the broker log. Success metrics: 100% match on share count and direction, zero logic/order mismatches, and realized round-trip cost within the modeled 1bp/side plus fees on the burn-in sample. If any mismatch appears, or if realized costs materially exceed the model, keep the sleeve paper-only and fix the implementation before promotion. No 1999-2017 confirmation applies because this is a process control, not an alpha hypothesis.
review.verdict_reason: This is good deployment hygiene, but it is not a trading rule and cannot be evaluated as a return-generating hypothesis on our historical market data. We already shadow-trade variants, so the proposal adds little new information for the purposes of bot research; implement it as an internal gate if desired, but do not waste backtest/validation capacity on it.

name: Intraday hard exits instead of close-only stops
one_line: For any stop-based exit, trigger on an intraday stop or time stop rather than waiting for the daily close, so losers are cut before adverse drift continues.
parameter_choices: Use next-5-minute-bar execution after a breach; optionally pair with a same-day time stop if the stop is not hit.
disagreement: Close-only exits are simpler and reduce noise, but they can let losers compound on the worst sessions.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The cited passage is a practitioner opinion against closing-price-only stops and in favor of active stop orders. That supports the general direction of "don’t wait for the close," but it is not evidence that this exact stop overlay helps our Q desk, and it gives no threshold or validation.
review.exact_rule_change: This is not a direct change to the current Q desk because it has no close-only stop to replace. The closest testable translation is a new protective overlay on the trend sleeve: after a TQQQ entry, if price trades 2.0% below entry on any 5-minute bar, exit at the next 5-minute bar open; otherwise keep the existing 15:55 exit. One new parameter: 2.0% stop distance.
review.mechanism: It could cut the largest intraday losses on bad market days instead of letting a loser drift all session, which might help the 3x trend sleeve’s crash give-back. The downside is obvious: TQQQ is noisy, so a hard stop is likely to convert ordinary volatility into whipsaw exits and miss rebounds.
review.data_missing: None for a bar-based stop test; our minute OHLCV is enough, including synthetic 3x backfill before real TQQQ exists.
review.already_tried_note: We already rejected classic stop/target tinkering on the old ORB bot, and the current intraday sleeve already exits intraday. But we have not specifically tested a hard intraday stop overlay on the trend sleeve, so this is only indirectly similar to prior attempts.
review.overfit_note: The stop distance is a free knob and the effect will be highly regime-dependent. A threshold that looks good on 2018-2026 could simply be fitting 2020/2022 path shapes and fail on the older unseen regimes.
review.expected_effect: Best case, slightly smaller tail losses on crash days. More likely, lower CAGR from extra whipsaws and premature exits; this is more a drawdown-management tweak than a clear profit edge.
review.test_protocol: If we test it at all, pre-register one stop distance and do not tune it after looking. Compare current Q desk vs. the trend-sleeve stop overlay on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (using the same synthetic 3x backfill logic before TQQQ exists). Success requires higher net CAGR after costs in both periods, with no meaningful worsening of max drawdown; if it only improves drawdown while lowering return, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: As stated, this is not a genuine improvement to the live Q desk: the intraday sleeve already uses intraday exits, and the only new part would be an arbitrary stop overlay on the trend sleeve. That adds a high-whipsaw, high-overfit knob with only anecdotal support and no clear path to higher net profit.

name: Daily loss cap and volatility-scaled sizing
one_line: Scale position size by realized volatility and stop trading for the day if a loss cap is hit, so a few bad trades cannot erase a week of gains.
parameter_choices: Cap daily loss around 1-2% of equity; size positions so per-trade risk is a fixed fraction of equity after volatility adjustment.
disagreement: Some systems avoid hard daily stops, but a small leveraged cash account needs tighter drawdown control.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: B4 is an anecdote about large red days dominating many small winners; B11 is a generic warning against oversizing. Neither source gives a daily loss-cap rule or volatility-targeting formula, so the proposal is an adaptation rather than direct support.
review.exact_rule_change: Scale the total Q desk notional each day by a 20-day realized-vol target: size = base_size × clamp(1.0% / σ20d, 0.5, 1.5); if combined mark-to-market PnL from the prior close falls to -1.5% of starting equity, flatten all open positions and stay flat until the next session.
review.mechanism: Lower exposure when QQQ volatility is high should reduce the worst leveraged-ETF days and some crash give-back. A hard daily loss cap can stop a bad session from compounding into a much larger drawdown. The catch is that Midas already allows only one intraday round trip per day, so the loss cap mostly affects the overnight trend sleeve and may just cut off recoveries in ordinary noisy sessions.
review.data_missing: None.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly on the Q desk. We have rejected classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot, which is adjacent, but we have not tested a daily equity kill switch or vol-targeted sizing here.
review.overfit_note: Only two real knobs if pre-registered, but the daily-cap threshold can be tuned to a single backtest path. Because the system uses 3x ETFs and whole shares, a small threshold change can flip whether the stop fires on a handful of path-dependent days.
review.expected_effect: Vol scaling might modestly reduce variance and improve Sharpe if the bot is currently too large in high-vol regimes. The daily loss cap is likely too tight for a 3x ETF desk at 1-2%: it will probably fire on normal noise, lowering drawdown a bit but also lowering net profit. Net effect is uncertain and could easily be negative.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the parameters before looking: target daily vol 1.0% and daily loss cap 1.5%.
