Backtest the current Q desk vs this modified version on 2018-2026, then confirm on 1999-2017 with no retuning. Primary metrics: CAGR and Sharpe; secondary: max drawdown and worst day. Pass only if both periods improve on CAGR and Sharpe and do not worsen max drawdown. If the combined rule fails, split the tests and try vol scaling alone; do not tune the loss cap by eye.
review.verdict_reason: The source support is weak and the fit to this bot is poor. A 1-2% daily cap is too tight for a leveraged ETF desk and will usually trigger on ordinary 3x noise rather than only on true blowups. Since Midas already allows only one intraday round trip per day, the cap adds little protection and mostly risks suppressing the edge. Volatility sizing is worth a separate clean test, but this bundled proposal should be rejected as stated.

name: Gap-risk controls for single-name swing sleeves
one_line: Any future individual-stock swing setup must either stay flat overnight or carry an explicit max-gap-loss rule and event-risk filter.
parameter_choices: No overnight holding by default; if overnight is allowed, require a max allowed gap-risk threshold and exclude known event windows.
disagreement: Staying flat overnight may miss some gains, but it sharply reduces blow-up risk from news gaps.
books: How to Day Trade (sample)

review.source_support_note: The source directly supports the broad caution of avoiding overnight exposure in individual stocks because of violent news gaps. It does not, however, specify a quantified max-gap-loss rule or a systematic event-risk filter; those parts are our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: For any future single-name swing sleeve, force all positions flat by 15:55 New York time; no overnight holds.
review.mechanism: Avoids uncontrolled overnight news gaps (earnings, offerings, FDA/litigation, delistings) that can overwhelm stop losses and turn a small loss into a large one. In a cash account, it also prevents capital from being trapped in a name that gaps against us before the open. The tradeoff is giving up favorable overnight gap-ups.
review.data_missing: We can backtest flat-overnight vs overnight using our minute/daily bars and measure realized gap losses, but we do not have earnings calendars, news, or other event labels needed for a real event-risk filter. A true max-gap-loss rule is also only retrospective unless we can actually hedge or have pre-market/event data.
review.already_tried_note: The core no-overnight rule is already covered by the rejected 'overnight holding' work. The event-filter / explicit gap-threshold variant has not been separately tested, but we lack the data to do it properly.
review.overfit_note: The no-overnight version has almost no knobs, but once you add a max-gap threshold or event window it becomes easy to tune to past disasters. With no event labels, any threshold choice would be arbitrary and prone to sample-hacking.
review.expected_effect: For a future single-name sleeve, lower tail losses and lower max drawdown, but likely lower raw return from missing favorable overnight gaps. For the current Q desk, effect should be near zero because the live sleeves are ETF-based and mostly intraday/market-wide.
review.test_protocol: No test now on the current bot. If a single-name swing sleeve is ever added, pre-register two versions with identical entry/exit logic, universe, and costs: (A) allow overnight holds, (B) force flat by 15:55 ET. Compare net expectancy, max drawdown, and worst 1% overnight gap loss on 2018–2026, then confirm on 2007–2017. Do not fit an event filter without a real earnings/news calendar.
review.verdict_reason: The only implementable part is the no-overnight rule, and that has already been tested/rejected in our prior overnight-holding work. The explicit event-risk filter is not feasible with our current data. Since Midas currently does not trade single-name swing sleeves, this is not an actionable alpha test for the bot today.

name: Fast regime exits and no shorts in persistent uptrends
one_line: Disable short-side mean reversion in persistent uptrends, and replace slow support-based exits with faster trend-flattening exits like EMA or MACD slope breaks.
parameter_choices: Require trend confirmation over multiple bars before shorting; flatten on a faster trend break rather than waiting for support to be revisited.
disagreement: Support-based exits and countertrend shorts can catch larger reversals, but they are the easiest way to get trapped in runaway trends.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The books support the failure mode, not our exact implementation: they warn that shorts entered on static support/resistance can be trapped in rising markets, and they explicitly suggest a faster trend exit such as a 20-day EMA. That is close to a no-shorts-in-uptrends / faster-exit overlay, but the exact QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ regime rule is our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the current 200-day SMA trend sleeve as-is, but add a single daily 20-day EMA overlay computed from the prior completed QQQ close: (1) block any SQQQ entry whenever QQQ is above its 20-day EMA; (2) if the overnight TQQQ trend position is on and QQQ closes below its 20-day EMA, flatten that TQQQ position on the next 5-minute bar open. No other rules change.
review.mechanism: This should stop the bot from shorting into persistent daily uptrends, where the intraday mean-reversion short is most likely to get run over, and it should get the overnight trend sleeve out sooner when momentum weakens. The hoped-for gain is fewer runaway short losses and less crash give-back, at the cost of some missed profitable shorts and more whipsaws.
review.data_missing: None.
review.already_tried_note: The live desk already has a daily trend gate and an intraday long/short sleeve, so this is a modification rather than a new setup. The exact 20-day EMA overlay has not been listed among the rejected tests, but similar price-only ideas and stop/exits have already been explored.
review.overfit_note: Only one fixed lookback, so this is not a knob-fest. But it touches two sleeves at once and can look good simply by suppressing shorts in bull markets, while failing in sideways/down markets by over-filtering profitable mean reversion or whipsawing the trend sleeve.
review.expected_effect: Likely reduces SQQQ tail losses and may improve drawdown, but it also removes some countertrend profits and may exit the trend sleeve too early. Net effect is probably modest unless short-side losses are currently a meaningful drag.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the 20-day EMA overlay before looking. Backtest baseline Q desk vs. the modified desk with all other assumptions unchanged, using prior-close QQQ EMA only (no lookahead). Evaluate 2018-2026 first, then confirm on 1999-2017; report net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, total trades, and short-sleeve expectancy separately. Adopt only if the modified version improves Sharpe or drawdown in 2018-2026 and does not materially worsen the same metrics in 1999-2017; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is cheap, fully implementable with existing data, and it targets a real failure mode for the bot. The source support is only partial, so I would not spend much time on variants, but this specific fixed-overlay test is worth doing once.

name: Automated circuit breakers and no discretionary overrides
one_line: Add runtime sanity checks, a kill switch, and a strict no-manual-intervention policy so the bot halts on anomalous order flow or PnL behavior instead of being rescued ad hoc.
parameter_choices: Trip on abnormal reject rates, repeated order bursts, or daily PnL breaches; only allow restart after a logged post-mortem.
disagreement: Human intervention can sometimes save a broken session, but it also breaks reproducibility and can amplify losses.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The sources directly support the general rule: B5-c012-02 explicitly recommends runtime sanity checks and a hard kill switch for anomalous order flow/PnL behavior, and B5-c019-08/B11-c008-02/B11-c012-04 all argue against manual intervention and missed/late exits. What they do not provide is evidence that this improves returns, only that it can prevent operational disasters.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a live-only hard kill switch: if the bot sees 3 consecutive order rejects or any 15-minute data-feed stall, it cancels all resting orders, flattens positions, and disables new orders until the next session; no manual overrides or discretionary re-entry before the next trading day.
review.mechanism: This only helps if something goes operationally wrong: bad feed, duplicate-order loop, broker reject storm, or human panic. It can prevent a small system failure from turning into a large loss and keeps live behavior reproducible. It does not add alpha to the Q desk itself, and if the trigger is too sensitive it will just shut down good sessions.
review.data_missing: We do not have the telemetry needed to test the real idea: broker reject/ack logs, order timestamps, feed-latency or stale-data flags, or operator override logs. Historical OHLCV can only test a crude PnL stop-loss proxy, which is not the same as a runtime circuit breaker.
review.already_tried_note: The desk is already mostly systematic and the backtests/shadow desks reduce discretion, but we have not separately validated a formal circuit breaker or hard no-override governance rule.
review.overfit_note: There are few knobs, but any attempt to tune trip thresholds from historical PnL would be easy to overfit to specific bad days and may simply optimize for drawdown at the expense of the strategy's valid recovery behavior.
review.expected_effect: Mostly lower operational blow-up risk; near-zero expected alpha. In backtest terms, the PnL effect is likely neutral to slightly negative because false trips would stop trades that the current rules would have taken.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend alpha backtest budget on this as a return rule. If implemented, run it as an ops safeguard in paper trading and log every reject, feed stall, and kill-switch trip for at least 20-30 live sessions. Success is zero unhandled anomalies and an acceptably low false-trip rate, not higher CAGR. If you insist on a proxy, simulate only a fixed intraday PnL breaker on history and reject it unless it reduces max drawdown materially without lowering full-period CAGR on both 2018-2026 and 1999-2017.
review.verdict_reason: This is good engineering hygiene, not a trading edge. The real trigger conditions require execution/telemetry data we do not have, and the only historical proxy is a stop-loss-like rule that is easy to overfit and likely to cut valid returns. Implement it directly as a safety policy if desired, but do not consume research/test bandwidth on it.

name: Task-specific benchmark and return reporting
one_line: Evaluate every sleeve against cash, QQQ buy-and-hold, and a simple baseline like a 200-day filter, using annualized time-weighted returns and the same cost assumptions throughout.
parameter_choices: Report daily, weekly, and full-sample annualized TWR; benchmark ladder = cash, QQQ, and a 200-day filter baseline.
disagreement: A single benchmark can hide whether the sleeve adds alpha or just beta or leverage.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)

review.source_support_note: The books directly support benchmarking against an appropriate comparator and annualizing returns; the time-weighted return idea is also directly supported for handling deposits/withdrawals. However, the specific benchmark ladder (cash, QQQ buy-and-hold, and a 200-day filter) is our adaptation, not something the sources state as a trading edge.
review.exact_rule_change: No change to live trading logic; change the evaluation standard: for every sleeve and variant, compute net daily chain-linked time-weighted return (TWR) using the bot's same cost model, report it annualized, and compare it against three fixed benchmarks: cash (0%), QQQ buy-and-hold, and a QQQ 200-day SMA filter baseline. Use this same reporting and promotion gate for 2018–2026 and the unseen period.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself, but it should stop us fooling ourselves. The benchmark ladder separates true timing skill from plain Nasdaq beta and from simple trend-following leverage, so we do not promote a sleeve that only looks good because QQQ rallied. Annualized TWR also makes cross-period comparisons honest when cash balances and exposure change over time.
review.data_missing: None. We already have the price history needed for QQQ, cash-equivalent returns, and the 200-day filter baseline, plus the transaction cost assumptions needed to net the returns.
review.already_tried_note: We already compare some sleeves to each other and to broad market behavior in backtests, but not with a standardized benchmark ladder and not as a fixed promotion rule using annualized TWR everywhere.
review.overfit_note: This is mostly a reporting and validation standard, so there are essentially no fit knobs. The main risk is not overfitting the metric; it is using the metric as if it were a trading edge when it is only a measurement discipline.
review.expected_effect: Improves attribution and model selection, reduces false positives, and makes it harder to mistake beta or leverage for alpha. It is useful for deciding what to keep, but it should not be expected to materially raise returns on its own.
review.test_protocol: Implement the reporting standard on all current sleeves and recent variants. For each sleeve, compute net daily TWR, annualize it, and report excess return versus cash, QQQ buy-and-hold, and the QQQ 200-day filter baseline. Run this on 2018–2026 and on the unseen 1999–2017 sample using the same cost assumptions. Success criterion: the metric should change promotion decisions in a sensible way, i.e. sleeves that only beat cash but not QQQ or the 200-day baseline should be demoted, while sleeves that retain positive excess return versus the appropriate benchmark in both subperiods remain candidates. If the standardized ladder does not alter any decisions or reveal beta masquerading as alpha, it is still accepted as a reporting standard, but not counted as a return-improving change.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and directly supported as a validation method. It is not a new trading edge, but it is worth codifying immediately because it can prevent wasted tests and bad promotions.

name: Live-vs-backtest bias calibration
one_line: After launch, measure paper/live slippage, rejection, and fill bias by setup and time of day, then adjust expected returns and sizing only by the observed bias.
parameter_choices: Calibrate after the first 20-50 live trades or 1-3 months, with separate estimates by sleeve and session.
disagreement: Some traders keep backtest assumptions fixed, but explicit bias calibration prevents persistent optimism or pessimism from distorting sizing.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The cited book explicitly recommends quantifying backtester optimism/pessimism after a few live deployments. It does not specifically argue for sleeve/session bucketed calibration or for using that estimate to resize trades; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the Q desk signals unchanged. For each sleeve, once there are 30 completed live trades, compute a rolling average of realized net PnL minus modeled backtest net PnL for that sleeve, subtract that bias from the sleeve's next-trade expected return before sizing, and set that sleeve to zero size if the adjusted expected return is not positive.
review.mechanism: This would not create alpha; it is execution hygiene. If our assumed spread/impact and fill model are too optimistic, the bot is otherwise oversized and overstates edge. A live bias haircut makes sizing closer to what the market actually delivers, which can reduce surprise losses and prevent persistent overbetting, especially in the intraday sleeve.
review.data_missing: We need live order logs with submit/reject/fill status, timestamps, actual fill prices and sizes, plus the modeled fill and modeled PnL for the same orders. Historical OHLCV alone cannot estimate live-vs-backtest bias. The proposed 20-50 live-trade sample is also too small for stable session bucketing.
review.already_tried_note: We already run shadow desks live, so the raw comparison can be logged. But the explicit bias-adjusted sizing rule itself has not been tested; current backtests still use fixed cost assumptions.
review.overfit_note: There is only one real knob, but the estimate comes from a tiny, regime-sensitive live sample. The main danger is not curve-fitting history; it is reacting to noise and a few bad fills.
review.expected_effect: Small, if any. It should help only when live fills systematically deviate from the model; otherwise it will do almost nothing or add noise. It does not address trend whipsaw, crash give-back, or the flat intraday years.
review.test_protocol: Do not treat this as a historical alpha test. Implement it first as a shadow overlay on live/paper trading only, with the rule frozen at a 30-trade sleeve-level lookback and no time-of-day split. For each completed trade, log modeled net PnL from the pre-trade assumptions and realized net PnL from the actual fills. After the first 30 live trades in a sleeve, apply the rolling bias haircut to future sizing in that sleeve. Judge it over the next 60+ live trades per sleeve against the uncalibrated baseline using two metrics: absolute forecast error between modeled and realized net PnL, and realized net PnL per unit gross exposure. Adopt only if forecast error drops by at least 25% and realized net PnL does not fall. If you insist on a historical replay, use it only as an accounting unit test, not as evidence of trading value.
review.verdict_reason: Useful as live monitoring, but not a pre-launch test: it depends on actual fill/rejection logs that we do not have historically, and 20-50 live trades are too few to estimate a stable bias, especially by session. It is worth implementing after the bot has enough live fills, but it is not a new alpha hypothesis we should spend backtest cycles on now.

name: Bounded parameter grid search with horizon matching
one_line: Search only a small pre-registered grid of parameter values, and force each indicator/lookback to match the sleeve’s holding horizon instead of using one generic setting.
parameter_choices: Use a narrow grid around the current values and set lookbacks separately for intraday, trend, and swing horizons.
disagreement: Broader searches can discover better settings, but they also invite overfit unless the grid is narrow and pre-committed.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)

review.source_support_note: B7 directly supports the horizon-matching half of the idea: indicators should fit the holding horizon. B5 supports searching over parameter combinations and horizons in general. Neither source supports the bounded, pre-registered grid as a proven edge; that part is our own extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not use a generic shared lookback across sleeves. For the existing Q desk, lock the current sleeve-specific defaults as the center of a pre-registered 3-point grid: trend sleeve SMA lookback = 200 trading days with candidates {100, 200, 300}; intraday noise-band sigma lookback = 14 trading days with candidates {7, 14, 28}. Pick one pair on 2018-2026, then freeze it for confirmation on older data. No other parameters may be tuned in that run.
review.mechanism: If the signal memory matches the sleeve’s holding horizon, the indicator should be less stale and less noisy. That can reduce lag into reversals, cut some trend whipsaws, and make the intraday band less prone to false flips. The bounded grid also limits how much the backtest can cherry-pick parameters.
review.data_missing: None; this uses only the price/volume series already in hand.
review.already_tried_note: The live desk already uses separate lookbacks (200-day trend, 14-day intraday sigma), and the team has already done historical tuning/backtesting. What has not been separately tested is a formal, pre-registered bounded grid with explicit horizon matching.
review.overfit_note: Even a small grid can overfit when you choose the winner on 2018-2026 and then judge it on the same market regime family. With two sleeves and multiple interacting lookbacks, the apparent gain may just be lucky retuning rather than a durable edge.
review.expected_effect: Likely modest. If the current lookbacks are mismatched, this can improve timing and reduce some whipsaw and crash give-back. If they are already close to optimal, expect little or no improvement. The main benefit is better parameter discipline, not a new alpha source.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact grid before looking: trend SMA 100/200/300 days and intraday sigma 7/14/28 days. Evaluate all candidates on 2018-2026 against the current Q desk using after-cost daily net return, Sharpe, and max drawdown. Select one candidate only once. Then rerun that frozen candidate unchanged on the older sample: 1999-2017 for the daily trend sleeve and 2007-2017 for minute-level intraday logic. Adopt only if the candidate beats the baseline in both periods on net return and Sharpe, and does not worsen max drawdown in either period by more than 5 percentage points.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap, but this is mostly a parameter-tuning wrapper, not a new trading edge. The bot already uses sleeve-specific horizons, so the likely gain is small and the overfit risk is real. Run it only as part of a concrete retune of an existing sleeve, not as a standalone alpha hunt.

name: Prototype one new signal from each loss period
one_line: When a sleeve underperforms, mine that loss period for one concrete new hypothesis, prototype it, and reject it if it is redundant with an existing signal.
parameter_choices: Allow one new hypothesis per loss cluster; require incremental out-of-sample lift over the current sleeve before keeping it.
disagreement: Iterating from losses can uncover real edges, but too many brainstormed variants can explode the search space.
books: Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The source says almost exactly this: mine live loss periods for new signal ideas, prototype/validate them, and drop anything that is just a duplicate of an existing signal. The only extrapolation is turning that research advice into a formal bot-development policy.
review.exact_rule_change: No live trading rule change. Research gate only: for each sleeve loss cluster, allow exactly one new hypothesis, prototype it, and keep it only if it adds incremental out-of-sample edge and is not redundant with an existing signal.
review.mechanism: Indirect only: it could reduce duplicated sleeves and force us to target the actual failure mode behind a drawdown. It does not itself improve entries, exits, sizing, or crash exits.
review.data_missing: No extra market data is missing. The limitation is conceptual: this is a research workflow, not a standalone trading signal, so it only becomes testable after you define a concrete candidate hypothesis to attach to each loss cluster.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the explicit rejected list. That said, it is close to our existing habit of iterating on weak spots, so the novelty is more process discipline than a new edge.
review.overfit_note: Loss periods are a rich source of post hoc stories. With only a handful of independent regime clusters, this can easily become multiple testing with a narrative for every failure. It is very easy to fit 2018–2026 and fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: No standalone PnL edge. Best case: better research hygiene and fewer redundant signals. Worst case: a formalized excuse to overfit whatever just lost money.
review.test_protocol: Do not evaluate the meta-rule as PnL by itself. If you want to test it, pre-register all loss clusters on 2018–2026, generate exactly one candidate signal per cluster using only that cluster, and compare: (1) candidate vs current sleeve on 2018–2026, (2) the same candidate on unseen 1999–2017 (and 2007–2017 for minute rules), and (3) a random-candidate baseline. Accept only if the candidate adds positive net daily return and Sharpe in both periods without materially increasing drawdown and without redundancy versus existing signals. Otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is a research workflow, not a tradable edge. It cannot improve the bot by itself, and the freedom to mine loss periods is exactly how you manufacture false discoveries. Test the concrete signal that comes out of a loss cluster, not the meta-policy.

name: QQQ RSI(2) volatility-shock skip rule
one_line: Keep the existing RSI(2) dip-buy edge, but skip entries when the decline is too fast or too large versus recent realized volatility.
parameter_choices: Skip if the drop exceeds about 1.5-2.5x recent ATR or if the intraday range is unusually extreme versus the last 20 days.
disagreement: Aggressive dips often mean revert, but the worst losers cluster in volatility shocks and trending selloffs.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book quote supports the general warning against buying a sharp decline ('catching a falling knife'), but it does not specify an RSI(2) rule, ATR thresholds, or a volatility-shock filter. Our proposed filter is an adaptation of that warning, not something stated by the source.
review.exact_rule_change: For the existing daily QQQ RSI(2) dip-buy, add one pre-entry shock filter: compute shock = max((prev_close - close)/ATR14, true_range/ATR20), using QQQ daily bars. If shock > 2.0, skip the RSI(2) long entry; otherwise take the trade exactly as before. No other RSI(2) parameters change.
review.mechanism: RSI(2) mean reversion should work best on ordinary pullbacks, not on volatility shocks and persistent selloffs. This filter tries to avoid the days where oversold stays oversold and the trade becomes a falling-knife loss. If it works, it should cut tail losses and maybe improve Sharpe, even if it reduces trade count a bit.
review.data_missing: None for a daily-bar implementation. QQQ daily OHLCV back to 1999 is enough to compute RSI(2), ATR14, and true range. No news, options, L2, or intraday quotes are required.
review.already_tried_note: The base QQQ RSI(2) dip-buy edge is already known in our research, but this specific volatility-shock skip rule is not on the rejected list. So this is a modification of an existing sleeve, not a previously rejected setup.
review.overfit_note: It is easy to tune the shock definition and threshold to the 2018-2026 sample and accidentally suppress only the bad-looking trades in-sample. The idea has only one real threshold, but the choice of ATR window, shock metric, and cutoff can still be overfit if we start iterating.
review.expected_effect: Best case: modestly higher Sharpe and lower drawdown for the QQQ RSI(2) sleeve by avoiding crash-like entries. Base case: mostly neutral. Failure mode: it cuts off some of the strongest V-shaped rebounds and lowers CAGR.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the filter with shock > 2.0 and do not retune it. Backtest baseline RSI(2) vs filtered RSI(2) on identical QQQ data, fills, and costs. Evaluate 2018-2026 first, then lock the rule and confirm on 1999-2017. Compare net CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, worst 5% trade loss, and trade count. Keep the filter only if it improves after-cost CAGR and Sharpe in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown versus baseline; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, feasible, and directly tied to an existing edge. The source is only a generic warning, so expectations should be modest, but the test is simple enough that we should run it once rather than guess.

name: Binary edge checklist and no-discretion rule
one_line: Trade only when every predefined edge variable is present; no extra confirmation, judgment overrides, or forecasting filter.
parameter_choices: Require all conditions vs a relaxed subset; keep the checklist fixed per sleeve; log every missing condition and compare against any discretionary-confirmation version.
disagreement: Some traders believe extra context, post-loss confirmation, or forecasting improves judgment; this rule assumes those additions mostly inject random variables and delay valid trades.
books: Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The quoted passages explicitly argue for exactly this style of rule: use only the predefined edge variables, make the edge binary and objective, and avoid outside information or post-loss confirmation. That is a direct match to the proposed no-discretion checklist. However, the source is philosophy/opinion, not evidence that this improves P&L.
review.exact_rule_change: For each sleeve, hard-code a binary pre-trade gate: execute only if 100% of that sleeve’s predefined checklist conditions are true; set manual_override = off and extra_confirmation_filters = 0. No forecasting filter, no ad hoc confirmation, no post-loss exception.
review.mechanism: This can only help if we currently allow human or code-level discretion to override signals. In that case it reduces rule drift, hindsight bias, and missed trades from extra confirmation. It does not add predictive information, so on a bot that is already fully mechanical the expected trading-edge improvement is near zero; it is mainly a governance/reproducibility change, not alpha.
review.data_missing: We can backtest the strict binary gate from existing price data, but we do not have logged human discretionary/confirmation decisions to measure the true counterfactual. Any 'discretionary version' would have to be a synthetic proxy, not actual judgment.
review.already_tried_note: The live Q desk is already rule-based and already avoids judgment overrides, so the core principle is already in production. What has not been tried is a deliberate discretionary overlay, which is not our operating mode and not a real candidate edge.
review.overfit_note: The checklist itself is a free-form variable factory: the more conditions you add, the easier it is to tune them to 2018–2026 and fail out of sample. The only knob that matters is which conditions you choose, and that is exactly where hindsight overfit creeps in.
review.expected_effect: Near-zero on backtested expectancy if the bot is already mechanical; possible reduction in operator error only. If extra confirmation filters are added, trade count will usually fall and expectancy will likely worsen unless the new filter is a genuine predictive variable.
review.test_protocol: No separate alpha test on the 'no-discretion' principle alone. First audit the implementation: every signal must map to a fixed checklist and manual overrides must be disabled. If you insist on a benchmark, compare the current Q desk to one pre-registered synthetic 'confirmation-heavy' proxy built only from existing price variables, using net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count on 2018–2026 and 1999–2017; require improvement in both periods after costs and no large trade-count collapse. Otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is a process rule, not a market edge, and the Q desk already runs on hard rules with no stated discretion. The source supports the philosophy, but it does not create a new tradable hypothesis. With no human judgment data to remove and no new price signal, testing this would mostly measure our compliance with a rule we already follow.

name: Post-run-up de-risking and no streak scaling
one_line: After a winning streak or fresh equity high, temporarily cut size and forbid increasing exposure because of recent wins.
parameter_choices: Trigger after 3, 5, or 8 consecutive wins; cut size by 25%, 50%, or 75% for 1-5 trades or days; compare against a hard no-upsize rule.
disagreement: Some traders want to press winners; this rule assumes streaks mostly raise overconfidence and boom-bust risk rather than signal quality.
books: Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Douglas supports the *behavioral premise* that winning streaks can lead humans to overcommit and then blow up, but he does not provide a quantified trading rule, nor does he address an automated fixed-rule bot. The cited material is anecdotal/opinion-based, so the link to this exact de-risking rule is indirect.
review.exact_rule_change: If the Q desk closes 3 consecutive trading days with positive net PnL, apply a 0.5 exposure multiplier to both sleeves for the next 3 trading days; do not lift the cap early because the equity curve makes a new high.
review.mechanism: The only plausible benefit is to reduce exposure after a hot run if those wins were late-regime and prone to mean reversion, which could slightly cap give-back. But this bot has no psychology or discretionary size creep, so the source's real mechanism does not exist here. In practice this rule is more likely to cut size during the periods when the system is already working, especially in persistent-trend regimes.
review.data_missing: None beyond the bot's own realized trade PnL / equity curve, which we already have from backtests.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tested. It is adjacent to position-sizing work, but not the same as the already-rejected ORB/stop-target tweaks. This specific streak-triggered de-risking rule has not been separately evaluated.
review.overfit_note: There are several arbitrary knobs (streak length, cut size, hold duration, and whether to trigger on PnL or equity highs). It is easy to fit one sample period and accidentally suppress the strategy's strong runs.
review.expected_effect: Most likely lower CAGR and slightly lower Sharpe; any drawdown benefit is uncertain and probably small. The rule does not address the bot's real weaknesses (trend whipsaws and crash give-back) and may simply underweight the best regimes.
review.test_protocol: If forced to test, pre-register exactly one rule: 3-day winning streak  0.5 exposure for the next 3 trading days. Compare against the current Q desk on 20182026 using identical fills/costs, then confirm on 19992017. Success requires higher net CAGR and no worse max drawdown in both periods. Do not sweep 3/5/8 or 25/50/75% unless the single fixed rule shows a real edge.
review.verdict_reason: This is a human-psychology rule, but Midas is an automated fixed-size system with no overconfidence or discretionary size escalation to correct. On this bot, streaks are more likely to indicate that the edge is working than that risk is rising, so cutting size after wins is probably just a return haircut. There is no strong data basis and the likely net effect is negative.

name: Orthogonal feature-family and regime blind-spot audit
one_line: Regularly test fresh feature families and regime buckets outside the desk’s current logic to surface blind spots instead of reinforcing familiar patterns.
parameter_choices: Test separate families such as trend, mean reversion, volatility, breadth, calendar, relative strength, and volume; evaluate each in separate regime buckets and frozen holdouts.
disagreement: The debate is whether the current desk already covers the useful space or whether a broader search finds genuinely uncorrelated edges.
books: Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The source item explicitly recommends broadening validation beyond the current desk logic into orthogonal price/volume features and separate regimes, which is close to this idea. But it is a validation philosophy from an opinion piece, not a trading rule with demonstrated edge.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a quarterly blind-spot audit gate: each quarter, backtest exactly one pre-registered orthogonal feature family from {trend, mean reversion, volatility, breadth, calendar, relative strength, volume} across fixed regime buckets {bull, bear, high-vol, low-vol}; only promote a candidate if its returns are sufficiently orthogonal to the current Q desk (|corr| <= 0.30) and it improves net results in both 2018-2026 and 1999-2017.
review.mechanism: This could uncover a genuinely new sleeve or a regime filter the current trend/intraday logic misses, especially one that behaves differently in the desk's weak regimes. The audit itself does not create alpha; its value is only in finding a separate edge or preventing us from ignoring one.
review.data_missing: None for the stated families. We can compute trend, mean reversion, volatility, breadth, calendar, relative strength, and volume from our OHLCV data. Minute-level breadth before 2018 is unavailable, but the proposed audit does not require it.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact quarterly audit gate, but the team already runs broad historical price/volume tests and holdouts, plus shadow desks. So the marginal novelty is low; this is mostly formalizing existing research practice.
review.overfit_note: This opens a huge search space across feature families and regime buckets, with a strong multiple-testing problem. Without strict pre-registration and family-wise correction, it will mostly surface noise that fits 2018-2026 by luck.
review.expected_effect: At best, it helps discover a new uncorrelated sleeve or a useful regime filter. On its own, it does not improve live PnL; if anything, it mainly improves research hygiene.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one audit cycle before looking at results. Test one new family at a time on 2018-2026, using fixed regime buckets and no parameter tuning beyond the two declared thresholds. Compare each candidate's standalone net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and correlation to the current Q desk. Promote only if it beats the current desk net of costs in 2018-2026 and also holds up on the unseen 1999-2017 period, with |corr| <= 0.30 to the existing desk. If no candidate survives family-wise correction and both periods, do not spend live-test capacity on this process.
review.verdict_reason: This is a research process, not a concrete trading edge. We already have broad price/volume backtesting and holdout capability, so the incremental value is low while the false-discovery risk is high. Unless it names a specific candidate family or rule to trade, it should not consume bot test slots.

name: Intraday open/close hygiene
one_line: Skip the open/close noise in the intraday sleeve by excluding the first few and last few minutes of the session, and treat the opening minutes as a no-trade zone when volatility is highest.
parameter_choices: Exclude 09:30-09:35 and 15:55-16:00; compare against the current 10:00-15:30 schedule; optionally widen the opening no-trade window if opening volatility is elevated.
disagreement: No real disagreement on the direction; the books differ only on whether to skip just the first 5 minutes or to guard the opening price-discovery window more broadly.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source explicitly recommends restricting intraday analysis/trading to 9:35–15:55 to avoid open/close bias and notes the first minutes after the open are a volatile price-discovery period. That supports the hygiene idea, but it is execution advice, not evidence of alpha, and Midas already uses a wider 10:00–15:30 buffer.
review.exact_rule_change: No incremental rule change: keep the intraday sleeve on the current 10:00–15:30 schedule; do not add a separate 09:35/15:55 hygiene filter. If a sensitivity check is forced, the only pre-registered variant is 09:35–15:55 with the existing 30-minute cadence and one-round-trip cap unchanged.
review.mechanism: Skipping the most chaotic minutes can reduce false breakouts and poor fills when spreads are widest. On Midas, though, the sleeve already avoids the open and close by a wider margin, so the marginal mechanism is basically gone.
review.data_missing: None; minute OHLCV is enough, and the same synthetic-3x handling used elsewhere can cover pre-2018 history.
review.already_tried_note: The live intraday sleeve already runs only from 10:00 to 15:30, which is stricter open/close hygiene than the proposed 09:35/15:55 buffer. So the concept is already covered, just not isolated as this exact variant.
review.overfit_note: Time-of-day windows are easy to tune to 2018–2026 and accidentally fit one regime. Even with only one schedule change, the effect size is likely tiny, so backtest noise can masquerade as improvement.
review.expected_effect: Near zero at best, and likely slightly negative after accounting for fewer tradable minutes and the fact that the bot already skips the most problematic open/close window.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on testing it, pre-register one sensitivity variant only: 09:35–15:55 vs the current 10:00–15:30 intraday window, same signal logic, same costs, same one-round-trip cap. Evaluate net daily return, Sharpe, hit rate, and max drawdown on 2018–2026, then confirm on unseen 2007–2017 minute history. Keep only if both periods improve after costs and drawdown does not worsen.
review.verdict_reason: This is not a new edge for Midas: the bot already avoids the open and close more aggressively than the source example, so the proposed hygiene tweak is mostly redundant. Best case is tiny; most likely outcome is no change or a slight loss from reducing usable time.

name: Intraday cadence experiment
one_line: Re-test the intraday signal cadence: 30-minute checks versus continuous few-second monitoring versus a lower-frequency schedule.
parameter_choices: Current 30-minute bins; every few seconds; or a reduced cadence such as only a few checks per day / once daily as a control.
disagreement: The sources conflict: one recommends continuous updating, while another warns that watching the market all day can encourage overtrading.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)

review.source_support_note: B1 supports the implementation idea of evaluating state variables continuously; B1-c007-07 says 2- or 5-minute bars can stand in for higher-frequency data; B7 warns that watching all day can induce overtrading. None of these sources directly show that cadence alone improves this specific sleeve's PnL.
review.exact_rule_change: Intraday noise-area sleeve only: change the polling cadence from every 30 minutes to every 5 minutes on QQQ bars, while keeping the existing band/VWAP entry-exit logic and the max one round trip per day. Do not attempt true few-second monitoring with the current feed.
review.mechanism: Faster polling can catch brief band/VWAP crossings sooner, so entries and exits are less stale and intraday give-back may shrink. The downside is that the signal may just become noisier, and with next-5-minute-open fills plus a one-trade cap, the improvement is likely small.
review.data_missing: True sub-minute/tick/quote data and order-book data are missing, so genuine few-second monitoring and its slippage cannot be tested directly.
review.already_tried_note: The live desk already uses the 30-minute baseline, so the control exists; however I do not see evidence that alternative polling frequencies have been isolated and tested as a separate factor.
review.overfit_note: Only one obvious knob if we keep the candidate set small (e.g. 5/15/30/60 minutes), but cadence is a fragile implementation choice and can easily look good only on the in-sample window.
review.expected_effect: Likely flat to modestly better at best; more likely the benefit is too small to matter after costs, with some risk of extra false triggers and lower Sharpe.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register a small cadence grid: 5, 15, 30, and 60 minutes, with all other rules unchanged. Test on 2018-2026 first, using the same fill model and costs, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 minute data. Compare against the current 30-minute baseline on net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and average net trade. Keep a candidate only if it beats 30-minute in both periods on net daily return and Sharpe, with no worse max drawdown and not materially higher turnover (for example, no more than 20% higher).
review.verdict_reason: The feasible 5-minute proxy is cheap to backtest with our existing data and could improve intraday timing a little; the true few-second version is not testable with our feed, so it should be dropped rather than deferred.

name: Late-day execution ramp for the trend sleeve
one_line: Replace the fixed 15:55 MOC on the trend sleeve with a close-aware execution schedule that ramps into the close using urgency based on close-volume risk.
parameter_choices: Simple MOC; a progressive late-day ramp; more front-loaded when risk aversion or gap risk is high; more VWAP-like when urgency is low.
disagreement: Almgren-Chriss is a continuum: higher risk aversion front-loads, while zero risk aversion tends toward VWAP; the source gives no empirical winner.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general execution concept: target-close orders, forecasting closing volume, and the Almgren-Chriss trade-off between impact and timing risk. It does not provide evidence that a late-day ramp beats a simple 15:55 MOC for this bot, or that a close-volume proxy from minute bars will work well enough to matter.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the single 15:55 MOC on the trend sleeve with a 20-minute late-day ramp. Default schedule: execute 25% of the required shares at 15:35, 25% at 15:40, 25% at 15:45, and 25% at 15:50, using the same direction and size as the current trend-sleeve rebalance. If QQQ cumulative volume through 15:30 is below its 60-day median for that clock time, switch to a front-loaded schedule of 50% / 30% / 15% / 5% on the same timestamps. No other signal, sizing, or exit rule changes.
review.mechanism: This could reduce end-of-day implementation shortfall if the close is thin or jumpy, because the order is not forced into one last print. On normal days, spreading the order should approximate VWAP and reduce impact. The problem is that the trend sleeve is low-turnover, so the likely gain is just a few bps on a small number of regime-change days.
review.data_missing: We can simulate the ramp from minute bars and use intraday volume as a proxy for close-liquidity risk, but we do not have auction imbalance data, MOC print data, or order-book/quote data. That means the exact 'close-volume risk' signal is only approximable, not directly measured.
review.already_tried_note: The live trend sleeve uses a fixed 15:55 MOC, but this specific ramped execution variant has not been tested. It is also not the same as the already-rejected overnight-hold or stop/target ideas.
review.overfit_note: There is only one real threshold and the event count is tiny: the trend sleeve only changes position on infrequent 200-day-SMA regime flips. That makes any threshold easy to noise-fit on 2018-2026 and impossible to trust if it only helps a handful of trades.
review.expected_effect: Likely tiny and possibly zero. Best case: a small reduction in slippage/auction pain on volatile close days. More likely: no measurable difference after costs, because the order size is small and the schedule changes exposure by only minutes.
review.test_protocol: Freeze the ramp schedule and the 60-day volume threshold before looking. Replay the current Q desk with only the trend-sleeve execution timestamp changed: baseline = single 15:55 MOC; variant = 20-minute ramp with the low-volume front-load rule. Primary metric: trade-level implementation shortfall versus the 16:00 close, in bp per share, plus the trend sleeve's net daily PnL. Secondary metrics: full-bot CAGR, Sharpe, and max drawdown. Build on 2018-2026 with actual minute bars; confirm on unseen 2007-2017 using the existing synthetic-3x proxy where needed, and require the sign of the effect to be the same in both periods. If the variant does not improve execution shortfall by at least ~1 bp per round trip and does not improve full-bot net return in both periods, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a pure execution micro-optimization on a very low-turnover sleeve. The source only gives generic execution advice, our data cannot directly observe auction/imbalance risk, and the number of actual trend-sleeve flips is too small to estimate a few-basis-point effect reliably. Even if it works mechanically, the P&L lift is likely below noise and not worth burning testing attention on.

name: Explicit protective exits
one_line: Add programmable stop-loss, trailing-stop, and take-profit logic to the ETF sleeves instead of relying only on band or end-of-day exits.
parameter_choices: No source-specified thresholds; test stop-loss, trailing-stop, and profit-target levels independently.
disagreement: The source supports the capability, not the optimal levels.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: B2 only says Python/broker APIs can place stop-losses, trailing stops, and take-profits; that is a capability statement, not evidence they improve returns. B3 is just a rule-of-thumb about downside speed, and B11 is a generic risk mindset. None of the quoted sources show that adding protective exits to a QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ system improves expectancy.
review.exact_rule_change: If we test this at all, make it a single first-pass rule: trend sleeve only, add a 5.0% trailing stop from the highest ETF close since entry; if hit, exit at the next 5-minute bar open and then stay in cash until the next 15:55 trend decision. Keep the existing band/VWAP/EOD exits unchanged; do not add take-profit logic in the first test.
review.mechanism: The only plausible benefit is cutting the rare worst crash give-back on the long trend sleeve. The problem is that TQQQ/SQQQ are 3x noisy, so a stop will also trigger on ordinary volatility and will often close positions before the existing band/VWAP/EOD logic would have done so. That tends to reduce the right tail and may increase churn more than it helps drawdown.
review.data_missing: No extra data is required. Minute OHLC is enough to simulate a conservative stop, though exact intrabar first-touch ordering is unknown without tick/quote data.
review.already_tried_note: Classic stop/target tweaks on the old ORB bot were already rejected, which is the same family of knob-turning. On the current Q desk, we already have multiple exit layers (band/VWAP/EOD), so this is partly redundant even though it has not been tested on this exact sleeve.
review.overfit_note: There are many free choices hidden inside the idea: stop type, stop distance, whether it is trailing or hard, whether it applies to one sleeve or both, and whether the reference price is the ETF or the underlying. With only 8 years of real ETF minute data, it is very easy to fit 2018-2026 and fail unseen periods.
review.expected_effect: At best, slightly smaller crash drawdowns on the trend sleeve. More likely, lower net return from whipsaw exits and lost trend capture, especially because the bot already has band/VWAP/EOD exits and trades leveraged ETFs where normal noise is large relative to any plausible stop.
review.test_protocol: If you insist on a test, pre-register exactly one trailing-stop distance and do not sweep it. Compare current Q desk vs. Q desk + 5.0% trailing stop on the trend sleeve only. Run 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 using the synthetic 3x series where needed; for minute-level behavior, also check 2007-2017 separately. Primary metric: net daily return after costs; secondary metrics: max drawdown, worst day, and trade count. Approve only if the variant improves net return in both periods and does not worsen drawdown; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic stop/target knob, not a source-backed edge. On leveraged ETFs it is very likely to fire on noise, overlap with the bot's existing exits, and cap winners. The idea is feasible to backtest, but the source support is weak and the overfit risk is high, so it is not a good use of test budget unless you narrow it to a single, pre-registered crash-stop experiment.

name: Alternate MA trend filter
one_line: Benchmark alternative moving-average regime filters against the current 200-day SMA trend sleeve.
parameter_choices: 100-day, 150-day, and 200-day SMA; short-over-long crossover; 10-bar EMA as a fast confirmation filter.
disagreement: Shorter/faster filters should react sooner but are more whipsaw-prone; the cited examples are illustrative rather than performance-backed.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
Technical Analysis Masterclass
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: The sources only support the general notion that moving averages/crossovers are used to define trend. They do not provide empirical evidence that 100/150/200-day filters beat the current 200-day rule, and the 10-bar EMA item is just a worked coding example, not strategy evidence.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the current QQQ 200-day SMA regime gate for the overnight trend sleeve with a 150-day SMA gate: at 15:55 New York, if QQQ closes above its 150-day SMA, keep the trend sleeve in TQQQ at 50% of equity overnight; otherwise hold that 50% in cash. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: A shorter regime filter may get the bot out of deteriorating trends earlier, so it could reduce the 2022-style crash give-back and some sideways-market whipsaws. The tradeoff is more false exits in choppy periods, so this only helps if the earlier exit benefit outweighs the extra churn.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected ORB, gap, last-half-hour, overnight, 12-1 momentum, and noise-area on IWM/DIA, but not alternative daily trend filters on QQQ/TQQQ. This is a distinct tweak to the existing trend sleeve, not a previously rejected setup.
review.overfit_note: A single pre-registered 150-day replacement is only one knob, so the risk is manageable. But if we let ourselves search across 100/150/200-day and crossover/EMA variants on the same sample, this quickly turns into data-mining.
review.expected_effect: Possible modest improvement in crash exits and regime-change response, but likely more whipsaws and lower participation in long uptrends. I would not expect a dramatic full-sample lift unless the shorter filter materially improves 2022-like exits.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one candidate only: 150-day SMA replacing the current 200-day SMA for the overnight trend sleeve. Backtest it with the exact existing Q desk costs and execution rules on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Compare against the current 200-day rule on net daily return after costs, Sharpe, and max drawdown. Accept only if the 150-day rule beats the current rule in both periods and does not worsen max drawdown; otherwise reject. Do not tune among multiple MA lengths after looking at 2018-2026.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible from existing daily QQQ data, cheap to test, and directly targets a known weakness of the live trend sleeve. The evidence is weak and the expected edge is probably small, but it is worth one strict pre-registered test — not a moving-average fishing expedition.

name: Supervised intraday meta-filter
one_line: Put a simple supervised model in front of the noise-area breakout and only trade when the model says the next bar has positive edge.
parameter_choices: Labels can be next-bar direction (+1/-1/0) or next-bar return; try standardized LASSO/Ridge first, then a shallow decision tree, and optionally bag them.
disagreement: Linear sparse models and nonlinear trees are alternative families; the books do not show one dominating the other.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the building blocks of a supervised meta-filter: next-bar up/down labels, LASSO/Ridge shrinkage, decision trees, standardized inputs, and bagging. None of them specifically justify putting a learned filter in front of the Q desk’s noise-area breakout, so that is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Replace the raw QQQ noise-area trigger with a rolling standardized LASSO logistic meta-filter: re-fit on the prior 2 trading years of QQQ 30-minute OHLCV features (e.g., last 6 bar returns, realized vol, volume z-score, open-to-price distance, VWAP distance, and band distance), and only take the existing breakout trade when the model’s predicted probability of a favorable next 30-minute return is at least 0.55 in the breakout direction; otherwise skip the trade.
review.mechanism: This could reduce false breakouts in chop and low-edge regimes by only allowing the intraday sleeve to trade when recent price/volume context looks supportive. If it works, we get fewer bad entries, lower cost drag, and a higher average expectancy per trade without changing the core band logic.
review.data_missing: No missing data for a first-pass test. We can build 30-minute features from the 1-minute QQQ/SPY OHLCV we already have; no order book, news, options, or fundamentals are required.
review.already_tried_note: We have rejected other breakout-style and noise-area variants (ORB, IWM/DIA noise-area), but not this exact supervised QQQ meta-filter. It is close enough to existing rejected intraday ideas that we should be skeptical, but it is not a duplicate.
review.overfit_note: High risk: many possible feature sets, label choices, and thresholds, while the true edge in next-bar prediction is likely tiny. A learned filter can easily fit 2018–2026 and fail on 2007–2017 because regime shifts are large and the sample of true breakout opportunities is still limited.
review.expected_effect: Best case: modestly better intraday Sharpe and fewer losing trades in choppy years. More likely: a small improvement or no change, with a real chance of overfitting and lower trade count.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one model and one threshold only: standardized LASSO logistic regression, trained on a rolling 2-year window, with a 0.55 probability threshold to allow the existing long/short breakout trade in the matching direction. Compare the filtered sleeve vs the current raw noise-area sleeve on identical execution/cost assumptions. Primary metrics: daily net return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. First evaluate on 2018–2026; then freeze the rule and confirm unchanged on unseen 2007–2017 minute data. Keep it only if both periods improve on net return and Sharpe without worsening max drawdown materially; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully data-feasible, and directly targets the intraday sleeve’s weak spots. The overfit risk is high, so the bar for success should be strict, but this is still worth one clean pre-registered test rather than a whole new research program.

name: Pairs / basket mean-reversion sleeve
one_line: Add a separate mean-reversion sleeve on liquid ETF or large-cap pairs that pass cointegration or reduced-rank checks.
parameter_choices: Screen each leg for nonstationarity first; then test cointegration or reduced-rank VAR; candidate setups can use VAR(5) / residual windows k=5, 10, 20.
disagreement: Cointegration, reduced-rank VAR, and low-vol linear-combination methods are different ways to build the same sleeve; they are not identical rules.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the general concept of cointegration/reduced-rank linear combinations for pairs trading, and they argue for adding complementary, uncorrelated sleeves. They do not support this specific implementation on Midas, and they do not address the cash-account/no-short constraint.
review.exact_rule_change: This is a new strategy, not a tweak to the current Q desk. No executable rule change for the current bot: a true cointegration pairs sleeve needs a short leg, which Midas cannot hold in a cash account. If shorting is ever added, the concrete test would be: ETF-only pairs, 252-day Engle-Granger screen, enter when spread residual z-score reaches ±2, exit when z returns to 0.
review.mechanism: In theory, a stationary spread can mean-revert and add a low-correlation return stream. On Midas that mechanism breaks because the payoff requires trading both legs, and the bot cannot short. Without a short leg, you are not trading the spread; you are just making a directional proxy, which is a different strategy with no direct support here.
review.data_missing: We have enough OHLCV to compute cointegration/reduced-rank screens and residual z-scores, but we do not have short/borrow capability or borrow-cost data, so a true pairs-trading payoff cannot be implemented or simulated realistically in the current account.
review.already_tried_note: No explicit pairs/cointegration sleeve has been tested. The rejected mean-reversion ideas in the backlog were QQQ RSI(2), noise-area on IWM/DIA, and ORB variants, which are different setups.
review.overfit_note: Pair selection, lookback window, stationarity filter, hedge ratio, and entry/exit thresholds create a large multiple-testing problem. With only a handful of broad live regimes, this kind of sleeve is easy to fit on 2018–2026 and then fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: As-is, no actionable improvement: the sleeve is not implementable in this bot. If shorting were later enabled, it might add a weakly correlated mean-reversion stream, but the edge is likely small and fragile after costs.
review.test_protocol: Do not test now. Only if shorting is added later: pre-register a fixed ETF universe, use 252-day Engle-Granger pairs, enter at residual z=±2 and exit at z=0, build on 2018–2026, then confirm on 1999–2017. Compare net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, turnover, and correlation to the current Q desk; require improvement in both periods after costs.
review.verdict_reason: A true pairs/cointegration sleeve needs a short leg, and Midas is a cash account with no short selling. We can compute the statistics, but we cannot trade the payoff, so this is not a viable test for the current bot. Even if converted into a proxy long-only version, it becomes a different strategy with high selection and threshold overfit risk.

name: Loss-streak / drawdown cooldown
one_line: After a losing streak or drawdown, temporarily cut size or disable the intraday sleeve.
parameter_choices: Trigger after consecutive losing trades or days, or after a daily drawdown; pause the sleeve for the rest of the day or next session, or reduce size sharply.
disagreement: Douglas argues each trade is independent and should not be conditioned on the last few outcomes.
books: Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)
The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: B7 and B8 explicitly say to trade less / add a circuit breaker after a losing streak, and B11 says recent losses distort risk perception. But all of that is trader-behavior advice, not evidence that an automated QQQ intraday sleeve has positive expectancy after a loss streak. Applying it here is an extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add a cooldown to the intraday sleeve only: if the sleeve closes 2 consecutive losing sessions net of all costs, disable the intraday sleeve for the next 1 session, then resume the normal noise-area rules. Leave the trend sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could help only if the intraday sleeve’s losses cluster in bad regimes, so a short cooldown skips the next few trades after the sleeve starts failing. It is not a human-psychology fix here, because the bot cannot revenge-trade; it is just a crude regime gate based on recent realized P&L. Best case: slightly lower drawdown and fewer loss clusters. Worst case: it shuts off right before the rebound day.
review.data_missing: Nothing material. We can compute consecutive losing intraday sessions and sleeve-level realized P&L from the existing minute bars and cost model.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and not the same as the ORB stop/target tweaks. This exact loss-streak cooldown on the Q desk has not been tried.
review.overfit_note: There are many nearby variants (1/2/3 losing sessions, pause 1 day vs several days, size cut vs flat). The signal is weak and easy to fit to a few ugly patches, especially since the sleeve already trades at most once per day.
review.expected_effect: At best, modestly lower drawdown in the intraday sleeve during bad patches; more likely, a small return haircut from skipping some recoveries. It does not address the trend sleeve’s crash give-back, and because the sleeve only trades once per day, the rule is more likely to suppress the rebound than prevent any real "revenge trading."
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one version: 2 consecutive losing intraday sessions trigger a 1-session cooldown. Compare baseline Q desk vs. cooldown Q desk on 2018-2026 first, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Use the same fills/costs and only prior realized sleeve P&L to trigger the rule. Primary metric: total-book net CAGR/day. Secondary: Sharpe, max drawdown, and intraday sleeve CAGR. Keep the rule only if net CAGR improves in both periods and drawdown does not worsen; if the benefit appears only in one subperiod or comes solely from lower trade count, reject.
review.verdict_reason: Cheap, fully data-feasible, and the rule is concrete enough to pre-register. The evidence is weak and the bot is not a discretionary trader, so this is low-priority, but it is still worth one clean test as a simple regime gate on the intraday sleeve.

name: Win-streak de-risking
one_line: After a strong winning streak, halve size for a few trades to counter euphoria and protect gains.
parameter_choices: After a winning streak, cut size to 50% for the next few trades, then restore if performance normalizes.
disagreement: Douglas’s view is that the next trade is independent, so any recency-based de-risking must justify itself out-of-sample.
books: Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Douglas explicitly argues for counteracting euphoria/overconfidence after a winning streak, and the source note suggests an automatic de-risking overlay. But this is psychology advice, not evidence that streaks have predictive value for future trade outcomes in an automated bot.
review.exact_rule_change: Per sleeve, if the last 3 closed trades in that sleeve were all net winners after costs, set that sleeve’s size multiplier to 0.5 for the next 3 entries in that sleeve, then revert to 1.0.
review.mechanism: The only plausible benefit is variance control: if profits cluster and are often followed by churn or give-back, cutting size briefly could reduce drawdown from the next few trades. For Midas, though, there is no human euphoria to correct, so this mostly just reduces exposure after the bot has already done well. That makes it more likely to lower expected return than to improve it.
review.data_missing: None. The rule uses realized closed-trade PnL and trade sequencing, which we can compute from our backtest/live logs.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected-idea list, and nothing equivalent has been tested.
review.overfit_note: The streak threshold and cooldown length are arbitrary lag parameters. It is easy to fit a short-lived post-streak effect in 2018-2026 that disappears out of sample, and the number of trigger events may be modest, especially if applied per sleeve.
review.expected_effect: At best a small drop in volatility or drawdown; more likely a lower CAGR and little/no Sharpe improvement. In a fully systematic bot, win streaks are not a causal risk factor.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register exactly one overlay: per sleeve, after 3 consecutive closed winning trades, cut that sleeve to 50% size for the next 3 entries, then restore to 100%. Backtest on 2018-2026 using the same fills/costs as the current Q desk, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017. Compare net daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and MAR versus the current desk. Keep it only if both periods improve net daily return and Sharpe and do not worsen max drawdown. If the rule triggers too rarely for a meaningful sample (for example, fewer than ~50 cooldown activations in 2018-2026), discard as underpowered.
review.verdict_reason: This is a human-psychology rule being imported into a fully automated system. We have no reason to believe recent wins predict worse future performance for this strategy, and the overlay mainly reduces exposure after the edge has already shown up. It does not target the bot’s real weaknesses (trend whipsaws and crash give-back), so it is not worth spending test budget on.

name: Dynamic sleeve allocation
one_line: Move away from a fixed 50/50 split and allocate between the trend sleeve, intraday sleeve, and cash based on recent sleeve volatility and realized performance.
parameter_choices: Compare static 50/50 to volatility-weighted and performance-weighted splits; allow the better recent sleeve to get a larger share.
disagreement: No source gives a formula; this is an allocation experiment built from general diversification advice.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)

review.source_support_note: The sources support the broad *idea* of allocating capital across sleeves and diversifying risk, but they do not give a concrete dynamic rule. The ‘AI can suggest allocations’ claim is generic opinion, and the ARIMA/trend-noise example is only a modeling analogy. Nothing in the sources justifies recent-P&L weighting or a specific inverse-vol formula; that part is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: At the daily 15:55 rebalance, keep the current state when the trend sleeve is off (0% trend / 100% intraday). When the trend sleeve is on, replace the fixed 50/50 split with a 20-trading-day inverse-realized-volatility split between the trend sleeve and the intraday sleeve: target weight_i = (1/vol_i) / sum(1/vol), rounded to whole shares, with each sleeve clipped to a 25%–75% band. Do not use trailing P&L weights in the first test.
review.mechanism: This is just risk scaling. If one sleeve has been choppier lately, it gets less capital, which may reduce drawdown and make compounding smoother. It does not create a new edge; it only tries to stop the worse sleeve from dominating the book. Recent-return weighting is the dangerous part because it will mostly chase noise across two sleeves on the same underlying.
review.data_missing: None. We can compute sleeve-level returns and realized vol from the price data we already have.
review.already_tried_note: Not explicitly. The live shadow desks use fixed splits, but I do not see an existing dynamic sleeve-allocation test or inverse-vol sizing test in the rejected list.
review.overfit_note: If you let recent performance drive the weights, this becomes a regime-chasing exercise with several plausible lookbacks and caps. With only two sleeves, coarse whole-share sizing, and the same underlying, it is very easy to fit 2018–2026 luck and lose it out-of-sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: a modest reduction in volatility and max drawdown, with little change in raw edge. Worst case: no improvement or worse results from overreacting to recent sleeve performance. I would not expect the performance-weighted version to add stable alpha.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one version only: 20-day inverse-vol weights, 25/75 cap, whole-share rounding, daily 15:55 updates, and no trailing-return weighting. Backtest against the current fixed 50/50 Q desk on 2018–2026, then on untouched 1999–2017. Compare net daily CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, and turnover after all costs. Adopt only if it improves net CAGR in both periods or, at minimum, keeps CAGR roughly unchanged while reducing drawdown materially without a turnover spike. If it only helps in-sample, reject it. Do not run a trailing-P&L weighting test unless this simpler version already wins out-of-sample.
review.verdict_reason: The source support is weak and the performance-weighted version is too noisy, but the inverse-vol sizing variant is cheap, fully feasible with our data, and could plausibly reduce drawdown without adding new market risk. Test that narrow version now; do not waste time on recent-P&L chasing unless the simpler sizing rule already proves itself out-of-sample.

name: Research/execution instrumentation and staged rollout
one_line: Separate signal from execution, log the full order life cycle, simulate bad fills or rejections in backtests, and deploy new rules at minimum size first.
parameter_choices: Stateless signal layer plus separate execution layer; log every signal, order, and fill; add a rejection or miss-fill rate in simulation; live test at the smallest feasible size before scaling.
disagreement: No substantive disagreement; these are operational controls rather than competing trading rules.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)
Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python
How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)
Learn Algorithmic Trading (Donadio, Ghosh)
The Trading Code (Jason Cam, Bookey summary)
Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: Multiple sources directly support the components of this proposal: split signal from execution, fully reconstruct/log the order life cycle, simulate random rejections/miss-fills, and deploy new algorithms at very low risk before scaling. The evidence is operational best practice, not proof of trading alpha.
review.exact_rule_change: Do not change the Q desk entry/exit logic. Refactor it into a stateless signal layer plus a separate execution layer; log every signal, order, cancel, and fill; and in backtests apply a fixed 1% random intraday reject/miss-fill rate. Any new rule that goes live starts at 1 share until it passes a probation period.
review.mechanism: This does not create alpha by itself. It reduces hidden implementation errors, makes backtests more honest under imperfect execution, and tells us whether the edge survives missed fills and slippage. Starting live at 1 share limits damage while we verify that the paper model matches reality.
review.data_missing: We can simulate the reject/miss-fill layer from existing bar data, but we do not have historical order-event logs or true rejection/fill data. Live rollout telemetry has to be collected going forward.
review.already_tried_note: You already run shadow desks, which is a crude staged rollout, but the brief does not mention full order-lifecycle logging or an explicit reject-fill simulator.
review.overfit_note: Very few knobs and no alpha-mining. The main risk is not overfitting; it is confusing process hygiene with a trading edge.
review.expected_effect: Better debugging and safer deployment; more honest backtests under imperfect execution. Little or no direct PnL uplift by itself.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the execution model before looking: run the current Q desk with and without a 1% random intraday reject/miss-fill layer on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 (minute-level where QQQ minute data exists). Compare daily CAGR, Sharpe, max drawdown, trade count, and sensitivity of expectancy to execution noise. Promote only if the ranking versus the baseline is unchanged and the degradation under the reject model is small (for example, <5% in daily CAGR and no material DD increase). For live rollout, keep any new rule at 1 share until realized fills/slippage stay within the simulated envelope for at least 20 trades.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible, cheap, and directly useful for preventing false positives from perfect-fill assumptions. It is not a trading edge, but it is a prerequisite for trustworthy testing and safer rollout.

name: Microstructure data upgrade for intraday execution
one_line: If tick, quote, or depth data is added later, compare event-time features and depth-aware throttles against fixed-bar intraday execution.
parameter_choices: Event-time vs 1-minute vs 5-minute features; Level I vs Level II/III; best-queue or spread-based throttles.
disagreement: Added market-data complexity may not improve fills or edge enough to justify the cost.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the general premise: trading data can arrive irregularly, so event-time/point-process methods may be appropriate, and Level I quote data is often insufficient for serious execution. But it does not show that this specific upgrade improves PnL for our Q desk.
review.exact_rule_change: Execution overlay only: if we later add tick/quote data, replace the intraday sleeve's fixed 30-minute decision clock with event-time checks on each quote/trade update, and require Level II quote depth (not just Level I) before sending the order. Default depth = Level II; default clock = event-time.
review.mechanism: Could reduce stale intraday signals and avoid sending TQQQ/SQQQ orders when liquidity is poor, which may lower slippage and missed fast moves. It only helps the intraday sleeve; it does not fix trend whipsaws or crash give-back.
review.data_missing: We do not have tick, quote, or Level II/III depth data for QQQ/TQQQ/SQQQ; only 1-minute bars and daily OHLCV.
review.already_tried_note: The current bot already uses fixed-bar intraday execution, so the baseline exists. The event-time/depth-gated overlay itself has not been tested.
review.overfit_note: Microstructure features offer many degrees of freedom, are noisy, and are easy to tune to 2018-2026. With no depth data and likely small incremental edge, the risk of finding a fragile improvement is high.
review.expected_effect: Small at best. If anything, it should slightly improve fills and reduce some bad intraday entries, but the gain is likely too small to materially change total bot performance after costs.
review.test_protocol: Not testable with current data. If tick/quote/L2 data is acquired, pre-register three intraday execution variants on the QQQ noise-area sleeve only: baseline fixed 30-minute checks with 5-minute bar fills; event-time checks on quote/trade updates; event-time plus Level II depth gate. Hold the trend sleeve unchanged. Compare net PnL after costs, average slippage from signal to fill, fill rate, Sharpe, and max drawdown on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen history (2007-2017 at minimum; 1999-2017 if the same microstructure history is available). Require a clear improvement in both in-sample and out-of-sample; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: Conceptually reasonable as an execution upgrade, but it cannot be tested with our current dataset because we lack tick/quote/depth data.

name: MA(1) noise filter for intraday returns
one_line: Use a simple MA(1) model as a noise filter or residual estimator before triggering intraday entries.
parameter_choices: q in {1,2,3}; fit on raw returns or signal residuals; filter threshold on residual z-scores.
