disagreement: The extra filter may just overfit short-run noise and add lag.
books: Algorithmic Trading and Quantitative Strategies (Velu, Hardy, Nehren)

review.source_support_note: The source supports the model-order choice (keep MA very small, often q=1 for finance), but it does not show that an MA(1) residual filter improves intraday trading entries. The trading use is still our adaptation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing 30-minute noise-area sleeve, but before each entry check fit an MA(1) to the prior 14 trading days of QQQ 5-minute close-to-close returns (reuse the current 14-day lookback). Compute the one-step-ahead residual z-score; only enter if z >= +1.0 for a long breakout or z <= -1.0 for a short breakout. Otherwise skip that check. q=1 and z-threshold=1.0 are fixed defaults.
review.mechanism: This is meant to block trades when the latest move is just short-lived noise or bid-ask bounce rather than a persistent push. In theory that could cut false intraday breakouts and churn in sideways tape, but it also adds lag and can miss good moves.
review.data_missing: None. We can compute this from the 1-minute QQQ bars we already have and the existing fill assumptions. No order book, news, options, or other external data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact rule. But it is another smoothing/gating layer on the intraday sleeve, so it overlaps with prior signal-tweaking / stop-target fiddling more than it creates a genuinely new return source.
review.overfit_note: The effect, if any, will come from very short-horizon autocorrelation that is regime-dependent and easy to fit away. A thresholded MA residual adds another knob and can look good in 2018-2026 while disappearing elsewhere.
review.expected_effect: Best case: fewer low-quality intraday entries and lower turnover. More likely: a bit less whipsaw but also less participation in good moves, so net PnL ends up flat to slightly worse.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register q=1 and z-threshold=1.0 before looking. Compare the current desk to the same desk with only this intraday MA(1) gate added; leave the trend sleeve unchanged. Build on 2018-2026 using the same costs and next-5-minute-open fills. Then confirm on unseen minute-level history (2007-2017, and 1999-2017 where synthetic 3x is needed). Primary metrics: after-cost mean daily return, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Only keep it if both OOS periods improve in mean daily return and Sharpe, max drawdown is not worse, and trade count is not cut by more than about 25%.
review.verdict_reason: Feasible and cheap, but the source only justifies keeping MA order small, not a real trading edge. This is a generic smoothing filter with high lag/overfit risk, and it does not target the bot's main weaknesses as directly as regime or volatility filters would.

name: Bollinger-plus-RSI technical overlay
one_line: Test short Bollinger envelopes and RSI(14) as an intraday regime filter or small overlay on QQQ.
parameter_choices: Bollinger length 15 with 1.5σ vs 2.0σ; RSI length 14; entry/skip thresholds around 30/50/70.
disagreement: These common indicators may add whipsaws without improving net return after costs.
books: Algorithmic Trading: A Hands-On Approach Using Python

review.source_support_note: The sources only show that Bollinger(15, 1.5σ) and RSI(14) are common indicator defaults in example code. They do not provide trading evidence that combining them as a QQQ intraday filter improves returns, so the support is mostly parameter support, not strategy support.
review.exact_rule_change: On the intraday sleeve only, compute Bollinger bands and RSI on 5-minute QQQ closes with BB(15, 1.5) and RSI(14). Take a long TQQQ trade only when QQQ closes above the upper band and RSI(14) > 50; take a short SQQQ trade only when QQQ closes below the lower band and RSI(14) < 50; otherwise skip that 30-minute signal.
review.mechanism: At best this could filter out some chop by requiring extension plus momentum confirmation. In practice it mostly reuses the same price information already embedded in the noise-area/VWAP logic, so any reduction in whipsaws is likely to be offset by fewer trades and missed reversals.
review.data_missing: None. We can compute Bollinger bands and RSI from our minute bars; no order-book, news, options, or fundamental data is needed.
review.already_tried_note: Not this exact combination, but it is the same family of price-only technical overlays. Similar knob-turning around existing band/stop rules has not been promising in prior ORB work.
review.overfit_note: There are multiple ways to tune this (bar size, Bollinger width, RSI threshold, gate vs size-down, long/short asymmetry). On QQQ, these indicators are highly correlated with the existing signal, so it is easy to fit 2018-2026 noise and fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: slightly fewer bad intraday fills. Base case: no meaningful lift after costs. Likely outcome: lower turnover and no durable edge, possibly worse because the filter throws away winners.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one frozen variant only: BB(15, 1.5) and RSI(14) computed on 5-minute QQQ closes, with a single midpoint threshold of 50. Apply it only as a gate on the existing intraday sleeve; leave the trend sleeve unchanged. Compare base Q desk vs filtered Q desk on 2018-2026 using the same fill/cost model, then confirm on unseen 1999-2017 QQQ minute history. Primary metrics: full-bot net CAGR/day and Sharpe; secondary: max drawdown, turnover, and intraday trade count. Accept only if the overlay improves the primary metrics in both periods without worsening drawdown or materially reducing net return after costs; otherwise discard.
review.verdict_reason: This is a weak, redundant price-only overlay with no external information and no clear structural reason to beat the current band/VWAP logic after costs. It is highly prone to overfitting the same QQQ noise it is meant to filter, so I would not spend a test slot on it unless higher-priority regime/sizing ideas are exhausted.

name: Trade-budget anti-overtrading guard
one_line: Impose a hard daily/weekly trade budget and skip marginal or boredom trades, especially on low-volatility days.
parameter_choices: Max intraday attempts per day; weekly round-trip cap; minimum volatility-to-cost ratio or expected-edge threshold.
disagreement: The current cap may already be sufficient, and stricter limits could leave money on the table.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book support is only the generic principle that traders should avoid overtrading and boredom trades. It does not give a quantitative trade budget, a volatility threshold, or evidence that adding a second throttle improves a systematic ETF strategy. The concrete cap/filter here is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Keep the existing 1 intraday round-trip-per-day cap, and add two extra guards to the Q desk intraday sleeve: (1) weekly intraday round-trip cap = 3 per calendar week; (2) minimum volatility-to-cost ratio = 3.0, using the existing 14-day sigma estimate at 10:00, so the intraday sleeve is disabled for the whole day if the ratio is below 3.0.
review.mechanism: This is meant to reduce churn in quiet weeks and skip marginal low-volatility setups whose expected move is too small to pay for spread/impact. In principle that could improve average trade quality and cut fee drag. In practice, Midas already limits itself to one intraday round trip per day, so the incremental benefit is likely tiny and the extra throttle may simply delete some of the better intraday days.
review.data_missing: none
review.already_tried_note: The live Q desk already has a hard one-round-trip-per-day cap, which is the main anti-overtrading guard. A weekly cap and an explicit volatility-to-cost gate have not been tested, but they are only tighter versions of an existing limit.
review.overfit_note: Two arbitrary thresholds on a low-frequency signal are easy to fit on 2018-2026 and then disappoint out of sample. The effect will be sensitive to small changes in cap and volatility cutoff, especially after costs.
review.expected_effect: Likely flat to slightly negative after costs. If it helps, the gain comes from skipping quiet-day noise and reducing turnover, but the more likely outcome is that it blocks a few profitable intraday trades while barely changing the bad ones because the bot is already tightly budgeted.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact settings above: weekly intraday cap = 3 and vol-to-cost gate = 3.0. Backtest against the current Q desk with all other rules unchanged. Compare on 2018-2026, then confirm on unseen 2007-2017 minute data and 1999-2017 where the synthetic 3x ETF model is used. Primary metric: net return per day after all costs. Secondary metrics: Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count. Only consider the change worthwhile if it improves net return/day and Sharpe in both periods without worsening max drawdown.
review.verdict_reason: This is mostly redundant with the bot’s existing one-round-trip-per-day cap. The source only supports the general warning against overtrading, not a quantified extra budget. The added weekly cap and volatility gate are arbitrary throttles on an already throttled system, so the most likely result is fewer trades and lower return, not a robust improvement.

name: VIX fear/complacency size overlay
one_line: Use VIX or another stress proxy to scale the sleeves up in fear and down in complacency.
parameter_choices: VIX percentile bands; size multipliers such as 0.5x/1.0x/1.5x; apply separately to trend and intraday sleeves.
disagreement: Fear may already be priced in, and VIX timing can be noisy or late.
books: The Naked Trader (Robbie Burns)

review.source_support_note: The book gives a broad contrarian slogan ('buy fear, sell confidence'), and the source item explicitly suggests using VIX/stress as a size overlay. But that is psychology, not a quantified or tested trading rule, so the support is only loosely related to this exact VIX-based sizing change.
review.exact_rule_change: At each 15:55 New York sizing decision, compute the rolling 1-year percentile rank of the most recent completed VIX close (no lookahead). Use it only to tilt the Q desk’s sleeve split, with total cash allocation still capped at 100%: VIX percentile >80% => trend sleeve 75% / intraday sleeve 25%; 20–80% => 50% / 50%; <20% => 25% / 75%. If whole-share rounding would exceed cash, scale both sleeves down proportionally.
review.mechanism: This is a regime-sizing bet, not new alpha. The only plausible edge is that high-VIX tapes tend to be more directional and better for the trend sleeve, while low-VIX tapes tend to be quieter and better for the intraday noise-area sleeve. So the overlay may reduce whipsaw by putting more of the book into the sleeve that should work better in that volatility regime. The big downside is that VIX is lagging and often spikes after the move, so it can easily be late and just reshuffle risk rather than add return.
review.data_missing: Daily VIX history (free) is needed; no news, options, L2, or minute VIX data required. The existing minute/daily price data is enough for the rest.
review.already_tried_note: Not on the rejected list, and no explicit VIX overlay has been run on the Q desk.
review.overfit_note: There are only a few knobs, but regime splits are easy to fit to crisis periods and then disappoint out of sample. If we let the percentile bands or split weights float, this becomes a very easy data-snooping exercise.
review.expected_effect: Likely small at best. It might help a bit if high-VIX periods are more trend-friendly and low-VIX periods are more intraday-friendly, but the VIX is a lagging stress proxy and leveraged ETFs suffer more volatility drag exactly when VIX is high. So the expected net effect is marginal and could easily be flat or worse.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the split rule before looking: 1-year rolling VIX percentile; 25/75, 50/50, 75/25 sleeve splits at <20%, 20-80%, >80%. Backtest the current Q desk vs the VIX-split version on 2018-2026 using only information available by the sizing time; then confirm unchanged on 1999-2017. Primary score: net daily return and max drawdown; secondary: Sharpe and turnover. Adopt only if both periods improve versus the current Q desk and drawdown does not get worse; if it only helps the in-sample period or only one sleeve, reject.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap and feasible, but the source is just a contrarian aphorism, VIX is a lagging proxy, and this is more likely to reshuffle regime exposure than create real alpha. Worth testing only after higher-priority volatility-targeting and crash-exit ideas.

name: Swing execution timing test
one_line: For swing entries and exits, compare 15:55 MOC decisions against next-day open or other outside-hours timing.
parameter_choices: MOC vs next open vs after-hours-implied timing; hold length 1-5 days; optional gap filters.
disagreement: Close execution may still dominate because next-open gaps can erase the edge.
books: Swing Trading For Dummies (excerpt)

review.source_support_note: The excerpt only says swing traders can place orders outside market hours when they cannot watch intraday. That is workflow advice, not evidence that MOC beats next-day open or vice versa. The specific close-vs-open execution comparison is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: For any pre-registered swing sleeve, execute entries and exits at the 15:55 New York close (MOC) instead of waiting for the next-day open; default hold length = 3 trading days; gap filter = none.
review.mechanism: This can help only by reducing stale-signal and overnight-gap risk. If the signal is generated from end-of-day information, waiting until the next open exposes us to news and gaps that can erase the edge. On liquid ETFs, the close is usually the cleaner benchmark fill.
review.data_missing: We can test close vs next-day open from our OHLC data. We cannot model true after-hours-implied fills or precise outside-hours execution without after-hours minute/quote data; we only have regular-session minute bars and limited daily premarket summaries.
review.already_tried_note: Not directly tested as a timing rule, but it is adjacent to the already-rejected overnight-holding theme. Do not treat it as a new alpha source; it is only an execution benchmark.
review.overfit_note: If we fix one hold length and no gap filter, the test is simple. The overfit risk comes from sweeping 1-5 day holds and adding gap filters until one timing wins.
review.expected_effect: Likely small and possibly zero. If anything, MOC should be slightly better than next-open on liquid ETFs because it avoids overnight gap noise, but the difference is probably modest and may vanish after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register one swing benchmark before looking: use QQQ RSI(2) dip-buy as the test sleeve, with entry when RSI(2) < 10 at the close and exit after 3 sessions or when RSI(2) > 70, whichever comes first. Run two execution variants only: (A) execute at 15:55 MOC, (B) execute at the next-day open. Use identical sizing and our standard 1 bp/side plus SEC fee model. Compare 2018-2026 and 1999-2017 separately on net expectancy per trade, CAGR, Sharpe, and max drawdown. Adopt MOC only if it beats next-open in both periods by a clear economic margin (at least a few bps per trade net) and does not worsen drawdown; otherwise reject the timing idea.
review.verdict_reason: It is cheap, fully testable with our data for close/open execution, and worth one pre-registered benchmark on a known swing edge. The source is weak, but the question is concrete enough to answer without extra data or many knobs. Do not widen it into a sweep over hold lengths or gap filters.

name: Sector-mania time-degradation exit
one_line: For a future sector-rotation sleeve, de-risk or exit once breadth or attention proxies roll over, instead of riding the move indefinitely.
parameter_choices: Breadth/relative-strength roll-over trigger; holding-time cap; exit fraction on first vs second deterioration signal.
disagreement: Time-based exits may cut the biggest winners too early and proxy signals may be noisy.
books: How to Swing Trade (Brian Pezim, Andrew Aziz)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general trading instinct—get out of hot-sector manias early and do not be the last out—but it does not state a specific breadth/attention rollover rule or a staged de-risking plan. The proposed trigger is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: This is not a change to the current Q desk; it requires a new sector-rotation sleeve. If we ever add one, use a staged exit: cut the position to 50% when the held sector ETF’s 10-day relative strength vs SPY turns negative, then exit the rest after 20 trading days if that deterioration persists.
review.mechanism: If a sector run is becoming crowded, relative strength and participation usually fade before the price fully breaks. A staged exit could harvest the early part of the move and reduce late-stage giveback. For Midas, that only helps if we first add a sector-rotation sleeve; it does nothing for the current QQQ trend/intraday sleeves.
review.data_missing: We can do rough price/volume proxies on liquid sector ETFs from our OHLCV data, but we do not have true sector constituent breadth, news, search/attention, or options data. The exact breadth/attention version is not directly testable as written.
review.already_tried_note: Not this rule, but the broad relative-strength/cross-sectional momentum family has already been tried and rejected (12-1 momentum failed 1999–2017). We do not currently have a sector-rotation sleeve to modify.
review.overfit_note: Many discretionary knobs hide inside the idea (proxy choice, thresholds, time cap, partial-exit fraction), and the relevant event class is rare. Easy to fit 2018–2026 and fail out of sample.
review.expected_effect: Best case: smaller late-stage givebacks and a bit less drawdown on rare sector blow-offs. Base case: noisy signal that clips big winners and lowers CAGR. Not a current improvement to the bot.
review.test_protocol: Do not spend a main test slot on this as a standalone idea. If we later define a simple sector-ETF rotation sleeve, pre-register the entry first, then compare baseline vs. the staged-exit version on 2018–2026 and confirm on 1999–2017. Keep the same sizing and entries; only change the exit. Success requires higher net Sharpe and lower max drawdown in both periods, with no material loss in CAGR; otherwise reject.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic exit heuristic for a strategy we do not currently trade. The quoted source is only anecdotal support for the broad idea, not for the actual rule, and our data lack true breadth/attention proxies. With rare episodes and many knobs, the overfit risk is too high relative to the likely benefit.

name: Chart-structure features on OHLCV
one_line: Add explicit chart-structure features such as trendline breaks, consolidation breaks, support/resistance, and retracement depth.
parameter_choices: Pivot lookbacks 20/50/100 bars or daily; breakout tolerance bands; retracement-depth thresholds.
disagreement: These handcrafted patterns may be redundant with the current band logic and could overfit.
books: Trading in the Zone (Mark Douglas)

review.source_support_note: The book supports the general idea that traders learn to see trends, trendlines, consolidations, support/resistance, and retracements, but it does not claim these chart distinctions are profitable rules. Using them as an automated filter is our extrapolation.
review.exact_rule_change: Add one daily chart-structure filter to the trend sleeve: at 15:55 New York, keep the existing 50% TQQQ trend position only if QQQ's last price is at least 0.2% above the highest close of the prior 20 trading sessions; otherwise move that 50% sleeve to cash. Leave the intraday sleeve unchanged.
review.mechanism: This could reduce trend-sleeve whipsaws by requiring an actual breakout instead of just being above the 200-day SMA. In theory it might also get us out earlier when price fails at a prior resistance level, but it will likely miss some slow-grind uptrends and cut exposure in the best trend years.
review.data_missing: No additional data needed; this can be computed from daily or minute OHLCV alone.
review.already_tried_note: We already use simple price-structure logic (200-day SMA trend gate and intraday bands), but we have not separately tested an explicit QQQ breakout/support-resistance filter like this.
review.overfit_note: This family has many subjective choices (pivot lookback, breakout tolerance, swing definition) and is very easy to fit on 2018-2026 while failing on 1999-2017. The source is conceptual, not statistical.
review.expected_effect: At best a modest reduction in whipsaws and maybe slightly smaller crash give-back. More likely it lowers trade frequency and total exposure enough to hurt CAGR after costs.
review.test_protocol: Pre-register the exact rule above with no parameter search. Compare the current Q desk versus the Q desk plus this breakout filter on 2018-2026 and on unseen 1999-2017 using the same costs and fill assumptions. Evaluate net return/day, Sharpe, max drawdown, and trade count for the total strategy and the trend sleeve. Require improvement in both periods; if the filter improves one period but not the other, or reduces return without a clear drawdown benefit, reject it.
review.verdict_reason: This is a generic chart-reading idea with weak evidence and high degrees of freedom. The bot already uses simple price-structure filters, so this is likely redundant and overfit-prone. It is computable, but the expected edge is too small and too easy to fit to justify spending testing budget unless the rule is narrowed to one very specific objective variant.
